chapters.title: Episode 1 — Telemachus
paragraphs: Big, cheerful Buck Mulligan came up from the stairway, carrying a bowl of shaving foam with a mirror and razor balanced on top. His yellow bathrobe hung loosely behind him in the gentle morning breeze. He held the bowl up high and said in a grand voice:
"I will go to the altar of God." It was Latin — the words a priest says at the start of Mass.
He stopped, peered down the dark winding stairs, and called out loudly:
"Come up, Kinch! Come up, you scaredy-cat!"

He walked forward seriously and climbed onto the round gun platform at the top of the tower. He turned around and pretended to bless the tower, the land around it, and the mountains in the distance — three times, like a priest would. Then he spotted Stephen Dedalus and leaned toward him, making quick signs of the cross in the air, making silly gurgling noises and shaking his head. Stephen, annoyed and still sleepy, leaned his arms on the top of the staircase and looked coldly at Mulligan's long face and pale hair.
Buck Mulligan peeked under the mirror for a moment, then quickly covered the bowl.
"Back to barracks!" he said firmly.
He added in a preacher's voice:
"For this, my dear friends, is the real thing: body and soul and blood. Quiet music, please. Close your eyes, everyone. One moment. A little trouble with the white blood cells. Silence, all."

He looked sideways up at the sky and gave a long, slow whistle, then waited, paying close attention. His white teeth gleamed with spots of gold fillings. Two sharp whistles answered back through the calm air.
"Thanks, old pal," he called out cheerfully. "That'll do nicely. Switch off the current, will you?"

He hopped off the gun platform and looked seriously at Stephen, gathering the loose folds of his bathrobe around his legs. His round, shadowy face reminded you of a wealthy church leader from the Middle Ages. A pleasant smile spread quietly across his lips.
"The mockery of it!" he said happily. "Your ridiculous name — an ancient Greek name!"

He pointed his finger in a friendly, teasing way and walked over to the low wall at the edge of the tower, laughing to himself. Stephen Dedalus got up, followed him halfway, and sat down on the edge of the gun platform, watching as Mulligan propped his mirror on the wall, dipped his brush in the bowl, and lathered up his cheeks and neck for shaving.
Buck Mulligan's cheerful voice continued.

"My name is silly too: Malachi Mulligan — it has a nice rhythm to it. But it sounds Greek, doesn't it? Light and sunny, just like me. We should go to Athens someday. Will you come if I can get my aunt to give us the money?"
He set the brush aside and cried out with delight:
"Will he come? The skinny bookworm!"
Then he stopped joking and began to shave carefully.
"Tell me, Mulligan," Stephen said quietly.
"Yes, my dear?"
"How long is Haines going to stay in this tower?"
Buck Mulligan showed his freshly shaved cheek over his right shoulder.

"Goodness, isn't he awful?" he said honestly. "A big, heavy Englishman. He thinks you're not a proper gentleman. These English! Full of money and bad digestion. Just because he went to Oxford. You know, Dedalus, you actually have proper Oxford manners. He can't figure you out. Oh, my nickname for you is the best: Kinch, the knife-blade."
He shaved carefully over his chin.
"He was raving all night about a black panther," Stephen said. "Where does he keep his gun?"
"What a crazy person!" Mulligan said. "Were you scared?"

"I was," Stephen said with feeling. "Out here in the dark with a man I don't know, raving and moaning to himself about shooting a black panther. You've saved people from drowning before. I'm no hero, though. If he stays here, I'm leaving."
Buck Mulligan frowned at the shaving foam on his razor. He hopped down and began searching through his trouser pockets.
"Bother!" he cried.
He came over to Stephen and, reaching into Stephen's top pocket, said:
"Lend me your handkerchief to wipe my razor."
Stephen let him pull out a dirty, crumpled handkerchief. Buck Mulligan wiped the razor blade clean. Then, looking at the handkerchief, he said:
"The poet's handkerchief! A new color for Irish art: snot-green. You can almost taste it, can't you?"
He climbed back up to the wall and gazed out over Dublin Bay, his pale hair stirring slightly in the breeze.
"God!" he said quietly. "Isn't the sea wonderful? The green sea. Look at it, Dedalus — the Greeks had a word for it. The sea is like a great, sweet mother. Come and look."
Stephen stood up and went over to the wall. Leaning on it, he looked down at the water and at the mail boat heading out of Kingstown harbour.
"Our mighty mother!" Buck Mulligan said.
He turned his sharp grey eyes from the sea to Stephen's face.
"Your aunt thinks you killed your mother," he said. "That's why she won't let me have anything to do with you."
"Someone killed her," Stephen said gloomily.

"You could have just knelt down when your dying mother asked you to," Buck Mulligan said. "I don't believe in religion any more than you do. But think of your mother begging you with her last breath to kneel down and pray for her. And you refused. There's something dark in you..."
He paused and went back to lathering his other cheek. A patient smile crossed his lips.
"But what an actor you are!" he murmured to himself. "Kinch, the greatest performer of them all!"
He shaved evenly and carefully, in silence.

Stephen leaned his elbow on the rough granite wall and rested his forehead on his hand, staring at the worn edge of his black coat sleeve. A sadness that wasn't quite grief filled his heart. He thought of his mother, who had died not long ago. In a dream, she had come to him — thin and wasted, in her burial clothes, smelling of candle wax and rosewood. He looked past his worn sleeve at the sea, which Mulligan had just called a great sweet mother. The water looked like a dull green mass. He remembered a white bowl that had stood beside her bed when she was dying.
Buck Mulligan wiped his razor again.
"Ah, poor fellow!" he said kindly. "I should give you a shirt and some handkerchiefs. How are those second-hand trousers?"
"They fit well enough," Stephen answered.
Buck Mulligan shaved under his lower lip.

"The joke of it," he said cheerfully. "They should be called second-leg. Who knows who wore them before. I have a lovely grey pair with a stripe. You'd look great in them. I'm serious, Kinch. You look really well when you're properly dressed."
"Thanks," Stephen said. "I can't wear them if they're grey."
"He can't wear them," Buck Mulligan told his own face in the mirror. "Rules are rules. He refuses to pray for his dying mother, but he can't wear grey trousers."
He folded his razor neatly and felt his smooth chin with his fingers.
Stephen turned from the sea to look at Mulligan's round face with its blue-grey eyes.
"That fellow I was with at the pub last night," said Buck Mulligan, "says you've gone mad. He works at the mental hospital with Dr. Connolly Norman."
He swept the mirror through the air to catch the sunlight, now bright on the sea. His teeth gleamed white as he laughed. His whole strong body shook with laughter.
"Look at yourself," he said, "you terrible poet!"

Stephen leaned forward and looked at the mirror held out to him, which had a crack running through it. His hair was sticking up. He saw himself as others see him. He wondered who had given him this face.
"I took the mirror from the maid's room," Buck Mulligan said. "It works fine for her. My aunt always hires plain-looking servants for me, so I won't be distracted. And the maid's name is Ursula."
Laughing again, he pulled the mirror away from Stephen.
"Like the monster in Shakespeare's play, angry at not seeing his own face in the mirror," he said. "If Oscar Wilde were alive to see you!"
Drawing back and pointing, Stephen said bitterly:
"That mirror is a symbol of Irish art. The cracked looking-glass of a servant."
Buck Mulligan suddenly linked his arm through Stephen's and walked with him around the tower, his razor and mirror clinking in his pocket.
"It's not fair to tease you like that, Kinch, is it?" he said kindly. "You've got more spirit than any of them."
Stephen thought to himself: He's dodging the subject again. He's afraid of my sharp words, just as I'm afraid of his. The cold steel pen.

"Cracked looking-glass of a servant!" Mulligan went on. "Tell that to the rich Englishman downstairs and get some money out of him. He's loaded with cash and thinks you're not a gentleman. His father made his fortune selling medicine overseas. Honestly, Kinch, if you and I could work together, we might do something great for Ireland."
Stephen thought of his friend Cranly's arm. Now it was Mulligan's arm linked with his.

"And to think you have to beg from these people," Mulligan continued. "I'm the only one who really understands you. Why don't you trust me more? What do you have against me? Is it Haines? If he causes any trouble here, I'll sort him out."
Stephen remembered a scene from university — young men from wealthy families laughing and shouting in someone's rooms, chasing each other around, having rough fun.
He remembered shouts from windows in the evening, echoing across the college courtyard. A gardener pushing his lawn mower on the dark grass.
Stephen thought about their ideas: about creating something new, something Irish.
"Let him stay," Stephen said. "There's nothing wrong with him except at night."
"Then what is it?" Buck Mulligan asked impatiently. "Spit it out. I'm completely honest with you. What do you have against me?"
They stopped walking and looked toward Bray Head, which lay on the water like the snout of a sleeping whale. Stephen gently freed his arm.
"Do you want me to tell you?" he asked.
"Yes, what is it?" Buck Mulligan answered. "I don't remember anything."
He looked into Stephen's face. A light breeze ruffled his uncombed fair hair, and there were little sparks of worry in his eyes.
Stephen, weighed down by his own voice, said:
"Do you remember the first day I came to your house after my mother died?"
Buck Mulligan frowned quickly and said:
"What? Where? I can't remember. I only remember ideas and feelings. Why? What happened?"
"You were making tea," Stephen said, "and you went across the landing to get more hot water. Your mother and a visitor came out of the drawing room. She asked you who was in your room."
"Yes?" Buck Mulligan said. "What did I say? I've forgotten."
"You said," Stephen answered, "'Oh, it's only Dedalus whose mother is dead.'"
A blush rose to Buck Mulligan's cheek, making him look younger.
"Did I say that?" he asked. "Well? What's wrong with that?"
He shook off his discomfort nervously.

"And what is death anyway?" he asked. "Your mother's or mine or anyone's? You only saw your own mother die. I see people die every day at the hospital and I study their bodies in the medical school. Death is an ugly thing, and that's all it is. It doesn't really matter. You wouldn't kneel down and pray for your mother when she was dying, just because you're too proud. I didn't mean to upset you about your mother's memory."
He had talked himself into confidence. Stephen, hiding the hurt that the words had caused, said very coldly:
"I'm not thinking about the insult to my mother."
"What then?" Buck Mulligan asked.
"The insult to me," Stephen answered.
Buck Mulligan spun around on his heel.
"Oh, you're impossible!" he exclaimed.

He walked off quickly around the wall. Stephen stood where he was, gazing over the calm sea toward the headland. The sea and headland grew dim before his eyes. He could feel his pulse beating behind his eyes, and his cheeks burned.
A voice from inside the tower called loudly:
"Are you up there, Mulligan?"
"I'm coming," Buck Mulligan answered.
He turned to Stephen and said:
"Look at the sea. Does it care about insults? Come on down, Kinch. The Englishman wants his breakfast."
His head paused at the top of the staircase:
"Don't mope about it all day," he said. "I say things without thinking. Stop brooding."
His head disappeared, but his booming voice echoed up from the stairway:
He sang a few lines of poetry as he went down: about not brooding over love's bitter sadness.

Stephen stood alone, watching shadows move silently across the peaceful morning sea. The water shimmered white in the distance, catching the early light. He thought of the poem Mulligan had just sung, about waves and words and music.

A cloud began to cover the sun slowly, darkening the bay to a deeper green. Stephen remembered singing that same sad song alone in the house. His mother's door had been open — she had wanted to hear his music. He had gone to her bedside, silent with sadness and pity. She had been crying. The song was about love's bitter mystery.
Where was she now?

He thought of her secrets: old fans with feathers, dance cards powdered with perfume, and amber beads locked away in a drawer. A birdcage had hung in the sunny window of her house when she was a girl. She had once laughed at a funny song in a show when she was young:
The song went: "I am the boy that can enjoy invisibility."
Those happy memories felt far away now, folded up and put away like old clothes.
He thought again of the sad song: stop brooding.

More memories came to him. A glass of water his mother would drink before going to church. An apple filled with brown sugar, roasting by the fire on a dark autumn evening. Her careful hands picking at the children's shirts to keep them clean.
In a dream, silently, she had come to him after her death — thin and wasted in her burial clothes, smelling of candle wax and rosewood, bending over him with silent, secret words.

He remembered her dying eyes, staring out from death, shaking his soul. The candle that lit her suffering face. Her rough, loud breathing while everyone around her knelt and prayed. He remembered the Latin prayers that were said for the dying.
He pushed the dark thoughts away.
No, Mother! Let me be. Let me live.
"Kinch, ahoy!"
Buck Mulligan's voice sang out from inside the tower. It came closer up the stairs, calling again. Stephen, still shaken by his dark thoughts, heard warm sunlight and friendly words behind him.
"Dedalus, come down, there's a good fellow. Breakfast is ready. Haines is sorry for waking us last night. It's all fine."
"I'm coming," Stephen said, turning.
"Please, for goodness' sake," Buck Mulligan said. "For my sake and for everyone's sake."
His head disappeared and popped back up again.
"I told Haines your idea about Irish art. He thinks it's very clever. Ask him for some money, will you?"
"I get paid this morning," Stephen said.
"The school job?" Buck Mulligan said. "How much? Four pounds? Lend me one."
"If you want it," Stephen said.
"Four shining gold coins!" Buck Mulligan cried with delight. "We'll have a wonderful time. Four mighty coins!"
He flung up his hands and stomped down the stone stairs, singing out of tune in a funny accent:
He sang a silly song about having a merry time drinking on coronation day.

Warm sunshine sparkled over the sea. The shaving bowl shone where it sat, forgotten, on the wall. Stephen wondered: should I bring it down? Or leave it there all day, a symbol of their forgotten friendship?

He went over to it and held it in his hands for a while, feeling how cool it was. He thought about how he used to carry things in church when he was a boy at school. He was different now, and yet still the same person. A servant, serving someone who was also a servant.

In the gloomy round living room of the tower, Buck Mulligan moved briskly around the fireplace in his bathrobe, the yellow glow of the fire appearing and disappearing behind him. Two shafts of daylight fell across the stone floor from the high windows, and where they met, smoke and the smell of frying food floated in the air.
"We'll choke in here!" Buck Mulligan said. "Haines, open that door, will you?"
Stephen set the shaving bowl on the shelf. A tall figure rose from the hammock and went to the doorway to open the inner doors.
"Have you got the key?" a voice asked.
"Dedalus has it," Buck Mulligan said. "I'm choking in here!"
He called out without looking up from the fire:
"Kinch!"
"It's in the lock," Stephen said, coming forward.

The key turned roughly twice, and when the heavy door was pushed open, welcome light and fresh air came flooding in. Haines stood in the doorway, looking outside. Stephen dragged his suitcase to the table and sat down to wait. Buck Mulligan tossed the fried food onto a plate, then carried the plate and a large teapot to the table, setting them down with a sigh of relief.
"I'm melting," he said. "Now then — Kinch, wake up! Bread, butter, honey. Haines, come in. The food is ready. Where's the sugar? Oh no, there's no milk."
Stephen fetched the loaf of bread, the pot of honey, and the butter dish from the shelf. Buck Mulligan sat down, annoyed.
"What kind of place is this?" he said. "I told the milk woman to come after eight."
"We can drink the tea without milk," Stephen said thirstily. "There's a lemon in the cupboard."
"Oh, forget your fancy ideas!" Buck Mulligan said. "I want proper milk."
Haines came in from the doorway and said quietly:
"That woman is coming up with the milk."
"Thank goodness!" Buck Mulligan cried, jumping up from his chair. "Sit down. Pour out the tea. The sugar is in the bag. I can't deal with these eggs right now."
He divided the fried food onto three plates, saying:
"In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." He was joking around, as usual.
Haines sat down to pour the tea.
"I'm giving you two lumps of sugar each," he said. "But I say, Mulligan, you really do make strong tea."
Buck Mulligan cut thick slices from the loaf and said in a funny old woman's voice:
"When I makes tea, I makes tea, as old Mrs. Grogan used to say. And when I makes water, I makes water."
"It certainly is tea," Haines said with a smile.
Buck Mulligan went on cutting bread and doing the voice:
"'So I do, Mrs. Cahill,' says she. 'Well, ma'am,' says Mrs. Cahill, 'just make sure you don't make them both in the same pot!'"
He tossed a thick slice of bread to each of them, stuck on the end of his knife.
"That's real folk humor," he said seriously to Haines. "For your book about Irish folklore."
He turned to Stephen and asked in a puzzled voice, raising his eyebrows:
"Can you remember, brother, whether Mrs. Grogan's story appears in any famous old book?"
"I doubt it," said Stephen seriously.
"Do you now?" Buck Mulligan said in the same tone. "And why is that?"
"I imagine," Stephen said as he ate, "it never existed in any book. Mrs. Grogan was probably just a made-up character."
Buck Mulligan's face lit up with delight.
"Charming!" he said in a sweet, proper voice, showing his white teeth and blinking pleasantly. "Do you think so? Quite charming!"
Then, suddenly changing his expression, he growled in a rough voice as he hacked at the bread again:
He started singing a silly old song about old Mary Ann.
He sang that she doesn't care a bit.
He kept going with the song, getting sillier.
He sang the last line with his mouth full.
He stuffed his mouth with fried food and chewed noisily.
The doorway darkened as someone appeared.
"The milk, sir!"
"Come in, ma'am," Mulligan said. "Kinch, get the jug."
An old woman came forward and stood near Stephen.
"That's a lovely morning, sir," she said. "Thanks be to God."
"To whom?" Mulligan said, glancing at her. "Ah, yes, of course!"
Stephen reached back and took the milk jug from the shelf.
"The country folk," Mulligan said to Haines casually, "are very religious."
"How much milk, sir?" asked the old woman.
"A quart," Stephen said.

He watched her pour the rich white milk into the measuring cup and then into the jug. She was old and wrinkled, but there was something dignified about her, as if she carried the weight of Ireland's history on her shoulders. Stephen thought of her as a kind of messenger from an ancient world, delivering milk in the early morning just as women had done for hundreds of years.
"It is good milk indeed, ma'am," Buck Mulligan said, pouring it into their cups.
"Taste it, sir," she said.
He drank some at her suggestion.
"If we could all eat good food like this," he said to her loudly, "we wouldn't have the whole country full of bad teeth and upset stomachs. People living in bogs, eating cheap food."
"Are you a medical student, sir?" the old woman asked.
"I am, ma'am," Buck Mulligan answered.
"Well, fancy that," she said.
Stephen listened in silence. He noticed how the old woman respected Mulligan because he was a medical student, and how she listened carefully to Haines — but she paid no attention to Stephen himself.
"Do you understand what he says?" Stephen asked her.
"Is it French you're speaking, sir?" the old woman said to Haines.
Haines spoke to her again, more confidently.
"Irish," Buck Mulligan said. "Do you speak any Irish?"
"I thought it was Irish," she said, "by the sound of it. Are you from the west of Ireland, sir?"
"I am an Englishman," Haines answered.
"He's English," Buck Mulligan said, "and he thinks we should speak Irish in Ireland."
"We really should," the old woman said, "and I'm ashamed I don't speak it myself. I'm told it's a wonderful language."
"Wonderful doesn't even begin to describe it," said Buck Mulligan. "Pour us some more tea, Kinch. Would you like a cup, ma'am?"
"No, thank you, sir," the old woman said, putting the handle of the milk can on her arm and getting ready to leave.
Haines said to her:
"Do you have your bill? We'd better pay her, Mulligan, hadn't we?"
Stephen refilled the three cups.

"The bill, sir?" she said, stopping. "Well, it's seven mornings at a pint — that's twopence each — so that's a shilling and twopence. And these three mornings at a quart — fourpence each — that's another shilling. So it's two shillings and twopence altogether, sir."
Buck Mulligan sighed, took a big bite of thickly buttered bread, stretched out his legs, and began searching his trouser pockets for money.
"Pay up and look pleasant," Haines said to him with a smile.
Stephen poured a third cup, adding just a small spoonful of tea to the thick, rich milk. Buck Mulligan found a coin, held it up, and twisted it between his fingers.
"A miracle!" he cried.
He slid the coin across the table to the old woman, saying:
"There you are, dear. That's all I can give you."
Stephen placed the coin in her hand.
"We'll owe you twopence," he said.
"That's fine, sir," she said, taking the coin. "Good morning, sir."
She gave a little curtsy and left, while Buck Mulligan sang softly after her:
He sang a tender little song about giving everything he had.
He sang the last line of the song.
He turned to Stephen and said:
"Seriously, Dedalus, I'm broke. Hurry off to your school and bring us back some money. Today we poets must celebrate. Ireland expects every man to do his duty!"
"That reminds me," Haines said, standing up, "I need to visit your National Library today."
"Let's go swimming first," Buck Mulligan said.
He turned to Stephen and asked cheerfully:
"Is today the day for your monthly bath, Kinch?"
Then he said to Haines:
"Our poetic friend here only washes once a month."
"All of Ireland is washed by the Gulf Stream," Stephen said as he drizzled honey over a slice of bread.
Haines, who was tying a scarf around his shirt collar in the corner, spoke up:
"I'd like to write down some of your clever sayings, if you'll let me."
Stephen thought to himself: He's talking to me. They wash and scrub themselves clean. But what about the dirt on the conscience? There's always a spot that won't come out.
"That one about the cracked looking-glass of a servant being the symbol of Irish art — that's really good," Haines said.
Buck Mulligan kicked Stephen's foot under the table and said warmly:
"Wait till you hear what he has to say about Shakespeare's Hamlet, Haines."
"Well, I do mean it," Haines said, still speaking to Stephen. "I was just thinking about it when that poor old woman came in."
"Would I make any money from it?" Stephen asked.
Haines laughed and, picking up his soft grey hat, said:
"I don't know, I'm sure."
He walked to the doorway. Buck Mulligan leaned across to Stephen and said roughly:
"You've gone and ruined it now. Why did you say that?"
"Well?" Stephen said. "The problem is getting money. From whom? From the milk woman or from him? It's a toss-up."
"I was talking you up to him," Buck Mulligan said, "and then you come along with your gloomy attitude."
"I don't see much hope," Stephen said, "from her or from him."
Buck Mulligan sighed dramatically and put his hand on Stephen's arm.
"What about from me, Kinch?" he said.
Then, suddenly changing his tone, he added:
"To tell you the truth, I think you're right. They're no use to us. Why don't you play along with them like I do? Forget them all. Let's get out of this dump."
He stood up and took off his bathrobe, saying with a sigh:
"Mulligan removes his garments."
He emptied his pockets onto the table.
"There's your handkerchief," he said.
And putting on his stiff collar and tie, he talked to himself as he rummaged through his trunk for a clean handkerchief. He threw a soft black hat across the room.
"And there's your Latin Quarter hat," he said.
Stephen picked it up and put it on. Haines called to them from the doorway:
"Are you coming, you two?"
"I'm ready," Buck Mulligan answered, heading for the door. "Come on, Kinch. You've eaten everything we left, I suppose." He walked out with a grand, solemn manner, saying seriously:
"And going forth, he met Butterly."

Stephen took his walking stick from where it leaned against the wall, followed them out, and as they went down the ladder, pulled the heavy iron door shut and locked it. He put the big key in his inside pocket.
At the bottom of the ladder, Buck Mulligan asked:
"Did you bring the key?"
"I have it," Stephen said, walking ahead of them.
He walked on. Behind him he heard Buck Mulligan swatting at ferns and grass with his heavy bath towel.
"Down, sir! How dare you, sir!" Mulligan said to the plants.
Haines asked:
"Do you pay rent for this tower?"
"Twelve pounds," Buck Mulligan said.
"To the British government," Stephen added over his shoulder.
They stopped while Haines looked at the tower and said:
"Rather cold in wintertime, I should think. A Martello tower, you call it?"
"The Prime Minister Billy Pitt had them built," Buck Mulligan said, "when the French might have invaded. But ours is the center of the world — the navel of the earth."
"What is your idea of Hamlet?" Haines asked Stephen.
"No, no," Buck Mulligan shouted. "I can't handle all his complicated ideas right now. Let me have a drink first."
He turned to Stephen, straightening his yellow waistcoat:
"You couldn't explain it in less than three drinks, could you, Kinch?"
"It's waited so long," Stephen said tiredly, "it can wait longer."
"You've got me curious," Haines said pleasantly. "Is it some kind of puzzle?"
"Oh, please!" Buck Mulligan said. "It's actually quite simple. He proves that Hamlet's grandson is Shakespeare's grandfather and that Shakespeare is the ghost of his own father."
"What?" Haines said, starting to point at Stephen. "He himself?"
Buck Mulligan swung his towel around his neck and, bending with laughter, whispered to Stephen:
"Oh, ghost of Kinch the elder! A son searching for a father!"
"We're always tired in the mornings," Stephen said to Haines. "And it's rather a long story to tell."
Buck Mulligan walked on, raising his hands.
"Only a drink can loosen the tongue of Dedalus," he said.
"What I mean is," Haines explained to Stephen as they walked, "this tower and these cliffs remind me of Elsinore — the castle in Hamlet. You know, 'that beetling cliff above the sea.'"

Buck Mulligan turned for an instant toward Stephen but didn't speak. In that bright, silent moment, Stephen saw his own reflection between their colorful clothes — himself in his cheap, dark mourning suit.
"It's a wonderful play," Haines said, stopping them again.
Haines gazed southward over the bay with his pale, steady eyes. The bay was empty except for the faint smoke of the mail boat on the bright horizon and a single sail near the rocks.
"I read a religious interpretation of it somewhere," he said thoughtfully. "The Father and Son idea. The Son trying to be united with the Father."

Buck Mulligan immediately put on a big, silly grin. He looked at them with wide eyes, blinking with playful craziness. He bobbed his head up and down, the brim of his straw hat wobbling, and began to sing in a quiet, silly voice:
He sang a funny song about Jesus, making fun of the idea in a lighthearted way — about having a Jewish mother and a father who was a bird.
He held up a warning finger.
He sang another silly verse, about making water into wine and back again.
He grabbed Stephen's walking stick in farewell and ran to the edge of the cliff, flapping his hands like wings, singing:
He sang a final verse, a funny goodbye song about rising from the dead and flying away.
He bounded ahead of them toward the swimming hole, flapping his hands like wings, leaping lightly, his hat bobbing in the fresh wind that carried his cheerful cries back to them.
Haines, who had been trying not to laugh, walked beside Stephen and said:

"We shouldn't laugh, I suppose. He's being rather disrespectful about religion. I'm not a believer myself, mind you. But his good humor takes the sting out of it somehow, doesn't it? What did he call it?"
"The ballad of joking Jesus," Stephen answered.
"Oh," Haines said, "you've heard it before?"
"Three times a day, after meals," Stephen said dryly.
"You're not a believer, are you?" Haines asked. "I mean, in the strict sense. Creation from nothing and miracles and a personal God."
"There's only one sense of the word, it seems to me," Stephen said.
Haines stopped and took out a smooth silver cigarette case with a green stone set in it. He opened it and offered Stephen a cigarette.
"Thank you," Stephen said, taking one.
Haines took one himself and snapped the case shut. He put it back in his pocket, pulled out a lighter, and lit Stephen's cigarette, cupping his hands around the flame.
"Yes, of course," he said, as they walked on. "Either you believe or you don't. Personally, I can't accept the idea of a personal God. You don't believe in that, do you?"
"What you see before you," Stephen said with grim humor, "is a terrible example of free thinking."

He walked on, trailing his walking stick beside him, its metal tip squeaking along the path. He thought to himself: Mulligan wants that key. It's mine — I paid the rent. But now I eat his food. Should I give him the key too? Everything? He'll ask for it. I could see it in his eyes.
"After all," Haines began...
Stephen turned and saw that Haines's cool gaze was not entirely unfriendly.
"After all, you should be able to free yourself," Haines said. "You seem to be your own master."
"I am a servant of two masters," Stephen said. "An English one and an Italian one."
"Italian?" Haines said, puzzled.
Stephen thought of the Catholic Church — old, demanding, and jealous of its power.
"And a third," Stephen said, "who wants me for odd jobs."
"Italian?" Haines said again. "What do you mean?"
"The British Empire," Stephen answered, his cheeks reddening, "and the Roman Catholic Church."
Haines picked a bit of tobacco from his lip before speaking.
"I can quite understand that," he said calmly. "An Irishman would feel that way, I'm sure. We in England know we haven't treated you very fairly. It seems history is to blame."

Stephen thought about the grand old words of the Catholic Church — its ancient traditions, its slow changes over centuries, its great music and rituals. He thought of how the Church had fought against those who questioned its teachings throughout history, and how Mulligan's mockery was just another form of that ancient challenge.
"Hear, hear!" Stephen thought sarcastically to himself.
"Of course, I'm British," Haines went on, "and proud of it. I don't want to see my country fall into the wrong hands. That's our national problem right now."
Two men stood at the edge of the cliff, looking out to sea: a businessman and a boatman.
"She's heading for Bullock harbour," said one.
The boatman nodded toward the north of the bay.
"There's deep water out there," he said. "The tide will bring things in around one o'clock. It's been nine days now."
Stephen thought about a man who had drowned. He imagined a boat searching the empty bay, waiting for the body to float to the surface.

They followed the winding path down to the little beach. Buck Mulligan stood on a rock in his shirtsleeves, his untied tie flapping over his shoulder. A young man clung to a rock nearby, slowly kicking his legs in the deep water.
"Is your brother with you, Malachi?"
"No, he's down in the country. With the Bannons."
"Still there? I got a letter from Bannon. Says he's met a nice girl down there. He calls her his photo girl."
"A photo girl, eh?" said someone.

Buck Mulligan sat down to unlace his boots. An older man climbed up out of the water nearby, his face red and puffing. Water glistened on his bald head and the ring of grey hair around it, dripping down over his chest.
Buck Mulligan made way for the man to climb past, and jokingly crossed himself — touching his forehead, lips, and chest — the way you do in church.
"Seymour's back in town," the young man in the water said. "He's quit medical school and joined the army."
"Really?" Buck Mulligan said.
"He's going over next week. You know that girl, Lily?"
"Yes."
"She was out walking with him last night. Her father is very rich."
"Are they serious about each other?"
"You'd have to ask Seymour."
"Seymour, an army officer!" Buck Mulligan said, amazed.
He nodded to himself as he undressed, getting ready for his swim.
He made a joke, then suddenly looked alarmed, feeling his side under his flapping shirt.
"My rib is missing!" he cried with a laugh. "I'm a superman! Toothless Kinch and I — the supermen!"
He pulled off his shirt and threw it behind him onto his pile of clothes.
"Are you going in here, Malachi?"
"Yes. Make room."
The young man pushed himself backward through the water and reached the middle of the creek in two strong strokes. Haines sat down on a rock, smoking.
"Aren't you coming in?" Buck Mulligan asked.
"Later on," Haines said. "Not right after breakfast."
Stephen turned away.
"I'm going, Mulligan," he said.
"Give us that key, Kinch," Buck Mulligan said, "to keep my clothes from blowing away."
Stephen handed him the key. Buck Mulligan laid it across his pile of clothes.
"And twopence," he said, "for a drink. Toss it over."
Stephen threw two pennies onto the soft pile of clothes. Buck Mulligan stood up straight, put his hands together in front of him like a prayer, and said solemnly:
"He who takes from the poor lends to the Lord." He was quoting a famous philosopher, but joking about it.
His body plunged into the water.
"We'll see you again," Haines said, turning to smile at Stephen as he walked up the path.
Stephen thought about the Englishman's smile — as untrustworthy as a bull's horn or a horse's hoof.
"The Ship pub!" Buck Mulligan called from the water. "Half past twelve!"
"Good," Stephen said.
He walked along the path that curved upward away from the sea.
He thought of the Latin prayers for the dying — the same ones that had been said over his mother.
He thought of the priest getting dressed in his grey robes in a little alcove. He decided: I won't sleep at the tower tonight. But I can't go home either.

A voice called to him from the sea — sweet and clear. Turning the curve of the path, he waved his hand. The voice called again. Far out on the water, a brown head bobbed — smooth and round like a seal's.
Stephen thought one word: Usurper. Mulligan had taken over — the tower, the key, everything.

chapters.title: Episode 2 — Nestor
paragraphs: "You, Cochrane, what city sent for him?" Stephen asked the class.
"Tarentum, sir."
"Very good. And then what happened?"
"There was a battle, sir."
"Very good. Where was it?"
The boy stared blankly at the window, his face empty of any answer.

Stephen thought about how stories get passed down through time. History was like that — things happened, and then people told stories about them, and the stories were never quite exactly what had happened. He thought about the great forces of time and how everything eventually crumbles.
"I forget the place, sir. 279 B.C."
"Asculum," Stephen said, glancing at the name and date in the battered old history book.

"Yes, sir. And Pyrrhus said: 'Another victory like that and we're finished.'" This was the famous idea of a Pyrrhic victory — winning a battle but losing so many soldiers that it's almost like losing.

Stephen thought about that famous phrase. He imagined a general standing on a hill above a battlefield, looking down at all the soldiers who had been lost, speaking to his officers. Any general in any war might have felt the same way.
"You, Armstrong," Stephen said. "What happened to Pyrrhus in the end?"
"End of Pyrrhus, sir?"
"I know, sir. Ask me, sir," Comyn said eagerly.
"Wait. Armstrong, do you know anything about Pyrrhus?"

Armstrong had a bag of fig cookies hidden in his school bag. He was secretly eating them, rolling them between his hands and swallowing them quietly. Crumbs stuck to his lips. Stephen knew the boy came from a well-off family who lived on Vico Road in Dalkey.
"Pyrrhus, sir? Pyrrhus, a pier." Armstrong made a joke, confusing the ancient king's name with a pier — a walkway going out into the sea.

Everyone laughed — not because it was funny, but because they liked seeing someone be cheeky to the teacher. Armstrong looked around at his classmates, pleased with himself. Stephen knew they would laugh even louder soon, aware that he didn't have much control over them.
"Tell me now," Stephen said, tapping the boy's shoulder with the book, "what is a pier?"
"A pier, sir," Armstrong said. "A thing out in the water. A kind of bridge. Kingstown pier, sir."
Some laughed again. Two boys whispered in the back row. Stephen watched their faces, these children of comfortable families with their sweet breath and jangling bracelets.
"Kingstown pier," Stephen said. "Yes, a disappointed bridge." He meant that a pier is like a bridge that never reaches the other side.
The words puzzled the boys.
"How do you mean, sir?" Comyn asked. "A bridge goes across a river."

Stephen thought about Haines, the Englishman from the tower. He imagined impressing Haines tonight with clever conversation over drinks. But what was the point? He would just be a clever entertainer, a jester performing for someone richer and more powerful. He thought about how for Irish people, history was a sad story heard too often, and their country felt like a pawnshop — everything valuable had been taken away.

Stephen thought about the big 'what ifs' of history. What if Pyrrhus hadn't been killed? What if Julius Caesar hadn't been stabbed? These things happened and couldn't be wished away. They pushed out all the other possibilities that might have been. But could those other possibilities ever really have happened, since they didn't?
"Tell us a story, sir."
"Oh, do, sir. A ghost story."
"Where do you start reading in this?" Stephen asked, opening a different book.
"'Weep no more,'" Comyn said, finding the place.
"Go on then, Talbot."
"And the story, sir?"
"After," Stephen said. "Go on, Talbot."
A dark-haired boy opened his book and propped it up against his school bag. He began reading the poem in a halting, jerky way, glancing at the text as he went:

He read: "Weep no more, sad shepherds, weep no more, for Lycidas, your friend, is not dead, even though he lies beneath the water..." It was a famous poem by John Milton about a friend who had drowned.

While Talbot stumbled through the poem, Stephen's mind wandered. He thought about a philosopher named Aristotle and his ideas about what is possible and what is real. He remembered studying late at night in a library in Paris, surrounded by other students under glowing lamps. He thought about how the mind works — thought thinking about thought. The soul taking in everything, becoming the shape of everything it encounters.
Talbot repeated one of the lines:
"Through the dear might of Him that walked the waves,"
"Through the dear might..." He got stuck.
"Turn over," Stephen said quietly. "I don't see the next line."
"What, sir?" Talbot asked, leaning forward.

The boy turned the page and continued. The poem was about Jesus, who walked on waves. Stephen thought about how Jesus's shadow falls over all of us — believers and doubters alike. He thought of the Bible story about paying taxes: give to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God.
Stephen thought of a riddle: "Riddle me, riddle me, what is it? My father gave me seeds to sow."
Talbot slid his book into his bag.
"Have I read it all?" Stephen asked.
"Yes, sir. Hockey starts at ten, sir."
"Half day, sir. It's Thursday."
"Who can answer a riddle?" Stephen asked.
The boys bundled their books away, pencils clacking, pages rustling. Crowding together, they strapped up their school bags, all talking excitedly:
"A riddle, sir? Ask me, sir."
"Oh, ask me, sir."
"A hard one, sir."
"This is the riddle," Stephen said:
He recited: "The rooster crowed, the sky was blue, the bells in heaven were striking eleven. It's time for this poor soul to go to heaven."
"What is that?"
"What, sir?"
"Again, sir. We didn't hear you."
The boys' eyes grew bigger as Stephen repeated the riddle. After a moment of silence, Cochrane said:
"What is it, sir? We give up."
Stephen, clearing his throat, answered:
"The fox burying his grandmother under a holly bush." It was a nonsense answer — the kind of riddle where the answer has nothing to do with the question.
He stood up and gave a nervous laugh. The boys cried out in protest.
A hockey stick banged against the door, and a voice in the corridor called:
"Hockey!"

The boys scattered, sliding out of their seats, some jumping over the benches. In an instant they were gone, and from the storeroom came the clatter of hockey sticks and the noise of their boots and voices.

One boy, Sargent, who had stayed behind, came forward slowly with an open exercise book. His hair was messy and his neck was thin. Through his foggy glasses, his weak eyes looked up, asking for help. On his cheek was a fresh ink stain, shaped like a date, still damp.
He held out his exercise book. The word "Sums" was written at the top. Below were messy, sloping numbers, and at the bottom a crooked signature with loops and a blot: Cyril Sargent.
"Mr. Deasy told me to write them all out again," he said, "and show them to you, sir."
Stephen touched the edges of the book. He felt it was all rather pointless.
"Do you understand how to do them now?" he asked.
"Numbers eleven to fifteen," Sargent answered. "Mr. Deasy said I was to copy them from the blackboard, sir."
"Can you do them by yourself?" Stephen asked.
"No, sir."

Stephen looked at the boy — awkward, with his thin neck and tangled hair and ink stain. Not a child anyone would call handsome. Yet someone loved him — his mother had carried him in her arms and in her heart. Without her love, the world would have trampled him like a snail on the path. Stephen thought of his own mother, now gone, and of how a mother's love is perhaps the only truly real thing in life. He thought of the fox from his riddle, scraping at the earth beneath the stars.
Stephen sat beside Sargent and worked through the math problem. The sounds of hockey sticks rattled from the storeroom, and he could hear the boys shouting on the field outside.

Stephen watched the numbers on the page — squares and cubes doing a kind of dance in their mathematical patterns. He thought of the great thinkers of the past, like the Arab philosopher Averroes and the Jewish philosopher Moses Maimonides, who had worked with numbers and ideas long ago. They were gone from the world now, but their knowledge lived on — a kind of darkness that shines in brightness.
"Do you understand now? Can you do the second one yourself?"
"Yes, sir."

Sargent copied the numbers in long, shaky lines. His hand moved carefully but unsteadily, and a faint blush of shame showed through his dull skin. Stephen thought about the Latin phrase "amor matris" — a mother's love. Sargent's mother had fed him, protected him, hidden his weaknesses from others.

Stephen thought: I was like him once — these sloping shoulders, this awkwardness. My childhood stands beside me now. We both carry secrets in the dark rooms of our hearts — secrets tired of ruling us, ready to let go.
The math problem was finished.
"It's very simple," Stephen said, standing up.
"Yes, sir. Thanks," Sargent answered.
He dried the page with a piece of blotting paper and carried his exercise book back to his desk.
"You'd better get your hockey stick and go out to the others," Stephen said as the boy walked toward the door.
"Yes, sir."
In the corridor, his name was called from the playing field.
"Sargent!"
"Run on," Stephen said. "Mr. Deasy is calling you."

Stephen stood in the porch and watched the slow boy hurry toward the rough playing field where sharp voices argued. The teams were being sorted, and Mr. Deasy walked back across the field in his boots with gaiters, stepping over tufts of grass. When he reached the school building, the boys called out to him again. He turned his angry white mustache toward them.
"What is it now?" he kept calling without really listening.
"Cochrane and Halliday are on the same side, sir," Stephen said.
"Will you wait in my study for a moment," Mr. Deasy said, "till I sort this out."
And as he stepped fussily back across the field, his old man's voice cried sternly:
"What is the matter? What is it now?"
The boys' sharp voices called out from all sides. Their small bodies closed around him in the harsh sunshine that bleached the poorly-dyed hair on his old head.

Stephen waited in the study. The room smelled of stale smoke and worn leather chairs. On the sideboard was a tray of old coins — treasure from a bog. In a velvet case, faded with age, were twelve silver spoons shaped like the twelve apostles. Everything in this room felt old and unchanging.
Quick footsteps came over the stone porch and down the corridor. Mr. Deasy arrived at his desk, smoothing his bushy mustache.
"First, our little money matter," he said.
He pulled from his coat a leather pocketbook, opened it, and took out two banknotes, placing them carefully on the table.
"Two," he said, putting the pocketbook away.

Now he brought out a box for the gold coins. Stephen's hand moved nervously over some seashells piled in a stone bowl on the desk — whelks, cowrie shells, and a scallop shell like the symbol of Saint James. Old treasure. Dead treasure. Empty shells.
A gold coin fell, bright and new, onto the soft tablecloth.

"Three," Mr. Deasy said, turning his little savings box in his hand. "These are handy things to have. See — this slot is for gold sovereigns. This is for shillings. Sixpences, half-crowns. And here, crowns. See."
He counted out two more crowns and two shillings.
"Three pounds twelve," he said. "I think you'll find that's correct."
"Thank you, sir," Stephen said, quickly gathering the money and putting it all in his trouser pocket.
"No need to thank me," Mr. Deasy said. "You've earned it."
Stephen's hand went back to the shells. They were symbols of beauty and power, he thought. But the money in his pocket already felt dirty — symbols stained by greed.
"Don't carry it loose like that," Mr. Deasy said. "You'll pull it out somewhere and lose it. You should buy one of these little savings boxes. Very handy."
Stephen needed to say something.
"Mine would usually be empty," Stephen said.
He thought: the same room, the same hour, the same advice — and I'm the same person hearing it. Three times now. I feel tied down here. But I could break free in an instant if I wanted to.

"Because you don't save," Mr. Deasy said, wagging his finger. "You don't know what money is yet. Money is power. When you've lived as long as I have — well. If only young people knew. But what does Shakespeare say? 'Put money in your purse.'"
"Iago," Stephen murmured. That line was spoken by the villain Iago in Shakespeare's play Othello — not exactly the best person to quote about money.
He looked up from the shells to the old man's staring eyes.

"Shakespeare knew what money was," Mr. Deasy said. "He made money. A poet, yes, but an Englishman too. Do you know what is the pride of the English? Do you know the proudest words an Englishman can say?"
Stephen thought of the English, rulers of the seas, with their cold eyes looking out over the empty bay.
"That on his empire," Stephen said, "the sun never sets."
"Bah!" Mr. Deasy cried. "That's not even English — a Frenchman said that." He tapped his savings box against his thumbnail.
"I will tell you," he said seriously, "the proudest thing an Englishman can say: 'I paid my way.'"
Stephen thought: good man, good man.
"'I paid my way. I never borrowed a shilling in my life.' Can you feel what that means? 'I owe nothing.' Can you?"
Stephen thought of all the people he owed money to — Mulligan, nine pounds; Curran, ten guineas; McCann, one guinea; and several others. The money in his pocket wouldn't cover half of it.
"At the moment, no," Stephen admitted.
Mr. Deasy laughed with delight, putting away his savings box.
"I knew you couldn't," he said happily. "But one day you'll understand. We Irish are generous, but we must also be fair."
"I'm afraid of those big words," Stephen said, "that make us all so unhappy."
Mr. Deasy stared for a moment at a portrait over the fireplace — a picture of the Prince of Wales in Scottish dress.

"You think I'm an old fool and an old conservative," Mr. Deasy said thoughtfully. "I've seen three generations since the days of the great Irish leader O'Connell. I remember the terrible famine of 1846. Do you know that the Protestant lodges wanted Ireland to be independent twenty years before O'Connell even started fighting for it? You young rebels forget some things."
Stephen thought of the long, bitter history between Protestants and Catholics in Ireland — the violence, the slogans, the hatred.
Stephen made a small gesture, as if to say "go on."

"I have rebel blood in me too," Mr. Deasy said, "on my mother's side. But I'm also descended from Sir John Blackwood, who voted for the union between Ireland and England. We are all Irish, all descended from kings."
"Alas," Stephen said.
"Sir John's motto was 'By the straight path,'" Mr. Deasy said firmly. "He put on his riding boots and rode all the way to Dublin to cast his vote."
Stephen imagined the old saying about the rocky road to Dublin, and a gruff old gentleman on horseback.
He pictured the scene — people calling out greetings as Sir John rode past on his way to Dublin.

"That reminds me," Mr. Deasy said. "You could do me a favor, Mr. Dedalus, with some of your friends in the newspaper business. I have a letter here I want published. Sit down a moment while I finish copying the end."
He went to his desk near the window, pulled his chair in, and read some words from the sheet in his typewriter.
"Sit down. Excuse me," he said over his shoulder, "'the dictates of common sense.' Just a moment."
He peered at his manuscript and, muttering to himself, began slowly pressing the stiff keys of the typewriter, sometimes blowing on the page to erase a mistake.

Stephen sat down quietly. Around the walls hung framed pictures of famous racehorses — Repulse, Shotover, Ceylon — with tiny jockeys perched on their backs. Stephen imagined the crowds cheering as these great horses raced by.
"Full stop," Mr. Deasy told his typewriter keys. "'But prompt attention to this very important question...'"
Stephen thought about a time when his friend Cranly had taken him to the horse races — the mud, the noise of the bookmakers shouting odds, the smell of the food tent, the excitement of betting.
Shrill shouts rang from the boys' playing field, and a whistle blew.
A goal had been scored. Stephen thought about being out there among the boys, in the thick of the game — the struggle and energy of life. He imagined ancient battles, the clash of armies.
"Now then," Mr. Deasy said, standing up.
He came to the table, pinning his pages together. Stephen stood up.
"I've written it all out clearly," Mr. Deasy said. "It's about the foot and mouth disease that's affecting cattle. Just read through it. There can't be two opinions on the matter."
Stephen skimmed the letter. It was about cattle trade, disease, government neglect, and Mr. Deasy's ideas about how to fix everything. It was full of big words and historical references.
"I don't mince words, do I?" Mr. Deasy asked as Stephen read on.

The letter went on about a scientist named Koch, disease treatments, veterinary surgeons, and a cousin of Mr. Deasy's named Mr. Henry Blackwood Price who had connections in Austria. It ended by thanking the newspaper for printing it.

"I want this to be printed and read," Mr. Deasy said. "Mark my words — at the next outbreak, they'll stop Irish cattle from being exported. But this disease can be cured. My cousin writes to me that it's regularly treated in Austria. Those Austrian cattle doctors have offered to come here. I'm trying to get the government interested. Now I'm going to try the newspapers. I'm surrounded by difficulties, by scheming, by people working against me behind the scenes..."
He raised his finger and waved it in the air before he spoke.

"Mark my words, Mr. Dedalus," he said. "England is being ruined." He went on to say unkind things about Jewish people, blaming them for England's problems — which was unfair and wrong, the kind of prejudice that was sadly common in those days.
He stepped quickly to the window, his eyes coming alive in a beam of sunlight. He turned back again.
"Dying," he said, "if not already dead."
He quoted a line from the poet William Blake: "The cry from street to street shall weave old England's burial cloth."
His eyes stared wide, looking across the sunbeam where he stood.
"A merchant," Stephen said, "is simply someone who buys cheap and sells at a higher price — whether he's Jewish or not."
"They sinned against the light," Mr. Deasy said seriously. "And that is why they have wandered the earth ever since." This was another unfair thing people used to say.

Stephen thought about Jewish people he had seen — traders and merchants going about their business. He thought about how they had been treated unfairly for centuries, forced to wander, their patience and hard work never truly appreciated.
"Who hasn't sinned?" Stephen said.
"What do you mean?" Mr. Deasy asked.
He stepped forward and stood by the table, his jaw dropping uncertainly. He waited to hear what Stephen meant.

"History," Stephen said, "is a nightmare from which I am trying to wake up." This was one of the most famous lines Stephen would ever say — that the terrible things of the past haunt us like a bad dream.
From the playing field, the boys shouted. A whistle blew: another goal. Stephen wondered: what if that nightmare of history could kick you back?
"The ways of God are not our ways," Mr. Deasy said. "All of human history moves toward one great goal — showing forth the will of God."
Stephen pointed his thumb toward the window:
"That is God," he said.
"Hooray! Ay! Whee!" came the shouts of the boys playing outside.
"What?" Mr. Deasy asked, confused.
"A shout in the street," Stephen answered with a shrug. He meant that God was in the ordinary, everyday moments — even in the shouts of boys playing hockey.
Mr. Deasy pinched the bridge of his nose for a moment, thinking, then let go.

"I am happier than you are," he said. "We have made many mistakes. A woman brought trouble into the world — starting with Helen, whose beauty caused the Trojan War, and the Irish woman who first invited foreign invaders to Ireland. And a woman brought down the great Irish leader Parnell. Many errors, many failures — but I will fight for what is right to the very end."
He quoted a political slogan: "For Ulster will fight, and Ulster will be right!"
Stephen held up the sheets of paper.
"Well, sir," he began.
"I suspect," Mr. Deasy said, "that you won't stay in this teaching job for long. You weren't born to be a teacher, I think. Perhaps I'm wrong."
"A learner, rather," Stephen said.
And what would he learn here? Stephen wondered.
Mr. Deasy shook his head.
"Who knows?" he said. "To learn, one must be humble. But life is the greatest teacher of all."
Stephen rustled the papers again.
"About these letters," he began.
"Yes," Mr. Deasy said. "You have two copies there. If you could get them published right away."
The Telegraph and the Irish Homestead — those were the newspapers Stephen might try.
"I'll try," Stephen said, "and let you know tomorrow. I know two editors slightly."

"That will do," Mr. Deasy said briskly. "I also wrote last night to Mr. Field, the member of Parliament. There's a meeting of the cattle traders' association today. I asked him to bring my letter to their attention. See if you can get it into your two papers. Which ones are they?"
"The Evening Telegraph..." Stephen began.
"That will do," Mr. Deasy said. "There's no time to waste. Now I have to answer a letter from my cousin."
"Good morning, sir," Stephen said, putting the papers in his pocket. "Thank you."
"Not at all," Mr. Deasy said, searching through papers on his desk. "I enjoy a good debate with you, old as I am."
"Good morning, sir," Stephen said again, bowing slightly as Mr. Deasy bent over his desk.

Stephen walked out through the open porch and down the gravel path under the trees, hearing the shouts and crack of hockey sticks from the playing field. He passed the stone lions on the gate pillars — toothless guardians. He thought: I'll still help the old man with his letter. But Mulligan will give me a new nickname for it — something about me being the poet who befriends cows.
"Mr. Dedalus!"
Stephen thought: he's running after me. I hope it's not more letters.
"Just one moment."
"Yes, sir," Stephen said, turning back at the gate.
Mr. Deasy stopped, breathing hard, catching his breath.
"I just wanted to say," he said. "Ireland, they say, has the honor of being the only country that never persecuted Jewish people. Do you know that? No. And do you know why?"
He frowned seriously at the bright air.
"Why, sir?" Stephen asked, starting to smile.
"Because she never let them in," Mr. Deasy said with great seriousness.
Then he burst out laughing at his own joke — a great cough of laughter that shook his whole body. He turned and walked back, still laughing, waving his arms in the air.
"She never let them in!" he cried again through his laughter as he stamped along the gravel path. "That's why!"
The sun threw dancing spots of light through the leaves onto his old shoulders, like scattered gold coins.

chapters.title: Episode 3 — Proteus
paragraphs: Stephen walked along Sandymount Strand, the beach near Dublin, thinking hard about what we can really know about the world. He thought: I can see things — seaweed, the tide coming in, a rusty old boot. Green, blue-silver, rust — the world shows itself through colors. An ancient philosopher named Aristotle said we understand the world through our bodies. How? By bumping into things, of course! Stephen thought about the difference between what you can see through (like a window) and what you can't (like a door). He decided to try an experiment: shut your eyes and see what happens.

Stephen closed his eyes and listened to his boots crunching on seaweed and shells. He was still walking through the world even with his eyes shut. One step at a time. He thought about how things come one after another in time — that's how we hear them. He thought: wait, what if I fall off a cliff with my eyes shut? No — I'm doing fine in the dark. My walking stick hangs at my side, like a blind man's cane. He tapped it on the ground. Am I walking into forever along this beach? Crunch, crack, crunch. Mr. Deasy from the school would love all these seashells.
A little rhyme popped into his head: "Won't you come to Sandymount, Madeline the mare?"
Stephen thought: there it is — rhythm. Poetry starting on its own. He could hear the beat of the words like horses trotting.
He thought: open your eyes now. I will. Just one moment. What if everything has disappeared while my eyes were closed? What if I open them and find only darkness forever? Enough! I'll look and see.
He opened his eyes. Everything was still there, just as it had been — the beach, the sea, the sky. There all the time, whether he looked at it or not.

Two women came down the steps from a row of houses and walked onto the beach, their feet sinking into the soft sand. One of them carried a heavy bag — she was a midwife, a woman who helps deliver babies. Stephen thought about how one of her kind had brought him into the world. He thought about birth and how every person is connected to every other person through an invisible chain going all the way back to the very first people. He imagined calling up the Garden of Eden on a telephone.
He thought about Eve, the first woman in the Bible — she would have had no belly button, since she wasn't born from a mother. He thought about the beginning of everything.

Stephen thought about his own parents — his father, with the same voice and eyes as him, and his mother, now dead. God had willed Stephen into existence before time began, and could never un-will him. He thought about old arguments in the Church about whether God the Father and God the Son are made of the same substance. A man named Arius had spent his whole life arguing about it.
Fresh, playful winds blew around Stephen. He could see the waves coming — white-topped, like horses galloping in the wind. In Irish legends, the sea god Mananaan rode such horses across the water.

He reminded himself: I mustn't forget Mr. Deasy's letter for the newspaper. And afterward? Meet Mulligan at The Ship pub at half past twelve. And go easy with that money — don't spend it all foolishly.

Stephen slowed down. He wondered: should I visit my Aunt Sara? He imagined his father's mocking voice, complaining about the family Stephen's mother had married into — Uncle Richie and his drinking, and the whole embarrassing lot of them.
Stephen imagined ringing the bell at their shabby little cottage and waiting. They would peek out, worried he might be someone coming to collect a debt.
"It's Stephen, sir," the son Walter would call out.
"Let him in. Let Stephen in."
The door bolt would slide back and Walter would welcome him.
"We thought you were someone else."
Stephen imagined Uncle Richie lying in his big bed, blankets piled up, sticking out a strong arm over his knees. He'd only washed the top half of himself.
"Good morning, nephew."
Uncle Richie would push aside his paperwork — he was a lawyer of sorts — with a framed poem on the wall above his bald head. He'd whistle for Walter to come back.
"Yes, sir?"
"A drink for Richie and Stephen. Tell your mother. Where is she?"
"Giving Crissie her bath, sir."
Little Crissie, the baby of the family.
"No, Uncle Richie..." Stephen would begin.
"Call me Richie. Never mind your mineral water. I want whiskey!"
"Uncle Richie, really..."
"Sit down or I'll knock you down!"
Walter would look around helplessly for a chair.
"He has nothing to sit on, sir."
"Bring our best chair, you fool. Would you like a bite to eat? Don't be putting on airs here. Some bacon and a herring? No? Just as well. We've got nothing in the house anyway."
"Watch out!" Uncle Richie would cry in Italian, pretending to be in an opera.
He would start humming a tune from an opera, drumming his fists on his knees. "The greatest song in the whole opera, Stephen. Listen!"
His whistling would fill the room — surprisingly musical, with fancy trills and runs.
But this scene was only in Stephen's imagination. The wind on the beach was sweeter than any house.

Stephen thought about his family and their crumbling houses. When he was at school, he'd told the other boys his uncle was a judge and his uncle was a general. But there was no beauty in pretending. He thought about all the clever, strange people he knew — the long faces of his friends and teachers. He thought about priests and churches and old arguments about religion, going round and round for centuries.

He thought about how, all across Dublin at this very moment, priests were saying Mass in different churches — bells ringing here and there, bread being blessed and shared. A philosopher named William of Occam had once puzzled over how all these separate services could happen at the same time.

Stephen teased himself: Cousin Stephen, you'll never be a saint. You used to be so religious as a boy! You prayed to the Virgin Mary that you wouldn't have a red nose. He laughed at his younger self and all his foolish prayers and embarrassing moments.
What of it? Everyone has awkward memories.

He remembered being young and ambitious — reading two pages from seven different books every night, practicing serious faces in the mirror, planning to write great books with single letters for titles. He'd written what he called "epiphanies" — moments of deep truth — on special paper, with plans to send copies to all the great libraries if he died. He laughed at himself now: someone would read them thousands of years later! How grand he'd thought he was.

The sand changed under his feet. Now he walked on damp, crackling stuff — razor shells, squeaking pebbles, bits of wood eaten by shipworms. The sand flats smelled unpleasant. He walked carefully past a bottle stuck in the sand, past broken barrels on the shore, dark fishing nets, and a clothesline with shirts hanging on it. This was Ringsend, where fishermen and sailors lived.

He stopped. He'd already walked past the turn-off to Aunt Sara's house. Was he going there after all? It seemed not. Nobody was around. He turned northeast and walked across the firmer sand toward the Pigeonhouse — a building out near the harbor.
He remembered a French joke: "Who got you into this mess?" "The pigeon, Joseph." It was a play on words about the Holy Spirit, who is sometimes shown as a dove.
The answer to the joke was about Joseph and Mary — a Bible joke.

Stephen remembered a young Irishman named Patrice, Kevin Egan's son, whom he'd known in Paris. They used to drink warm milk together at a bar. Patrice had a round, cheerful face. He hoped to win the lottery. He was always reading books.
Patrice had once said in French: "It's hilarious, you know. I'm a socialist. I don't believe in God. But don't tell my father."
"Does he believe?" Stephen had asked in French.
"My father? Yes."
That was that. Patrice went on drinking his milk.

Stephen thought about his time as a student in Paris. His special hat, his gloves. Studying science — physics, chemistry, natural history. Eating cheap stew at crowded cafes, bumped by rude cab drivers. Pretending to be sophisticated: "When I was in Paris..." He thought about how strange it was — you carry tickets and papers to prove where you've been, to prove you're real. The other version of yourself, the one who stayed home — was that the real you?

He remembered walking proudly through Paris, imitating someone else's walk. He remembered being hungry, standing at the post office with a money order from his mother — eight shillings — and having the door shut in his face. Hunger and toothache. Waiting and waiting.
He'd planned to do great things in Paris, like the ancient Irish monks who had gone out to teach Europe. What had he actually brought back? Some torn French magazines and a telegram:
"Mother dying. Come home. Father."
Mulligan's aunt thought Stephen had killed his mother by refusing to pray at her deathbed. That's why she wouldn't have anything to do with him.
A silly rhyme came to him about Mulligan's aunt, and he hummed it to himself as he walked.

His feet fell into a proud marching rhythm on the sand. He walked along beside the boulders of the south wall, staring at them — huge stones piled up like the skulls of prehistoric animals. Golden light on the sea, on the sand, on the boulders. The sun was bright, the trees thin, the houses pale yellow.

He remembered Paris waking up in the morning — raw sunlight on the yellow streets, the smell of fresh bread, people starting their day. Women in a cafe eating pastries, men walking past with pleased expressions.

He remembered sitting with old Kevin Egan at noon in a Paris cafe. Kevin Egan was an Irish rebel who had fled to France long ago. He rolled his own cigarettes with ink-stained fingers and drank green absinthe. They sat among other men shoveling food down their throats. The waitress confused them — two Irishmen — with Dutchmen. Kevin Egan talked about Ireland, about revolutionaries and politicians, about hopes for Irish freedom. He was an old man living in the past, full of stories about people Stephen didn't know.

Stephen remembered Kevin Egan lighting a cigarette, the flame and sharp smoke filling their corner of the cafe. The old man told stories about how a rebel leader had escaped by disguising himself as a bride. Stories of lost leaders, betrayals, narrow escapes.

Kevin Egan had once been a young, strong man — he'd been involved in a bombing in London, then fled to Paris where he lived in hiding. Now he was old, loveless, homeless, separated from his wife. His wife was comfortable without him, living in a Paris street with a canary and two lodgers. "Tell my son you saw me, won't you?" he'd say. He'd taught young Patrice old Irish songs. He took Stephen by the hand like a character in an Irish ballad.
A snatch of song: "Oh, oh, the boys of Kilkenny..."
An old, weak hand pressing Stephen's. People had forgotten Kevin Egan. But he had not forgotten them. He remembered his homeland, like the Israelites remembering Zion in their exile.

Stephen had wandered near the edge of the sea. Wet sand slapped against his boots. The fresh air hit him, sharp and wild, full of brightness. He stopped — was he walking out toward the lighthouse? He felt his feet beginning to sink in the soft, wet sand. Time to turn back.

He turned and looked south along the shore, his feet sinking into the sand again. He thought about the tower back at Sandycove — the cold, round room where Mulligan and Haines would be waiting. The light would be shifting slowly across the floor. He wouldn't sleep there tonight. Mulligan had the key now. Take it all, keep it all. Stephen's soul walked with him, the shape of all shapes. He thought of Hamlet pacing on the walls of Elsinore, looking out at the dangerous sea.
The tide was coming in, following him. He'd have to get back by the road. He climbed over some seaweed-covered rocks and sat down on a flat stone, resting his walking stick in a crack between rocks.

A dead dog lay bloated on the seaweed. Nearby was the side of a sunken boat, buried in sand. Stephen thought about how sand and stones pile up like heavy words, like layers of history. He imagined a giant stomping around — "Fee-fi-fo-fum! I smell the blood of an Irishman!"

A living dog appeared in the distance, running across the wide sweep of sand. Stephen thought: is it going to come after me? No — let it be free. I have my stick. From farther away, two figures walked toward the shore across the wet sand. The dog was running back to them.

Stephen thought about the Viking ships that had once come to this very beach — Danish warriors with gold around their necks, riding low on the grey surf. He imagined whales stranded in the shallows, and poor, starving Dubliners running out with knives to cut the whale meat. Famine and plague. Their blood runs in me, he thought. He imagined himself walking among the ancient Dubliners on the frozen River Liffey, saying nothing to anyone.

The dog barked, ran toward Stephen, stopped, ran back. Stephen thought of all the pretenders in history — princes and rebels who pretended to be what they weren't. He thought about Mulligan saving people from drowning, while Stephen himself was afraid of a barking dog. He thought about the man who had drowned nine days ago. Could Stephen have saved him? He would have wanted to. He would have tried. But he wasn't a strong swimmer. He remembered the cold water at school, the fear of putting his face in. He thought of drowning: the horror in a dying man's eyes. He couldn't save anyone. He couldn't even save his own mother.
He noticed the man and woman walking on the beach. He could see the woman's skirt.

Their dog trotted around a bank of sand, sniffing everything. Suddenly it took off like a hare, ears back, chasing the shadow of a seagull skimming low. The man whistled sharply and the dog turned, bounded back, trotting on quick legs. At the edge of the water it stopped, ears pointing out to sea, snout lifted, barking at the waves. The waves curled toward it, one after another, rolling in from far out.

The man and woman were cockle-pickers — people who gather shellfish from the shallow water. They waded in, dipped their bags in the sea, and waded out again. The dog ran to them, jumped up on them, then dropped to all fours, then jumped up again, tongue hanging out. It ran ahead of them, then galloped off to where the dead dog lay. It stopped, sniffed, circled the dead body, nosed closer, sniffing all over. Stephen thought: poor creature. Here lies the body of a poor dead dog.
"Tatters! Get away from that, you mongrel!" the man shouted.

The shout brought the dog skulking back to its master, who kicked at it but missed. The dog slunk away in a wide curve. It wandered along the edge of the rocks, sniffing and marking its territory. Then it started digging in the sand — front paws dabbing and scratching. It was burying something, or digging something up. It scraped and scraped with its claws, then stopped to listen, then scraped again furiously.

Stephen thought about a strange dream he'd had the night before — or was it after Haines woke him? He remembered a hallway, a mysterious street. A man had led him somewhere, holding a melon to his face. It smelled sweet. "Come in," the man said. "You will see."

The man and woman shouldered their bags and trudged along. Stephen watched them — they looked like traveling people, weatherbeaten and rough. The man's feet were bare in his rolled-up trousers, a scarf around his unshaved neck. The woman followed behind, hair blowing around her face, a sack on her back, sand crusting her bare feet.
Stephen thought of an old thieves' song: "White your hands, red your mouth, and your body fair. Come lie down with me in the dark and kiss."

He thought about how the great thinker Saint Thomas Aquinas would have called such thoughts wrong — but then, the language of thieves and outlaws was no worse than the language of monks and priests. Different words for the same human desires.
They were passing now.

Stephen watched them from the corner of his eye. He thought about being seen — his odd hat. He thought about all the wandering people of the world, dragging their loads from east to west, following the sun. He thought about the tide and the moon, about birth and death. He was trying to capture a phrase for a poem, something about "mouth to her mouth's kiss."
He thought: wait, hold that idea. Let me write it down. "Mouth to her kiss." No — it needs to be two words. "Mouth to her mouth's kiss." Yes, that's it.

He whispered the words to himself, shaping them with his lips. The sounds seemed to echo like something enormous — planets roaring through space. He needed paper. He found Mr. Deasy's letter in his pocket, tore off the blank end, turned his back to the sun, and bent over a flat rock to scribble down the words. He'd forgotten again to take paper from the library.

His shadow fell over the rocks as he wrote. He thought: why doesn't my shadow stretch on forever, all the way to the farthest star? Somewhere out there, behind the bright sky, stars and whole worlds hide in the darkness. Here he sat with his walking stick, by the pale sea, under strange stars. Who was watching him? Who would ever read these scribbled words? He thought about seeing and distance and how the mind turns flat pictures into a sense of depth. You think my words are dark, he thought. Well, darkness is in our souls.

He thought of a girl he imagined trusting him — gentle hand, long eyelashes. But then he laughed at himself. What girl? Probably the woman he'd noticed in a bookshop window on Monday. She probably lived a very ordinary life. He told himself to stop daydreaming.
He felt lonely. Touch me, he thought. Soft eyes. Soft hand. I am alone here, quiet and sad. He longed for human contact — the word everyone knows: love.

He lay back on the rocks, stuffing his scribbled note and pencil into his pocket, his hat tilted over his eyes. He was copying the way Kevin Egan used to lie down for a nap. The sun shone on him through his eyelashes. He imagined a lush, warm garden with heavy plants and sweet-smelling fruits, leaves floating on brown water. For a moment, all pain was far away.
He thought of the poem again: stop brooding. No more turning aside.

He looked down at his boots — Buck Mulligan's old boots, borrowed and worn. He counted the wrinkles in the leather where someone else's feet had been. He thought about a girl in Paris whose shoe had once fit him perfectly. He thought about his friend Cranly, who was drifting away from him. Would Cranly leave him? So be it. He was what he was. All or nothing.

Water flowed in from the lake, covering the sand in golden-green pools, rising slowly. Stephen thought: my walking stick will float away if I don't move. No — wait — the water will pass, swirling past the low rocks. Better finish this job quickly. He listened to the waves: they seemed to speak in four words — seesoo, hrss, rsseeiss, ooos. The waves crashed among the rocks, then flowed smooth and quiet, spreading out in foam and flowers.

Under the rising tide he watched the seaweed lift and sway like lazy arms in the whispering water. Day after day, night after night, the weeds are lifted, flooded, and dropped again. They seem tired and sad. Saint Ambrose once heard the same sigh in the leaves and waves — everything waiting for something, never quite arriving, flowing out and flowing back, pulled by the moon.

Five fathoms deep out there, Stephen thought. "Full fathom five thy father lies" — that's Shakespeare, from The Tempest. He thought about the drowned man they were looking for. They'd said the body would come in at one o'clock, when the tide turned. He imagined the pale body rising from the water, bobbing toward shore. There he is. Quick, grab him. Pull him in.

Stephen imagined the drowned body in terrible detail — swollen, nibbled by fish. He thought about how everything changes into everything else: God becomes man, man becomes fish, fish becomes something else. We breathe the air that dead people breathed. We walk on their dust.
A sea-change, Stephen thought — brown eyes turned blue by salt water. Drowning at sea is said to be the gentlest of all deaths. Old Father Ocean. He tried to imagine it calmly.

He felt thirsty. Clouds were gathering. Was a storm coming? No, no dark clouds. He thought about lightning and about Lucifer, the fallen angel. Then he thought about being a pilgrim with a walking stick and sandals, heading west toward the evening lands.

He picked up his walking stick and poked at the sand gently. Evening would come whether he wanted it to or not. All days end. He tried to remember — when was the longest day this year?
