His teeth ached. They were getting bad. Should he spend some of his money at the dentist? Toothless Kinch, the superman — that's what Mulligan called him.
He thought: my handkerchief. Mulligan threw it to me earlier. Did I pick it up?
He felt through his pockets. No, he hadn't picked it up. He'd have to buy a new one.
He wiped his nose on his hand and flicked it onto a ledge of rock. Let whoever wants to see it, see it.
He thought: there might be someone behind me.

He looked over his shoulder. In the distance, moving through the air, he saw the tall masts of a three-masted sailing ship, its sails gathered up, heading upstream toward Dublin. It moved silently through the sky, like a ghost ship.
Stephen thought of the Roman numeral II — the second part of his day was about to begin.

chapters.title: Episode 4 — Calypso
paragraphs: Mr. Leopold Bloom liked to eat hearty breakfasts. He enjoyed thick soup, tasty gizzards, and roast heart. But most of all he loved grilled mutton kidneys with their rich, strong flavor.

He was thinking about kidneys as he moved quietly around the kitchen, setting up his wife's breakfast tray. The kitchen was cold and grey inside, but outside it was a gentle summer morning. It made him feel a little hungry.
The coals in the fire were glowing red.

Another slice of bread and butter — three, four — that was right. His wife didn't like her plate piled too high. He turned from the tray, lifted the kettle, and set it on the fire. It sat there, squat and dull. A cup of tea coming soon. Good. His mouth was dry. The cat walked stiffly around the table leg, tail held high.
"Meow!" said the cat.
"Oh, there you are," Mr. Bloom said, turning from the fire.
The cat meowed again and stalked around the table leg, just the way she walked across his writing desk. Purring. Scratch my head. Purr.
Mr. Bloom watched the sleek black cat with interest and affection. She was clean and beautiful — glossy fur, a white spot under her tail, bright green eyes. He bent down to her, hands on his knees.
"Milk for the kitty," he said.
"Mrrrow!" the cat cried.

People say cats are stupid, Bloom thought. But they understand what we say better than we understand them. She knows exactly what she wants. She can be mean, too — it's just her nature. He wondered what he looked like from the cat's point of view. As tall as a tower? No, she could jump over him easily.
"Afraid of the chickens, are you?" he said teasingly. "Afraid of the cluck-clucks. I never saw such a silly kitty."
"Mrrrrow!" the cat said loudly.

She blinked up at him with greedy, half-closed eyes, meowing sadly, showing her white teeth. He watched her eyes narrow with hunger until they looked like green stones. Then he went to the cupboard, took the jug of milk the milkman had just delivered, poured some warm, bubbly milk into a saucer, and set it slowly on the floor.
"Grrrr!" she cried, running to lap it up.

He watched her whiskers gleam in the faint light as she lapped three times. He wondered: is it true that if you cut a cat's whiskers, she can't catch mice anymore? Maybe the whiskers glow in the dark, or they work like feelers.

He listened to her lapping. What should I have for breakfast? Ham and eggs? No, no good eggs in this dry weather. He'd want fresh water too. Thursday wasn't the best day for a mutton kidney at Buckley's shop. Better get a pork kidney at Dlugacz's butcher shop while the kettle boils. The cat lapped more slowly, then licked the saucer clean. Why are cats' tongues so rough? To lap better, he supposed. Nothing else for her to eat. He looked around. No.

On quietly creaking boots he went up the stairs to the hall and paused by the bedroom door. Maybe his wife Molly would like something tasty. She liked thin bread and butter in the morning. But perhaps something special, just this once.
He said softly in the empty hallway:
"I'm going around the corner. Be back in a minute."
And then he added:
"You don't want anything for breakfast?"
A sleepy, soft grunt answered:
"Mm."

No, she didn't want anything. He heard a warm, heavy sigh as she turned over in bed, the brass rings of the bedstead jingling. He really needed to get those fixed. The bed had come all the way from Gibraltar, where Molly had grown up. Her father, old Tweedy, had bought it at an auction. He'd been a clever man — a soldier who'd risen through the ranks and was proud of it. He'd even made money collecting stamps.

Bloom took his hat from the peg above his heavy overcoat. He thought about stamps — little pictures you stick on letters. Inside the band of his hat was a white slip of paper. He checked: still there. Safe.

On the doorstep he felt in his back pocket for the door key. Not there. It was in the other trousers, the ones he'd changed out of. He'd have to get it later. He had a potato in his pocket — he carried one for good luck. He didn't want to go back upstairs and disturb Molly — she'd just turned over in bed. He pulled the front door shut very gently until it clicked. It looked closed. That would have to do until he got back.

He crossed to the sunny side of the street, avoiding a loose cellar cover at number seventy-five. The sun was getting near the steeple of George's church. It would be a warm day. His black funeral clothes would make it feel hotter. Black absorbs heat — or does it reflect it? He couldn't wear his light suit to a funeral anyway. His eyelids drooped pleasantly as he walked in the warm morning. He noticed the bread van delivering — though Molly preferred yesterday's bread, all crispy. He thought about traveling east, chasing the sunrise, moving around the world so fast you'd never grow a day older. He imagined walking through an ancient city — a sentry at the gate, winding streets with carpet shops, sellers calling out, drinking cool water scented with herbs. Wandering all day. The shadows of mosques, a girl playing a stringed instrument. He imagined the whole journey in his mind.
It was probably nothing like that in real life, Bloom thought with a smile. Just the kind of thing you read about in adventure books. A picture of a rising sun on the cover.

He passed Larry O'Rourke's pub. The smell of beer floated up from the cellar, and the doorway breathed out whiffs of ginger and tea and biscuits. Good location for a pub — right at the edge of the busy part of town.

O'Rourke was there, leaning against the counter in his shirtsleeves, watching his assistant mop the floor. Bloom decided not to stop and try to sell him an advertisement — the man knew his own business best.
He should probably stop and say a word — about the funeral, perhaps. Poor Dignam. That was a sad business.
Turning into Dorset Street, he called out a greeting through the pub doorway:
"Good day, Mr. O'Rourke."
"Good day to you."
"Lovely weather, sir."
"That it is."

Bloom wondered how pub owners made their money. Young fellows from the country came to Dublin, worked as bartenders, and somehow ended up owning their own places. Where did the money come from? He supposed it all added up — a little here, a little there, doing deals with suppliers.

How much would that come to per month? He passed Saint Joseph's school. He could hear children shouting inside, windows open to let in the fresh air. Boys learning their geography: names of islands. He thought of his own name — Bloom — and the mountain in Ireland called Slieve Bloom.

He stopped in front of Dlugacz's butcher shop window, looking at the sausages — dark ones and light ones, all hanging in rows. He tried to do some math in his head but gave up and just enjoyed looking at the shiny links of sausage, breathing in the warm, spicy smell.

A kidney sat on a patterned dish — the last one, oozing red. He stood behind a girl at the counter. She was buying sausages, reading from a list. Bloom noticed she was strong-looking. He wondered about her family — the father's name was Woods. She worked hard, you could tell.
The sharp-eyed butcher wrapped up the sausages the girl had ordered with his thick fingers.

Bloom picked up a page from a pile of advertising sheets on the counter. It showed a model farm in Palestine, near the Sea of Galilee. You could buy land there — plant olive trees, orange groves, almond trees. He read about the prices and payment plans.
The butcher wrapped up the girl's sausages and turned to her with a grin.
"Now, miss," he said.
She paid with a coin, holding out her thick wrist, smiling boldly.
"Thank you, miss. And one shilling threepence change. For you, please?" the butcher asked, turning to Bloom.
Mr. Bloom pointed quickly at the kidney. The girl walked outside into the sunshine and strolled lazily to the right. Bloom sighed. People are interesting to watch, he thought.
"Threepence, please."

Bloom took the soft, moist kidney and slipped it into his side pocket. Then he found three coins in his trouser pocket and placed them on the counter. The butcher quickly counted them into the cash register.
"Thank you, sir. Come again."
A spark of friendliness from the butcher's sharp eyes. Bloom looked away.
"Good morning," he said, moving toward the door.
"Good morning, sir."
The girl was gone. Oh well, what did it matter?

He walked back along Dorset Street, reading the advertisement about the farm in Palestine. A company was selling land — you could plant olive trees, orange trees, almonds, or lemons. You'd get a share of the harvest every year. Your name would be entered in the register forever.
It probably wouldn't amount to anything, Bloom thought. Still, there was an idea behind it.

He looked at the picture of cattle in a silvery heat haze. Silver-dusted olive trees. Quiet, long days of pruning and harvesting. He thought of olives packed in jars — Molly didn't like olives, she spat them out. And oranges wrapped in tissue paper in wooden crates. He remembered pleasant evenings with friends — the Citrons and the Mastianskys — Molly sitting in a basket chair. Nice to hold a cool, waxy piece of fruit, lift it to your nose, and smell the sweet perfume. Coming all the way from Spain, Gibraltar, across the Mediterranean.
A cloud began to cover the sun. Everything went grey.

No, not like Palestine at all, Bloom thought. A dead sea. A dead land. The Dead Sea — no fish, no plants, sunk deep in the earth. The cities of the Bible — Sodom, Gomorrah — all destroyed. Dead names. He thought about the oldest peoples, wandering everywhere, multiplying, dying, being born again. He watched an old woman cross the street, clutching a small bottle.
Loneliness.

A chill ran through him. He folded the page into his pocket and turned into Eccles Street, hurrying home. Cold feelings crept through him. But then he thought: I'm here now. Just bad morning thoughts. I need to start exercising again. He noticed the brick houses, the one still for rent, the "For Sale" signs. He longed to smell the tea brewing, the butter sizzling in the pan, to be near Molly's warm body again. Yes, yes.
Quick, warm sunlight came running along the pavement, bright as a girl with golden hair running to meet him.
Two letters and a card lay on the hallway floor. He stooped and picked them up. "Mrs. Marion Bloom." His heart skipped, then slowed. Bold handwriting. Mrs. Marion — someone was writing to his wife.
"Poldy!" Molly called from the bedroom. That was her pet name for him.
Entering the bedroom, he half-closed his eyes and walked through the warm yellow light toward her messy hair on the pillow.
"Who are the letters for?"
He looked at them. One from Mullingar.
"A letter for me from Milly," he said carefully, "and a card for you. And a letter for you."
He laid her card and letter on the bedspread near her knees.
"Do you want the blind up?"
As he pulled the blind halfway up, he noticed her glance at the letter and tuck it quickly under her pillow.
"Is that enough light?" he asked, turning.
She was reading the card, propped up on her elbow.
"She got the things," she said.
He waited until she put the card aside and curled herself back down with a cozy sigh.
"Hurry up with that tea," she said. "I'm dying of thirst."
"The kettle is boiling," he said.
But first he cleared off the chair — her striped petticoat, some laundry — piling it all on the foot of the bed.
As he went down the kitchen stairs she called:
"Poldy!"
"What?"
"Warm the teapot first."

The kettle was boiling, all right — steam puffing from the spout. He rinsed the teapot with hot water, put in four spoonfuls of tea, and poured the boiling water in. While the tea brewed, he put the frying pan on the coals and watched the butter slide and melt. He unwrapped the kidney — the cat meowed hungrily beside him. He dropped the wrapping paper for the cat and set the kidney sizzling in the butter. He sprinkled pepper on it from a chipped egg cup.
Then he opened Milly's letter and read it quickly. She mentioned a new hat, something from Mr. Coghlan, a picnic at a lake, a young student, and some songs.

The tea was ready. He filled his own special cup — a silly thing decorated with a fake crown, a birthday present from Milly when she was small. He smiled, remembering. She'd only been four or five. He'd given her a necklace of amber beads that she'd broken. He used to put folded bits of paper in the letterbox for her to find. He smiled as he poured.
He hummed a little song about Milly Bloom, his darling daughter.

He thought about an old music teacher, Professor Goodwin — a kind old man who used to bow politely when Molly performed. And the night little Milly had found a tiny mirror in the professor's hat and brought it into the living room. Everyone had laughed.

He poked the kidney with a fork and flipped it over, then put the teapot on the tray. He checked: everything there? Bread, butter, sugar, spoon, her cream. Yes. He carried the tray upstairs, his thumb hooked in the teapot handle.
He nudged the bedroom door open with his knee, carried the tray in, and set it on the chair by the bed.
"What took you so long!" she said.
She sat up briskly, making the bed jingle. He looked at her calmly. The warmth of her body rose into the air, mixing with the smell of the tea she poured.
A strip of torn envelope peeked out from under her pillow. Bloom paused to straighten the bedspread.
"Who was the letter from?" he asked.
Bold handwriting. Marion.
"Oh, Boylan," she said. "He's bringing the programme." Boylan was helping organize a concert tour.
"What are you going to sing?"
"A duet with J. C. Doyle," she said, "and 'Love's Old Sweet Song.'"
She smiled as she drank her tea.
"Would you like the window open a bit?"
She folded a slice of bread into her mouth and asked:
"What time is the funeral?"
"Eleven, I think," he answered. "I haven't seen the paper yet."
She pointed, and he looked around for something on the bed. He picked up various items — no, not those.
"No — that book," she said.
He looked further.
"It must have fallen," she said.
He searched around the bed and found the book on the floor.
"Show me," she said. "I put a mark in it. There's a word I wanted to ask you about."
She wiped her fingers on the blanket and searched through the pages with a hairpin until she found the word.
"Met him what?" he asked.
"Here," she said. "What does that mean?"
He leaned down and read near her polished thumbnail.
"Metempsychosis?"
"Yes. What on earth is that?"
"Metempsychosis," he said, frowning. "It's Greek. It means the passing of the soul from one body to another after death."
"Oh, just explain it in plain words!" she said.

He smiled at her teasing eyes. He thought about the picture above their bed — a painting of nymphs, figures from Greek mythology, that had come free with a magazine. He flipped through the book she was reading — a romantic adventure story.
"Did you finish it?" he asked.
"Yes," she said. "There's nothing bad in it. Does the girl stay in love with the first man the whole time?"
"I never read it. Do you want another book?"
"Yes. Get another one of those funny ones."
She poured more tea, watching it flow.
Bloom thought: I need to return that library book or they'll charge me. Reincarnation — that's an easier word for it.

"Some people believe," he said, "that after we die, we're born again in a different body. That we lived before, thousands of years ago, maybe on another planet. They say we've just forgotten. Some people say they can remember their past lives."
The cream swirled slowly through her tea. Bloom thought he should remind her of the right word: metempsychosis. An example would make it clearer.
He looked at the painting above the bed — the nymphs bathing. He thought about the ancient Greeks and how they believed people could be changed into animals or trees.
He turned the pages back.
"Metempsychosis," he said, "is what the ancient Greeks called it. They believed you could be reborn as an animal or a tree. What they called nymphs, for example."
Her spoon stopped stirring. She stared straight ahead, sniffing the air.
"There's a smell of something burning," she said. "Did you leave anything on the fire?"
"The kidney!" he cried suddenly.

He shoved the book into his pocket and hurried out toward the smell, stumbling down the stairs. Smoke was shooting up from the side of the pan. He jabbed a fork under the kidney and flipped it over. Only a little burnt. He tossed it onto a plate and let the brown gravy trickle over it.

Time for a cup of tea. He sat down, cut and buttered a slice of bread. He cut away the burnt part of the kidney and tossed it to the cat. Then he put a forkful of the good meat into his mouth, chewing with pleasure — done perfectly. A sip of tea. He cut some bread, dipped it in the gravy, and read Milly's letter more carefully as he ate.
The letter began: "Dearest Papa,"

She wrote: "Thanks so much for the lovely birthday present. It suits me perfectly. Everyone says I look wonderful in my new hat. I got mummy's lovely box of creams too. I'm doing really well in the photography business now. Mr. Coghlan took a photo of me and Mrs. — will send it when it's developed. We did great business yesterday — it was a fair day and everyone was in town. We're going to Lough Owel on Monday for a little picnic with some friends. Give my love to mummy and a big kiss for yourself. I hear them playing the piano downstairs. There's going to be a concert at the Greville Arms on Saturday. There's a young student who comes in some evenings named Bannon — his family are important people — and he sings that song about seaside girls. Tell him silly Milly sends her best. I must close now with fondest love."
"Your fond daughter, Milly."
"P.S. Sorry about the bad handwriting — I'm in a hurry. Bye-bye."

Fifteen yesterday, Bloom thought. Curious — the fifteenth of the month too. Her first birthday away from home. He remembered the summer morning she was born, running to fetch the midwife, Mrs. Thornton. She was a kind old woman who'd delivered lots of babies. She'd known right away that little Rudy wouldn't survive. Rudy would have been eleven now, if he'd lived. Bloom's little son, who had died as a baby.

He stared sadly at Milly's postscript. She was growing up — coming out of her shell. He remembered a row with her at a cafe about a bracelet. She'd refused to eat or speak. Twelve and six a week she was earning now. Not much, but she might do worse. He read the letter again, twice.
Well, she was a sensible girl — she knew how to look after herself. She was growing up fast, getting her own life. Nothing to worry about.

He smiled with worried affection at the kitchen window. He remembered catching her on the street once, pinching her cheeks to make them rosy. She'd been a bit pale — too much milk when she was little. He remembered her on a boat trip, not a bit seasick, her pale blue scarf flying in the wind.
He hummed a tune about a girl with dimpled cheeks and curls.
He thought about seaside girls and summer evenings with music. A torn envelope caught his eye. He thought about Boylan — friend of the family, always singing.
He hummed another tune: "Those girls, those lovely seaside girls."
Milly was growing up too. Young kisses — the first ones, now far in the past. And Molly — Mrs. Marion Bloom — lying upstairs, reading, braiding her hair.
A soft wave of sadness and regret flowed through him. Things change. Things happen. He could feel it coming — the future he couldn't prevent. Time moves forward.

Better that Milly was away, down in Mullingar. Keep her busy. She'd wanted a dog for company. Maybe he could visit her there. August bank holiday — only two and six for the return ticket. Six weeks away, though.

The cat, having cleaned all her fur, went back to the meat wrapping, sniffed it, then walked to the door. She looked back at him, meowing. She wanted to go out. Bloom thought: cats wait by doors, knowing they'll open eventually. She was restless. Maybe thunder in the air.
He felt heavy and full. He stood up and loosened his belt. The cat meowed at him.
"Meow!" he said back. "Wait till I'm ready."
It felt like a hot day was coming. He didn't want to bother going upstairs.
He wanted something to read. He hoped nobody would come knocking while he was busy.
In the table drawer he found an old magazine. He tucked it under his arm, went to the door, and opened it. The cat bounded up the stairs — she wanted to curl up on the bed.
He heard Molly's voice from upstairs:
"Come, come, kitty. Come."
He went out through the back door into the garden. He stood listening — quiet from next door. Maybe the neighbor was hanging out laundry. Fine morning.

He looked down at a row of spearmint growing by the garden wall. He thought about making a little garden — growing peas, lettuce, fresh greens. He'd need to dig up the whole place and add compost. The neighbor's hens would provide good fertilizer. Gardens always have their drawbacks, though — bees and flies.

He walked on, thinking about his hat — where had he left it? On the peg? On the floor? He couldn't remember. The hallstand was crowded with umbrellas and Molly's raincoat. He thought about various things — a barber he knew, wondering if he had time for a bath this morning.
That butcher Dlugacz had a deep voice. What was the name on that advertisement? Now, miss. An enthusiastic fellow.

He went to the outdoor toilet at the back of the garden. Better be careful not to get his trousers dirty — he needed them for the funeral. He went in under the low doorway, leaving the door slightly open. He checked through a crack — nobody watching from next door.

He settled down and unfolded his magazine on his knees. No great hurry. He found a short story: "Matcham's Masterstroke" by Mr. Philip Beaufoy. The writer had been paid a guinea a column — about three pounds, thirteen shillings and sixpence.

He read quietly, taking his time. The story wasn't particularly moving, but it was neat and well-crafted. Anybody could get printed these days, during the slow news season. The story began and ended on a positive note. He thought he might try writing something himself someday.

Maybe he and Molly could write something together. He remembered trying to write down the things Molly said while she was getting dressed in the morning. She talked about all sorts of things — nine fifteen: "Did Roberts pay you yet?" Nine twenty: "What did Gretta Conroy wear?" Nine twenty-three: "Why did I buy this comb?"
He remembered a night when a band played at a dance — morning hours, noon, evening, then night. The music marking the passage of time. Molly had been there, getting ready, fixing her hair.
Evening hours, he thought. Girls in grey. Night hours: dark and mysterious. It was a poetical idea — pink, then golden, then grey, then black. Day, then night.
He tore off half the page, finished up, pulled up his trousers, buckled his belt, and came out of the dim little building into the fresh air.
In the bright light, he checked his black trousers carefully — the bottoms, the knees. What time was the funeral? He should check the paper.
A dark sound from high above — the bells of George's church tolling the hour, loud and heavy.
The bells chimed: dong, dong, dong, dong, dong, dong.
Quarter to ten. The deep tone echoed through the air. A third bell followed.
Poor Dignam! Bloom thought. Time to get ready for the funeral.

chapters.title: Episode 5 — Lotus Eaters
paragraphs: Mr. Bloom walked along the quayside by the river, past warehouses and the telegraph office. He turned off the noisy main road into a quieter street. He passed some poor cottages where a boy lounged by a door, smoking, next to a bucket. A smaller girl with rough skin on her forehead watched him blankly. Bloom thought: someone should tell that boy smoking is bad for him. But then again, his life wasn't easy — waiting outside pubs to bring his father home. Bloom crossed Townsend Street, passed a church, and passed the undertaker's shop. The funeral was at eleven. Plenty of time.

In Westland Row he stopped at a tea shop window and read the labels on the packets: choice blend, finest quality, family tea. It was getting warm. He needed to get some tea from Tom Kernan — though you couldn't ask someone about tea at a funeral. While his eyes still read the labels, he quietly took off his hat, smoothed his hair, and slipped his hand inside. His fingers found a small card hidden behind the leather headband and moved it to his waistcoat pocket.

So warm. He smoothed his hair again, put his hat back on, and went back to reading the tea labels. The Far East — it must be lovely there. Gardens of the world, big lazy leaves, flowers everywhere. People in hot countries taking it easy, sleeping half the year away. Too hot to argue. He thought about floating in the Dead Sea — so salty you couldn't sink. He tried to remember the science of it — something about the weight of the body versus the weight of the water. Gravity — thirty-two feet per second per second.

He crossed the road and sauntered toward the post office, rolling his newspaper into a baton and tapping it against his leg. He tried to look casual — just dropping in. He darted a quick look through the post office door. Nobody around. He went in.
He handed a card through the brass window.
"Are there any letters for me?" he asked.

While the postmistress looked through a slot, he gazed at a recruiting poster on the wall — soldiers of all kinds on parade. He held his rolled newspaper under his nose, smelling the fresh ink on the paper. She probably hadn't written back. He'd gone too far last time.
The postmistress handed him back his card with a letter. He thanked her and glanced quickly at the typed envelope.
It was addressed to "Henry Flower, Esq." at this post office. Henry Flower — that was Bloom's secret name, the one he used for writing to a pen pal he'd never met.

He slipped the card and letter into his pocket and looked again at the soldiers on the poster. He found the regiment that Molly's father, old Tweedy, had been in — the Royal Dublin Fusiliers. Red coats. Too flashy, Bloom thought.

He strolled out of the post office and turned right. His hand went into his pocket, and his finger worked under the envelope's flap, tearing it open in small jerks. Something was pinned inside — a photo maybe? Or hair? No.
Oh no — there was M'Coy, someone he didn't really want to talk to right now. He'd have to get rid of him quickly.
"Hello, Bloom. Where are you off to?"
"Hello, M'Coy. Nowhere in particular."
"How's things?"
"Fine. How are you?"
"Just keeping alive," M'Coy said.
M'Coy noticed Bloom's black tie and dark clothes and asked respectfully:
"Is there any... no trouble, I hope? I see you're..."
"Oh, no," Mr. Bloom said. "Poor Dignam, you know. The funeral is today."
"Of course, poor fellow. What time?"
Bloom thought about what was pinned to the letter. Not a photo. Maybe a badge of some kind.
"E... eleven," Mr. Bloom answered.
"I should try to get out there," M'Coy said. "Eleven, is it? I only heard about it last night. Who told me? Holohan. You know Hoppy?"
"I know him."

While M'Coy talked, Mr. Bloom gazed across the road at a fancy horse-drawn carriage outside a hotel. A woman stood waiting while a man searched his pockets for change. She wore a stylish coat with a rolled collar, standing with her hands in her pockets.
"I was with Bob Doran," M'Coy went on, "he's been having a rough time, and Bantam Lyons. Down in Conway's pub, we were."

M'Coy kept talking, but Bloom was watching the elegant woman across the road. She raised a gloved hand to fix her hair. He could see her clearly in the bright light — the shine of her fawn-colored outfit.
"And he said: 'Sad thing about our poor friend Paddy! What Paddy?' I said. 'Poor little Paddy Dignam,' he said."
The woman seemed to be heading for the train station — off to the country, probably. She wore high brown boots with laces. The man was still fiddling with the change.
"'Why?' I said. 'What's wrong with him?'" M'Coy continued.
Bloom watched the elegant woman. Fine stockings.
"Yes," Mr. Bloom said, trying to pay attention.
He shifted slightly to see past M'Coy's head.

"'What's wrong with him?' he said. 'He's dead,' he said. And he got all upset. 'Is it Paddy Dignam?' I said. I couldn't believe it. I'd seen him just last Friday in the pub. 'Yes,' he said. 'He's gone. Died on Monday, poor fellow.'"
Bloom tried to watch the woman getting into the carriage. But just then—
A heavy tram came clanging between them, blocking his view with its loud bell.
He'd lost sight of her. Oh well. These things always happen at the worst moment.
"Yes, yes," Mr. Bloom said with a sigh. "Another one gone."
"One of the best," M'Coy said.
The tram passed. The carriage drove off toward the bridge, the woman's gloved hand on the rail.
"Wife well, I suppose?" M'Coy asked, changing the subject.
"Oh, yes," Mr. Bloom said. "Very well, thanks."
He unrolled his newspaper and read absently:
There was an advertisement: "What is home without Plumtree's Potted Meat? Incomplete. With it, a home of happiness."
"My wife has just got a singing engagement," M'Coy said. "At least, it's not settled yet."
Not this again, Bloom thought. M'Coy always wanted to borrow things.
Mr. Bloom turned his large, calm eyes toward M'Coy.
"My wife too," he said. "She's going to sing at a big event in Belfast on the twenty-fifth."
"Is that so?" M'Coy said. "Glad to hear it. Who's organizing it?"
Bloom thought of Molly upstairs, not even out of bed yet. Her letter. The cat. The torn envelope.
He hummed a bit of "Love's Old Sweet Song" in his head.
"It's a kind of tour," Mr. Bloom said thoughtfully. "There's a committee organizing it. Part shares and part profits."
M'Coy nodded, picking at his upper lip.
"Oh, well," he said. "That's good news."
He moved to leave.
"Well, glad to see you looking well," he said. "See you around."
"Yes," Mr. Bloom said.

"Tell you what," M'Coy said. "Could you put my name down at the funeral? I'd like to go but I might not be able to — there's a drowning case at Sandycove that might come up, and I'd have to go with the coroner. Just put my name down if I'm not there, will you?"
"I'll do that," Mr. Bloom said, moving to get away. "That'll be all right."
"Right," M'Coy said brightly. "Thanks. I'd go if I could. Just C. P. M'Coy will do."
"That will be done," Mr. Bloom answered firmly.
That fellow is always trying something, Bloom thought. He's the type who borrows things and never returns them. Bob Cowley had lent him a suitcase for a concert and never got it back.

Mr. Bloom smiled as he strolled toward Brunswick Street. M'Coy and his wife — Bloom knew her voice wasn't anything special. A thin, freckled soprano. But M'Coy was always comparing their situations — your wife and my wife, as if they were in the same league.
Bloom wondered if M'Coy was following him.

Mr. Bloom stopped at a corner and looked at the colorful advertising posters on the walls. Ginger ale, summer sales. He noticed a theater poster — a play called "Leah" was on tonight, with Mrs. Bandmann Palmer. He'd like to see it. She'd played Hamlet last night — a woman playing a man's part. He thought about his own father, who used to talk about the great actresses he'd seen. His father had once waited all afternoon outside a London theater to get a ticket. The old man would talk about the scene where the blind old father recognizes his son's voice by touch.
"Nathan's voice! His son's voice!" — the line from the play went through Bloom's mind. His father had loved that scene, about a son who left his father to die of grief.
"Every word is so deep, Leopold" — that's what his father used to say.
Poor Papa, Bloom thought. He was glad he hadn't gone into the room to see his father's face at the end. That terrible day. Well, perhaps it was for the best.
Mr. Bloom walked around the corner, past the tired horses of a carriage stand. No use thinking about it. Time for the horses' feedbags too. He wished he hadn't run into M'Coy.

He walked closer and heard the horses crunching their oats, their big, gentle eyes watching him pass. Poor animals. They didn't know or care about anything, with their noses stuck in their feedbags. But they seemed content enough. All their needs taken care of.
He took the letter from his pocket and hid it inside his folded newspaper. He might run into the letter-writer on this street. The side lane would be safer.

He passed a shelter for cab drivers. He thought about their life — out in all weathers, no choice about where they go, no will of their own. He hummed a tune from the opera — the same one Molly was going to sing.
He hummed: "Give me your hand... la la lala la la."

He turned into Cumberland Street and stopped in the shelter of a wall. Nobody around. A timber yard with stacked wood. Ruined buildings. He stepped carefully over an old hopscotch court on the ground. Near the timber yard, a small child sat alone playing marbles. A wise-looking cat watched from a sunny windowsill. Bloom didn't want to disturb them. He remembered playing marbles himself as a boy, at an old woman's school. He opened the letter inside the newspaper.
A flower fell out — yellow, with flattened petals. So she wasn't angry after all. What did the letter say?
It began: "Dear Henry,"

The letter read: "I got your last letter and thank you for it. I'm sorry you didn't like my last letter. Why did you send the stamps? I'm very annoyed with you. I called you a naughty boy because I don't like that other word. Please tell me what it really means. Aren't you happy at home, you poor naughty boy? I wish I could do something for you. Please tell me what you think of me. I think of you often — you have no idea. I've never felt so drawn to someone. Please write me a long letter and tell me everything. If you don't, I'll have to punish you! Oh, how I long to meet you. Don't ignore my request. Then I'll tell you everything. Goodbye, naughty darling. I have such a headache today. Write back soon to your longing —"
"Martha."
"P.S. Do tell me what kind of perfume your wife uses. I want to know."

He carefully took the flower from its pin, smelled it — almost no scent — and placed it in his breast pocket. The language of flowers, he thought. People like using flowers because they're silent — no one can overhear. He read the letter again slowly, murmuring words here and there.

A small pleasure opened his lips. Her letters had changed since the first one. He wondered if she'd written it herself. She was playing a role — a respectable girl, pretending to be annoyed. He wondered what she really wanted.
He fingered the letter in his pocket and pulled out the pin that had held the flower. An ordinary pin. He threw it on the road. Funny how women always seem to have pins everywhere.
He thought of Dublin voices and an old song he'd heard, about a girl who lost the pin holding her clothes together.
The song went: "Oh, Mary lost her pin... she didn't know what to do to keep it up, to keep it up."
Martha had a headache, she said. He thought about her sitting all day typing, straining her eyes. And what was that about perfume?
The song echoed in his head: "To keep it up."
He thought about two women from the Bible — Martha and Mary. Martha was the busy one, always working; Mary was the quiet one, sitting and listening. Mysterious.
"To keep it up," the song went again in his head.

He imagined a nice, quiet evening. No more wandering about. Just sitting peacefully somewhere. Telling stories about places you'd been, strange customs from other lands. Quiet dusk. Someone listening with big, dark, soft eyes. He'd tell her more and more. Everything. Then a sigh. Silence. Long, long rest.
Walking under the railway bridge, he took out the envelope, tore it into small pieces, and scattered them in the air. The white shreds fluttered and sank in the damp air, then disappeared.

Henry Flower. You could tear up anything, he thought. A hundred-pound check would tear just the same — just a bit of paper. He thought about how much money the Guinness family had made from porter — millions of pounds. He tried to work out the math: twopence a pint, fourpence a quart...
What was he saying — barrels? He meant gallons. About a million barrels, give or take.
A train clattered heavily overhead, coach after coach. He imagined barrels of porter rolling around in his head, sloshing and churning, flooding out everywhere in a great lazy river.

He reached the open back door of All Hallows Church. Stepping into the porch, he took off his hat and tucked the card back behind the leather headband. He thought: I should have tried to get a free train pass from M'Coy to visit Milly in Mullingar.

He noticed a sign about a sermon on the church door. He thought about religion — how the Catholics, Protestants, and Buddhists all seemed to have their own way of doing things. Clever, the way the Catholic Church worked — priests trained for years, knowing exactly what to say and do.
The cold, stony smell of the church called to him. He stepped down the worn stone steps, pushed through the swing door, and entered quietly from the back.

A service was going on — some kind of group prayer. Bloom watched as the priest moved along the altar rail, giving communion to a row of women who knelt with their heads bowed. One by one, he placed the small white wafer on each tongue. Bloom thought about the whole ritual: Latin words, the mystery of it. He found it strange and impressive at the same time — this idea of bread becoming something sacred.

He moved aside as the women passed back down the aisle, heads still bowed, finding their seats. Bloom sat in a corner of a bench, holding his hat and newspaper. He watched the people around him, heads bowed, waiting for the communion wafer to dissolve. It was like a kind of family gathering, he thought — everyone together, sharing something. It must make them feel less alone. He thought about faith and miracles and all the things people believe in.

He watched the priest put away the communion cup and kneel briefly. He noticed the priest's big grey boot sole showing under his robes. He saw the letters on the priest's back: I.H.S. — which Molly once told him stood for "I Have Suffered."

Bloom thought about Martha's letter again: "Meet me one Sunday after prayers. Don't deny my request." He imagined her showing up at a church with a veil and a black bag. All sorts of people come to church — saints and sinners alike.

The priest rinsed out the chalice and drank the last of the wine. Bloom thought about how the ceremony used wine instead of ordinary drinks — more elegant than beer. The priest didn't share the wine with the congregation. Probably wise, Bloom thought — otherwise you'd have people coming in just for a free drink.

Mr. Bloom looked toward the choir. No music today. Pity. He thought about Molly's beautiful singing voice. She'd once sung a song from Rossini so beautifully that everyone stopped to listen. He could feel the thrill of it in the air.
The Latin words of the song echoed in his mind: "Who is the man..."

He thought about old church music — Mozart, Palestrina. Those old popes had loved music and art. Monks would chant during the day and then brew their own drinks in the evening — Benedictine, Chartreuse. The monasteries had a good life going, in some ways.

He saw the priest come down from the altar, bless everyone, and turn to face the congregation. Everyone crossed themselves and stood up. Mr. Bloom stood up too, looking around over the tops of people's hats. Then everyone knelt again, and the priest read a prayer from a card, with the altar boy answering in Latin:
"O God, our refuge and our strength..."

Mr. Bloom leaned forward to catch the words. This part was in English. He thought about the whole system of the Catholic Church — confession, penance, forgiveness. It was a powerful organization, running like clockwork. People would go in and whisper their secrets to a priest in a dark box. Then they'd come out feeling lighter. The Church had it all figured out — the doctors of theology had mapped out the whole thing centuries ago.
The priest prayed:
"Blessed Michael, archangel, defend us in the hour of conflict. Be our protection against wickedness. And do thou, O prince of heaven, by the power of God, thrust Satan down to hell."
The priest and the altar boy stood up and walked off. The service was over. The women stayed behind for their own private prayers.
Time to go, Bloom thought. Better leave before someone came around with the collection plate.

He stood up and noticed two of his waistcoat buttons had been open the whole time. He buttoned them discreetly as he walked down the aisle and out through the main door into the daylight. He paused by the holy water font, watching two people dip their hands in. Trams passed on the street. He checked the time — quarter past ten. Still time. He should get that skin lotion made up at the chemist. Sweny's, in Lincoln Place — chemist shops rarely move locations. He'd visit the old Huguenot graveyard nearby someday.
He walked south along Westland Row. But the prescription was in his other trousers. And he'd forgotten the door key too. What a bother, this funeral business. Well, poor Dignam, it wasn't his fault.

The chemist turned back through his prescription book, page after page. He was a shriveled old man with a sandy smell about him. Bloom thought about how working with drugs all day must age you. The shelves were full of bottles and potions — ointments, herbs, disinfectants. All those Latin names on the jars. The smell alone was almost enough to cure you.
"About a fortnight ago, sir?" the chemist asked.
"Yes," Mr. Bloom said.
He waited at the counter, breathing in the sharp smell of chemicals, the dusty smell of sponges.
"Sweet almond oil and tincture of benzoin," Mr. Bloom said, "and then orange-flower water..."
The lotion certainly did make Molly's skin lovely and white.
"And white wax too," he said.

He thought about Molly's dark eyes. She'd look at him from the bed, the sheet pulled up to her eyes. Old homemade beauty recipes were often the best — strawberries for the teeth, oatmeal in buttermilk for the skin. And you'd want a nice perfume too. That orange-flower water smelled so fresh. The soaps here smelled nice too. He should get a bath around the corner — the Turkish baths. A good soak would make him feel fresh for the whole day, though a funeral would be rather gloomy regardless.
"Yes, sir," the chemist said. "That was two and nine. Have you brought a bottle?"
"No," Mr. Bloom said. "Make it up, please. I'll call back later today. And I'll take one of these soaps. How much are they?"
"Fourpence, sir."
Mr. Bloom lifted a bar of soap to his nose. Sweet, lemony wax.
"I'll take this one," he said. "That makes three and a penny altogether."
"Yes, sir," the chemist said. "You can pay for everything when you come back."
"Good," Mr. Bloom said.
He strolled out of the shop with the newspaper under his arm and the neatly wrapped soap in his left hand.
Suddenly someone grabbed his arm — it was Bantam Lyons.
"Hello, Bloom. What's the latest news? Is that today's paper? Let me see it a minute."
The man had shaved off his mustache again, Bloom noticed. Trying to look younger. He did look younger — younger than Bloom, actually.
Bantam Lyons's yellowish fingers unrolled the newspaper. The man could use a wash himself, Bloom thought. Dandruff on his shoulders.
"I want to check on that French horse running today," Bantam Lyons said. "Where is it?"
He rustled through the pages, chin pressing on his high collar. He was looking for the horse racing results. Better just give him the paper and be done with it, Bloom thought.
"You can keep it," Mr. Bloom said.
"Wait — Ascot. Gold Cup. Half a second. Maximum the Second..." Bantam Lyons muttered.
"I was just going to throw it away," Mr. Bloom said.
Bantam Lyons suddenly looked up with a sharp, suspicious expression.
"What's that?" he said quickly.
"I said you can keep it," Mr. Bloom answered. "I was about to throw it away."
Bantam Lyons hesitated, looking at Bloom strangely. Then he shoved the newspaper back into Bloom's hands.

"I'll risk it," he said. "Here, thanks." And he ran off toward the corner. Bloom didn't understand what that was about. (Bantam Lyons thought Bloom was giving him a horse racing tip — "Throwaway" was actually the name of a horse in the race.)
He sped off. Good riddance, Bloom thought.
Mr. Bloom folded the newspaper neatly and tucked the soap into it, smiling. Silly man. Everyone seemed to be gambling these days — even delivery boys stealing money to place bets.

He walked cheerfully toward the Turkish baths. The building looked like a little mosque, with its red bricks and pointed towers. He noticed a poster for college sports — a cyclist bent double, not a very good advertisement. If they'd made it round like a wheel, it would look better.
There was Hornblower standing at the college gate. Bloom nodded to him — worth staying on good terms, in case he wanted to drop in someday.
Beautiful weather, really. Perfect for cricket. You could sit around all day under parasols. It was a heat wave, but it wouldn't last. Nothing does. Always passing, the stream of life.
He looked forward to a bath — clean warm water, cool enamel tub, gentle steam.

He imagined himself lying in the warm water, his pale body floating, surrounded by the scent of lemon soap, buoyed up gently. He pictured himself relaxed and weightless, like a flower floating in a stream.

chapters.title: Episode 6 — Hades
paragraphs: Martin Cunningham poked his top-hatted head into the creaking funeral carriage and sat down neatly. Mr. Power stepped in after him, ducking his tall frame.
"Come on, Simon."
"After you," Mr. Bloom said politely.
Mr. Dedalus — Stephen's father — covered his head quickly and climbed in, saying:
"Yes, yes."
"Are we all here?" Martin Cunningham asked. "Come along, Bloom."

Mr. Bloom got in and sat in the last empty seat. He pulled the door shut, slamming it twice until it closed tight. He put his arm through the strap and looked out the window at the houses along the avenue, where the window blinds were lowered out of respect for the dead man. He noticed an old woman peeking out through one blind, pressing her nose against the glass. People always took an extraordinary interest in death. He thought about all the things that happen when someone dies — the washing, the dressing, the laying out of the body.
They all waited in silence. Bloom felt something hard under him — oh, it was the bar of soap in his back pocket. He'd need to move it when he got a chance.

They waited. Then they heard wheels turning ahead of them, then horses' hooves. The carriage jerked and began to move, creaking and swaying. Other carriages followed behind. They passed the house of the dead man — number nine — with its door slightly open and a black ribbon on the knocker. They moved at walking pace.
They waited, knees bumping, until the carriage turned onto the tram tracks. The wheels rattled over the cobblestones and the glass windows shook in their frames.
"Which way is he taking us?" Mr. Power asked, looking out both windows.
"Irishtown. Ringsend. Brunswick Street," Martin Cunningham said.
Mr. Dedalus nodded, looking out.
"That's a fine old custom," he said, noticing people on the street taking off their hats as the funeral passed. "I'm glad to see it hasn't died out."

They all watched through the windows as people along the road lifted their hats and caps in respect. The carriage turned off the tram track onto a smoother road. Mr. Bloom spotted a thin young man dressed in black, wearing a wide hat.
"There's a friend of yours going by, Dedalus," he said.
"Who's that?"
"Your son and heir." Bloom meant Stephen Dedalus.
"Where is he?" Mr. Dedalus asked, craning his neck across the carriage.
The carriage lurched around a corner past some run-down houses, then swerved back to the tram track, rolling noisily along. Mr. Dedalus fell back in his seat, saying:
"Was that Mulligan rascal with him?"
"No," Mr. Bloom said. "He was alone."
"Probably down visiting his Aunt Sally," Mr. Dedalus said scornfully, insulting his wife's relatives.
Mr. Bloom smiled joylessly as they passed along Ringsend Road, past a bottle factory and a bridge.
Bloom thought about Richie Goulding, one of those relatives — a man who thought he was grand but was going downhill with back problems. His wife was always rubbing ointment on his back.
"Stephen is mixed up with a bad crowd," Mr. Dedalus snarled. "That Mulligan is a terrible character. I'll write a letter to his mother one of these days that will open her eyes wide."
He shouted over the noise of the wheels:
"I won't have that rascal ruin my son!"

Mr. Bloom glanced from Mr. Dedalus's angry mustache to the mild faces of Mr. Power and Martin Cunningham. Mr. Dedalus was a noisy, stubborn man, but he loved his son fiercely. Bloom thought: he's right to feel that way. It's something special, having a son to watch grow up. If little Rudy had lived... Bloom's baby son had died long ago, and the sadness never fully went away.
Bloom thought about how Molly had been expecting Rudy, and how he might have helped the boy grow up, learn things, become independent.
"Are we late?" Mr. Power asked.
"Ten minutes," Martin Cunningham said, checking his watch.
Bloom thought about his daughter Milly — she was so like her mother Molly. Growing up fast. Soon she'd be a woman. Her letter from Mullingar. The young student she'd mentioned. Life goes on.
The carriage tilted as they went around a bend, and all four men swayed together.
"Corny might have given us a more comfortable carriage," Mr. Power said.
"He might," Mr. Dedalus agreed, making a joke about why Corny Kelleher might not have.
He closed one eye. Martin Cunningham began to brush crumbs from the leather seat beneath him.
"What is this?" he said. "Crumbs?"
"Someone seems to have had a picnic in here," Mr. Power said.
They all raised themselves and looked disapprovingly at the old, worn leather seats. Mr. Dedalus wrinkled his nose, frowned, and said:
"Unless I'm very much mistaken... What do you think, Martin?"
"Same thought crossed my mind," Martin Cunningham said. The seat smelled bad.
Mr. Bloom settled back down. He was glad he'd taken a bath that morning. His feet felt clean, at least. Though he wished Mrs. Fleming had done a better job darning his socks.
Mr. Dedalus sighed.
"After all," he said, "it's the most natural thing in the world." He meant that even death is natural.
"Did Tom Kernan show up?" Martin Cunningham asked, stroking his beard.
"Yes," Mr. Bloom answered. "He's behind us with Ned Lambert and Hynes."
"And Corny Kelleher himself?" Mr. Power asked.
"He'll be at the cemetery," Martin Cunningham said.
"I met M'Coy this morning," Mr. Bloom said. "He said he'd try to come."
The carriage stopped suddenly.
"What's wrong?"
"We've stopped."
"Where are we?"
Mr. Bloom stuck his head out the window.
"The Grand Canal," he said.

Bloom thought about the gas works nearby. People said the gas fumes could cure whooping cough. He was glad Milly had never caught it — poor children doubled up with terrible coughing fits. He thought about his father's old dog, Athos. His father's dying wish had been: "Be good to Athos, Leopold." The dog had pined away after his master died.
A raindrop splashed on Bloom's hat. He drew back and saw a quick spray of dots on the grey pavement. Curious — like water through a strainer.
"The weather is changing," he said quietly.
"Pity it didn't stay fine," Martin Cunningham said.
"The country needs the rain," Mr. Power said. "But look — the sun is coming out again."
Mr. Dedalus peered through his glasses at the cloudy sun and silently cursed the sky.
"The weather is as unpredictable as a baby," he said.
"We're off again."
The carriage wheels turned stiffly and they swayed gently. Martin Cunningham twirled his beard.
"Tom Kernan was brilliant last night," he said. "And Paddy Leonard making fun of him to his face."
"Oh, tell Simon about it," Mr. Power said eagerly. "Wait till you hear his impression of Ben Dollard singing 'The Croppy Boy.'"
"It was marvelous," Martin Cunningham said grandly, imitating Kernan's voice: "'His singing of that simple ballad is the most powerful performance I have ever heard in my whole experience.'"
"'Powerful,'" Mr. Power said, laughing. "He's completely obsessed with that word."
"Did you read Dan Dawson's speech?" Martin Cunningham asked.
"I didn't," Mr. Dedalus said. "Where is it?"
"In the paper this morning."
Mr. Bloom took the newspaper from his inside pocket. He remembered: I need to change that library book for Molly.
"No, no," Mr. Dedalus said quickly. "Later, please."

Mr. Bloom glanced down the edge of the paper, scanning the death notices: Callan, Coleman, Dignam, Fawcett... He read the little memorial messages: "Sadly missed... To the great grief of his family... Aged 88 after a long illness."
There was a poem in the death notices: "It is now a month since dear Henry departed to his home above in the sky, while his family weeps and mourns, hoping someday to meet him on high."
Bloom wondered: did I tear up that envelope? Yes. And where did I put Martha's letter? He patted his waistcoat pocket. Still there. Safe.
They passed the school, the timber yard, the cab stand. The carriage horses nodded their heads sleepily. Two of them, full as ticks. The cab drivers raised their hats as the funeral passed.

A traffic controller straightened up by a tram post outside Bloom's window. Bloom thought: couldn't they invent something automatic instead? But then that fellow would lose his job. Though someone else would get a job making the new invention.
They passed a concert hall — nothing on there. A man in a pale suit wore a black armband. Not much grief on display there.

They went past Saint Mark's church, under the railway bridge, past the Queen's Theatre, in silence. Bloom noticed theater posters — the play "Leah" was on tonight. He wondered if he could go see it. He thought about what shows were coming next week.
Bloom thought: Boylan is coming to see Molly this afternoon. Her songs.
They passed a memorial fountain. "Who was that for?" Bloom wondered.
"How do you do?" Martin Cunningham said, raising his hand in greeting to someone on the street.
"He doesn't see us," Mr. Power said. "Yes, he does. How do you do?"
"Who?" Mr. Dedalus asked.
"Blazes Boylan," Mr. Power said. Boylan was the man organizing Molly's concert tour.
Just at that moment I was thinking about him, Bloom thought uncomfortably.
Mr. Dedalus leaned across to wave. From a doorway, the white flash of a straw hat waved back. Boylan — a well-dressed figure — walked on.

Mr. Bloom looked down at his own fingernails, pretending to examine them. He thought about Boylan and tried not to feel bothered. He checked his nails — well trimmed, at least. He thought about Molly and felt a twinge of sadness.
He clasped his hands between his knees and looked around at his companions' faces.
Mr. Power asked:
"How is the concert tour going, Bloom?"
"Oh, very well," Mr. Bloom said. "I hear good reports. It's a good idea, you see..."
"Are you going yourself?"
"Well, no," Mr. Bloom said. "Actually, I have to go down to County Clare on some private business. The idea is to tour the main towns. What you lose in one place, you make up in the next."
"Quite so," Martin Cunningham said.
"Do you have good performers?" someone asked.
"Oh yes," Mr. Bloom said. "All the best. J. C. Doyle and John MacCormack, I hope."
"And Madame Bloom," Mr. Power said with a smile. "Last but not least."
Mr. Bloom unclasped and clasped his hands politely. They passed a statue with flowers laid at its base. The carriage wheels turned noiselessly past another statue.
An old man on the curb held out his goods for sale, his mouth opening and closing:
"Four bootlaces for a penny!"
Bloom thought about the old man — once a respectable lawyer, now selling shoelaces on the street. A terrible fall in life.
He thought about Molly, now probably awake, doing her hair, humming a tune from the opera. Her beautiful singing voice — a rich, warm tone like a songbird.

Bloom glanced at Mr. Power's pleasant face. Grey around the ears. He thought about Power's complicated personal life — people said he kept a lady friend, which wasn't fair to his wife. But who really knew the truth?
They passed under the huge statue of Daniel O'Connell, the great Irish leader.
Martin Cunningham nudged Mr. Power.
"One of the tribe of Reuben," he said, pointing to someone on the street. It was a mean comment about a Jewish moneylender.
A tall, dark-bearded figure, bent on a walking stick, came around a corner, showing them his curved back.
"In all his glory," Mr. Power said sarcastically.
Mr. Dedalus looked after the stumping figure and said mildly:
"The devil take him!"
Mr. Power collapsed in laughter, hiding his face from the window as they passed a statue.
"We've all been to the moneylender at some point," Martin Cunningham said broadly.
He caught Mr. Bloom's eye. He stroked his beard and added kindly:
"Well, nearly all of us." Martin was being sensitive — he knew Bloom was Jewish, or at least had a Jewish father.
Mr. Bloom began speaking eagerly to change the subject:
"There's a really good story going around about Reuben J. and his son."
"About the boatman?" Mr. Power asked.
"Yes. Isn't it good?"
"What is it?" Mr. Dedalus asked. "I haven't heard it."
"There was a girl involved," Mr. Bloom began, "and the father decided to send the son away to the Isle of Man, out of trouble. But when they were both..."
"What?" Mr. Dedalus asked. "That useless boy of his?"
"Yes," Mr. Bloom said. "They were both on the way to the boat, and the son tried to..."
"Good riddance!" Mr. Dedalus cried. "I wish he had!"
Mr. Power laughed behind his hand.
"No," Mr. Bloom said, "the son himself..."
Martin Cunningham cut in to tell the story properly:
"Reuben J. and his son were walking along the quay to catch the boat, and the young man suddenly broke free and jumped over the wall into the River Liffey."
"Good heavens!" Mr. Dedalus exclaimed. "Is he dead?"

"Dead? Not at all!" Martin Cunningham cried. "A boatman grabbed a pole and fished him out by the seat of his trousers. He was hauled up on the quay, more dead than alive. Half the town was there to watch."
"Yes," Mr. Bloom said. "But the funny part is..."
"And Reuben J.," Martin Cunningham said, "gave the boatman a two-shilling coin for saving his son's life."
A stifled laugh came from behind Mr. Power's hand.
"Oh, he did," Martin Cunningham confirmed. "Like a hero. A silver two-shilling piece. For saving a life!"
"Isn't that a good story?" Mr. Bloom said eagerly.
"One shilling and eightpence too much," Mr. Dedalus said dryly — meaning the life wasn't even worth twopence.
Mr. Power's choked laughter burst out in the carriage.
They passed Nelson's Pillar, a tall column in the center of Dublin.
"Eight plums a penny!" called a street seller. "Eight for a penny!"
"We'd better look a bit more serious now," Martin Cunningham said.
Mr. Dedalus sighed.
"Ah, poor little Paddy wouldn't have minded us having a laugh," he said. "He told plenty of good jokes himself."
"God forgive me," Mr. Power said, wiping his wet eyes. "Poor Paddy! I never thought when I saw him just last week, healthy as ever, that I'd be following his coffin like this. He's gone from us."
"As decent a little man as ever wore a hat," Mr. Dedalus said. "He went so suddenly."
"Heart failure," Martin Cunningham said.
He tapped his own chest sadly.
Bloom thought: poor Dignam had been a heavy drinker. A red face from too much drink. He'd spent a lot of money making that face redder.
Mr. Power gazed sadly at the passing houses.
"He had a sudden death, poor fellow," he said.
"The best kind of death," Mr. Bloom said.
They all turned to stare at him.
"No suffering," he explained. "A moment and it's all over. Like dying in your sleep."
No one said anything.
Bloom looked out at the dull side of the street — offices, a temperance hotel, a railway guide shop. He thought about the politician Parnell and his broken heart.
White horses with white feathered plumes came galloping around a corner, pulling a tiny coffin. A child's funeral, rushing past.
"Sad," Martin Cunningham said. "A child."

Bloom thought of his own lost son, little Rudy, who had died as a baby. A tiny wrinkled face. A small body in a small white coffin. He remembered how the burial society pays for such things — a penny a week.
"Poor little thing," Mr. Dedalus said. "It's better off out of this world."
The carriage climbed a hill more slowly. Bloom thought of an old rhyme about a pauper's funeral: "Rattle his bones over the stones, only a pauper, nobody owns."
"In the midst of life..." Martin Cunningham began the old saying about death.
"But the worst of all," Mr. Power said, "is when a man takes his own life."
Martin Cunningham quickly checked his watch, coughed, and put it back.
"The greatest disgrace for a family," Mr. Power added.
"Temporary madness, of course," Martin Cunningham said firmly. "We must be understanding about it."
"They say a man who does that is a coward," Mr. Dedalus said.
"It's not for us to judge," Martin Cunningham said.

Mr. Bloom was about to speak but closed his mouth. He looked at Martin Cunningham — a big man with kind, intelligent eyes. Like Shakespeare's face. Always a good word to say. Bloom knew that Martin understood, because Bloom's own father had taken his own life — poisoned himself in a hotel room. Bloom thought about Martin's own difficulties too — his wife was a terrible drinker who pawned the furniture every Saturday.
A song floated through Bloom's mind — something about a geisha, which his thoughts connected to Martin's wife causing scenes.
Martin looked away. He knows about my father, Bloom thought.

Bloom remembered the afternoon of the official investigation into his father's death. The red-labeled bottle on the table. The stuffy hotel room. The servant who'd found the body. Yellow streaks on his father's face. The official verdict: accidental overdose. And the letter — "For my son Leopold."
No more pain. No more waking up. Nobody owns.
The carriage rattled swiftly along the next street.
"We're moving fast," Martin Cunningham said.
"I hope the driver doesn't tip us over," Mr. Power said.
"I hope not," Martin Cunningham said. "There's going to be a great car race in Germany tomorrow. The Gordon Bennett race."
"By Jove, that will be worth watching," Mr. Dedalus said.

As they turned into Berkeley Street, a street organ played a lively tune behind them. Bloom recognized the song. They passed a hospital — the Mater Misericordiae. Near his own house on Eccles Street. He thought about hospitals and dying and birth — one hospital for the dying, another for births, right across from each other.
The carriage galloped around a corner and stopped.
"What's wrong now?"
A herd of cattle was crossing the road — branded animals with swishing tails, moving slowly on soft hooves. Frightened sheep ran bleating through and around them.
"Emigrants," Mr. Power said — meaning the cattle were being shipped to England.
"Huuuh!" the cattle driver shouted, cracking his switch. "Out of the way!"

Bloom thought: Thursday, of course. Tomorrow is slaughter day. These animals would be shipped to Liverpool for English roast beef. He thought about the meat trade and all the by-products — hide, hair, horns — used for soap and other things.
The carriage pushed through the herd.
"I don't understand why they don't run a tram line from the park gate to the docks," Mr. Bloom said. "All these animals could be moved by train."
"Exactly," Martin Cunningham agreed. "Instead of blocking up the streets."

"Yes," Mr. Bloom said, "and another thing I've often thought — they should have special funeral trams, like they have in Milan. Run a line right to the cemetery gates. A funeral tram with a hearse car attached. Don't you see what I mean?"
"Oh, that's ridiculous!" Mr. Dedalus said. "What next — a dining car?"
"That would put poor Corny out of business," Mr. Power added.
"Why?" Mr. Bloom asked, turning to Mr. Dedalus. "Wouldn't it be more dignified than galloping through the streets?"
"Well, there's something in that," Mr. Dedalus admitted.
"And," Martin Cunningham said, "we wouldn't have accidents like the time the hearse tipped over at Dunphy's corner and the coffin slid onto the road."
"That was terrible," Mr. Power said, looking shocked. "The coffin fell right into the road!"
"First around Dunphy's corner," Mr. Dedalus said with dark humor. "Like a racing car."
"Thank the Lord that went okay," Martin Cunningham said.
Bloom imagined poor Dignam tumbling out of a broken coffin onto the road. He thought about what happens to a body after death — how it changes. Not pleasant to think about.
"Dunphy's," Mr. Power announced as they turned right.
Dunphy's corner — funeral carriages were lined up outside a pub. Bloom thought: we'll probably stop here on the way back for a drink in Dignam's memory.
Bloom thought about whether a dead body could still bleed if cut. He supposed the blood would stop circulating. But some might still ooze out.
In silence they drove along the road. An empty hearse trotted past, coming back from the cemetery — it seemed almost relieved to be empty.
They crossed a bridge over the Royal Canal.
Water rushed loudly through the canal locks. A man stood on a barge loaded with peat, drifting slowly. A horse waited on the towpath.

They watched him pass. Bloom thought about the waterway stretching all across Ireland — he could take a canal trip to see Milly in Mullingar. Or cycle there. He imagined dropping down through lock after lock all the way to Dublin, carrying peat from the bogs. The man on the barge raised his straw hat in salute as the funeral passed.
They drove on. Nearly there now.
"I wonder how our friend Fogarty is doing," Mr. Power said.
"Better ask Tom Kernan," Mr. Dedalus said.
"How so?" Martin Cunningham asked. He made a joke about Fogarty being left behind.
"Though lost to sight, to memory dear," Mr. Dedalus said — an old saying about people who are gone.
The carriage turned left toward Finglas Road.

They passed a stone-cutter's yard on the right. The last stretch now. Bloom could see the cemetery — white shapes appearing on the narrow strip of land: stone angels, figures kneeling in grief, hands reaching upward. Headstones and monuments. "The Best Obtainable — Thos. H. Dennany, Monumental Builder and Sculptor."
They passed it.
An old tramp sat on the curb outside the cemetery worker's house, emptying dirt from his enormous, dusty boot. After life's journey, Bloom thought.
They passed gloomy gardens and dark houses, one after another.
Mr. Power pointed.
"That's where the Childs murder happened," he said. "The last house."
"So it is," Mr. Dedalus said. "A terrible case. He was accused of murdering his brother. But the lawyer got him off."
"The prosecution had no real evidence," Mr. Power said.
"Only circumstantial," Martin Cunningham added. "The legal principle is: better for ninety-nine guilty people to go free than for one innocent person to be wrongly convicted."
They all looked at the dark, shuttered house — empty, abandoned, the garden overgrown. Murder's ground. It looked like a place gone to ruin.
Bloom thought about Milly — he should probably write and tell her he was coming to visit, rather than showing up by surprise. She was fifteen now.

The high railings of the cemetery rippled past their windows. Dark poplar trees, white stone shapes. More and more white forms appeared among the trees — headstones and monuments and angels, streaming past in silence.

The carriage wheel scraped against the curb and stopped. Martin Cunningham reached back, wrenched the handle, and shoved the door open with his knee. He stepped out. Mr. Power and Mr. Dedalus followed.
Time to move that soap. Mr. Bloom quickly shifted the bar of soap from his back pocket to his handkerchief pocket. He stepped out of the carriage, still holding his newspaper.

It was a modest funeral — just the hearse and three carriages. Beyond the last carriage, a street seller stood with his cart of cakes and fruit. Bloom noticed the funeral cakes — simnel cakes stuck together. Who ate those things?
He followed his companions. Mr. Kernan and Ned Lambert followed behind, with Hynes after them. Corny Kelleher stood by the open hearse and took out two wreaths, handing one to Dignam's eldest boy.
Bloom wondered: where did that child's funeral go? The small one they'd seen earlier.
A team of heavy horses plodded past from Finglas, pulling a wagon with a huge granite block. The driver saluted the funeral.

The coffin was already there ahead of them. Bloom watched the horse that had pulled the hearse — it looked around at the coffin with a dull eye, the collar tight on its neck. Bloom thought: do these horses know what they carry every day? There must be twenty or thirty funerals a day. And that's just this cemetery.
Some mourners were already coming out through the gates — a hard-faced woman and a girl whose face was stained with tears, holding the woman's arm, looking up for permission to cry.

The undertaker's men shouldered the coffin and carried it through the gates. Bloom followed, thinking: dead weight. He felt heavier himself after his bath this morning. The family and friends walked behind the coffin. Corny Kelleher and the boy followed with their wreaths.
Everyone walked together.
Martin Cunningham whispered to Mr. Power:
"I was in agony when you were talking about suicide in front of Bloom."
"What?" Mr. Power whispered. "Why?"
"His father poisoned himself," Martin Cunningham whispered. "Had a hotel in Ennis. Remember Bloom said he had to go to County Clare? It's the anniversary."
"Oh no!" Mr. Power whispered. "I had no idea."
He glanced behind at Bloom, who was walking with dark, thoughtful eyes.
"Was Dignam insured?" Mr. Bloom asked the men near him.
"I believe so," Mr. Kernan answered. "But the policy was heavily in debt. Martin is trying to get one of the children into a school."
"How many children did he leave?"
"Five. Ned Lambert is trying to get one of the girls a job."
"A sad case," Mr. Bloom said gently. "Five young children."
"A great blow for the poor wife," Mr. Kernan added.
"Indeed," Mr. Bloom agreed.
Death has the last laugh, Bloom thought.

He looked down at his polished black boots. Dignam's wife had outlived her husband. One always outlives the other. He thought about Queen Victoria, who had mourned her husband Albert for decades, but in the end had started wearing flowers in her hat again. Life goes on. But for the dead — no more warm beds.
"How are you, Simon?" Ned Lambert said softly, shaking hands. "Haven't seen you in ages."
"Never better," Mr. Dedalus said. "How are things in Cork?"
"I was down there for the races at Easter," Ned Lambert said. "Same old same old. Stayed with Dick Tivy."
"And how is Dick?"
"Not a hair on his head," Ned Lambert answered.
"Good Lord!" Mr. Dedalus said. "Dick Tivy bald?"
"Martin is going to take up a collection for the Dignam children," Ned Lambert said. "A few shillings each. Just to keep them going until the insurance comes through."
"Yes, yes," Mr. Dedalus said. "Is that the eldest boy up front?"
"Yes," Ned Lambert said. "With the wife's brother. John Henry Menton is behind — he put down a pound."
"I bet he did," Mr. Dedalus said. "I used to tell Paddy he should have stayed in Menton's office. John Henry isn't the worst person in the world."
"How did Paddy lose that job?" Ned Lambert asked. "Drinking, was it?"
"Many a good man's weakness," Mr. Dedalus said with a sigh.

They stopped at the door of the cemetery chapel. Mr. Bloom stood behind Dignam's young son, looking at the boy's neatly combed hair and thin neck inside his brand-new collar. Poor boy! Had he been there when his father died? Bloom thought about last moments — how dying people sometimes recognize someone one final time. The undertaker's men carried the coffin into the chapel.

After a moment, Bloom followed the others inside, blinking in the dim light. The coffin lay on a stand before the altar, with four tall yellow candles at its corners. Corny Kelleher placed a wreath at each front corner and motioned for the boy to kneel. The mourners knelt in various spots. Mr. Bloom stood near the back, carefully put his newspaper on the floor, and knelt on it. He held his black hat on his left knee and bowed his head.
A server came out carrying a brass bucket, followed by the priest in white robes, holding a little book against his round belly.
They stopped by the coffin and the priest began to read in a croaking voice.
Bloom thought about the priest — Father Coffey, a name that sounded like "coffin." He was a big, stocky man who seemed to boss everyone around.
The priest read the Latin prayer: "Do not judge your servant harshly, O Lord."

Bloom thought: the Latin makes people feel the ceremony is more important. This was a cold, gloomy place to work. The priest must sit here all morning waiting for the next funeral. Bloom's knees were getting sore.
His kneecap ached. He shifted. That was better.

The priest took a stick with a knob at the end from the boy's bucket and sprinkled holy water over the coffin. He walked to the other end and sprinkled it again. Then he put it back. It was all written down — he had to do exactly these steps.
The priest recited more Latin: "And lead us not into temptation."
The young server piped the responses in a high voice.

Bloom thought: that must be holy water. The priest must get tired of this job — shaking that sprinkler over every coffin, day after day. Middle-aged men, old women, children, young girls. Every single day he says the same prayers and sprinkles the same water. Today it's Dignam's turn.
The priest read: "Into paradise."
He says that about everyone, Bloom thought. That they're going to paradise. A tiresome job. But he has to say something.

The priest closed his book and left, followed by the server. Corny Kelleher opened the side doors and the gravediggers came in, lifted the coffin again, carried it out, and loaded it onto their cart. Corny Kelleher gave one wreath to the boy and one to the brother-in-law. Everyone followed them out into the mild, grey air. Mr. Bloom came last, folding his newspaper back into his pocket. The coffin cart wheeled off to the left, its metal wheels grinding on the gravel. The mourners followed along a lane between rows of graves.
A tune started in Bloom's head — he told himself not to hum at a funeral.
"The O'Connell circle," Mr. Dedalus said, pointing out a large monument.
Mr. Power looked up at the tall cone-shaped memorial.
"The great Daniel O'Connell is buried here," he said, "in the middle of his people. But his heart is buried in Rome. How many broken hearts are buried here, Simon!"
"Her grave is over there," Mr. Dedalus said, meaning his dead wife's grave. "I'll be stretched beside her soon enough. Let God take me whenever He wants."
He broke down and began to cry quietly, stumbling a little. Mr. Power took his arm.
"She's better where she is," he said kindly.
"I suppose so," Mr. Dedalus said weakly. "I suppose she is in heaven, if there is a heaven."
Corny Kelleher stepped aside to let the mourners pass.
"Sad occasions," Mr. Kernan began politely.
Mr. Bloom closed his eyes and bowed his head twice in silent sympathy.
"The others are putting their hats back on," Mr. Kernan said. "I suppose we can too. We're at the back. This cemetery is cold and damp."
They put their hats on.
"The priest read the service rather quickly, don't you think?" Mr. Kernan said disapprovingly.
Mr. Bloom nodded, looking into Kernan's quick, searching eyes. He thought: Kernan might be a Freemason — not sure. We're walking together at the back. Both outsiders in a way.
Mr. Kernan added:
"The Protestant service used in Mount Jerome cemetery is simpler and more impressive, I must say."
Mr. Bloom agreed cautiously. The language was certainly different — English instead of Latin.
Mr. Kernan said solemnly:
"'I am the resurrection and the life.' Now that is a line that touches a man's deepest feelings."
"It does," Mr. Bloom agreed.

But Bloom thought privately: your heart may be touched, but what about the man lying six feet under? A heart is just a pump, when you come down to it — pumping thousands of gallons of blood every day. One day it stops, and that's that. The idea of resurrection — everyone digging themselves out of their graves on Judgment Day — seemed strange. Where would they find all their parts after centuries underground?
Corny Kelleher fell into step beside them.
"Everything went perfectly," he said. "Didn't it?"
He looked at them with his slow eyes.
"As it should," Mr. Kernan agreed.
"What?" Corny Kelleher asked.
Mr. Kernan assured him everything was fine.
"Who is that fellow behind us, walking with Tom Kernan?" John Henry Menton asked someone. "I know his face."
Ned Lambert glanced back.
"Bloom," he said. "His wife is Madame Marion Tweedy — the singer, the soprano."

"Oh, of course," John Henry Menton said. "I haven't seen her in some time. She was a fine-looking woman. I danced with her, it must be fifteen or seventeen years ago, at Mat Dillon's place in Roundtown."
He looked behind at Bloom.
"What does he do?" he asked. "Wasn't he in the stationery business? I had a run-in with him once at lawn bowls."
Ned Lambert smiled.
"Yes, he used to work at Wisdom Hely's," he said. "He sold blotting paper."
"What on earth did she marry someone like that for?" John Henry Menton said. "She could have done much better."
"She's still a fine woman," Ned Lambert said. "He does some work selling advertisements now."
John Henry Menton stared ahead with his large eyes.
The coffin cart turned into a side lane. A portly man rose from among the grasses and raised his hat in greeting. The gravediggers touched their caps.
"John O'Connell, the cemetery caretaker," Mr. Power said, pleased. "He never forgets a friend."
Mr. O'Connell shook all their hands silently. Mr. Dedalus said:
"I've come to pay you another visit."
"My dear Simon," the caretaker answered quietly, "I'd be happy never to have your business."
He walked on beside Martin Cunningham, jingling two big keys behind his back.
"Did you hear the one about Mulcahy from the Coombe?" he asked.
"I didn't," Martin Cunningham said.
They all leaned in to listen as the caretaker told his joke in a quiet, respectful voice.

"They say two men had a bit too much to drink one foggy evening and came out here looking for a friend's grave — a man called Mulcahy from the Coombe neighborhood. They finally found the right headstone. One of them read the name: 'Terence Mulcahy.' The other one was squinting up at a statue of Jesus that the widow had put on top."
