The caretaker glanced at a monument as they passed. He continued:

"And after staring up at the statue, the second man says: 'Not a bit like Mulcahy. That's not him at all. Whoever made that didn't know him.'" He thought the statue of Jesus was supposed to be a portrait of Mulcahy!
The caretaker smiled at their laughter and fell back to walk with Corny Kelleher, accepting the funeral paperwork.
"He tells jokes on purpose," Martin Cunningham explained to Hynes. "To cheer people up."
"I know," Hynes said.
"It's pure kindness," Martin Cunningham said. "Nothing else."

Mr. Bloom admired the caretaker — a cheerful, prosperous-looking man. Everyone wanted to stay on his good side. Bloom thought about various things: an advertisement he needed to arrange, wondering if Martha's letter was safe, noticing his own beard needed a shave. He wondered what it was like to be married to the cemetery caretaker — living right next to all those graves.

The caretaker had seen a lot of burials in his time, Bloom thought. The ground must be completely honeycombed with graves. He kept the place neat, though — trimmed grass, tidy edges. Some people said the Chinese grew poppies in their cemeteries. Bloom thought about how the dead nourish the earth — the soil must be very rich here.
Bloom thought about what happens underground — things he'd rather not dwell on. But he thought about how the cells in a body keep changing and living, in a way, long after the person is gone.

The cemetery caretaker seemed cheerful enough about his job, Bloom thought. It must give him a sense of perspective, seeing everyone come and go. He probably had good jokes — like the one about the bulletin: "Mr. Spurgeon went to heaven at 4 a.m. Reply at 11 p.m.: Not arrived yet." The dead themselves would probably enjoy a good joke. You have to laugh sometimes. Even Shakespeare knew that — he put comic gravediggers in Hamlet.
"How many funerals tomorrow?" the caretaker asked Corny Kelleher.
"Two," Corny said. "Half past ten and eleven."

The caretaker pocketed his papers. The coffin cart had stopped. The mourners moved to either side of the open grave, stepping carefully between the other graves. The gravediggers carried the coffin to the edge and looped straps around it.

Bloom thought: we come to bury Paddy Dignam. He wondered about a mysterious man in a raincoat — a mackintosh — who had appeared among the mourners. Who was he? Nobody seemed to know. It was strange how someone always turns up at a funeral whom nobody expects. Bloom thought about Robinson Crusoe — even on a desert island, someone has to bury you in the end.
A little song came to mind: "Oh, poor Robinson Crusoe! How could you possibly do so?"

Poor Dignam, Bloom thought. His last resting place, in a wooden box. When you think of all the coffins, it does seem like a waste of wood. They could invent something reusable — but people are particular about these things. Everyone wants their own coffin. An Irishman's house is his coffin, Bloom thought darkly.

Mr. Bloom stood at the back, hat in hand, counting the bare heads. Twelve mourners. With himself, thirteen. No, wait — the mysterious man in the mackintosh made thirteen. Thirteen — supposedly an unlucky number. Where had that man come from?
Bloom noticed Ned Lambert's nice tweed suit — a touch of purple in it. He thought about his own grey suit that needed turning. And someone should have picked the loose threads off Lambert's jacket.
The coffin slid out of sight, lowered by the men straddling the grave supports. They scrambled out and everyone removed their hats. Twenty seconds of silence.
Pause.
If we were all suddenly someone else, Bloom thought.
Far away, a donkey brayed. Rain coming? No. Bloom thought: you never see a dead donkey — they hide when they're dying. His own father had gone away to die alone too.

A gentle breeze blew around the bare heads. The boy stood by the grave holding his wreath with both hands, staring quietly into the dark hole. Mr. Bloom moved behind the caretaker. He thought about death — the moment when you realize it's happening. The confusion. The dark room, people whispering around you. The last struggle. And then — gone. People talk about you for a while, then forget.
Bloom thought about the prayers being said for Dignam's soul. He hoped Dignam was in a better place, not a worse one.

He wondered if the caretaker ever thought about the grave waiting for him too. Everyone shivers when someone walks over the spot where they'll be buried someday. Bloom thought of his own family plot toward Finglas — his mother and little Rudy buried there.

The gravediggers took up their spades and began throwing heavy clumps of clay onto the coffin. Mr. Bloom turned his face away. A terrible thought crossed his mind: what if the person was still alive? No, no — Dignam was definitely dead. He'd died on Monday. Still, they really should have some way of making absolutely sure — maybe a telephone in the coffin, just in case.
The clay fell more softly now. The grave was almost filled. Out of sight, out of mind. The dead begin to be forgotten.

The caretaker walked away and put his hat on. He'd had enough. The mourners began putting their hats back on too, one by one, trying not to be too obvious about it. Mr. Bloom put on his hat and watched the caretaker navigate expertly through the maze of graves.
Hynes was jotting something in his notebook. He was writing down the names of the mourners for the newspaper report.
"I'm just taking the names," Hynes said quietly. "What's your first name? I'm not sure."
"L," Mr. Bloom said. "Leopold. And you might put down M'Coy's name too. He asked me to."
"Charley," Hynes said, writing. "I know him."
Bloom thought about M'Coy and his various jobs. He'd once worked at a newspaper and had left under a cloud — something about missing money. But Bloom had promised to put his name down, so he did.
"And tell me," Hynes said, "do you know that fellow who was over there in the..."
He looked around.
"The mackintosh? Yes, I saw him," Mr. Bloom said. "Where is he now?"
"McIntosh," Hynes wrote down, thinking that was the man's name. "I don't know who he is. Is that his name?"
He walked away, looking around for the man.
"No," Mr. Bloom began, turning. "Wait — Hynes!"
But Hynes didn't hear him. The man in the mackintosh had vanished completely. Where had he gone? Not a trace.
A gravedigger came up beside Mr. Bloom to pick up a spare spade.
"Oh, excuse me!" Bloom said, stepping aside quickly.
He stepped nimbly out of the way.

Brown, damp clay was rising in the grave now, almost level with the ground. The gravediggers rested their spades. Everyone uncovered their heads once more. The boy propped his wreath against the corner of the grave; the brother-in-law placed his on a mound of earth. The gravediggers knocked the clay off their spades on the grass, wiped them clean, and walked toward their cart. One plucked a tuft of grass from his spade handle. Another walked slowly away with his spade over his shoulder, its blade glinting blue. At the graveside, someone coiled up the coffin strap. The brother-in-law slipped some money into someone's hand — a tip for the gravediggers.
The mourners drifted away slowly, wandering along different paths, stopping now and then to read a name on a headstone.
"Let's walk past the chief's grave," Hynes said, meaning the grave of the great Irish leader Charles Stewart Parnell. "We have time."
"Let's," Mr. Power agreed.
They turned right, lost in thought. Mr. Power said in a hushed voice:
"Some people say Parnell isn't really in that grave. That the coffin was filled with stones. That one day he'll return."
Hynes shook his head.
"Parnell will never come again," he said. "He's there. All that was left of him. Peace to his memory."

Mr. Bloom walked alone along a row of graves, past stone angels with sad faces, crosses, broken pillars, and family vaults. Hands carved in prayer, eyes looking upward — all of old Ireland's hopes and sorrows turned to stone. He thought: it would be more sensible to spend all this money on charity for the living. He planned to visit Dignam's grave in a few weeks and pay the gardener who kept it tidy. Bloom noticed how tombstones never told you anything interesting about the person — just names and dates. It would be better if they said what the person actually did. 'So-and-so, wheelwright.' Or 'I cooked good Irish stew.' He thought about wreaths and flowers on graves — flowers were more poetic than those bronze things that never wither. Everlasting flowers expressed nothing at all.

A bird sat tamely on a poplar branch — so still it looked stuffed. It knew nobody would throw stones at it here. Bloom remembered little Milly as a child, burying a dead bird in a matchbox in the back garden, making a tiny gravestone of daisies and broken china.

Bloom looked at a statue of the Sacred Heart — Jesus showing his heart. It should be painted red, he thought, like a real heart, not white. He thought about how Ireland was dedicated to the Sacred Heart. The statue didn't look very happy about it.
How many people here! Bloom thought. All of them once walked the streets of Dublin. As you are now, so once were they.

How could you possibly remember everyone? Eyes, walk, voice. Well, the voice — they could put a recording in every grave. After dinner on Sunday, put on a gramophone of great-grandfather talking. Otherwise, you forget what people looked like after fifteen years.
A sudden noise — a rattle of pebbles. Bloom stopped. He looked down into a stone crypt.
Some animal down there. Wait. There it goes.
A fat grey rat waddled along the side of the crypt, pushing pebbles as it went. An old-timer — it knew its way around. The rat squeezed itself under the stone base and disappeared. Good hiding place.
Who was buried there? The remains of Robert Emmet, the Irish revolutionary, was said to be buried somewhere in this cemetery.
The rat's tail was gone now.

Bloom thought about rats and what they do in graveyards — better not to dwell on it. He thought about other ways people disposed of the dead — cremation, burial at sea. Drowning was said to be the most peaceful death — your whole life flashes before your eyes. He thought about how news of a fresh burial must spread through the rat population underground. They probably could smell it.

The cemetery gates glimmered ahead — still open. Back to the world of the living. Bloom thought: enough of this place. Every visit brings you a little closer to your own turn. He thought about ghosts and hauntings. But then he pushed those thoughts away. There was plenty to see and hear and feel in life yet. Warm living beings near you. Warm beds. Warm, full-blooded life.
Martin Cunningham appeared from a side path.

Bloom noticed John Henry Menton — the lawyer. He remembered Menton from years ago at Mat Dillon's house, where they'd all had happy evenings together. Menton had taken a dislike to Bloom ever since Bloom had beaten him at lawn bowls — just a lucky shot. And Molly had been there too, laughing under the lilac trees with Floey Dillon. Menton was the type who felt embarrassed when women were around.
Bloom noticed a dent in the side of Menton's hat. Probably from the carriage door.
"Excuse me, sir," Mr. Bloom said, stepping up beside them.
They stopped.
"Your hat is a little crushed," Mr. Bloom said, pointing.
John Henry Menton stared at him for a moment without moving.
"There," Martin Cunningham said helpfully, also pointing to the dent.
John Henry Menton took off his hat, pushed out the dent, and smoothed the fabric carefully with his sleeve. He jammed the hat back on his head.
"It's fine now," Martin Cunningham said.
John Henry Menton gave a short nod.
"Thank you," he said curtly.

They walked on toward the gates. Mr. Bloom fell behind a few steps, feeling foolish. He shouldn't have bothered. Martin Cunningham knew how to handle men like Menton — could wrap them around his little finger.
Cold fish, Bloom thought. Never mind. He'll feel sorry later, when he realizes I was just trying to be kind.
Thank you indeed! How grand we are this morning!

chapters.title: Episode 7 — Aeolus
paragraphs: IN THE HEART OF DUBLIN

In front of Nelson's tall column in the middle of Dublin, trams slowed down and switched tracks, heading off to all the different neighborhoods around the city. Tram drivers called out their routes, and the conductors rang their bells.
—Rathgar and Terenure!
—Come on, Sandymount Green!
Two trams, one with two levels and one with just one, rolled away from the stops and glided along their tracks side by side.
—Start, Palmerston Park!
THE KING'S MAIL

Under the porch of the big post office, shoe-shiners called out to customers and polished away. The royal mail carts, painted bright red with the king's initials on them, were parked along the street, ready to carry letters all across Ireland.
NEWSPAPER PEOPLE
Big, heavy-booted workers rolled barrels out of a warehouse and bumped them up onto a delivery cart. The barrels thudded dully as they were loaded up.
—There it is, Red Murray said. Alexander Keyes.
—Just cut it out, will you? Mr. Bloom said. And I'll take it around to the Telegraph office.
A man named Davy Stephens came out of an office wearing a big cape coat and a small hat, carrying a roll of papers under his cape like a royal messenger.
Red Murray's long scissors snipped the advertisement out of the newspaper in four clean cuts.
—I'll go through the printing room, Mr. Bloom said, taking the cut-out square of paper.
—Of course, if he wants a short article about it too, Red Murray said helpfully, with a pen tucked behind his ear, we can write him one.
—Right, Mr. Bloom said with a nod. I'll mention that to him.
We. He said "we" like he owns the place, Bloom thought.
WILLIAM BRAYDEN, THE IMPORTANT OWNER
Red Murray touched Mr. Bloom's arm with the scissors and whispered:
—Brayden.
Mr. Bloom turned and saw the fancy doorman tip his cap as a grand-looking gentleman walked in between the newspaper signs. This was Mr. Brayden, the newspaper's owner.
—Don't you think his face looks like a painting of Jesus? Red Murray whispered.
The office door squeaked softly as it swung. They always build one door across from another so the wind can blow through.
Bloom thought about it — yes, the man did have that kind of oval face with a beard. He also looked a bit like Mario, the famous opera singer.
—Or like Mario, Mr. Bloom said.
—Yes, Red Murray agreed. But people used to say Mario looked like Our Savior.
Bloom pictured the opera singer with rosy cheeks and thin legs, hand on his heart, singing in the opera called Martha.

Come back, you lost one,
     Come back, you dear one!
THE CHURCH AND THE NEWSPAPER
—The Archbishop phoned down twice this morning, Red Murray said seriously.
They watched Mr. Brayden's legs and boots disappear up the stairs.
A telegram boy hopped in quickly, tossed an envelope on the counter, and dashed off with a quick word:
—Freeman!
Mr. Bloom said slowly:
—Well, he's one of our saviors too, in a way.
With a small smile, Bloom pushed through a side door and walked along the warm, dark hallway toward the printing room. He wondered if the newspaper owner would really help save the business.
He pushed through a glass swinging door and stepped over scattered packing paper, making his way through rows of clanking machinery toward Mr. Nannetti's reading room.
SAD NEWS ABOUT A WELL-KNOWN CITIZEN

Bloom noticed Hynes was there too — probably writing about the funeral. The printing machines thumped and banged. This morning they were printing the story about the late Mr. Patrick Dignam's funeral. The machines were powerful enough to crush a person. They ruled the world, these machines.
HOW A GREAT NEWSPAPER IS MADE
Mr. Bloom stopped behind the foreman, Mr. Nannetti, and admired his shiny bald head.

It was strange that Nannetti had never visited Italy, even though he was Italian. He was a member of the city council now. Bloom thought about what really sold newspapers — it was the advertisements and special features, not the serious articles.

The machines clanked away in a steady rhythm. Thump, thump, thump. Bloom thought about what would happen if someone got stuck in the machines and nobody knew how to stop them — they'd just keep printing the same thing over and over.
—Well, get it into the evening edition, councillor, Hynes said.
People were saying Nannetti might become Lord Mayor someday. He had powerful friends backing him.
The foreman, without speaking, scribbled "press" on a corner of the page and signaled to a typesetter, sliding the sheet silently over the dirty glass screen.
—Right, thanks, Hynes said, moving off.
Mr. Bloom stood in his way.
—If you want to collect your pay, the cashier is just about to go to lunch, Bloom said, pointing over his shoulder.
—Did you? Hynes asked.
—Mm, Mr. Bloom said. Go quickly and you'll catch him.
—Thanks, old man, Hynes said. I'll ask him for some money too.
He hurried off eagerly toward the Freeman's Journal office.
Three shillings I lent him weeks ago, Bloom thought. He's hinted three times about paying it back but never does.
THE ADVERTISEMENT MAN AT WORK
Mr. Bloom laid his newspaper clipping on Mr. Nannetti's desk.
—Excuse me, councillor, he said. This advertisement, you see. Keyes, you remember?
Mr. Nannetti looked at the clipping for a moment and nodded.
—He wants it in for July, Mr. Bloom said.
The foreman moved his pencil toward it.
—But wait, Mr. Bloom said. He wants it changed. Keyes, you see. He wants two keys drawn at the top.
The machines made such a racket. But Nannetti didn't seem to hear it at all. Iron nerves, that man had.
The foreman turned around patiently and, lifting an elbow, began to scratch slowly at his jacket.
—Like that, Mr. Bloom said, crossing his two pointer fingers at the top.
Let him think about that first, Bloom thought.
Mr. Bloom, glancing up, saw the foreman's yellowish face and, beyond him, the huge rolls of paper feeding into the printing machines. The machines clanked and clattered away.
Slipping his words carefully into the pauses between the machine noises, Bloom drew a quick sketch on the worn wooden desk.
HOUSE OF KEY(E)S
—Like that, see. Two crossed keys here. A circle. Then here the name. Alexander Keyes, tea, wine and spirit merchant. And so on.
Better not tell him how to do his job, Bloom thought.
—You know yourself, councillor, just what he wants. Then around the top in big letters: The House of Keys. You see? Do you think that's a good idea?
The foreman scratched his side quietly.

—The idea, Mr. Bloom said, is the House of Keys. You know, councillor, like the parliament on the Isle of Man. It hints at home rule for Ireland. Tourists come over from the Isle of Man. It catches the eye. Can you do that?
Bloom thought about asking Nannetti how to pronounce an Italian word, but decided not to — it might be embarrassing if Nannetti didn't know.
—We can do that, the foreman said. Have you got the design?

—I can get it, Mr. Bloom said. It was in a Kilkenny newspaper. He has a house there too. I'll just run out and ask him. Well, you can print that and just add a little article drawing attention to it. You know the usual kind of thing. A high-class licensed place. Long-standing business.
The foreman thought for a moment.
—We can do that, he said. But tell him to give us a three months' renewal on the ad.

A typesetter brought Nannetti a freshly printed page to check. He began looking it over carefully. Mr. Bloom stood by, listening to the loud thumps of the machines and watching the quiet typesetters at their letter cases.
SPELLING CHECK

He wants to make sure every word is spelled right, Bloom thought. Proofreading fever. He remembered a spelling puzzle someone had told him about — how to spell "embarrassment" with all those double letters.
I should have said something funny about his hat, Bloom thought. When he put on his top hat, I could have said "Looks as good as new!" That would have been clever. Oh well, too late now.
The nearest printing machine jerked forward, pushing out the first batch of folded newspapers. The machine seemed almost human in the way it called for attention, doing its best to keep up.
IMPORTANT CHURCHMAN WRITES FOR THE PAPER
The foreman suddenly handed back the page, saying:
—Wait. Where's the archbishop's letter? It's supposed to be reprinted in the Telegraph. Where's what's-his-name?
He looked around at the loud, busy machines.
—Monks, sir? a voice asked from nearby.
—Yes. Where's Monks?
—Monks!
Mr. Bloom picked up his clipping. Time to get out of here, he thought.
—Then I'll get the design, Mr. Nannetti, he said, and you'll give it a good spot in the paper, I know.
—Monks!
—Yes, sir.

Three months' renewal, Bloom thought. But first I need to take care of something else. I'll try to get the deal done anyway. August would be a good time — it's horse show month. Lots of tourists in town for the show.
A LONG-TIME WORKER

He walked through the room past an old man wearing spectacles and an apron. Old Monks, who had worked there for years and years. He must have handled so many different things over the years — funeral notices, pub ads, and all kinds of stories.
THE FEAST OF PASSOVER

Bloom stopped to watch a typesetter neatly arranging the metal letters. The man read everything backwards — it took real skill to do that. Bloom thought of his father reading from his Jewish prayer book at Passover, with the pages going from right to left.

Mr. Bloom walked through the printing room and out onto the landing. Now he had to decide — should he take the tram all the way out to find Mr. Keyes, or phone first? Better to phone and save the trip. He could call from the newspaper office.
THAT SOAP AGAIN
He went down the stairs. Someone had scrawled all over the walls with matches. There was always a heavy, greasy smell in the printing works.
He took out his handkerchief to wipe his nose and found the bar of soap he'd put in that pocket earlier. Better move it before he lost it. He tucked it safely into his hip pocket.
What perfume does your wife use? Bloom remembered the advertisement. He thought about going home, but decided against it. No. Not now.
A sudden burst of laughter came from the Evening Telegraph office. Bloom recognized the laugh — it was Ned Lambert. He'd pop in for a moment to use the phone.
He entered quietly.
IRELAND, GREEN JEWEL OF THE SEA
—The ghost walks, Professor MacHugh murmured softly to the dusty window, munching on a biscuit.
Mr. Dedalus, Stephen's father, stared at Ned Lambert from the empty fireplace and asked sourly:
—Good grief, wouldn't that writing give you a stomachache?
Ned Lambert, sitting on the table, read aloud from the newspaper:
—"Or again, notice how the little stream babbles along its way, past mossy banks and whispering trees..." It went on and on like that, using the fanciest, most over-the-top language imaginable.
—He must have switched drinks halfway through writing that, Mr. Dedalus joked.
Ned Lambert laughed so hard he slapped the newspaper against his knees, repeating the silliest phrases.
—"The thoughtful heart and the overhanging leaves." Oh, boys! Oh, boys!
—And then he looked at the plain and said it was beautiful, Mr. Dedalus added sarcastically, looking from the fireplace to the window.
—That's enough, Professor MacHugh cried from the window. I don't want to hear any more of that stuff.
He nibbled on his water biscuit, still hungry, and got ready to eat the one in his other hand.
Bloom thought it was all very showy, empty writing. He noticed Ned Lambert was taking a day off — funerals tend to upset your schedule. Lambert had connections to important people.
—Just another burst of bad writing, Ned Lambert said.
—What is it? Mr. Bloom asked.
—A recently discovered masterpiece of terrible writing, Professor MacHugh answered with mock grandness. It's called "Our Lovely Land."
A QUICK RESPONSE
—Whose land? Mr. Bloom asked simply.
—Excellent question, the professor said between bites. With an emphasis on "whose."
—Dan Dawson's land, Mr. Dedalus said.
—Is it his speech from last night? Mr. Bloom asked.
Ned Lambert nodded.
—But listen to this, he said.
The doorknob bumped Mr. Bloom in the back as someone pushed the door open.
—Excuse me, J. J. O'Molloy said, coming in.
Mr. Bloom quickly stepped aside.
—I beg your pardon, he said.
—Good day, Jack.
—Come in. Come in.
—Good day.
—How are you, Dedalus?
—Well. And yourself?
J. J. O'Molloy shook his head.
SAD
He used to be the cleverest young lawyer around, Bloom thought. But he's been going downhill lately. That unhealthy reddish color in his cheeks wasn't a good sign. Money troubles, probably.
—"Or again if we but climb the great tall mountains..." Ned Lambert continued reading the awful speech.
—You're looking well, someone said to O'Molloy.
—Is the editor here? J. J. O'Molloy asked, looking toward the inner door.
—Very much so, Professor MacHugh said. He's in his office with Lenehan.
J. J. O'Molloy walked over to a desk and began flipping through old newspaper files.
O'Molloy's law practice was shrinking, Bloom thought. He used to have such promise. Now he had gambling debts and money problems.
—Oh, listen to this for goodness' sake, Ned Lambert begged. "Or again if we but climb the great tall mountains..."
—Rubbish! the professor interrupted impatiently. Enough of this windy nonsense!
—"Mountains," Ned Lambert went on, "towering high on high, to bathe our souls, as it were..."
—Bathe his face, more like, Mr. Dedalus said. Is he taking any medicine for this terrible writing?
—"As it were, in the peerless view of Ireland's beautiful scenery, unmatched anywhere in the world, with lovely woods and rolling plains..."
HIS COUNTRY ACCENT
—The moon! Professor MacHugh said. He forgot to mention the moon.
—"And wait till the glowing moon shines forth to spread its silver light..."
—Oh! Mr. Dedalus groaned. That's enough, Ned. Life is too short.
He took off his silk hat and ran his fingers through his bushy hair in frustration.
Ned Lambert tossed the newspaper aside, laughing with delight. A moment later, Professor MacHugh burst out laughing too.
—Doughy Daw! he cried. That was the writer's nickname.
WHAT PEOPLE WERE SAYING

It's all very well to laugh at it now, Bloom thought, but people eat up that flowery stuff when they hear it. The writer, Dan Dawson, had made a good living for himself — he used to be in the bakery business, which is why people called him "Doughy Daw."
The inner office door flew open and a red-faced man with bright blue eyes stuck his head in. He had a crest of feathery hair standing up on top of his head. In a loud voice he demanded:
—What is it?
—And here comes the big man himself! Professor MacHugh announced grandly.
—Oh, stop it, you old professor! the editor said, recognizing him.
—Come on, Ned, Mr. Dedalus said, putting on his hat. I need a drink after listening to that.
—Drink! the editor cried. No drinks until after work!
—Quite right, Mr. Dedalus said, heading out. Come on, Ned.
Ned Lambert slid down from the table. The editor's blue eyes drifted toward Mr. Bloom with a half-smile.
—Will you come along, Myles? Ned Lambert asked the editor.
FAMOUS VICTORIES
—North Cork! the editor cried, marching to the mantelpiece. We won every time! North Cork and Spanish officers!
—Where was that, Myles? Ned Lambert asked thoughtfully.
—In Ohio! the editor shouted.
—So it was, Ned Lambert agreed.
As he passed out, he whispered to J. J. O'Molloy:
—He's getting a bit excitable. Poor fellow.
—Ohio! the editor crowed in a high voice from across the room. My Ohio!
—A perfect rhythm! the professor said. Long, short, and long.
OH, WINDS OF CHANGE!
He took out a piece of dental floss and twanged it between his teeth.
—Bing-bang, bang-bang.
Mr. Bloom, seeing that everyone was distracted, headed for the inner office door.
—Just a moment, Mr. Crawford, he said. I just need to make a phone call about an advertisement.
He went in.
—What about that opinion piece for this evening? Professor MacHugh asked, coming over to the editor and putting a firm hand on his shoulder.
—That'll be all right, Myles Crawford said more calmly. Don't worry about it. Hello, Jack. Everything's fine.
—Good day, Myles, J. J. O'Molloy said. Is that fraud case in court today?
The telephone buzzed inside the office.
—Twenty-eight... No, twenty... Double four... Yes.
PICK THE WINNER
Lenehan came out of the inner office carrying the racing pages.
—Who wants a sure bet for the Gold Cup horse race? he asked. Sceptre with O. Madden riding.
He tossed the racing pages onto the table.
A group of barefoot newsboys rushed through the hallway, and the door was flung open.
—Shh, Lenehan said. I hear footsteps.

Professor MacHugh strode across the room and grabbed one of the boys by the collar as the others scrambled out and ran down the steps. The racing pages fluttered up in the breeze and floated softly around the room.
—It wasn't me, sir! It was the big fellow who pushed me, sir!
—Throw him out and shut the door, the editor said. There's a gale blowing in here.
Lenehan started picking up the scattered papers from the floor, groaning as he bent down.
—We were just waiting for the racing results, sir, the newsboy explained. It was Pat Farrell who pushed me, sir.
He pointed at two faces peeking in around the doorway.
—Him, sir.
—Get out of here, Professor MacHugh said firmly.
He pushed the boy out and shut the door with a bang.
J. J. O'Molloy was turning through newspaper files, looking for something.
—Continued on page six, column four, he murmured.
—Yes, Evening Telegraph here, Mr. Bloom phoned from the inner office. Is the boss there?... Yes, Telegraph... Where?... Oh! Which auction rooms?... I see... Right. I'll catch him.
BUMP!
The phone bell rang again as Bloom hung up. He came out quickly and bumped into Lenehan, who was still picking up papers.
—Pardon me, Lenehan said, grabbing Bloom's arm for a moment and making a face.
—My fault, Mr. Bloom said. Are you hurt? I'm in a hurry.
—My knee, Lenehan said.
He made a funny face and rubbed his knee, complaining:
—Getting old is no fun!
—Sorry, Mr. Bloom said.
He went to the door and paused, holding it open. J. J. O'Molloy was flipping through heavy newspaper pages. From the hallway came the sounds of the newsboys — two shrill voices and a harmonica.

We are the boys of Wexford
     Who fought with heart and hand.
BLOOM LEAVES
—I'm just running around to Bachelor's Walk, Mr. Bloom said, about this Keyes advertisement. I need to sort it out. They tell me he's at Dillon's.
He looked at their faces uncertainly for a moment. The editor, who had been leaning against the mantelpiece with his head propped on his hand, suddenly swept out his arm grandly.
—Go! he said. The world is before you.
—Back in no time, Mr. Bloom said, hurrying out.
J. J. O'Molloy took the racing pages from Lenehan's hand and read them quietly.
—He'll get that advertisement placed, the professor said, watching through the window. Look at those young rascals chasing after him.
—Show me! Where? Lenehan cried, running to the window.
STREET PARADE
Both men smiled at the window, watching a line of playful newsboys following Mr. Bloom down the street, the last one waving a white paper in the breeze like a kite.
—Look at that little rascal copying his walk! Lenehan said, laughing. Oh, that's too funny! He's imitating the flat way Bloom walks!
Lenehan began doing a silly dance across the floor, sliding past the fireplace to hand the papers to J. J. O'Molloy.
—What's going on? Myles Crawford said, startled. Where did the other two go?
—Who? the professor said, turning. They've gone around to the pub for a drink. Paddy Hooper is there with Jack Hall. They came over last night.
—Come on, then, Myles Crawford said. Where's my hat?
He walked jerkily into the back office, jingling his keys in his pocket. The keys clinked against the wood as he locked his desk drawer.
—He's had quite a bit to drink already, Professor MacHugh said in a low voice.
—It seems that way, J. J. O'Molloy said, pulling out a cigarette case. But things aren't always what they seem. Who has matches?
A PEACE OFFERING
He offered a cigarette to the professor and took one himself. Lenehan quickly struck a match and lit both their cigarettes. J. J. O'Molloy opened his case again and offered it around.
—Thank you very much, Lenehan said, helping himself.
The editor came back from the inner office with a straw hat tilted on his head. He sang dramatically, pointing at Professor MacHugh:

'Twas fame and glory that tempted thee,
     'Twas power that charmed thy heart.
The professor grinned.
—Eh? You old Roman Empire fan? Myles Crawford teased.
He took a cigarette from the open case. Lenehan lit it for him neatly and said:
—Quiet, everyone! I have a brand-new riddle!
—The Roman Empire, J. J. O'Molloy said thoughtfully. It does sound grander than the British Empire, doesn't it?
Myles Crawford blew a big puff of smoke toward the ceiling.
—That's the point, he said. We Irish are the ones caught in the middle. We don't have a chance.
THE GREATNESS OF ANCIENT ROME
—Wait a moment, Professor MacHugh said, raising his hands. We shouldn't get carried away by fancy words. When we think of Rome — imperial, powerful, commanding.
He spread his arms wide from his worn shirt cuffs and paused:

—But what was their civilization really? Big, I'll admit, but brutal. Sewers — that's what they built. The Jewish people, out in the wilderness, said: "Let us build a place to worship God." But the Romans? They just built drains and roads for conquering people.
—And our own ancestors liked running water too, Lenehan joked.
—They were gentlemen of nature, J. J. O'Molloy murmured. But we also got Roman law from them.
—And Pontius Pilate was its most famous judge, Professor MacHugh replied.
—Do you know that story about the chief judge Palles? J. J. O'Molloy asked. It was at a fancy dinner. Everything was going smoothly...
—First my riddle, Lenehan insisted. Are you ready?
Mr. O'Madden Burke, a tall man in a gray tweed suit, came in from the hallway. Stephen Dedalus followed behind him.
—Come in, everyone! Lenehan called out.
—I'm escorting a young visitor, Mr. O'Madden Burke said in a grand voice. Youth led by Experience visits Fame.
—How do you do? the editor said, shaking Stephen's hand. Come in. Your father just left.
Lenehan announced to everyone:
—Silence! What opera is like a railway line? Think about it, and answer!
Stephen handed over some typed pages, pointing to the title and signature.
—Who wrote this? the editor asked.
Part of the page was torn off.
—Mr. Garrett Deasy, Stephen said. He was a schoolmaster.
—That old complainer, the editor said. Who tore it? Was he in a rush?

Stephen thought of some lines of dark poetry:
On swift sail flaming
     From storm and south
     He comes, pale vampire,
     Mouth to my mouth.
—Good day, Stephen, the professor said, coming over to look. Foot and mouth disease? Are you interested in that?
Stephen, the poet who befriended cattle farmers.
TROUBLE IN A RESTAURANT
—Good day, sir, Stephen answered, blushing. The letter isn't mine. Mr. Garrett Deasy asked me to bring it to the newspaper.
—Oh, I know him, Myles Crawford said, and I knew his wife too. She was the most difficult woman ever! She once threw soup at a waiter in a restaurant because it was too hot!
Stephen thought about how through history, arguments over love had led to great conflicts. Like Helen of Troy — because of her, the Greeks fought for ten years.
—Is he a widower? Stephen asked.

—Sort of, Myles Crawford said, glancing at the typed letter. It was about an Irishman who once saved the Austrian Emperor's life. Don't forget — Irish people have done brave things all over the world!
—The real question is whether the Emperor remembered to thank him, J. J. O'Molloy said quietly. Saving important people is often a thankless job.
Professor MacHugh turned to him.
—And if he didn't? he said.
—I'll tell you what happened, Myles Crawford began. A Hungarian one day...
FIGHTING FOR LOST CAUSES

—We Irish were always loyal to lost causes, the professor said. Success never really suited us. What made us great was our imagination and fighting spirit, even when we couldn't win. I teach young people whose own language was taken away from them.
LORD, HAVE MERCY!
A smile brightened his dark-rimmed eyes.
—The Greek language! he said with passion. What a shining word — "Kyrie"! The beauty of the Greek language, the language of the mind. "Lord, have mercy!" That's what it means.
He walked away from them toward the window.
—They went out to fight, Mr. O'Madden Burke said sadly, but they always lost.
—Boo-hoo! Lenehan pretended to cry. Poor fighters!
He whispered something near Stephen's ear:
LENEHAN'S FUNNY POEM

—"There once was a professor named MacHugh
Who wore glasses of darkest black hue.
Since he mostly sees double,
Why bother with trouble?
I can't get the joke. Can you?"
Stephen thought about how someone had said Mulligan was in mourning — in mourning for an ancient writer. And about mothers who die.
Myles Crawford stuffed Stephen's pages into his side pocket.
—That'll be fine, he said. I'll read the rest later. It'll be all right.
Lenehan held up his hands.
—But my riddle! he said. What opera is like a railway line?
—Opera? Mr. O'Madden Burke's face twisted as he tried to figure it out.
Lenehan announced happily:
—The Rose of Castile! Get it? Rows of cast steel — like railway tracks! Ha!
He poked Mr. O'Madden Burke playfully in the ribs. Mr. O'Madden Burke leaned back dramatically on his umbrella, pretending to faint.
—Help! he sighed. I feel terribly weak.
Lenehan stood on his tiptoes and fanned Burke's face with the racing pages.
The professor walked past Stephen and Mr. O'Madden Burke, brushing their loose neckties.
—Paris, past and present, he said. You two look like French revolutionaries.
—Like fellows who blew up a fortress, J. J. O'Molloy joked. Or did you two cause some international trouble?
ALL THE TALENTS
—We were only thinking about it, Stephen said.
—All the talents gathered here, Myles Crawford said. Law, the classics...
—Horse racing, Lenehan added.
—Literature, the press.
—If Bloom were here, the professor said, we'd have advertising too.
—And Mrs. Bloom, Mr. O'Madden Burke added. She's a wonderful singer. Dublin's favorite.
Lenehan gave a loud, fake cough.
—Ahem! he said very softly. I need some fresh air! I caught a cold in the park. The gate was open. Get it?
"YOU CAN DO IT!"
The editor put his hand on Stephen's shoulder nervously.
—I want you to write something for me, he said. Something sharp and clever. You can do it. I can see it in your face.
Bloom thought about those words — "I can see it in your face." They reminded him of something his teacher used to say.

—Forget about this foot-and-mouth disease letter! the editor cried scornfully. Who cares about boring meetings? Give the readers something exciting! Something that'll make people sit up and pay attention!
—We can all offer food for thought, Mr. O'Madden Burke said.
Stephen looked up at the editor's bold, staring eyes.
—He's trying to recruit you for the newspaper, J. J. O'Molloy said to Stephen.
THE GREAT GALLAHER

—You can do it, Myles Crawford said again, clenching his fist. Wait. We'll amaze all of Europe, just like Ignatius Gallaher used to say. He was an Irish journalist who made it big — started right here in this office, doing odd jobs, and ended up working for the biggest newspapers in the world!
He pushed past them to the newspaper files.
—Look at this, he said, turning around. The New York World once sent a cable asking for a special report. Remember that?
Professor MacHugh nodded.

—The New York World! the editor said excitedly, pushing back his straw hat. They wanted the story of the Phoenix Park murders — a famous event in Irish history. The whole thing was solved using a newspaper advertisement!
—That old carriage driver, Fitzharris, Mr. O'Madden Burke said. They say he runs a shelter for cab drivers now, down by the bridge.
—Is that the fellow? Myles Crawford asked.
—And poor Gumley is down there too, guarding stones for the city at night.
Stephen turned in surprise.
—Gumley? he said. Really? A friend of my father's?

—Never mind Gumley, Myles Crawford said impatiently. The point is what Gallaher did. He was a genius! He sent the whole story by telegraph using nothing but an advertisement from the newspaper as a map. He marked locations with letters — here's the park gate, here's where it happened, here's the escape route.
He flipped through the old newspaper files and jabbed his finger at a page.
—Take page four — say there's an ad for coffee. Got that? Right.
The telephone buzzed.
A FARAWAY VOICE
—I'll answer it, the professor said, going.
—B marks the park gate. Good.
His finger jumped from point to point on the newspaper page.
—T is the government house. C is where the crime happened. K is Knockmaroon gate.
The editor's neck wobbled with excitement. His shirt collar was coming loose, and he shoved it back into his waistcoat.
—Hello? Evening Telegraph here... Hello?... Who's there?... Yes... Yes... Yes.
—F to P is the route the driver took through the city streets to create an alibi. Got that? X marks the pub.
The professor came back from the inner office.
—Bloom is on the telephone, he said.
—Tell him to go away, the editor said. X marks the pub, see?
CLEVER, VERY
—Clever, Lenehan said. Very.
—Gave them the whole story, Myles Crawford said proudly.
Stephen thought: History — a nightmare from which you can never escape.
—I was there when it happened, the editor said proudly. Dick Adams, the kindest man from Cork you'd ever meet, and myself.
Lenehan bowed to the air, announcing:
—"Madam, I'm Adam." And "Able was I ere I saw Elba." Those are palindromes — they read the same forwards and backwards!
—History! Myles Crawford cried. Our newspaper was the first to break that story. A woman designed the whole thing using an advertisement. That was real journalism!
—The father of exciting journalism, Lenehan confirmed.
—Hello?... Are you there?... Yes, he's still here. Come on over.
—Where do you find a journalist like that nowadays? the editor cried.
He tossed the newspaper pages down.
—Very clever indeed, Lenehan said to Mr. O'Madden Burke.
—Very smart, Mr. O'Madden Burke agreed.
Professor MacHugh came back from the inner office.
—Speaking of famous crimes, he said, did you hear that some street sellers were in court...

—Oh yes, J. J. O'Molloy said eagerly. Lady Dudley was walking in the park after the big storm and wanted to buy a picture of Dublin. And the picture turned out to be the very scene from the old crime. The lady had no idea!

—Those street sellers are small-time, Myles Crawford said dismissively. But the lawyers and journalists of the old days — now those were real talents. Men like Whiteside, Isaac Butt, and others with silver tongues!
His mouth twitched with frustration.
Stephen thought: Would anyone want to be kissed by that nervous, twitching mouth?
RHYMES AND REASONS
Stephen's mind played with words: Mouth, south. Is the mouth south somehow? Rhymes: two words that sound the same, paired together.
He thought of beautiful lines from Dante's Italian poetry about peace and wind and speaking.
He imagined groups of girls in colorful dresses — green, rose, purple — walking gracefully through the air, like figures from a painting.
—Speak up for yourself, Mr. O'Madden Burke said to Stephen.
ENOUGH FOR TODAY...
J. J. O'Molloy spoke up with a pale smile.

—My dear Myles, he said, putting out his cigarette, you're twisting my words. I'm not arguing against journalism. But your Cork friends were just as brilliant in the courtroom. A judge once made one of them apologize three times in court — and it was the funniest thing!
GLORY DAYS
—Great writers worked for this very newspaper, the editor cried. Irish patriots! This paper was established in 1763! Where are writers like that today?
—Well, J. J. O'Molloy said, what about Bushe, the lawyer?
—Bushe? the editor said. Well, yes. Bushe. He does have something special.
—He should have been a judge long ago, the professor said. If only... but never mind.
J. J. O'Molloy turned to Stephen and said quietly:
—One of the most beautiful speeches I ever heard was by Seymour Bushe. It was in a murder trial. Bushe was defending the accused.
Shakespeare's words echoed: "And in the porch of my ear did pour."
Stephen wondered: How did they find out the man was murdered? He died in his sleep — so how could they know?
—What was the speech about? the professor asked.
ITALY, TEACHER OF THE ARTS
—He spoke about justice, J. J. O'Molloy said. He compared Roman law with the older law from the Bible — an eye for an eye. And he described Michelangelo's famous statue of Moses in the Vatican.
—Ah.
—A few well-chosen words, Lenehan said. Everyone be quiet!
There was a pause. J. J. O'Molloy took out his cigarette case.
A moment of quiet. Nothing unusual yet, Stephen thought.
Someone thoughtfully struck a match and lit a cigar.
Stephen thought about how sometimes one small, ordinary moment can change the course of your whole life.
A BEAUTIFUL SPEECH
J. J. O'Molloy continued, choosing his words carefully:

—He described the statue of Moses as: that stone figure in frozen music, horned and powerful, showing the eternal spirit of wisdom. If anything made by human imagination could truly capture the divine, then this statue was it — the reflection of God's own face.
His thin hand made a graceful wave through the air.
—Beautiful! Myles Crawford said immediately.
—Inspired words, Mr. O'Madden Burke said.
—Did you like that? J. J. O'Molloy asked Stephen.
Stephen blushed, moved by the beauty of the words. He took a cigarette from O'Molloy's case. Lenehan lit everyone's cigarettes and took one too.
—Much thanks.
A MAN OF GOOD CHARACTER

—Professor Magennis was asking about you, J. J. O'Molloy said to Stephen. What do you really think of those mystical poets? That group around the writer A. E., with their talk of ancient wisdom and hidden knowledge?
Stephen wondered: They were talking about me? What did they say? But he didn't ask.

—No, thank you, Professor MacHugh said, waving away the cigarette case. Wait a moment. Let me tell you about the finest speech I ever heard. It was by John F. Taylor, at a college debate about whether Ireland should have its own language.
He turned to Myles Crawford and said:
—You know Gerald Fitzgibbon, the judge. So you can picture his style of speaking.
—He's working with Tim Healy now, J. J. O'Molloy said, on the college property commission.
—He's having a good time, Myles Crawford said. Go on. What happened?
—It was a brilliant speech, the professor said. Fitzgibbon argued against the Irish language with great skill and cleverness. He poured scorn on the idea with such polished words...
He paused, closed his lips for a moment, then eagerly raised his hand to adjust his spectacles.
ON THE SPOT
In a serious tone he addressed J. J. O'Molloy:

—Taylor was sick that day. He came from his bed to speak. He hadn't prepared anything — there wasn't even a reporter to write it down. His dark, thin face showed he hadn't shaved. But his eyes burned with purpose.
The professor looked from face to face, then down at the ground, remembering. His worn collar showed behind his bent head.
—When Fitzgibbon finished, John F. Taylor stood up to reply. As best as I can remember, here is what he said.
He raised his head firmly. His eyes were alive with memory behind his thick glasses.
He began:

—"Mr. Chairman, ladies and gentlemen: I was deeply impressed by the words just spoken. It seemed to me that I had been carried back to ancient Egypt, to the time when the Israelites were slaves there."
Everyone stopped to listen, their cigarettes held still in the air. The smoke rose in thin lines.
—"And it seemed to me that I heard the voice of an Egyptian ruler speaking with the same pride and scorn. I heard his words, and their meaning became clear to me."
FROM THE ANCIENT WRITERS
Stephen thought about what he'd read in Saint Augustine — that good things can be damaged, which proves they're good, because only good things can be ruined.

—"'Why won't you accept our ways?' the Egyptian said. 'You are just wandering shepherds. We are a mighty civilization. You have no cities, no wealth. Our cities are full of busy people. You have nothing but a wilderness. We have the great river Nile.'"
Nile.
Stephen pictured the scene: child, grown man, stone statue.
By the Nile, mothers knelt among the bulrushes with their babies. A young man grew strong as a fighter. And finally, the stone statue — horned, bearded, heart of stone.
—"'You worship a small, unknown god,' the Egyptian continued. 'Our temples are grand and mysterious, home to mighty gods. You know only humble obedience. We command the thunder and the seas.'"
A rumble of hunger interrupted the professor's speech. He raised his voice bravely above it:

—"'But,' Taylor said, 'ladies and gentlemen, if the young Moses had listened to that argument — if he had given in and accepted that way of thinking — he would never have gone to the mountaintop. He would never have spoken with God in the burning bush. He would never have come down carrying the stone tablets of the law in his hands. He would never have said the words that changed history forever.'"
The professor stopped and looked at them, enjoying the silence that followed.
A WARNING!
J. J. O'Molloy said, with some sadness:
—And yet Moses died without ever reaching the Promised Land.
—And after a long illness, he died suddenly, Lenehan added, trying to be funny. With a great future behind him!
The sound of bare feet came rushing through the hallway and pattering up the staircase — the newsboys were back.
—Now that was real oratory, the professor said, and nobody disagreed.

Gone with the wind, Stephen thought. All those great speeches, all those huge gatherings at historic places. Miles of listening ears. The speaker's words, shouted and scattered on the wind. A whole people sheltered within someone's voice. Dead sounds. But was it really just words?
I have money, Stephen thought suddenly.
—Gentlemen, Stephen said. May I suggest we all go get something to eat?
—You take my breath away! Mr. O'Madden Burke said with a smile. Are you inviting us? Well, I think it's the perfect time for a visit to a fine old eating place.
—All in favor, say "aye," Lenehan announced. The motion is carried! Which restaurant shall it be? I vote for Mooney's!
He led the way, saying:
—We will firmly refuse to have anything too strong to drink, won't we? Yes, we won't.
Mr. O'Madden Burke followed close behind, swinging his umbrella:
—Lead on!
—Chip off the old block! the editor cried, clapping Stephen on the shoulder. Let's go. Where are those papers?
He fumbled in his pocket, pulling out the crumpled typed pages.
—Foot and mouth disease article. Right. That'll go in the paper. Where are they? That's all sorted.
He shoved the pages back into his pocket and went into the inner office.
LET'S HOPE
J. J. O'Molloy, about to follow him, said quietly to Stephen:
—I hope you'll see your writing published. Myles, one moment.
He went into the inner office, closing the door behind him.

—Come along, Stephen, the professor said. That was a fine speech, wasn't it? It had a grand vision of the future. The fall of the ancient city of Troy. The great empires rise and fall. People are always dreaming of the Mediterranean.
The first newsboy came clattering down the stairs behind them and rushed out into the street, yelling:
—Racing special!
Dublin, Stephen thought. I have much, much to learn.
They turned left along Abbey Street.
—I have a vision too, Stephen said.
—Yes? the professor said, skipping to keep up. Crawford will follow us.
Another newsboy raced past them, yelling:
—Racing special!
DEAR OLD DUBLIN
Dubliners, Stephen thought.
—Two Dublin ladies, Stephen began his story. They're elderly and devoted churchgoers. They've lived fifty and fifty-three years in a small lane in Dublin.
—Where's that? the professor asked.
—Off Blackpitts, Stephen said.
Stephen's mind flickered with dark images of the city at night.
Now go on, he told himself. Dare to tell the story. Let there be life.
—They want to see the views of Dublin from the top of Nelson's Pillar. They save up their coins in a little red money box. They shake out the pennies and carefully count every last one.
—Wise women, Professor MacHugh said.
REAL LIFE

—They buy some cold meat and bread from a dining room on Marlborough Street... They also buy two dozen ripe plums from a girl at the base of the Pillar... Then they give their tickets to a large man with a wide smile at the ticket booth... and slowly, panting and puffing, they climb the winding staircase all the way to the top.
Their names are Anne Kearns and Florence MacCabe. Anne Kearns has a sore back that she treats with holy water from Lourdes. Florence MacCabe takes pills every night and has been doing so for years.
—Interesting contrast, the professor said, nodding. Old-fashioned ladies. I can picture them. What's keeping our friend?
He turned to look for the editor.
A crowd of newsboys rushed down the steps, scattering in all directions with their white papers fluttering. Right behind them came Myles Crawford, his hat tilted like a halo, puffing and blowing.
—Come on! the professor called, waving his arm.
He started walking again beside Stephen.
BLOOM RETURNS
—Yes, the professor said. I can see your two old ladies.
Mr. Bloom, out of breath, caught up with them near some newspaper offices and called out:
—Mr. Crawford! Just a moment!
—Racing special! the newsboys shouted.
—What is it? Myles Crawford said, slowing down.
A newsboy shouted a silly made-up headline in Mr. Bloom's face:
—Terrible tragedy! A child attacked by a pair of bellows!
TALKING TO THE EDITOR

—Just this advertisement, Mr. Bloom said, pushing through to the steps and catching his breath. He pulled the clipping from his pocket. I spoke with Mr. Keyes just now. He'll renew for two months, he says. Then he'll think about a longer deal.
K.M.A.
—Tell him he's not getting special treatment! Myles Crawford said, throwing out his arm. Tell him that straight!

The editor seemed nervous and ready for a fight, Bloom thought. Everyone was going off for a drink. Lenehan was tagging along as usual. He wondered if young Stephen Dedalus was leading this group. The young man seemed bright — he had a good pair of boots, at least.
—Well, Mr. Bloom said, looking back at the editor, if I can get the design, I think it's worth a short article. He'd give us the ad. I'll tell him...
ABSOLUTELY NOT!
—He can forget about special treatment! Myles Crawford shouted over his shoulder. Any time he likes, tell him!
Mr. Bloom stood there thinking it over, about to respond, but the editor had already marched off.
TRYING TO GET SOMETHING

—Sorry, Jack, the editor said to J. J. O'Molloy, raising his hand. I'm in trouble myself. I was looking for someone to lend me money just last week. I'm sorry, Jack. With all my heart, I would if I could.
J. J. O'Molloy made a long face and walked on silently. They caught up with the others and walked side by side.
—When they've eaten the meat and bread, Stephen continued his story, and wiped their twenty fingers on the paper the bread was wrapped in, they move closer to the railing at the top of the Pillar.
—Something for you, Myles, the professor explained. Two old Dublin women on top of Nelson's Pillar.
WHAT A STORY!
—That's new, Myles Crawford said with interest. That's a real story. Two old ladies on a day out. What then?

—But they're afraid the Pillar might fall, Stephen went on. They look out at the rooftops and try to figure out which churches are which: the blue dome of Rathmines, Adam and Eve's, Saint Laurence O'Toole's. But they can't agree about anything.
THOSE CHEEKY OLD LADIES
—Easy now, Myles Crawford said. Let's keep it proper. We're in the Archbishop's area here.
—And they settle down on their striped skirts, Stephen continued, looking up at the statue of Nelson — the famous admiral who was known for having only one hand and for having a mistress.
—One-handed scoundrel! the professor cried. I like that. I see what you mean.
SPEED AND EXCITEMENT — THE OLD LADIES ARE AMAZED

—Looking up gives them a stiff neck, Stephen said, and they're too tired to look up or down or even to talk. They put the bag of plums between them and eat them one by one, spitting the pits out over the railing down onto the street below.
He gave a sudden, loud, young laugh to finish the story. Lenehan and Mr. O'Madden Burke heard him, turned, waved, and led the way across the street toward Mooney's pub.
—Finished? Myles Crawford said. Well, as long as they don't do anything worse than spit plum pits.
A WISE MAN DEFEATS PROUD ENEMIES. TROY FALLS AGAIN.

—You remind me of Antisthenes, the professor said. He was an ancient Greek thinker known for his sharp wit. No one could tell if he was harder on other people or on himself. He lived in an interesting time.
Poor Penelope, Stephen thought. Always waiting.
They got ready to cross O'Connell Street.
HELLO THERE!

At different spots along the street, trams stood still on their tracks with their poles reaching up. They were headed to neighborhoods all around Dublin. But at that moment everything had stopped — all the power was off, and the trams stood frozen in place.
WHAT? WHERE?
—But what do you call this story? Myles Crawford asked. Where did they get the plums?
THE PROFESSOR AND THE STUDENT DISAGREE ON A TITLE
—Call it, wait, the professor said, thinking hard. Call it... let me see. Call it: "God has given us this rest" — a quote from the ancient Roman poet Virgil.
—No, Stephen said. I call it "A Distant View of the Promised Land" or "The Story of the Plums."
—I see! the professor said.
He laughed heartily.

—I see! he said again, delighted. Moses and the Promised Land — because the old ladies looked out from the top of the pillar but could never actually reach the places they saw, just like Moses saw the Promised Land but never entered it. We gave him that idea, he said to J. J. O'Molloy.
NELSON'S PILLAR STANDS TALL ON THIS FINE DAY
J. J. O'Molloy sent a tired sideways look toward the Nelson statue and said nothing.
—I see, the professor said.
He stopped on the pavement island around Sir John Gray's statue and looked up at Nelson through a crooked smile.
THE OLD LADIES CAN'T HELP THEMSELVES
—One-handed scoundrel, he said, smiling. That phrase tickles me, I must say.
—It tickled the old ladies too, Myles Crawford said, if the truth be known.

chapters.title: Episode 8 — Lestrygonians
paragraphs: Pineapple candy, lemon drops, butterscotch. A girl with sticky fingers was scooping handfuls of sweets for a group of schoolboys. Some kind of school outing. Too many sweets are bad for stomachs. The candy shop had a royal sign saying they made sweets for the King himself.
A serious-looking young man from the YMCA, standing among the warm sweet smells of a candy shop, handed Mr. Bloom a flyer.
Heart-to-heart talks, it said.
Bloo... Me? No, Bloom thought. That's not my name.
Blood of the Lamb, the flyer read.

Mr. Bloom walked slowly toward the river, reading the flyer. "Are you saved?" it asked. "All are washed in the blood of the lamb." It was a religious leaflet about a preacher named Elijah who was coming to Dublin.

Is coming! Is coming!! Is coming!!!
     All heartily welcome.

It's all a business, Bloom thought. Those traveling preachers make good money. He remembered seeing an advertisement for a glow-in-the-dark crucifix from a company in Birmingham. Imagine waking up in the middle of the night and seeing it glowing on the wall!

It must be made with phosphorus, Bloom thought. Like how fish glows in the dark. He remembered going down to the kitchen pantry one night — his wife Molly had wanted something. The Malaga raisins, that was it.

From the corner, Bloom glanced along Bachelor's Walk. He spotted Dedalus's daughter standing outside Dillon's auction rooms. She must be waiting for her father. Bloom recognized her eyes right away — they were just like her father's. Poor girl, waiting around with nowhere to go. Fifteen children that family had. Was it music she was studying?
Good heavens, that poor girl's dress is falling apart, Bloom thought. She looks underfed too. Probably living on potatoes and margarine. That kind of poor diet catches up with you eventually.

As Bloom stepped onto O'Connell Bridge, a puff of smoke rose from a brewery barge carrying stout for export to England. He'd heard that sea air makes beer go sour. It would be interesting to visit the brewery someday. He'd heard it was like a whole world inside — they even had their own railway.
Looking down from the bridge, he saw seagulls wheeling between the stone walls of the river. The weather must be rough out at sea. The gulls dipped lower, looking for food.
They flew lower. Looking for food, Bloom thought. Wait.

He crumpled up the religious flyer and threw it down to the gulls. The paper ball bobbed on the river, ignored by the birds. They weren't fooled. Just like the time he threw stale cake from a boat and the gulls had swooped right down for it.

The hungry famished gull
     Flaps o'er the waters dull.

That's how poets write, Bloom thought — matching sounds together. But Shakespeare didn't use rhymes. He used blank verse instead. It was the flow of the words that made it beautiful. The thoughts behind them, solemn and deep.

Hamlet, I am thy father's spirit
     Doomed for a certain time to walk the earth.
—Two apples a penny! Two for a penny! a woman called out.
Bloom looked at the shiny apples stacked neatly on her stand. They must be from Australia at this time of year. Their peels were polished bright — she probably rubbed them with a cloth.
Wait, Bloom thought. Those poor birds.

He stopped and bought two small cakes from the old apple woman for a penny. He broke the crumbly pastry and threw the pieces down into the River Liffey. The gulls swooped down silently — first two, then all of them — diving after the food. They grabbed it eagerly and flew away.

Knowing how greedy and clever the gulls were, Bloom shook the last crumbs from his hands. They hadn't expected that treat. It was like manna from heaven for them. Seabirds eat fish all day, so their meat tastes fishy. Swans sometimes came swimming up from further down the Liffey to clean their feathers.

The gulls flapped around weakly. I'm not going to throw any more, Bloom thought. A penny was quite enough. Not even a squawk of thanks from them. He thought about how different animals taste depending on what they eat.
His eyes looked for an answer from the river and spotted a rowboat rocking gently on the slow, syrupy waves. On its side was a painted advertisement.

Kino's
     11/—
     Trousers

Good idea, advertising on a boat, Bloom thought. He wondered if the owner paid rent to the city for floating the sign there. You can't really own water, can you? It's always flowing — like the stream of life. All kinds of places make good spots for advertisements.
If he...?
Oh!
Eh?
No... No.
No, no. I don't believe it. He wouldn't surely?
No, no.

Mr. Bloom walked on, pushing away a troubling thought. It was after one o'clock. The time ball at the Ballast Office had dropped, marking the hour. He remembered a fascinating little astronomy book by Sir Robert Ball. The word "parallax" had always confused him — something about how things look different depending on where you stand.

Mr. Bloom smiled as he passed two windows. His wife Molly was right, in her way. She'd asked him what "metempsychosis" meant — just a big word for reincarnation, the idea that souls are reborn. She wasn't exactly clever with words, but she had her own kind of sense.

A line of men in white coats walked slowly toward him, each carrying a sandwich board with red letters. They reminded Bloom of the priest at the funeral that morning. He read the red letters on their five boards: H.E.L.Y.S. — the name of a stationery shop. Bloom used to work there.

He crossed Westmoreland Street. A bicycle shop. Horse races were on today. How long ago was it since he'd worked at Hely's? That was the year Phil Gilligan died. They were living on Lombard Street then.

He'd been happier then, Bloom thought. Or was that really him? Their snug little room with the red wallpaper. He remembered giving little Milly her bath. The cozy smell of her bathwater. She'd been born in 1889, so she was fifteen now, working at a photographer's shop in Mullingar.
He walked along the curb.

Stream of life, Bloom thought. What was the name of that odd-looking fellow who used to peer in the window when they lived on Lombard Street? He had weak eyes. Something with "Pen" — Penrose? His memory was getting worse. It was years ago, of course. Was Molly working at that time? Yes, she had a job at that dressmaker's shop. She'd earned good money there.

Bartell d'Arcy was the singer then, just starting his career. He used to walk Molly home after choir practice. A conceited fellow with his waxed mustache. He'd given her a song called "Winds That Blow from the South."

There was a windy night when Bloom went to pick Molly up. A meeting was happening at the Mansion House. He and Molly walked home together through the wind. A sheet of her music blew out of his hand. They'd been so happy together.
He remembered Molly getting ready for bed. Sitting up taking out her hairpins. Little Milly tucked up safe in bed. Happy times. That was the night...
—Oh, Mr. Bloom! How do you do?
—Oh, how do you do, Mrs. Breen?
—No use complaining. How is Molly these days? Haven't seen her in ages.
—She's doing wonderfully, Mr. Bloom said cheerfully. Milly has a job down in Mullingar, you know.
—Go away! Isn't that lovely for her?
—Yes. At a photographer's. Getting on brilliantly. How is everyone at your house?
—Everyone's keeping busy, Mrs. Breen said.
Bloom wondered how many children she had. No sign of any with her today.
—You're wearing black, I see. You haven't had a...
—No, Mr. Bloom said. I've just come from a funeral.
This is going to keep coming up all day, Bloom thought. Who died, when, what of? It'll follow me around like a bad penny.
—Oh dear me, Mrs. Breen said. I hope it wasn't anyone close to you.
Might as well get her sympathy, Bloom thought.
—Dignam, Mr. Bloom said. An old friend of mine. He died quite suddenly, poor fellow. Heart trouble, I believe. The funeral was this morning.
A silly song ran through Bloom's head about funerals.
—So sad to lose old friends, Mrs. Breen said, her eyes looking sorrowful.
That's quite enough about that, Bloom thought. Better change the subject. Ask about her husband.
—And how is your husband?
Mrs. Breen rolled her eyes dramatically.
—Oh, don't be talking! she said. He's driving me crazy. He's in a solicitor's office right now, looking up the law on insults. He has me worn out! Wait till I show you.

The warm smell of mock turtle soup and freshly baked jam pastries poured out from a nearby restaurant. The rich, heavy smell tickled the top of Mr. Bloom's throat. Good pastry needs butter, the best flour, and brown sugar, or you can taste the difference.
She opened her handbag — old, chipped leather. Hatpins, Bloom noticed. Those things should have safety guards. Someone could poke an eye out on the tram. She rummaged through the bag.
—There must be a new moon out, she said. He's always worse then. Do you know what he did last night?
Her hand stopped rummaging. Her eyes fixed on Bloom, wide with alarm but also somehow amused.
—What? Mr. Bloom asked.
Just let her talk, Bloom thought. Look her in the eye. Show you believe her.
—Woke me up in the middle of the night, she said. He'd had a nightmare.
Bad dreams from eating too much, probably.
—He said the ace of spades was walking up the stairs!
—The ace of spades! Mr. Bloom said.
She took a folded postcard from her handbag.
—Read that, she said. He got it this morning.
—What is it? Mr. Bloom asked, taking the card. U. P.?
—"U. P." — as in "up," she explained. Someone is playing a mean trick on him. It's a terrible thing to do, whoever's behind it.
—It certainly is, Mr. Bloom agreed.
She took the card back with a sigh.
—And now he's going to a lawyer's office. He says he's going to sue someone for ten thousand pounds.
She folded the card back into her messy bag and snapped it shut.

She was wearing the same blue dress she'd had two years ago, Bloom noticed. It was getting faded. Her hair was wispy, and her hat was old-fashioned with fake grapes on it. She used to dress much better. Life had been hard on her.
Bloom noticed a woman passing by who gave Mrs. Breen a mean look. How cruel people can be, he thought.
He kept looking at her kindly, hiding his thoughts. The smell of soup from the restaurant was making him very hungry. He could see flakes of pastry on her dress and a smudge of flour on her cheek.
Time to change the subject, Bloom thought.
—Do you ever see Mrs. Beaufoy? Mr. Bloom asked.
—Mina Purefoy? she said.
Bloom realized he'd mixed up the names. He'd been thinking about Beaufoy, the writer. But Mrs. Purefoy was who he meant.
—Yes.
—I actually stopped by the hospital to ask about her on my way here. She's in the maternity hospital on Holles Street. She's been having a very difficult time — three days now.
—Oh, Mr. Bloom said. I'm sorry to hear that.
—Yes, Mrs. Breen said. And she has a whole house full of children at home. The nurse says it's been a very difficult birth.
—Oh, Mr. Bloom said.
His eyes showed deep sympathy as he took in the news. He made a soft clicking sound of pity.
—I'm so sorry to hear that, he said. Poor woman! Three days! That's terrible for her.
Mrs. Breen nodded.
—She was taken ill on Tuesday...
Mr. Bloom gently touched her elbow, warning her:
—Careful! Let this man pass.

A bony, strange-looking man came striding along the curb from the river, staring with an intense gaze at the sun through thick glasses. A tiny hat sat tight on his head. He carried a folded coat, a walking stick, and an umbrella all dangling from one arm.
—Watch him, Mr. Bloom said. He always walks on the outside of the lampposts. Watch!
—Who is he, if you don't mind me asking? Mrs. Breen said. Is he a bit odd?
—His name is Cashel Boyle O'Connor Fitzmaurice Tisdall Farrell, Mr. Bloom said, smiling. Watch!
—Well, he certainly has enough names! she said. My Denis will end up like that one of these days.
She broke off suddenly.
—There he is, she said. I must go after him. Goodbye. Remember me to Molly, won't you?
—I will, Mr. Bloom said.

He watched her hurry through the crowd toward the shops. Denis Breen shuffled out of the restaurant in a short coat and worn shoes, hugging two heavy law books to his chest. Mrs. Breen caught up to him and they walked on together, her talking steadily into his ear.
Poor man's gone a bit crazy, Bloom thought.

Mr. Bloom walked on easily, watching the strange Mr. Farrell ahead of him with his funny walk. There were plenty of eccentric people in Dublin, Bloom thought. Everyone seemed a little unusual in their own way.

Bloom thought he knew who had sent that rude postcard to Mr. Breen. Probably Alf Bergan or Richie Goulding, having a laugh. Poor Mr. Breen would go storming into the lawyer's office with the postcard. The lawyer would find it hilarious.
He passed the Irish Times office. There might be replies waiting for him there — he'd placed a personal advertisement. But he'd leave them for now. He had enough to deal with today.

The Irish Times was the best paper for small advertisements, Bloom thought. He scanned the ads in his mind: cooks wanted, housemaids wanted, shop assistants needed. He wondered who placed all these ads and what stories lay behind them.

Poor Mrs. Purefoy! Bloom thought. Her husband was very strict and religious. He even timed how many times he chewed his food — thirty-two chews per minute. Despite all his careful eating, his sideburns kept growing like weeds.

Bloom stood at a crossing, thinking about lunch. Should he have a cheap meal at Rowe's? Or a better one at the Burton? He also needed to check on something at the National Library. He'd head toward the Burton.
He walked on past a tea shop. Tea, tea, tea. He'd forgotten to ask Tom Kernan for money.
Oh dear, Bloom thought about poor Mrs. Purefoy again. Three days of suffering. Terrible. The first baby is always the hardest. And then all those children at home waiting for their mother.
Not stillborn, of course, Bloom hoped. Those cases weren't even officially recorded. Such sadness for nothing.

Bloom thought about pregnant women — how different they looked before and after, the peaceful look in their eyes when it was all over. Old Mrs. Thornton used to be the best midwife. She'd delivered Milly — a fine healthy baby.

In front of the grand old Irish Parliament building, a flock of pigeons flew about, having their fun after meals. Bloom watched them from below, amused. It must be exciting to fly through the air like that.
A group of police officers marched out of College Street in single file, their faces red and sweaty from a big lunch. They patted their truncheons as they walked.

Bloom walked past the statue of the poet Thomas Moore, placed above a public fountain. The statue's finger pointed roguishly. All kinds of places are good for statues. He hummed the old song: "There is not in this wide world a valley so sweet."
He watched the last police officer pass. You wouldn't want to cross those fellows, Bloom thought. Jack Power had stories about what happened to troublemakers in the police cells.
—Up the Boers! someone shouted.
—Three cheers for De Wet!
—We'll hang Joe Chamberlain on a sour apple tree!

A bunch of young lads were shouting political slogans, Bloom thought. They were full of fire now, but in a few years half of them would be working for the government themselves. When war comes, everyone marches off together, no matter what side they were on before.
You never know who you're talking to in Dublin, Bloom thought. There are spies everywhere. Even in the old days, one of the rebels had turned informer and betrayed his friends. You had to be careful.
—Are those yours, Mary? someone called out flirtatiously.
—I don't wear such things... Stop or I'll tell the missus on you! Out half the night, she teased back.
—Great times are coming, Mary. Wait and see.
—Oh, go along with your great times!
Bloom noticed the barmaids and shop girls chatting. Dublin was full of life.

Bloom thought about Irish revolutionaries and their methods. James Stephens had the best idea — organizing in small circles of ten, so if one person was caught, they could only betray their own small group. Secret societies were clever that way.

To lead people, you need a certain charm, Bloom thought. Parnell had it. Arthur Griffith, the political leader, was intelligent but didn't have that spark with crowds. And as for flowery speeches about "our lovely land" — that was just hot air.

His smile faded as he walked and a heavy cloud covered the sun, darkening the front of Trinity College. Trams passed each other, coming and going, clanging their bells. The same things happened day after day — police marching, trams going, people hurrying about. Nothing ever really changed.

Cities were always passing away, Bloom thought. One generation replaced by the next. Houses, streets, miles of pavement — all changing owners over time. One landlord goes, another comes. People step into the same rooms, sit on the same chairs, look through the same windows.
No one is really anything special, Bloom thought.
This is the worst time of the day, Bloom thought. Everything feels dull and gloomy around lunch. He felt empty inside.

He passed the Provost's house at Trinity College. The head of the college was named Dr. Salmon — "Tinned Salmon" would be a good nickname, sealed up in that big fancy house like a fish in a tin. Bloom hoped there would be a good hot lunch waiting somewhere.
The sun came out again slowly, sending glints of light off the silverware in a shop window. Just then, John Howard Parnell passed by without noticing — brother of the famous Irish leader.

There he is, Bloom thought. He looks just like his famous brother Charles — the same haunting face. It was a coincidence seeing him after just thinking about Parnell. You think about someone a hundred times and never run into them, but sometimes the coincidences just line up.
—Of the two-headed octopus... someone was talking loudly on the street, giving some kind of lecture about politics.
Two figures passed behind Mr. Bloom along the curb. A man with a beard, pushing a bicycle. A young woman walking beside him.

And there he is too, Bloom thought. That's really a coincidence — the second one today. "Coming events cast their shadows before," as they say. It was the poet and thinker Mr. George Russell, known as A.E. He must be with one of his followers.

Bloom watched the tall figure in plain clothes with his beard and bicycle, a woman listening attentively at his side. Coming from the vegetarian restaurant. They ate only vegetables and fruit. Bloom thought it odd to never eat meat. He supposed there was something noble about it, but he wasn't convinced.

Her stockings are loose around her ankles, Bloom noticed. How sloppy. Those literary types are all dreamy and cloudy, thinking about symbols and art. Maybe it was their vegetarian diet that made them so vague and airy.

The dreamy cloudy gull
     Waves o'er the waters dull.

He crossed at the corner of Nassau Street and stopped in front of a shop window to look at field glasses. Or maybe he'd drop in and chat with young Sinclair at old Harris's shop. But he was probably at lunch. Bloom needed to get his old glasses fixed for the theater.
He half-closed his eyes and tried to see something in the distance. If you imagined it was there, you could almost see it. Almost.

He turned around and, standing between shop awnings, held out his right hand at arm's length toward the sun. He'd always wanted to try this. Yes — the tip of his little finger blocked out the entire sun. It was something to do with where the light rays crossed.

Now that he thought about it, Bloom remembered that the time ball dropped at Greenwich time, connected by an electric wire. He'd like to visit the observatory someday and learn about the stars and planets. Maybe if he could get an introduction to one of the professors there.
Ah.
His hand fell back to his side.

You never really know anything about the universe, Bloom thought. Gasballs spinning around, crossing each other's paths. The same cycle over and over — gas, then solid, then a world, then cold, then a dead frozen rock drifting through space. Everything comes from somewhere and goes to nothing.
He walked on past a French restaurant.

Wait, Bloom thought. The full moon was that night two weeks ago. That was when they were walking by the river. Molly was humming a song. "The young May moon, she's beaming, love." But there was someone on the other side of her. Him. Boylan. That was the night...
Stop. Stop. If it happened, it happened, Bloom thought. Must keep going.
Mr. Bloom, breathing faster, slowed his walking as he passed a court.

He noticed Bob Doran's heavy shoulders ahead of him — the man who went on a drinking binge every year at this time. People drink to find courage to say or do things they normally wouldn't. Bloom thought about the different places and ways people fall apart.
