Yes, thought so. Doran was heading into a music hall. A glass of plain water would do him more good. Before that venue used to be a theater where all sorts of shows played. Dublin's entertainment world was always changing.

Was I happier then? Bloom wondered. Was that the same me, or am I different now? He was twenty-eight then, Molly twenty-three. After they moved from Lombard Street, something changed. He could never feel the same after little Rudy died. You can't bring back time. It's like trying to hold water in your hand.

Grafton Street was bright and busy with colorful shop awnings. Ladies in fine dresses, the jingle of horse carriages, hooves clopping on the hot pavement. Dublin's fanciest shopping street was alive with activity.

He passed the windows of a silk shop, admiring the displays. Ribbons cascaded down. Delicate Chinese silks. A tilted jar poured a flood of deep red fabric — beautiful, rich-colored cloth. The French Huguenots had brought that craft to Ireland centuries ago.
Pincushions, Bloom thought. He'd been meaning to buy one for ages. Molly stuck pins everywhere around the house.

He glanced at a small scratch on his forearm. Nearly healed. He thought about buying Molly a birthday present. Her birthday was September eighth — almost three months away. But maybe she wouldn't like what he picked. Women had strong opinions about gifts.
Gleaming silks, petticoats on slim brass rails, rows of smooth silk stockings — all displayed in the shop window.
No use looking back, Bloom thought. What happened had to happen.
High voices. Warm silk in the sunshine. Jingling horse carriages. Everything in the world seemed designed for women — homes, fine fabrics, silver, spicy fruits. The world's wealth on display.
A warm, pleasant feeling settled over Bloom's mind. His thoughts went soft and dreamy, surrounded by the beauty of the street.
Duke Street. Here we are. Time to eat, Bloom thought. The Burton restaurant. He'd feel better after a meal.
He turned the corner, his mind still wandering. The jingle of carriages, the scent of perfume. A beautiful summer day in Dublin.
—Jack, love!
—Darling!
—Kiss me, Reggy!
—My boy!
—Love!

Feeling a flutter in his chest, Bloom pushed open the door of the Burton restaurant. But a terrible smell hit him — greasy meat juice and mushy vegetables. It was like watching animals at feeding time.
Men, men, men.

Men were perched on high stools at the bar, hats shoved back, calling for more free bread, gulping down sloppy food. Their eyes bulged as they wiped their mustaches. A pale young man polished his knife and fork, waiting for his meal.
—Roast beef and cabbage.
—One stew.
The smells were overwhelming — food, smoke, spilled drinks. The whole place reeked.
Bloom's stomach turned.

He couldn't eat a bite in here. Men were shoveling food in like machines — one fellow sharpening his knife and fork, an old man picking at his teeth, another chewing with his mouth full. It was disgusting.
Bloom looked around at all the people eating, wrinkling his nose.
—Two pints here.
—One corned beef and cabbage.
That fellow was ramming a forkful of cabbage into his mouth as if his life depended on it. It made Bloom nervous just watching. The man ate like he was born doing it.

A messy waiter collected clattering plates. A man at the bar blew the foam off his drink, splashing some on the floor. Another diner sat with knife and fork straight up, elbows on the table, ready for seconds. A man had gravy dripping from his thick lips.
Mr. Bloom raised two fingers uncertainly to his lips. He looked around.
—Not here, he decided. I don't see what I want.
Out. I hate messy eaters, Bloom thought.
He backed toward the door. He'd get a light snack at Davy Byrne's instead. Just enough to keep him going. He'd had a good breakfast, after all.
—Roast and mashed, here.
—Pint of stout.
Everyone for himself in there, Bloom thought. Gulp, grab, gulp.
He came out into the cleaner air and turned back toward Grafton Street. Eat or be eaten, he thought. That's the law of nature.

Maybe in the future there'd be communal kitchens, Bloom imagined, where everyone would line up with their bowls to be fed. But that seemed wrong somehow. People need variety and choice. Different tastes, different foods. There's no accounting for taste, as they say.

There is a lot to be said for vegetarian food, Bloom thought. The fine flavors — garlic, onions, mushrooms, truffles. He felt sorry for the animals too. Poor creatures in the slaughterhouse. And the fishermen pulling fish out of the water. Everything alive wants to keep living.
Some people drink hot blood as a health cure, Bloom thought. It made him shudder to think about it.
Ah, I'm hungry, Bloom thought.

He entered Davy Byrne's — a quiet, respectable pub. The owner wasn't much of a talker, which Bloom liked. Once in a great while he'd offer someone a free drink. He'd once cashed a check for Bloom when he needed it. A decent man.
What shall I have? Bloom thought, checking his watch. What about a shandy?
—Hello, Bloom, Nosey Flynn said from his corner seat.
—Hello, Flynn.
—How are things?
—Very well, thanks... Let me see. I'll have a glass of burgundy wine and... let me see.

Bloom looked at the sardines on the shelves. He could almost taste them just by looking. What about a sandwich? He saw the potted meats and remembered a silly advertisement: "What is home without Plumtree's Potted Meat? Incomplete." They'd printed it right under the death notices. What a terrible place to put a food ad!
—Have you got a cheese sandwich?
—Yes, sir.

Some olives would be nice too, Bloom thought. He liked Italian olives best. A glass of good wine would wash it all down nicely. He thought about nice salads and how his friend Tom Kernan was good at preparing them with olive oil.
—Wife well? the barman asked.
—Quite well, thanks... A cheese sandwich, then. Gorgonzola, have you?
—Yes, sir.
Nosey Flynn sipped his drink.
—Is Molly doing any singing these days?
Flynn doesn't know much about music, Bloom thought. But no harm in telling him. It's free publicity.
—She's booked for a big concert tour at the end of this month. You may have heard about it.
—No. Oh, that sounds great! Who's organizing it?
The barman served Bloom's order.
—How much is that?
—Seven pence, sir... Thank you, sir.
Mr. Bloom cut his sandwich into thin strips. He hummed a little tune to himself as he ate.
—Mustard, sir?
—Thank you.
He put dabs of yellow mustard under each strip of sandwich.
—The tour? he said. Well, it's like a company arrangement, you see. Part shares and part profits.
—Oh, now I remember, Nosey Flynn said, putting his hand in his pocket. Who was it telling me? Isn't Blazes Boylan involved in it?

A sudden jolt of anxious warmth hit Mr. Bloom in the chest at the mention of Boylan's name. He looked up at the clock. Two o'clock. Pub clock was five minutes fast. Time was moving on. Not yet, though. There was still time.
His stomach tightened with a longing, yearning feeling.
Wine.
He sipped the rich wine slowly, then set his glass down carefully.
—Yes, he said. He's the organizer, actually.
Nothing to worry about, Bloom told himself.
Nosey Flynn sniffled and scratched himself.
—He's had some good luck lately, Nosey Flynn said. Jack Mooney was telling me about that boxing match Blazes Boylan was involved in. Made a tidy profit from it.
Bloom hoped the drop on Flynn's nose wouldn't fall into his drink. No — he sniffed it back up.
—For nearly a month before the fight, Flynn went on, they kept the boxer on a strict diet. No drinking at all. Boylan's a tough fellow.
Davy Byrne, the pub owner, came out from behind the bar, wiping his lips with a napkin.
—Here's the man himself, Nosey Flynn said. Can you give us a tip for the Gold Cup horse race?
—I don't bet on horses, Mr. Flynn, Davy Byrne said. I never put money on a horse.
—You're right about that, Nosey Flynn agreed.

Mr. Bloom ate his sandwich strips with satisfaction — fresh, clean bread with tangy mustard and the strong flavor of cheese. Sips of wine soothed his tongue. This was good wine, proper stuff. Food always tastes better in cool weather.
Nice quiet bar, Bloom thought. Nice piece of wood in that counter. Nicely polished. He liked the way it curved.
—I wouldn't touch horse racing, Davy Byrne said. It's ruined many a man.
Gambling licenses and prizes, Bloom thought. Heads I win, tails you lose. The house always benefits.
—True enough, Nosey Flynn said. Unless you have inside information. Lenehan gets some good tips. He fancies Sceptre for today's race. But Zinfandel is the favorite.
—Is that so? Davy Byrne said...
He went to the window and picked up his account book to check the figures.
—I could tell you stories about champion horses, Nosey Flynn said, sniffling. He told a long tale about a famous filly who had won a race in a thunderstorm.
He drank from his glass, running his fingers down the ridges.
—Ay, he said with a sigh.

Mr. Bloom chewed thoughtfully, watching Nosey Flynn. Flynn wasn't the brightest fellow. Bloom wondered if he should mention the horse tip he'd heard from Lenehan. But Flynn probably already knew. Better to let him figure it out — or lose more money trying.

The wine-softened bread and mustard and cheese melted together in Bloom's mouth. Nice wine, he thought. It tasted better because he wasn't terribly thirsty. The bath that morning had helped. Just a light bite was all he needed. Then around six o'clock he could have a proper dinner.

The gentle warmth of the wine spread through his body. He'd needed that. He'd been feeling so out of sorts all morning. His eyes wandered over the shelves of tins — sardines, lobster. He thought about all the strange things people eat — shellfish, snails, seaweed. Who first figured out what was safe to eat?
Two flies buzzed on the windowpane, stuck together.

The wine glowed on his tongue. He thought about grapes being crushed in French vineyards, warmed by the sun. The taste seemed to unlock a memory. He remembered a happy day on Howth Head with Molly, lying among the wild ferns above the bay. The beautiful view, the warm sun. It had been a perfect day.
Me then. And me now, Bloom thought.
The flies buzzed, still stuck.

Bloom's eyes traced the patterns in the oak counter. Beauty is found in curves, he thought. Like the curves of ancient statues in the museum — Venus, Juno. You could see them in the round hall, those beautiful carved figures from long ago.
Nature was calling, and Bloom finished his wine, got up, and walked to the back of the pub toward the washroom.
When the sound of his footsteps had faded, Davy Byrne said, looking up from his book:
—What does Bloom do for a living? Isn't he in insurance?
—He left that job ages ago, Nosey Flynn said. He sells advertising space for the Freeman's Journal newspaper now.
—I know him by sight, Davy Byrne said. Is he in some kind of trouble?
—Trouble? Nosey Flynn said. Not that I've heard. Why?
—I noticed he was wearing black — mourning clothes.
—Was he? Nosey Flynn said. So he was, now that you mention it. I asked him how things were at home. You're right. So he was in black.
—I never bring up the subject, Davy Byrne said kindly, if I see a gentleman going through a hard time. It only reminds them of their troubles.

—It's not his wife, anyway, Nosey Flynn said. I saw him just the other day coming out of a dairy shop with a jar of cream, taking it home to her. She's doing fine. Hasn't changed a bit — still a fine-looking woman.
—And he's working for the Freeman? Davy Byrne asked.
Nosey Flynn pursed his lips.
—He doesn't buy cream from the money he makes selling ads, if you know what I mean. He has other ways of getting by.
—How so? Davy Byrne asked, looking up from his book.
Nosey Flynn made quick, mysterious gestures in the air. He winked.
—He's a Freemason, he said knowingly.
—You don't say? Davy Byrne said.
—Very much so, Nosey Flynn said. Ancient free and accepted order. He's a member in good standing. They look after their own, those Freemasons. I was told that by someone — well, I won't say who.
—Is that a fact?
—Oh, it's a fine organization, Nosey Flynn said. They stick by you when you're in trouble. Very exclusive, though. Hard to get in.
Davy Byrne smiled, yawned, and nodded all at once.
—Ahhhhhh!
—There was one woman, Nosey Flynn said, who supposedly hid in a clock to spy on their secret meetings. But they discovered her and made her swear to keep their secrets forever.
Davy Byrne, recovering from his yawn, said with watery eyes:
—Is that true? Bloom seems like such a quiet, decent man. I've often seen him in here and I've never once seen him behave badly.

—You'd never get him drunk, Nosey Flynn said firmly. He always leaves when things get lively. Didn't you see him check his watch? He always does that. His first move when someone offers him a drink is to check the time. He makes sure he has an appointment to get to.
—There are people like that, Davy Byrne said. He's a trustworthy man, I'd say.
—He's not bad at all, Nosey Flynn said, sniffling. He's been known to help people out with money too. Give credit where it's due. Bloom has his good qualities. But there's one thing he'll never do.
Flynn traced an imaginary signature on the bar with his finger.
—I know, Davy Byrne said. He won't put things in writing.
—Nothing on paper, Nosey Flynn confirmed.
Paddy Leonard and Bantam Lyons came into the pub. Tom Rochford followed behind them, looking uncomfortable and pressing his hand to his chest.
—Good day, Mr. Byrne.
—Good day, gentlemen.
They stopped at the counter.
—Who's buying? Paddy Leonard asked.
—I'm sitting down, anyway, Nosey Flynn said. That counts for something.
—Well, what'll everyone have? Paddy Leonard asked.
—I'll have a ginger ale, Bantam Lyons said.
—How much? Paddy Leonard cried. Since when do you drink ginger ale? What's yours, Tom?
—How's the stomach? Nosey Flynn asked Tom Rochford.
Tom Rochford pressed his hand to his chest and hiccupped.
—Could I trouble you for a glass of fresh water, Mr. Byrne? he said.
—Certainly, sir.
Paddy Leonard looked at his friends with disbelief.
—Would you look at what I'm buying drinks for! he said. Water and ginger ale! Two fellows who used to drink with the best of them. I bet one of you has a secret tip on a horse for the Gold Cup.
—Is it Zinfandel? Nosey Flynn asked.
Tom Rochford poured some powder from a twisted paper into his water glass.
—This terrible indigestion, he said before drinking.
—Baking soda is very good for that, Davy Byrne suggested.
Tom Rochford nodded and drank.
—Is it Zinfandel you fancy?
—I'm not saying a word! Bantam Lyons said with a wink. I'm going to bet five shillings on my own pick.
—Tell us your tip, will you? Paddy Leonard demanded. Who told you?
Mr. Bloom, on his way out of the pub, raised three fingers in a friendly wave.
—See you later! Nosey Flynn called out.
The others turned to look.
—That's the man who gave me the tip, Bantam Lyons whispered.
—Nonsense! Paddy Leonard scoffed. Mr. Byrne, sir, we'll have two small whiskeys after that, and a...
—Ginger ale, Davy Byrne added politely.
—Yes, Paddy Leonard said. A baby's bottle for the little one.

Mr. Bloom walked toward Dawson Street, running his tongue over his teeth. Something green — spinach, maybe — would have been good for cleaning his teeth. He thought about X-ray machines and how they could see inside people.

In a lane, a hungry little terrier dog was being sick on the cobblestones, then licked it up again. Bloom walked past carefully. His second time having lunch today, in a manner of speaking — first the Burton, now Davy Byrne's. Like that opera character Don Giovanni.
He hummed the closing notes of a song:

Don Giovanni, you have invited me
     To come to supper tonight.
He felt better now. The wine had picked him up nicely. He still needed to check on something at the National Library.

Bloom passed a plumber's shop with toilet equipment displayed in the window. An odd thing to put in a shop window, but it made him think about how food travels through the body. Strange thoughts you have after lunch.
—To come to supper tonight, he hummed.
What does that word mean exactly? Bloom wondered. Tonight perhaps.

Don Giovanni, thou hast me invited
     To come to supper tonight,
     The rum the rumdum.
Doesn't sound quite right, Bloom thought.

Bloom did some mental arithmetic. The Keyes advertisement — if he got it — would earn about two pounds ten. Plus the three shillings Hynes owed him. And if he got Billy Prescott's ad too... about five guineas total. He'd be sitting pretty.
He could buy Molly one of those nice silk petticoats, the color of her new garters.
Today. Today. Don't think about today, Bloom told himself.

Maybe they could take a holiday to the seaside, Bloom thought. English resort towns — Brighton, Margate. Piers in the moonlight. Molly's voice floating out over the water. He passed a man dozing against a wall, chewing on a crust.

Mr. Bloom turned past a confectioner's window full of unsold tarts. He passed a bookshop selling pamphlets with titles like "Why I Left the Church of Rome." The shop was run by do-gooders who used to offer poor children soup if they'd change their religion. People called the children "soupers" as an insult.
A young blind man stood tapping the curbstone with his thin cane, waiting to cross. No tram was coming. He obviously wanted to get across.
—Do you want to cross? Mr. Bloom asked kindly.
The blind young man didn't answer. His face tightened with a slight frown. He moved his head uncertainly.
—You're on Dawson Street, Mr. Bloom said. Molesworth Street is right across. Do you want to cross? There's nothing in the way.
The cane moved out trembling to the left. Mr. Bloom saw a delivery van parked nearby.
—There's a van there, Mr. Bloom said, but it's not moving. I'll help you across. Do you want to go to Molesworth Street?
—Yes, the young man answered. South Frederick Street.
—Come, Mr. Bloom said.
He gently touched the young man's thin elbow and took his hand to guide him forward.
Better say something casual, Bloom thought. Don't be condescending. Blind people can tell when you're being patronizing. Just make a normal remark.
—The rain held off, Bloom said.
No answer.

Bloom noticed stains on the young man's coat. He probably had trouble eating without seeing, Bloom thought. His hand felt like a child's — soft and sensitive. Like little Milly's hand when she was small. The blind young man was sizing Bloom up by his touch, probably.
—Thanks, sir, the blind young man said.
He knows I'm a man, Bloom thought. He can tell from my voice.
—All right now? First turn to the left.
The blind young man tapped the curbstone with his cane and went on his way, feeling ahead of him as he walked.

Mr. Bloom walked behind him, watching. Poor young fellow! How did he know that van was there? He must have sensed it somehow — maybe the size of it, the way sound bounced off it. Bloom had heard that blind people develop a kind of sixth sense about the space around them.
Penrose! Bloom remembered suddenly. That was the name of that odd fellow from the old neighborhood.

Bloom thought about how much blind people could learn to do — reading with their fingers, tuning pianos. People are always surprised that someone with a disability can be clever, as if only their eyes matter. Of course, when you lose one sense, the others become stronger.

Their sense of smell must be very powerful too, Bloom thought. Every street would have its own smell. Every person too. In spring and summer, the smells would change. They say you can't taste wine properly without being able to see it.

Bloom thought about how different the world must be for someone who couldn't see. So many things we take for granted — faces, colors, the beauty of a sunset. What kind of picture did the blind man have in his mind? He could hear voices, feel temperatures, sense when someone was near.
Bloom remembered he needed to stop by the post office. He had to send a reply to someone and mail a postal order. He'd take care of it today. But first, he needed to think it over.

Bloom gently touched his own hair, combed back above his ears. Then he felt his cheek. Smooth skin with fine, downy hair. He thought about different textures — the smoothness of skin in different places.
Walking past a pub, Bloom discretely felt his stomach. A bit soft, but not too bad.
He straightened his clothes.

Poor fellow! Bloom thought about the blind young man again. Hardly more than a boy. What dreams would he have, never having seen anything? Life must be like a dream for him. Where was the justice in being born that way? Bloom thought of all the terrible things that happen in the world — accidents, disasters. How could anyone believe God was good when such things happened?

Bloom noticed Sir Frederick Falkiner, the judge, going into the Freemasons' hall. A serious, important-looking man, fresh from a big lunch. Judges and lawyers, always telling stories about their court cases. Bloom thought about justice — some judges were harsh, others kind. And a guilty person always looks guilty, somehow.

Bloom noticed a poster: the Mirus Bazaar, sponsored by the Lord Lieutenant, happening on the sixteenth — today! It was raising money for Mercer's Hospital. The great oratorio The Messiah was first performed as a charity event too. Maybe he'd drop by Ballsbridge later and try to visit Mr. Keyes about the advertisement.
Mr. Bloom arrived at Kildare Street. First things first — the Library.
Straw hat in the sunlight. Tan shoes. Turned-up trouser cuffs. It was him. It was definitely him.
Bloom's heart jumped. Boylan! He quickly turned to the right toward the Museum. Away from him. The statues. The goddesses.
Is it him? Almost certainly. Don't look. The wine has made my face red. Why did I drink that? Too strong. Yes, it is him. That walk. Don't look. Keep going.
Walking quickly toward the museum gate with long strides, Bloom looked up at the building. Handsome architecture. Was Boylan following him? No, surely not.
Maybe he didn't see me, Bloom thought.
Bloom's breath came in short, nervous sighs. Quick — the cold stone statues inside. Safe in a minute.
No. He didn't see me. It's after two o'clock. He was just passing the gate.
My heart! Bloom thought.
He stared at the cream-colored stone curves of the building, trying to calm down. Beautiful Greek architecture.
Look for something in my pocket, Bloom thought. Look busy.
His hand quickly went into a pocket and pulled out a leaflet — Agendath Netaim, the advertisement about buying land in Palestine. Where had he put it?
Busy looking, he told himself. Act normal.
He shoved the leaflet back.
This afternoon, she said. Molly had said Boylan was coming this afternoon.
I'm looking for something, Bloom pretended. Yes, that. Try all pockets. Handkerchief. Newspaper. Where did I... Oh yes. Trousers. Potato — his good luck charm. Purse. Where?
Hurry. Walk calmly. Just another moment. My heart.
His hand searching through his pockets found the bar of soap in his hip pocket, along with a paper from the chemist's. Oh, soap — yes, there it is. He reached the museum gate.
Safe!

chapters.title: Episode 9 — Scylla and Charybdis
paragraphs: The friendly head librarian, Mr. Lyster, a Quaker gentleman, spoke in a gentle, purring voice to comfort his listeners:

—And we have, don't we, those wonderful pages where the great German writer Goethe wrote about Shakespeare. A great poet writing about another great poet. He described Hamlet as a hesitating soul, torn by doubts, just like people in real life.
He took a step forward on his creaking leather shoes, then a step back on the quiet library floor.
A silent library attendant opened the door slightly and beckoned to Mr. Lyster.

—Just a moment, Mr. Lyster said, already heading toward the door but still talking. The beautiful dreamer who comes to grief when he meets hard reality. One always feels that Goethe's observations are so true. True in the bigger picture.
With his shoes creaking, Mr. Lyster hurried off toward the door. Bald and eager, he listened carefully to the attendant's message, nodded, and was gone.
Two people left in the conversation, Stephen thought.
—Monsieur de la Palice, Stephen said with a sneer, was alive fifteen minutes before he died. In other words, that was an obvious observation.
—Have you found those six brave medical students, John Eglinton asked with a sharp tone, to write a great poem at your command? You call it "The Sorrows of Satan."
Smile, Stephen told himself. Smile like Cranly does.

Stephen thought of a silly rhyme:
First he tickled her
     Then he patted her
     Then he helped her out
     For he was a medical student
     A jolly old medi...
—I think you'd need one more person for Hamlet, Eglinton continued. Seven is a special number to mystics. The poet Yeats calls them the shining seven.

John Eglinton, with his glittering eyes and reddish hair, looked toward the shadowy figure of George Russell, known as A.E. — a bearded man with an almost holy look about him. Eglinton laughed quietly, but no one laughed with him.
Stephen thought of lines about Satan from Milton's Paradise Lost, weeping floods of tears, mixed with a rude line from Dante's poetry.
He keeps my foolish words as weapons against me, Stephen thought about Mulligan.

Stephen's mind wandered to thoughts about his friend Cranly and Irish patriots, about Kathleen — the symbol of Ireland — and her beautiful green fields. About people gathering in the shadows of the countryside.
Mulligan has my telegram, Stephen remembered.
This might be foolish, but I'll keep going, Stephen thought.

—Our young Irish poets, John Eglinton said critically, have yet to create a character that the world can place alongside Shakespeare's Hamlet. Though I admire the prince as much as old Ben Jonson did.

—All these questions are just for scholars to argue about, Russell declared from his shadowy corner. I mean, whether Hamlet represents Shakespeare or King James or the Earl of Essex. It's like clergymen arguing about whether Jesus really existed. Art should reveal ideas to us, spiritual truths. The deepest poetry is about beauty, not about individual lives.
A.E. has been talking to some American reporter, Stephen thought with amusement.
—The great thinkers were once students themselves, Stephen said politely. Aristotle was once Plato's student.
—And has remained so, one would hope, John Eglinton said calmly. You can picture Aristotle as a model student carrying his diploma under his arm.
He laughed again at Russell's smiling, bearded face.
Stephen's mind raced through religious and mystical ideas — the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit. All the spiritual mysteries that thinkers like Russell loved to discuss.
Stephen thought about all the mystical figures and secret societies that Russell was involved with — hidden masters, spiritual lodges, ancient wisdom.
Stephen's thoughts became playful and irreverent about the mystical groups.
Mr. Best entered the room — a tall, young, gentle man with a mild expression. He carried a new, clean notebook in his hand.
—That model student Aristotle, Stephen said, would find Hamlet's famous speech about life after death as shallow as anything Plato wrote.
John Eglinton frowned and said, growing annoyed:
—Upon my word, it makes me angry to hear anyone compare Aristotle with Plato!
—Which of the two, Stephen asked, would have kicked me out of his ideal society?
Stephen's mind played with philosophical definitions. What is a horse? What is space? What is God? His thoughts darted through centuries of philosophy in seconds.
Mr. Best came forward in a friendly way toward his colleague.
—Haines has left, he said. The Englishman from the tower.
—Has he?
—I was showing him a book about Irish mythology. He's very excited about Hyde's Love Songs of Connacht. I couldn't bring him in for the discussion. He's gone to the bookshop to buy a copy.
Stephen thought of a verse about sending a little book out into the world.
—The smoky Irish atmosphere is going to his head, John Eglinton commented.
We feel at home in England, Stephen thought bitterly. The Englishman is gone. I smoked his tobacco. Ireland — an emerald set in a ring of sea.

—People don't realize how powerful love songs can be, Russell warned mysteriously. The movements that change the world are born in the dreams of simple people on hillsides. For them, the earth isn't just a piece of land you can buy and sell.
Mr. Best turned a friendly face to Stephen after these words.

—The French poet Mallarmé, you know, Best said cheerfully, wrote wonderful pieces about Hamlet. He described him walking around, reading the book of himself, you know? Reading the book of his own mind.
His free hand made small, graceful gestures in the air.

Hamlet
or
The Absent-Minded One
A Play by Shakespeare
He repeated to John Eglinton:
—"A Play by Shakespeare" — you know, it's so French. The French point of view. "Hamlet or..."
—The absent-minded fellow, Stephen finished for him.
John Eglinton laughed.
—Yes, I suppose that would be the translation, he said. Excellent people, the French, but disappointingly short-sighted about some things.
Stephen thought about the extravagant murders in the play.

—A destroyer of souls is what the writer Robert Greene called Shakespeare, Stephen said. He was a butcher's son, after all — not afraid of violence. In the play, nine people die to avenge one death. Our Father who art in purgatory.
Stephen thought of his friend Cranly, who followed him silently like a soldier.
Lines from an old poem about enemies: "Pups and mothers of murderous foes whom none but we had spared..."
Caught between English smiles and American shouts. Between the devil and the deep sea, Stephen thought.
—He'll tell you that Hamlet is a ghost story, John Eglinton explained to Mr. Best. Like the fat boy in Dickens, he wants to make our flesh creep.
Listen! Listen! Oh, Listen! — the words of the Ghost in the play.
Stephen felt the words creeping through him.
"If thou didst ever..." the Ghost began to say.

—What is a ghost? Stephen asked with sudden energy. Someone who has faded from the world — through death, through absence, through changing times. London in Shakespeare's day was as far from his hometown of Stratford as wicked Paris is from innocent Dublin. Who is the ghost in Shakespeare's Hamlet? Who is King Hamlet?
John Eglinton leaned back in his chair to consider this.
Lifted, Stephen thought. I've got his attention.

—Picture this hour of the day in mid-June, Stephen said, asking with a quick glance for their attention. The flag is flying over the theater by the river Thames. Nearby, a bear named Sackerson growls in a pit. Sailors who traveled with the explorer Drake are chewing their tobacco. The audience is gathering.
Use everything you know, Stephen told himself. Make them your partners in the story.

—Shakespeare has left the French Protestant family's house on Silver Street and walks along the river by the swan pens. But he doesn't stop to watch the mother swan guiding her babies toward the reeds. The Swan of Avon has other things on his mind.
Setting the scene, Stephen thought. Help me, imagination!

—The play begins. An actor comes on stage in the shadows, wearing borrowed armor — a well-built man with a deep voice. He plays the ghost, the king. And the actor playing this ghost of a king is Shakespeare himself. He has been studying the role of Hamlet's dead father all year long.
"Hamlet, I am thy father's spirit,"

the ghost says, telling Hamlet to listen. Shakespeare speaks to a son — the son of his imagination, Prince Hamlet — and at the same time to the ghost of his own real son, Hamnet Shakespeare, who had died in Stratford.

Is it possible, Stephen wondered, that Shakespeare — a ghost himself because he was far from home — wearing the costume of a dead king, speaking his own words to a character with his own son's name... is it possible he was really speaking about himself and his own dead boy?
—But this prying into the private life of a great man, Russell interrupted impatiently.
Are you there, old friend? Stephen thought.

—It's only interesting to gossips, Russell continued. What matters is the plays themselves. When we read the poetry of King Lear, what does it matter how the poet lived? As a French writer said: "As for living, our servants can do that for us." Looking into the private lives of dead writers is cheap entertainment.
Mr. Best's face seemed to agree.
Stephen thought of a poem about waves washing over everything, carrying things away.
And what about that pound Russell lent me when I was hungry? Stephen thought.
I needed it, he answered himself.
Take this money, then.
Go on! You spent most of it, Stephen's conscience reminded him.
Do you plan to pay it back?
Oh, yes.
When? Now?
Well... No.
When, then?
I paid my way, Stephen told himself. I paid my way.
Easy now. He's from the north. You owe him.
Wait. Five months have passed. Every molecule in my body has changed since then. I'm a different person now. The other me got that money.
Buzz. Buzz. His thoughts buzzed.
But I, my essential self, remain the same through all these changing forms — held together by memory.
I am the one who made mistakes and the one who tried to do better.
A child once. Protected by Father Conmee from being punished at school.
I, I and I. Just me, Stephen thought.
A.E.I.O.U. — I owe you, he punned on the vowels.
—Do you mean to go against three centuries of tradition? John Eglinton demanded. Shakespeare's wife Anne Hathaway has been dead to literature since before she was born.

—She died, Stephen responded, sixty-seven years after she was born. She saw him born and saw him die. She held him as a baby. She had his children. And she placed coins on his eyelids to close them when he was dead.
Stephen thought of his own mother's deathbed. The candle. The covered mirror. The one who brought him into the world, lying there under cheap flowers.
I cried alone, Stephen remembered.
John Eglinton stared into his desk lamp, thinking.
—The world believes that Shakespeare made a mistake marrying her, he said, and got out of it as quickly as he could.
—Nonsense! Stephen said sharply. A man of genius doesn't make mistakes. His errors are deliberate — they're doorways to discovery.
Just then, the doorways of discovery opened to let in the librarian, Mr. Lyster, tiptoeing back on his creaking shoes.
—A difficult wife, John Eglinton said cleverly, is not exactly a useful doorway to discovery. What useful discovery did the philosopher Socrates learn from his famously nagging wife Xanthippe?

—He learned how to argue, Stephen answered. And from his mother, who was a midwife, he learned how to help ideas be born. But neither midwifery nor nagging could help him when the judges forced him to drink poison.
—But what about Anne Hathaway? Mr. Best's quiet voice asked. Yes, we seem to be forgetting her, just as Shakespeare himself forgot her.
Best looked from Russell's beard to Eglinton's bald head, then to the librarian, gently reminding them all.
—Shakespeare was clever with words, Stephen said, and had a good memory. He remembered Anne well enough as he walked to London, whistling the tune of "The Girl I Left Behind Me."
And when will it be my turn? Stephen wondered. When will I have my chance?
Come on! he urged himself.
—Ryefield, Mr. Best said brightly, lifting his new book. That's where they courted!
He read aloud happily for everyone:

"Between the acres of the rye
     These pretty country folk would lie."
Paris — city of pleasures, Stephen recalled.
A tall, bearded figure in plain homespun clothing rose from the shadows and checked a pocket watch.
—I'm afraid I need to leave for the newspaper office, Russell said.
Going already? Stephen thought. There might be something useful to gain here.
—Are you going? John Eglinton asked, his eyebrows rising. Shall we see you at Moore's gathering tonight? Piper is coming.
—Piper! Mr. Best exclaimed. Is Piper back in town?
Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers, Stephen thought playfully.
—I don't know if I can make it, Russell said. It's Thursday. We have our spiritual meeting. If I can get away in time.

Stephen thought mockingly about Russell's mystical group — sitting cross-legged in their meeting room, studying ancient texts, waiting for spiritual revelations. Believing in hidden masters and cosmic energy. All very earnest.
Stephen thought of a poem about a soul dwelling in a body for years.
—They say we're going to have a literary surprise, the librarian said in a friendly way. Mr. Russell is gathering together a collection of our younger poets' verses. We're all looking forward to it.
He looked anxiously around the lamplight at three faces shining in the dim room.
Look at this moment, Stephen told himself. Remember it.

Stephen looked down at his wide hat hanging from his walking stick over his knee. My helmet and sword, he thought. He pressed his two index fingers together — an old experiment of Aristotle's. With your fingers crossed, one thing can feel like two.
Listen, he told himself.

Stephen thought about the young poets whose work Russell was collecting — Colum, Starkey. George Roberts was handling the business side. Another man would give it a good review in the newspaper. Everyone was excited about the book. Did these young poets really have genius? Even Yeats had praised their work.
Stephen thought of Cordelia from King Lear — the loneliest, most faithful daughter.
Now, polish your argument, Stephen told himself.
—Thank you very much, Mr. Russell, Stephen said, standing up. If you would be kind enough to give this letter to Mr. Norman at the newspaper...
—Oh, yes. If he thinks it's important, it will go in. We receive so much mail.
—I understand, Stephen said. Thanks.
Stephen thought about the newspaper — a farmers' paper, really.

The playwright Synge has promised an article too, Russell said. Are people going to read our work? I feel they will. The Irish language society wants something in Irish. I hope you'll come round tonight. Bring Starkey along.
Stephen sat down.
The librarian came back from seeing Russell off. His face was slightly pink as he said:
—Mr. Dedalus, your views are most interesting.
He tiptoed forward on his creaking shoes, and under cover of the noise of people leaving, said quietly:
—Is it your view, then, that Shakespeare's wife was not faithful to him?
Stephen noticed his worried face. Why does he care? Is he just being polite, or does he feel something deeper?
—Where there is a making-up, Stephen said, there must have been a falling-out first.
—Yes.

Stephen's mind filled with images of Shakespeare as a fox — hunted, hiding, lonely. A man who charmed women but was also betrayed by them. The whole story of love and betrayal, woven like a fox's trail through the woods.
—Yes. So you think...
The door closed behind the last person leaving.
A peaceful quiet suddenly settled over the small vaulted room — warm, still air.
Like a lamp in an ancient temple, Stephen thought.
This is a place where people think about things that never happened — what Caesar might have done if he'd listened to the fortune-teller, what might have been, what was possible.
Books surrounded him like coffins of thought, preserved in the spice of words. The Egyptian god Thoth, protector of libraries, watched over them all.
The books are silent now, Stephen thought. But once these ideas were alive in people's minds. And still, even dead, they want to tell their stories, to make me act on their behalf.
—Certainly, John Eglinton said thoughtfully, of all great men, Shakespeare is the most mysterious. We know almost nothing about him except that he lived and suffered.
—But Hamlet is so personal, isn't it? Mr. Best pleaded. I mean, it's like a private diary, you know? I don't really care about who kills whom in the plot...
He rested his clean book on the edge of the desk with a defiant smile.
Little John Eglinton said:
—I was prepared for unusual ideas from what Mulligan told us, but I should warn you that if you're trying to shake my belief that Shakespeare IS Hamlet, you have a hard job ahead.
Bear with me, Stephen thought.
Stephen faced Eglinton's stern, wrinkled brow bravely. A dangerous look, like a legendary serpent whose gaze could kill.

—Just as our bodies are being woven and unwoven every day, Stephen said — molecules changing and shifting — so does the artist weave and unweave his own image. And just as the birthmark on my chest is in the same place it was when I was born, even though my whole body has changed around it, so through the changing events of his life, the artist always remains himself.
That's a good line from the Scottish poet Drummond, Stephen thought. He helped me over that tricky bit.
—Yes, Mr. Best said eagerly. I feel Hamlet is quite young. The bitterness might come from the father, but the scenes with Ophelia are surely written from the son's perspective.
He's got it wrong, Stephen thought. He sees me in the father. But I am in the son.
—That birthmark is the last thing to change, Stephen said with a laugh.
John Eglinton made a disapproving face.
—If that were the mark of genius, he said, genius would be everywhere. Shakespeare's later plays, which the great scholar Renan admired, breathe a very different spirit.
—The spirit of making peace, the librarian murmured.
—There can be no making peace, Stephen said, if there hasn't first been a breaking apart.
I already said that, Stephen realized.

—If you want to know what events cast their shadow over Shakespeare's darkest tragedies — King Lear, Othello, Hamlet, Troilus and Cressida — look to see when the shadow lifts. What softens the heart of a man who has been through terrible storms? What brings him peace?
Stephen pictured a man battered by waves, blinded by salt water.
—A child, Stephen said. A girl placed in his arms. Marina.
—Following obscure side paths instead of main roads is a constant temptation for clever people, John Eglinton objected. The main roads may be boring, but they lead somewhere.

Stephen thought about all the scholars chasing theories about Shakespeare — some claiming he was really Bacon, others finding secret codes in the plays. And the mystical writers hiding behind pen names. Where were they all heading?

"How many miles to Dublin?
     Three score and ten, sir.
     Will we be there by candlelight?"
—The scholar Mr. Brandes accepts The Tempest as the first play of Shakespeare's final period, Stephen said.
—Does he? And what does Mr. Sidney Lee say about it? Eglinton asked.

—Marina, Perdita, Miranda, Stephen said — a child of storm, a wonder, that which was lost. What was lost is given back to him: his daughter's child. In the play Pericles, the father says his dead wife looked just like this young girl. Will any man love the daughter if he hasn't first loved the mother?
—The art of being a grandfather, Mr. Best murmured softly.
—Won't he see his own youth reborn in her, with the memory of his younger self added to make a new image?
Do I even know what I'm talking about? Stephen wondered. Love. Yes. The word everyone knows.

—For a man of genius, his own image is the standard for everything he experiences, Stephen continued. He'll see other men of his bloodline as nature's failed attempts to copy him. But in his daughter, or his granddaughter, he'll see himself reborn.
The librarian's kind face brightened with hope.

—I hope Mr. Dedalus will develop his theory for everyone to hear, the librarian said. And we should mention other Irish Shakespeare scholars — George Bernard Shaw, for one. And Frank Harris, whose articles on Shakespeare are quite brilliant.
He stopped speaking happily and sat quietly among them, like a prize in their contest of ideas.
Stephen thought about how Shakespeare might have spoken tenderly to his wife in their early days. "Do you love me, dear?"

—That may be true too, Stephen said. There's a saying of Goethe's that Eglinton likes to quote: "Be careful what you wish for in youth because you'll get it in middle life." Why did Shakespeare write love poems to someone unfaithful? He was driving at something deeper.
They're listening, Stephen thought. And I'm pouring ideas into their ears.

—The soul had already been wounded deeply, Stephen continued. In Hamlet, poison is poured into the ear of a sleeping king. But those who are killed in their sleep can't know how they died unless God gives them that knowledge in the afterlife. That's what the Ghost reveals — the truth about his own murder.
—Amen! a voice called from the doorway.
Have you found me, my enemy? Stephen thought, recognizing the voice.
A pause in the performance.
Buck Mulligan appeared in the doorway with a cheeky grin, then strode forward cheerfully in his colorful way to greet the smiling group. Stephen's telegram — he still had it.
—You were talking about some kind of gassy, boneless creature, if I'm not mistaken? Mulligan asked Stephen with mock seriousness.
Mulligan tipped his Panama hat in a playful greeting, as if it were a toy.
They welcomed him warmly. They'll learn to respect what they now laugh at, Stephen thought.
A group of mockers, Stephen thought. False friends.

Stephen's mind raced through a dizzying summary of Christianity — God who sent Himself, who was betrayed, beaten, nailed up, died, rose again, and sat down at His own right hand. The whole story in one breathless thought.
[A mental picture flashed through Stephen's mind.]
He imagined veils falling away, flowers blooming, bells ringing in beautiful harmony.
—Yes, indeed, the librarian said pleasantly. A most interesting discussion. Mr. Mulligan, I'm sure, has his own theory about the play and about Shakespeare. All points of view should be represented.
He smiled at everyone equally.
Buck Mulligan pretended to think hard:
—Shakespeare? he said. I seem to know that name.
A bright, mischievous smile spread across his face.
—Oh, of course, he said, remembering with a grin. The fellow who writes like the Irish playwright Synge.
Mr. Best turned to him.
—Haines was looking for you, he said. Did you run into him? He'll meet you later at the café. He's gone to buy a book of Irish love songs.
—I came through the museum, Buck Mulligan said. Was he here?

—The great poet's countrymen, John Eglinton said, are perhaps getting tired of all our clever theories. I hear that an actress played Hamlet for the four hundred and eighth time last night in Dublin. Some scholars even believed the prince was really a woman. Perhaps we've had enough Shakespeare theories.

—The most brilliant theory of all is Oscar Wilde's story, Mr. Best said, lifting his shiny notebook. In "The Portrait of Mr. W. H.," Wilde claims the sonnets were written for a boy actor named Willie Hughes — a man of all hues, all colors.
—For Willie Hughes, you say? the librarian asked.
Or Will Himself? Stephen wondered. W. H. — who am I?
—I mean, for Willie Hughes, Mr. Best corrected himself. Of course it's all a playful argument — Hughes and hues and colors — but it's so typical of Wilde's cleverness. The very essence of his wit.
His glance touched their faces lightly as he smiled. He was a tame version of Wilde's spirit, Stephen thought.
Stephen thought mockingly: You're very clever. You spent the money I earned drinking with journalists.
How much did I spend? Oh, a few shillings, Stephen thought.
A few shillings on a bunch of newspaper men. Some humor, wet and dry.
Stephen thought about youth and cleverness, about desire and getting older.
Stephen's mind wandered through images of love and temptation.
Eve in the Garden. Sin. The serpent's kiss.
—Do you think it's only a joke? the librarian was asking. The person who mocks is never taken seriously, even when he's being most serious.
They discussed the seriousness of Mulligan's mockery.
Buck Mulligan studied Stephen's face for a moment. Then, wagging his head, he came closer and pulled a folded telegram from his pocket. His quick lips read it with a delighted smile.
—Telegram! he cried. Wonderful stuff! A telegram! Like an announcement from the Pope!
He sat on the corner of the desk, reading aloud with joy:
—"The sentimentalist is someone who wants to enjoy things without paying the emotional price." Signed: Dedalus. Where did you send it from? College Green. Have you spent all the money yet?
Joyfully he stuffed the telegram into his pocket, then put on a mock-Irish country accent:

—It's what I'm telling you, sir, we were feeling terrible sick, Haines and myself, when the telegram arrived. We needed a strong drink to settle us down. And there we were, waiting hours for you, with our tongues hanging out!
He pretended to wail:
—And you off sending us your big fancy words while we were dying of thirst waiting for you!
Stephen laughed.
Quickly, seriously, Buck Mulligan leaned in close.
—The writer Synge is looking for you, he whispered. He heard you were rude at his front door in Glasthule. He's furious.
—Me? Stephen exclaimed. That was your doing, not mine!
Buck Mulligan threw his head back, laughing at the dark ceiling.
—He'll get you! he laughed.
Stephen thought about Mulligan's harsh, mocking face — they'd argued over dinner in Paris. Mulligan was full of words but little real meaning. A man he'd met who was always looking for free drinks.
—Mr. Lyster, an attendant said from the doorway.
—... in which everyone can find something for themselves, the librarian was saying. So the judge Mr. Madden has found references to hunting in Shakespeare's plays... Yes? What is it?

—There's a gentleman here, sir, the attendant said, stepping forward with a business card. From the Freeman's Journal newspaper. He wants to look at the old files of the Kilkenny People newspaper from last year.
—Certainly, certainly, certainly. Is the gentleman...?
The librarian took the card, glanced at it without really seeing it, set it down, looked again, and asked:
—Is he...? Oh, he's out there!
Eagerly, Mr. Lyster hurried off into the daylit corridor, talking politely and helpfully.
—This gentleman? From the Freeman's Journal? The Kilkenny People? Of course. Good day, sir. We certainly have those...
A patient figure stood waiting in the corridor, listening.
—All the leading regional papers... Northern Whig, Cork Examiner, Enniscorthy Guardian, 1903... Will you please follow... This way, sir...
Politely and helpfully, he led the way to the newspaper archives, a dark figure following behind him.
The door closed.
—It's that fellow Bloom! Buck Mulligan cried.
He jumped up and snatched the business card from the desk.
—What's his name? Bloom, he read.
He went on rudely, making fun of Bloom's Jewish background:
—I found him over in the museum where I went to admire the Greek statues. He was staring at the statue of Venus. You should have seen his eyes!
Suddenly he turned to Stephen:
—He knows you. He knows your father. Oh, I'm afraid he's quite the admirer of beauty. His eyes were fixed on the finest statue of Venus in the place!

—We want to hear more of your theory, John Eglinton said, turning back to Stephen. We're getting interested in Mrs. Shakespeare. Until now we'd thought of her as a patient, stay-at-home wife, like Odysseus's Penelope.

—The ancient Greek thinker Antisthenes, Stephen said, awarded the prize for beauty not to the famous Helen of Troy, but to faithful Penelope — the one who waited at home. Shakespeare lived twenty years in London and during all that time, he never invited his wife to visit. He never set up a home for her there.
Stephen's mind flashed through memories of Paris streets.
—The finest society in London, Stephen continued. And Shakespeare's own landlord's wife, who always had a cup of wine ready for visitors.
Buck Mulligan looked upward with mock piety, pretending to pray:
—Blessed saints preserve us!
—And the daughters of kings, Stephen went on. And all sorts of high-society ladies. But in all those twenty years, what do you suppose poor Anne was doing back in Stratford?
Stephen imagined Shakespeare walking through London's herb gardens, his hair going gray. And far away at home, his wife...
Buck Mulligan rapped sharply on John Eglinton's desk.
—Whom do you suspect? he demanded.
—Think of him as the rejected lover in the sonnets, Stephen said. Rejected once, rejected twice. A nobleman stole the woman Shakespeare loved.
Stephen thought about love that was forbidden to speak openly.
—As an Englishman, John Eglinton put in, Shakespeare naturally admired the nobility.
Stephen thought of old walls in the sun where lizards dart about.

—It seems so, Stephen agreed. Perhaps, like Socrates, Shakespeare had a midwife's wisdom from his mother and a difficult marriage to sharpen his wit. But his wife, the older woman who had charmed a younger man, was no faithful Penelope. Somewhere along the way, she found comfort closer to home.
Stephen turned boldly in his chair.

—The proof is on your side to deny it, not mine, he said firmly. If you say Shakespeare didn't criticize his wife in Hamlet, then explain why she's never mentioned during the thirty-four years between their marriage and the day he wrote his will.

Oh, she is mentioned once, Stephen thought. When Shakespeare was living richly in London, she had to borrow forty shillings from a shepherd back home. And then there's the famous will — where he left her his "second-best bed."
He faced their silence.
John Eglinton responded about the will — lawyers had explained that she was entitled to her share of the estate by law, so the will wasn't as insulting as it seemed.
But Mulligan quipped mockingly about second-best beds.
Stephen played with the words in his mind: Left-her-his second-best bed. Left. Her. His. Second. Best.
Whoa!
—Country people didn't have much furniture back then, John Eglinton observed. Same as in Irish country life today.

—But he was a rich gentleman, Stephen argued. He had a coat of arms, land in Stratford, property in London. He was a businessman and investor. Why didn't he leave her the best bed if he wanted her comfortable?
—It's clear there were two beds — a best and a second-best, Mr. Best said with a clever smile.
—Separation from the dining table and the bedroom, Buck Mulligan translated from the Latin, and everyone smiled.
—Ancient history mentions famous beds, Eglinton mused. Let me think...

—Ancient history also mentions the philosopher Aristotle, Stephen said, who when he was dying far from home, freed his slaves, honored his teachers, asked to be buried near his dead wife, and told his friends to be kind. A beautiful death.
—Do you mean Shakespeare died like that too? Mr. Best asked with concern.
—He died after drinking too much, Buck Mulligan said bluntly. A quart of ale — a fine drink for a king! Oh, I must tell you what Professor Dowden said!
—What? both Best and Eglinton asked.
Stephen thought: William Shakespeare and Company, Limited. The People's William.

—It was wonderful! Buck Mulligan said with a sigh. I asked Dowden what he thought about certain accusations against Shakespeare. The old professor raised his hands and said: "All we can say is that life was very exciting in those days!" Wonderful!
Stephen's thoughts turned dark for a moment.
—The sense of beauty can lead us in the wrong direction, Mr. Best said to Eglinton.
John Eglinton replied firmly:
—The doctor can tell us what those words really mean. You can't have everything both ways.
Will they take away my best argument? Stephen worried.

—And the sense of property, Stephen said, bringing the discussion back on track. Shakespeare drew the character of Shylock from his own experience with money. He was himself a grain dealer and money lender. He hoarded corn during famine and charged interest on loans.
Stephen thought: I'm mixing philosophy, literature, and economics together nicely.
—Prove that Shakespeare was Jewish, John Eglinton dared. Your university teacher says he was a Roman Catholic.
I need to be careful here, Stephen thought.
—He was made in Germany, Stephen replied wittily, as the finest polisher of Italian stories.
—A man of infinite variety, Mr. Best reminded everyone. The poet Coleridge called Shakespeare "myriad-minded."
Stephen thought about friendship and what Saint Thomas Aquinas wrote about it.
—Saint Thomas, Stephen began...
—Pray for us! Monk Mulligan groaned, slumping into a chair.
He pretended to wail in a mock-Irish accent:
—It's destroyed we are! It's ruined we are from this day!
Everyone smiled at his performance.

—Saint Thomas, Stephen continued with a smile, wrote about how similar things are connected in nature. When a person hoards things selfishly — whether it's money or love — it reveals something about their character.
—Or his stubbornness, Buck Mulligan added.
—Poor Will Shakespeare is being treated roughly today, gentle Mr. Best said gently.
—Which Will? Buck Mulligan joked. We're getting confused with all the Wills.
—The will to live, John Eglinton said philosophically. For poor Anne, Shakespeare's widow, it became the will to die.
—Rest in peace, Stephen said.
A snatch of song ran through his mind: "What of all the will to do? It has vanished long ago..."

—She lies in that second-best bed, Stephen continued, like a queen in mourning. Even though you might prove that beds were rare and valuable in those days, as rare as motorcars are today. In her old age she turns to religion, as people often do when their hearts have been broken.

—History shows that to be true, Eglinton agreed. The generations replace each other. But as the saying goes, a man's worst enemies are often in his own family. I think Russell was right — what does it matter who Shakespeare was? The plays are what matter.

Stephen thought about Eglinton — a shy man, hiding behind his stern manner. He had a father who visited him sometimes, and Eglinton seemed embarrassed by it, as if he wanted to hide his humble origins.
Your own father, Stephen thought. Mulligan knows your old fellow too.
Stephen remembered rushing home from Paris to his mother's deathbed. He'd touched his father's hand on the quayside. His father's eyes wished him well but didn't really see him anymore.

—A father, Stephen said, fighting against a feeling of hopelessness, is a necessary evil. Shakespeare wrote Hamlet in the months after his own father died. Here was a man with grown-up daughters and thirty-five years of life behind him, looking at the world through the eyes of a young prince. Fatherhood — the relationship between a man and his son — is the great mystery. Who is the father of any son?
What am I trying to prove? Stephen wondered.
I know. Be quiet. I have my reasons, he told himself.
More, more, keep going.
Am I forced to say all this? he wondered.

—Fathers and sons are separated by a powerful bond of shame, Stephen continued. A deep, natural shame. In all of history, the most unthinkable crime has been against one's own parents. Sons and mothers, fathers and daughters — these relationships are sacred. But the bond between father and son is the strangest of all.
I thought of this idea in Paris, Stephen remembered.
—What connects them in nature? Stephen asked. A moment of chance.
Am I a father? Stephen wondered. What if I were?
His hand trembled with uncertainty.

—The ancient thinker Sabellius believed that the Father was Himself His Own Son, Stephen said. Saint Thomas Aquinas argued against this. But think about it: if a father who has no son isn't truly a father, and a son who has no father isn't truly a son, then fatherhood itself is a kind of idea that depends on the relationship existing.
John Eglinton's eyes brightened with pleasure behind his glasses.
Flatter him a little, Stephen thought. Just a touch.
—Himself his own father, Mulligan said to himself with mock amazement. Wait — I'm pregnant with an idea! A play is being born! Let me give birth to it!
He clutched his forehead with both hands, pretending to be in labor.

—As for Shakespeare's family, Stephen said, his mother's name lives on in the Forest of Arden. Her death inspired the scene with Volumnia in Coriolanus. His young son Hamnet's death is echoed in the death of young Arthur in King John. And Hamlet, the black prince, is the grown-up version of all Shakespeare's dead sons.
—The plot thickens, John Eglinton said.
The librarian tiptoed back in, his mask-like face showing he was in a hurry.
Door closed. Cell of quiet. Another day in the library.
Three listeners. They.
I, you, he, they, Stephen counted.
Come on, let's get to it, Stephen thought.

The discussion shifted into a more dramatic format, like a play:

STEPHEN: Shakespeare had three brothers — Gilbert, Edmund, Richard. Old Gilbert once told someone how he got a free pass from his brother Will to see a play in London.
JOHN EGLINTON: Names! What's in a name?
BEST: Richard is my name, actually. I hope you're going to say something nice about Richard! (Everyone laughed.)
BUCK MULLIGAN: (Humming softly, then quieter...)
Then he sang a silly medical students' song.

STEPHEN: In Shakespeare's plays, the villains — Iago, Richard the Third, Edmund in King Lear — two of them share the names of his own brothers. The last play was written while his brother Edmund was dying in London.
BEST: I hope Edmund gets what's coming to him in the play. I don't want Richard, my name, to be the villain... (Everyone laughed again.)
(More laughter.)
THE LIBRARIAN: (Speaking up) But he that steals my good name...

STEPHEN: (Building to a climax) Shakespeare hid his own name, William, throughout the plays — appearing as a minor character here, a clown there, like an old Italian painter hiding his own face in a dark corner of his canvas. In the sonnets, he plays with the word "Will" over and over — Will in the name of desire, Will in his own name.
Everyone seemed satisfied with that, Stephen thought. Me too.
Don't mention that Shakespeare was only nine when some of these events happened, Stephen reminded himself.
Stephen thought about Shakespeare's wife and her arms.
Wait to be courted and won, Stephen thought. But who will court me?
Stephen's mind raced through signs and symbols, through Italian phrases about his destiny and his name.
—What is that, Mr. Dedalus? the librarian asked. Was it some kind of sign from the heavens?
—A star by night, Stephen said. A pillar of cloud by day. Like the signs that guided Moses.
What more is there to say? Stephen wondered.
Stephen looked at his hat, his walking stick, his boots.
My crown, my sword, Stephen thought. But my boots are wearing out and there are holes in my socks. I need new everything.
—You make good use of your name, John Eglinton admitted. Dedalus is a strange enough name. I suppose it explains your wild imagination.
Me, Magee, and Mulligan, Stephen thought. Three M's.

Stephen thought of his mythical namesake — Daedalus, the fabulous inventor who built wings and flew. Where did he fly to? Stephen had taken a boat to France. Not exactly flying. More like a clumsy bird that falls into the sea.
Mr. Best eagerly lifted his book to speak:

—That's very interesting, you know, because we find the same brother theme in old Irish myths too. Just what you're saying. And in Grimm's fairy tales — the third brother who always wins the princess.
Best of the Best brothers, Stephen thought. Good, better, best.
The librarian hurried back over.
—I'd like to know, he said, which brother you... I understand you're suggesting there was some wrongdoing with one of the brothers... But perhaps I'm jumping ahead?
He caught himself, looked around at everyone, and held back.
An attendant called from the doorway:
—Mr. Lyster! Father Dineen wants to see you...
—Oh, Father Dineen! Right away!
Mr. Lyster hurried off once more with his creaking shoes.
John Eglinton pressed the point.
—Come, he said. Let's hear what you have to say about Richard and Edmund. You saved them for last, didn't you?
—In asking you to think about those two brothers, Uncle Richard and Uncle Edmund, Stephen answered, I feel I'm asking a lot. A brother is as easily forgotten as an umbrella.
Like a clumsy bird, Stephen thought of himself.
Where is your own brother? Stephen asked himself. At the pharmacy. And my friends — first Cranly, then Mulligan — now these men. I need to stop just talking and start doing. They're testing me. Act!
Like a clumsy bird again.
I'm tired of my own voice, Stephen thought. I'd give my kingdom for a drink.
Keep going, he told himself.

—You'll say those names were already in the old history books Shakespeare used for his plays, Stephen continued. But why did he choose those particular names? Richard — a wicked, twisted character — woos and wins a woman named Anne. Sound familiar? Then there's Edmund in King Lear, the illegitimate brother who betrays everyone.
—That was Shakespeare's way, John Eglinton defended. He mixed things up. He put the sea coast in a landlocked country and made Ulysses quote Aristotle. That's just how he worked.

—But why? Stephen answered his own question. Because the theme of the false brother, the usurping brother, the betraying brother — or all three in one — was always with Shakespeare. The theme of banishment runs through everything: banishment from the heart, banishment from home. And wherever the theme of betrayal appears, there too is the pain of a man whose trust was broken.
He laughed to free his mind from its own intensity.
Judge Eglinton summed up:
—The truth is somewhere in the middle, he declared. Shakespeare is both the ghost and the prince. He is everything.

—He is, Stephen agreed. The boy in Act One becomes the grown man in Act Five. In his plays, Shakespeare is everything at once — betrayer and betrayed, lover and hater. He acts and is acted upon. His tireless mind studied itself endlessly — and what he found was all of us.
—Cuckoo! Cuckoo! Mulligan called out rudely. Oh, what a scary word!
The dark dome of the library ceiling absorbed and echoed the word.
—And what a character Iago is! John Eglinton exclaimed. When all is said, the French novelist Dumas was right: "After God, Shakespeare has created the most."

—No one truly delights him, Stephen said. Not men, not women. He returns after a lifetime of wandering to the place where he was born, where he has always been, man and boy. His journey done, he plants his mulberry tree and dies. The last act of his life mirrors the first.
—Eureka! Buck Mulligan cried. Eureka! I've got it!
Suddenly happy, he jumped up and reached for Eglinton's desk in one stride.
—May I? he said. The Lord has spoken to me!
He began scribbling something on a slip of paper.
Stephen thought: Take some paper slips on your way out.
—Those who are married, Mr. Best announced cheerfully, shall all live happily. The rest shall stay as they are.
He laughed at John Eglinton, the unmarried scholar.
Stephen thought about the bachelors in the room, each reading Shakespeare alone at night.
—You are misleading us, John Eglinton said firmly to Stephen. You've brought us all this way to show us a love triangle. Do you actually believe your own theory?
—No, Stephen said immediately.
—Are you going to write it up? Mr. Best asked. You should make it into a dialogue, like the Platonic dialogues that Wilde wrote.
John Eglinton smiled.

—Well, in that case, he said, I don't see why you should expect to be paid for something you don't believe in yourself. The great scholars all think there's a mystery in Hamlet but none can quite solve it.
Help me believe, Stephen thought. Or help me not believe. Who helps with belief? Yourself. Who helps with doubt? Everyone else.
—You're the only writer for our journal who asks for money, Eglinton said. And the next issue is already filling up.
Stephen thought about the money he'd borrowed. Economics.
—For a guinea, Stephen offered, you can publish this whole discussion as an interview.
Buck Mulligan stood up from his scribbling, laughing, then said with pretend seriousness:
—I visited the poet Stephen at his summer home and found him deep in study, in the company of some very questionable characters.
He broke away.
—Come, Stephen. Come, wandering poet of the birds.
Come along. You've eaten everything we left for you, Mulligan said. I'll serve you scraps and leftovers.
Stephen stood up.
Life is many days, he thought. This day will end.
—We'll see you tonight, John Eglinton said. Our friend Moore says Mulligan must be there.
Buck Mulligan waved his paper slip and Panama hat.
—Mr. Moore, he said mockingly, lecturer on French literature to the youth of Ireland! I'll be there. Come, Stephen, we poets must drink. Can you walk straight?
Laughing, he led the way...
Drinking until eleven, Stephen thought. A fine Irish evening's entertainment.
Stumbling along...
Stephen followed the stumbling joker...
One day in the national library we had a discussion about Shakespeare, Stephen thought. And now I follow behind him, stepping on his heels.
Stephen, after greeting everyone sadly, followed the cheerful, well-groomed Mulligan out of the quiet library room into the blinding daylight.
What have I learned? Stephen wondered. From them? About myself?
Walk like Haines now — like an Englishman, Stephen thought.

In the reading room, Stephen noticed that the eccentric Mr. Cashel Boyle O'Connor Fitzmaurice Tisdall Farrell had signed the visitors' book with his ridiculously long name. And the librarian was chatting eagerly with a young priest about books.
—Oh, please do, sir... I shall be most happy...
Buck Mulligan amused himself with his own thoughts, nodding and murmuring:
—A happy fellow, that librarian.
The turnstile clicked as they passed through.
Is that...? A blue-ribboned hat... Someone writing idly... What? Did they look up?
The curved railing of the staircase swooped down smoothly.
Buck Mulligan, his Panama hat on like a helmet, walked step by step down the stairs, singing:

"John Eglinton, my dear John,
     Why won't you find a wife?"
He called out to the air:
—Oh, that chinless Eglinton! We went to see the Irish players at the Abbey Theatre, Haines and I. Our actors think they're creating new art for Europe, like the ancient Greeks!
He made a rude noise.
Stephen's mind went back to the questions he hadn't fully answered: Why didn't Shakespeare have more children? And his first child was a girl — what did that mean?
Too late for that now, Stephen thought. Move forward.
Back in the reading room, the two scholars still sat — stern Eglinton with his books, and gentle young Best with his fair hair, like a character from an ancient dialogue.
Eh... I just... wanted... I forgot... he..., Stephen's thoughts stumbled.
—Longworth and Atkinson were there... someone was saying.
Buck Mulligan skipped along nimbly, singing a silly song about a man named Atkinson who never dared to satisfy his thirst in case his wooden leg might fail him.
Just keep joking, Stephen thought. But know yourself.
Stephen stopped. Below him, someone looked up at him quizzically. He stopped too.
—Sad-faced joker, Buck Mulligan teased. The writer Synge has stopped wearing black clothes. Only crows, priests, and English coal are black.
A laugh escaped Mulligan's lips.

—The newspaper editor Longworth is very upset, Mulligan said, about that nasty review you wrote. The woman who got you the newspaper job — and you went and criticized her writing! Couldn't you have been nicer about it?
He went on down the steps, waving his arms gracefully and singing:
—"The most beautiful book from our country in our time. One thinks of Homer." A quote he was mocking.
He stopped at the bottom of the stairs.
—I have an idea for a play, he said seriously.
Stephen looked at the grand columned hall with its shadows.
In sweetly changing voices, Buck Mulligan read from his paper slip:
"Everyone His Own Wife — or — A Honeymoon at Home, a silly play by Buck Mulligan."
He turned a mischievous grin to Stephen:
—The disguise isn't very thick, I'm afraid. But listen to the characters.
He read dramatically:
—Characters!
He listed the silly character names of his made-up play, including a ruined gentleman, some medical students, an old woman, and various other ridiculous figures.
He laughed, shaking his head from side to side, and walked on with Stephen following. He told jokes to the shadows as they went:
—Oh, that night at the Camden Hall when you fell asleep on the floor and the ladies had to step over you!
—I was the most innocent fellow there, Stephen said quietly.
About to pass through a doorway, Stephen sensed someone behind him and stepped aside.
This is the moment, Stephen thought. The decision point. Where am I going? If Socrates goes out today, if Judas goes out tonight — what happens must happen.
My will against his will, Stephen thought. A vast sea between us.
A man passed between them, bowing politely in greeting.
—Good day again, Buck Mulligan called out.
The portico of the library opened before them.

Here I once watched the birds for signs, Stephen thought. Last night I dreamed I was flying. Easily. People wondered at it. Then I was in a strange street. Someone held out a melon to me. You will see, they said.
—The wandering stranger, Buck Mulligan whispered with comic fear. Did you see how he looked at you? That old sailor look. Oh Stephen, you're in danger!
The manner of a university man, Stephen thought.
Day. Sun like a wheelbarrow rolling over the bridge.
A dark figure walked ahead of them with the silent step of a cat, down and out through the gateway.
They followed.
Never mind his teasing, Stephen thought. Let him talk.
The gentle air outlined the edges of houses on Kildare Street. No birds in sight. Two thin plumes of smoke rose from the rooftops, and in a gentle breeze, softly drifted away.
Let it go, Stephen thought. Peace. Like the ancient priests blessing the wide earth.
Stop struggling, Stephen told himself. Find peace — like the wise priests in Shakespeare's Cymbeline, blessing the world from a great altar.

"Praise the gods
     And let our smoke climb up to them
     From our blessed altars."

chapters.title: Episode 10 — Wandering Rocks
paragraphs: Father John Conmee, a Jesuit priest, checked his smooth pocket watch as he came down the church steps. Five minutes to three. Just enough time to walk to Artane, where he needed to arrange a place at a school for a boy whose father had just died.

A one-legged sailor, swinging himself forward on his crutches, growled out a few notes of a song. He stopped in front of a convent and held out his peaked cap, hoping for some coins. The sisters had given him something last time.
Father Conmee crossed to Mountjoy Square. He thought briefly about soldiers and sailors who had lost their legs in wars and ended up in charity hospitals. A sad thought.
—Very well, indeed, Father. And you, Father?
Father Conmee was feeling very well indeed. He might go to the health spa for the waters. He asked after the boys at school. Everything seemed to be going splendidly.
Father Conmee was very glad to see the wife of a member of Parliament looking so well. He asked to be remembered to her husband and promised to visit.
—Good afternoon, Mrs. Sheehy.
Father Conmee tipped his silk hat and smiled politely as he took his leave, admiring how the jet beads of her veil sparkled in the sun.
Father Conmee walked on, smiling to himself as he remembered Father Bernard Vaughan's funny way of speaking with a London accent.
—Pilate! Why don't you hold back that howling mob? Father Conmee imagined Vaughan saying in his cockney voice.
He was a dedicated man, Father Vaughan. He truly did great good in his way. He loved Ireland and the Irish, he always said. His family was Welsh, though — or was it?
Oh, he mustn't forget — he needed to post that letter to the Father Provincial, his boss.

Father Conmee stopped three little schoolboys at the corner of Mountjoy Square. Yes, they were from his school, Belvedere. And were they being good boys at school? Very good. And which was the most well-behaved? Father Conmee smiled at the tiniest boy.
Father Conmee gave a letter from his pocket to a boy named Brunny Lynam and pointed to the bright red pillar-box at the corner of Fitzgibbon Street.
—But mind you don't post yourself into the box, little man, he said with a chuckle.
The three boys stared at Father Conmee with wide eyes and laughed:
—Oh, sir!
—Well, let me see if you can post a letter, Father Conmee said.
Young Brunny Lynam ran across the road and dropped Father Conmee's letter into the mouth of the bright red letter-box. Father Conmee smiled, nodded, and walked along the street, feeling pleased.

Mr. Denis J. Maginni, professor of dancing, walked by in a silk hat, fine coat, white tie, lavender trousers, canary-yellow gloves, and pointed patent leather boots. He walked with great dignity, as if performing a slow dance.
Was that not Mrs. McGuinness? Father Conmee wondered.
Mrs. McGuinness, a stately woman with silver hair, bowed to Father Conmee from the other side of the street. Father Conmee smiled and bowed back. How was she doing?
She carried herself so elegantly, like a queen. And to think she ran a pawnshop! Well, well. Such a queenly manner about her.

Father Conmee walked down Great Charles Street and glanced at a Protestant church on his left. A notice said the Reverend T. R. Greene would be speaking. He felt it was his duty to say a prayer for lost souls.
Father Conmee turned the corner and walked along the North Circular Road. It was surprising there was no tram line on such an important street. Surely there should be one.
A group of schoolboys with their satchels crossed from Richmond Street. They all raised their untidy caps. Father Conmee greeted them kindly. Christian Brothers' boys.
Father Conmee smelled incense drifting from Saint Joseph's Church on Portland Row. A church for elderly women. He raised his hat to the church as he passed.
Near Aldborough House, Father Conmee thought about the nobleman who had once wasted his fortune there. Now it was some kind of office.

Father Conmee began walking along the North Strand Road. Mr. William Gallagher, standing in his shop doorway, greeted him. Father Conmee greeted him back and noticed the unusual smells coming from the shop.
Father Conmee passed a pub where two men leaned lazily against the window. They saluted him and he saluted them back.
Father Conmee passed O'Neill's funeral home where Corny Kelleher was adding up figures in a book while chewing a blade of hay. A policeman on his beat saluted Father Conmee, who saluted him back.

Along Charleville Mall, Father Conmee saw a barge tied up under the trees, with a horse standing with its head hanging down and a bargeman sitting aboard, smoking and staring at a tree branch above him.
On Newcomen Bridge, Father Conmee stepped onto an outward-bound tram.
At the same time, another priest, Father Nicholas Dudley, stepped off an inward-bound tram onto the same bridge.
Father Conmee took the tram because he didn't like walking through the rough area past Mud Island.
Father Conmee sat in a corner of the tram, a blue ticket tucked carefully in one glove, while coins clinked from his other gloved hand into the conductor's palm.

It was a peaceful day. The gentleman with glasses sitting opposite Father Conmee had finished explaining something to the woman beside him — his wife, Father Conmee supposed. She opened her mouth in a tiny yawn.
Father Conmee noticed her perfume in the tram. He also noticed that the awkward-looking man on her other side was sitting uncomfortably on the edge of his seat.
Father Conmee remembered a time at church when he had difficulty placing a communion wafer in the mouth of an awkward old man whose head kept shaking.
