At Annesley Bridge, the tram stopped, and just as it was about to move again, an old woman suddenly stood up to get off. The conductor pulled the bell to hold the tram for her. She got off slowly.
From a billboard, a performer's face grinned down at Father Conmee as he passed.
Father Conmee thought about people of all races around the world — and about his sermon on the African missions, and about the millions of souls who had never heard of Christianity.
At the Howth Road stop, Father Conmee got off the tram. The conductor saluted him and he saluted back.

The Malahide Road was quiet, and it pleased Father Conmee. A pleasant road with a pleasant name. He thought about the noble family who had once lived there, the Talbots, hereditary admirals since the time of King Henry the Fourth.

Father Conmee, walking along, thought about his own little history book and about the grand old houses of the Jesuits, and about a sad story from centuries ago — a noblewoman who was locked away by her jealous husband for many years.
A lonely lady, no longer young, had once walked the shore of a lake, not startled when an otter splashed nearby. Who could know the secrets she carried in her heart?
Father Conmee thought about human weakness, which was necessary for continuing the human race, and about God's mysterious ways.
Father Conmee imagined himself in olden times, honored and respected, hearing people's confessions and smiling at noble faces in grand drawing rooms.
It was a charming day.
A gate in a field showed Father Conmee rows of cabbages, their big green leaves seeming to bow to him. The sky showed a flock of small white clouds drifting slowly across it.
Father Conmee read his prayer book as he walked through fields, his thin-socked ankles tickled by stubble. He remembered walking through these same fields years ago as a young man.
Father Conmee took off his gloves and pulled out his prayer book with its red-edged pages. An ivory bookmark showed him his place.
Afternoon prayers. He should have read them before lunch, but an important visitor had come.
Father Conmee quietly said the Our Father and Hail Mary and crossed himself. God come to my assistance.

He walked calmly, reading the afternoon prayers quietly as he went, until he reached a certain verse: "The beginning of thy words is truth: and every one of thy righteous judgments endureth for ever."

A young man with a red face appeared suddenly from a gap in a hedge, and after him came a young woman carrying wildflowers. The young man tipped his cap quickly; the young woman bent down and pretended to tie her shoe, blushing.
Father Conmee blessed them both solemnly and turned a thin page of his prayer book, continuing to read.

Corny Kelleher closed his big account book and glanced at a pine coffin lid standing in a corner of the funeral home. He got up, went over to it, and spun it on its edge to check its shape and size. He was pleased with how it was made.
Father John Conmee had stepped onto the tram at Newcomen Bridge a while ago.
Corny Kelleher locked his heavy boots together and stood chewing his blade of hay, his hat tilted down.
A policeman on his beat stopped to chat.
—That's a fine day, Mr. Kelleher.
—Ay, Corny Kelleher agreed.
—It's very warm, the policeman said.
Corny Kelleher spat a stream of hay-juice, while from a window on Eccles Street, a generous white arm tossed a coin down to someone below.
—What's the news? Kelleher asked.
—I saw that particular person last evening, the policeman whispered mysteriously.
The one-legged sailor crutched himself around the corner and jerked himself up Eccles Street. Toward a man standing in his doorway in shirtsleeves, he growled some notes of an old song:
—For England...
He swung himself violently forward past two of the Dedalus girls — Katey and Boody — then stopped and growled:
—home and beauty.
At a nearby building, J. J. O'Molloy's tired, worried face was told that Mr. Lambert was in the warehouse with a visitor.

A stout lady stopped, took a copper coin from her purse, and dropped it into the sailor's outstretched cap. He grumbled a thanks, glanced sourly at the windows of the houses, and swung himself forward again.
He stopped and growled angrily:
—For England...
Two barefoot boys, sucking long licorice laces, stopped near him and stared at his missing leg with their mouths open.
He swung himself forward powerfully, stopped, lifted his head toward a window, and sang out deeply:
—home and beauty.

From inside the house came the sound of cheerful whistling, which stopped after a moment. The window blind was pulled aside. A card reading "Unfurnished Apartments" slipped off the window and fell. A generous arm flung a coin out the window and it landed on the pavement.
One of the barefoot boys ran to pick it up and dropped it into the sailor's cap, saying:
—There, sir.
Katey and Boody Dedalus pushed open the door of the steamy kitchen.
—Did you bring the books to the pawnshop? Boody asked.
Maggy, their sister, was at the stove, pushing down a gray mass of laundry beneath bubbling soapy water. She wiped her brow.
—They wouldn't give us anything for them, she said.
Father Conmee was walking through the fields at that moment, his ankles tickled by stubble.
—Where did you try? Boody asked.
—McGuinness's pawnshop.
Boody stamped her foot and threw her schoolbag on the table.
—Curse her! she cried.
Katey went to the stove and peered at it, squinting.
—What's in the pot? she asked.
—Shirts, Maggy said. Just laundry.
Boody cried angrily:
—Is there nothing for us to eat?
Katey, lifting the kettle lid with a pad of her stained skirt, asked:
—And what's in this?
A heavy smell of soup rose up.
—Pea soup, Maggy said.
—Where did you get it? Katey asked.
—Sister Mary Patrick at the convent gave it to us, Maggy said.
Outside, the bellman at the auction house rang his bell.
—Clang!
Boody sat down at the table and said hungrily:
—Give it to me.
Maggy poured thick yellow soup from the kettle into a bowl. Katey, sitting across from Boody, quietly picked up crumbs from the table as she said:
—It's a good thing we have even this much. Where's Dilly?
—Gone to meet Father, Maggy said. Their father, Simon Dedalus.
Boody, breaking big chunks of bread into the yellow soup, added bitterly:
—Our father, who is never at home.
Maggy, pouring soup into Katey's bowl, scolded:
—Boody! Shame on you!
A crumpled piece of paper — the religious flyer that read "Elijah is coming" — floated lightly down the River Liffey, riding the current past bridges and ships, sailing eastward.
In Thornton's flower and fruit shop, a blonde girl arranged a wicker basket with rustling straw. Blazes Boylan handed her a bottle wrapped in pink tissue paper and a small jar.
—Put these in first, will you? he said.
—Yes, sir, the blonde girl said. And the fruit on top.
—That'll do nicely, Blazes Boylan said.
She arranged fat pears neatly in the basket, head to tail, with ripe peaches nestled between them.
Blazes Boylan strolled around the sweet-smelling fruit shop in his new tan shoes, picking up fruits and sniffing their scents — juicy tomatoes, plump and red.
The five sandwich-board men spelling H.E.L.Y.S. plodded past outside, their tall white hats bobbing.
Boylan suddenly turned from a box of strawberries, pulled out a gold watch, and held it at the end of its chain to check the time.
—Can you send these by tram? Right now?
In the distance, a dark figure under a stone archway browsed books on a street seller's cart.
—Certainly, sir. Is it in the city?
—Oh, yes, Blazes Boylan said. Just ten minutes away.
The blonde girl handed him a slip and pencil.
—Will you write the address, sir?
Blazes Boylan wrote at the counter and pushed the slip back to her.
—Send it right away, will you? he said. It's for someone who's not well.
—Yes, sir. I will, sir.
Blazes Boylan jingled coins merrily in his trouser pocket.
—How much do I owe you? he asked.
The blonde girl's slim fingers counted up the fruit.
Boylan glanced at the girl admiringly. He took a red flower from a tall glass vase.
—This one for me? he asked with a charming smile.
The blonde girl glanced sideways at him and blushed, noticing his slightly crooked tie.
—Yes, sir, she said.
She bent over to count the pears and peaches again, her cheeks pink.
Boylan held the red flower between his smiling teeth.
—May I use your telephone, miss? he asked playfully.
—But! said Almidano Artifoni, Stephen's old Italian music teacher.
He gazed over Stephen's shoulder at a statue of the writer Oliver Goldsmith.
Two carriages of tourists passed slowly, the women gripping the handrails. Pale-faced visitors, looking from Trinity College to the grand buildings across the street.

—I had the same ideas myself, Artifoni said in Italian, when I was young like you. But then I realized the world is a rough place. It's a shame. Because your voice — it could earn you money, you know.
—A sacrifice without blood, Stephen replied in Italian, smiling and swinging his walking stick gently.
—Let's hope so, the round-faced Italian said pleasantly. But listen to me. Think about it seriously.
By a statue of the Irish patriot Grattan, a tram from Inchicore unloaded a group of Scottish soldiers from a marching band.
—I'll think about it, Stephen said, glancing down.
—But seriously, eh? Artifoni pressed.
His heavy hand shook Stephen's warmly. Kind eyes. Then he turned quickly toward a Dalkey tram that was about to leave.
—There it goes! Artifoni said in hurried Italian. Come visit me and think it over. Goodbye, my dear fellow!
—Goodbye, teacher, Stephen said, tipping his hat. And thank you.
—For what? Artifoni called back. Excuse me — all the best!
Artifoni trotted after the Dalkey tram, waving his rolled-up music like a signal. But he was too late — the tram pulled away, and he was left standing among the crowd.
Miss Dunne hid a library novel far back in her desk drawer and rolled a sheet of fancy notepaper into her typewriter.
Too much mystery in that book, she thought. Is the man in love with that woman, Marion? She'd exchange it for something else at the library.
A disk slid down a groove in a machine, wobbled, stopped, and showed the number six.
Miss Dunne typed on the keyboard:
Outside, the five sandwich-board men with their tall white hats plodded past, spelling out H.E.L.Y.S., then turned and plodded back the way they'd come.

Miss Dunne stared at a big poster of a music-hall performer and doodled lazily on her notepad. The performer had mustard-colored hair and painted cheeks. She's not that pretty, Miss Dunne thought, and she doesn't look very nice.
The telephone rang loudly by her ear.

—Hello. Yes, sir. No, sir. Yes, sir. I'll ring them after five. Only those two, sir, for Belfast and Liverpool. All right, sir. Then I can leave after six if you're not back. A quarter past. Yes, sir. I'll ring right away.
She scribbled three numbers on an envelope.
—Mr. Boylan! Hello! That gentleman from the sports newspaper was here looking for you. Mr. Lenehan, yes. He said he'll be at the Ormond Hotel at four. No, sir. Yes, sir. I'll ring them after five.
Two pink faces turned in the flare of a small torch.
—Who's that? Ned Lambert asked. Is that Crotty?
—Ringabella and Crosshaven, a voice replied from the darkness, feeling for a foothold.
—Hello, Jack, is that you? Ned Lambert said, holding up his thin wooden stick among the flickering arches. Come on. Watch your step.
A match in the clergyman's raised hand burned with a long, soft flame, then was dropped. Its red spark died at their feet, and damp, musty air closed around them.
—How interesting! a refined voice said in the gloom.

—Yes, sir, Ned Lambert said heartily. We're standing in the historic council chamber of Saint Mary's Abbey, where a nobleman named Silken Thomas declared himself a rebel in 1534. This is the most historic spot in all of Dublin.
—No, Ned, the visitor corrected gently.
—He rode through Dame Walk, the clergyman said with his refined accent, if I remember correctly. The mansion was actually in Thomas Court.
—That's right, Ned Lambert agreed. Quite right, sir.
—If you would be so kind, the clergyman said, perhaps next time you could allow me to bring a camera...
—Certainly, Ned Lambert said. Bring your camera whenever you like. I'll clear those sacks away from the windows so you can get a good shot.
In the dim light, he moved about, tapping piles of grain sacks to show the best spots for photographs.
A man with a long face, a beard, and intense eyes sat nearby, bent over a chessboard.
—I'm deeply grateful, Mr. Lambert, the clergyman said. I won't take up any more of your valuable time...
—You're welcome, sir, Ned Lambert said. Drop in any time. Next week, perhaps. Can you see your way out?
—Yes, yes. Good afternoon, Mr. Lambert. Very pleased to have met you.
—The pleasure is mine, sir, Ned Lambert answered.
He walked his guest to the exit, then tossed his wooden stick playfully among the old stone pillars. With J. J. O'Molloy, he came out into the sunlight where workers were loading sacks onto carts.
He stopped to read the business card in his hand.
—The Reverend Hugh C. Love, from Rathcoffey, Ned said. Nice young fellow. He's writing a book about the old Fitzgerald family. He knows his history, I'll say that.
A young woman carefully picked a twig off her skirt.
—I thought you were planning some kind of conspiracy down there, J. J. O'Molloy joked.
Ned Lambert cracked his fingers in the air.

—Oh! he cried. I forgot to tell him the story about the Earl of Kildare after he burned down Cashel Cathedral. You know that one? "I'm terribly sorry I did it," says the Earl, "but I swear I thought the Archbishop was inside!"
The horses nearby started nervously as he passed. He slapped one on the side and called out:
—Steady, boy!
He turned to J. J. O'Molloy and asked:
—Well, Jack. What's the matter? What's troubling you? Hold on a second.
With his mouth wide open and his head tilted back, he stood still and then sneezed loudly.
—Achoo! he said. Blast it!
—The dust from those sacks, J. J. O'Molloy said politely.
—No, Ned Lambert gasped. I caught a cold the night before last, and there was a terrible draft...
He held his handkerchief ready for the next sneeze.
—I was at the funeral this morning — poor little... what's his name... Achoo! Good heavens!
Tom Rochford held a disk from a stack pressed against his chest.
—See? he said. Say it's act number six at the music hall. You put it in here, see. "Now Playing."
He slid the disk into the left slot of his machine. It shot down a groove, wobbled, and stopped, showing the number six.
Through the windows, important-looking lawyers passed by. Among them, Richie Goulding carried a legal bag for his law firm.
—See? Tom said. The last one I put in slides over here: "Finished." It's all about the mechanism. Leverage, see?
He showed them how the disks stacked up on the right side.
—Smart idea, Nosey Flynn said, sniffling. So anyone arriving late can see what's playing now and what acts are already finished.
—See? Tom Rochford said, pleased.
He put in another disk for himself and watched it slide, wobble, and stop on number four. "Now Playing."
—I'll see Boylan at the Ormond Hotel now, Lenehan said, and have a word with him. One good turn deserves another.
—Do, Tom Rochford said. Tell him I'm eagerly waiting.
—Goodbye, M'Coy said abruptly. When you two get going, there's no stopping you.
Nosey Flynn bent down toward the machine, sniffling at it.
—But how does this part work, Tommy? he asked.
—See you later, Lenehan called out.
He followed M'Coy out across the little square.
—Tom Rochford is a real hero, Lenehan said simply.
—I know, M'Coy said. You mean the drain rescue.
—Drain? Lenehan said. It was a manhole!
They passed a music hall where a performer's face smiled at them from a poster — the same one Miss Dunne had been looking at.
Walking down the path beside the music hall, Lenehan told M'Coy the whole story. A man had been stuck down a manhole, and Tom Rochford climbed down to save him, risking his own life.
—A true hero, Lenehan said.
At a crossroads, they paused to let an ambulance gallop past.
—This way, Lenehan said, walking right. I want to pop into Lynam's to check the horse racing odds. What time is it?
M'Coy looked at a nearby clock.
—After three, he said. Who's riding in the big race?
—O. Madden, Lenehan said. And she's a fine horse.
While Lenehan was inside, M'Coy waited on the street, carefully nudging a banana peel off the pavement with his toe. Someone could easily slip on that in the dark.
The gates of the Vice-Regal Lodge opened wide to let out the Lord Lieutenant's procession of carriages.
—Even money odds, Lenehan said, coming back. I bumped into Bantam Lyons in there. He's going to bet on some horse that someone gave him a tip about. This way.
They went up the steps and under Merchants' Arch. A dark figure was browsing books on a street seller's cart.
—There he is, Lenehan said.
—What's he buying, I wonder? M'Coy said, glancing back.
—Leopold the bookworm! Lenehan joked.
—He loves bargains at book sales, M'Coy said. I was with him once and he bought a book with beautiful astronomy plates for just a couple of shillings — pictures of the stars and the moon.
Lenehan laughed.
—I'll tell you a great story about stargazing, he said. Come over into the sun.
They crossed to a bridge and walked along the riverbank.
Young Patrick Dignam, the dead man's son, came out of a butcher's shop carrying a pound and a half of pork chops.
—There was a big fancy dinner at Glencree, Lenehan said eagerly. The annual banquet, you know. Formal affair. The Lord Mayor was there, and all sorts of important people.
—I know, M'Coy interrupted. My wife sang at one of those.
—Did she? Lenehan said.
In the meantime, the "Unfurnished Apartments" card reappeared in the window of number 7 Eccles Street.
Lenehan paused his story for a moment, then broke out laughing.
—But wait till I tell you, he said. I was in charge of the drinks. The Blooms were there — Leopold and Molly. We had wine and food galore.
—I know, M'Coy said. The year my wife was there...
Lenehan linked his arm through M'Coy's warmly.
—But listen, he went on. After midnight, we all piled into a carriage to go home. It was freezing cold. And I was sitting next to Mrs. Bloom in the back, and she was wrapped up in a fur rug...
He held his hands apart, frowning:
—I was tucking the rug around her and fixing her scarf the whole time. You know what I mean?
He made gestures in the air describing curved shapes, closed his eyes with delight, and whistled softly.

—Meanwhile, Lenehan continued with a sigh, Bloom was in the front of the carriage pointing out all the stars and conets to another man — the Great Bear, the constellation of Cassiopeia. While I was in the back with Mrs. Bloom! What a situation!
Lenehan leaned on the river wall, laughing helplessly.
—I can't take it, he gasped.
M'Coy's white face smiled and then grew serious. Lenehan walked on again, scratching under his cap.
—He's a well-rounded man, Bloom is, Lenehan said seriously. He's not your ordinary fellow. There's something of the artist about old Bloom.
Mr. Bloom browsed through books at a second-hand bookstall. He looked through a couple of old volumes with strange illustrations, then set them aside.
He glanced at another book and pushed it away.
—I've had that one already, he said.
The shopkeeper set two more books on the counter.
—Those are two good ones, he said.
The shopkeeper's breath smelled of onions. He was a messy old fellow in an unbuttoned waistcoat.
On O'Connell Bridge, many people noticed the elegant Professor Maginni, the dancing teacher, walking past in his fine clothes.
Mr. Bloom, now alone, looked at the book titles. He recognized some types of books and picked one up. He opened it. Just as he thought.
A woman's voice came from behind a curtain at the back of the shop. The shopkeeper was talking to someone.
No, Molly wouldn't enjoy that kind of book, Bloom thought. He'd gotten her one like it before.
He read the other title: Sweets of Sin. More to her taste, maybe. He opened it.
He read where his finger happened to fall.
The passage described a woman spending her husband's money on fancy dresses — not for him, but for another man.
Yes, Bloom thought. This one. Here. Try it.
He read another passage about a romantic scene between two characters.
Yes. I'll take this one, Bloom decided.
—You're late, one of the characters in the book spoke harshly.
The beautiful woman in the story took off her fine wrap, showing her elegant shoulders.
Mr. Bloom re-read the words: "The beautiful woman."
A warm feeling washed over him as he imagined the scene in the book.
Young! Young! he thought wistfully.
An elderly woman came out of the law courts nearby, having sat through a complicated legal case. She walked with a thin umbrella.
The shopkeeper emerged from behind the curtain, coughing roughly, his gray hair uncombed and his face unshaven.
Mr. Bloom stared at him.
Catching his breath, Bloom said:
—I'll take this one.
The shopkeeper looked up with watery eyes.
—Sweets of Sin, he said, tapping the book. That's a good one.
The bellman at Dillon's auction rooms shook his handbell twice and admired his reflection in a dusty mirror.

Dilly Dedalus — Stephen's younger sister — stood by the curb, listening to the auctioneer's voice inside. Lovely curtains were being sold for next to nothing. Things that had cost much more when new. Everything was going for a fraction of the price.
The bellman shook his bell again:
—Clang!
A bicycle race was going on nearby — riders with their necks stretched forward, legs pumping, rounding a corner past the college library.
Mr. Dedalus — Stephen and Dilly's father — came around the corner, pulling at his long mustache. He stopped near his daughter.
—It's time you showed up, she said.
—Stand up straight, for the love of heaven, Mr. Dedalus said. Are you trying to imitate your uncle John with his head hanging to one side? Stand up!
Dilly shrugged her shoulders. Mr. Dedalus put his hands on them and pushed them back.
—Stand up straight, girl, he said. You'll get a crooked spine. Do you know what you look like?
He let his own head drop forward and hunched his shoulders to show her what she looked like.
—Stop it, Father, Dilly said. Everyone is staring at you.
Mr. Dedalus stood up straight and tugged at his mustache again.
—Did you get any money? Dilly asked.
—Where would I get money? Mr. Dedalus said. There isn't a soul in Dublin who would lend me a penny.
—You did get some, Dilly said, looking him straight in the eye.
—How do you know that? Mr. Dedalus asked, his tongue in his cheek.
Mr. Kernan, pleased with a business deal he had just made, walked briskly along James's Street at that moment.
—I know you did, Dilly said. Were you at the pub?
—I was not, Mr. Dedalus said with a smile. Was it the nuns who taught you to be so saucy? Here.
He handed her a shilling.
—See if you can do anything with that, he said.
—I bet you got five shillings, Dilly said. Give me more than that.

—Wait a minute, Mr. Dedalus said, his tone turning harsh. You're just like the rest of them, aren't you? A pack of ungrateful children, ever since your poor mother died. But just you wait. You'll all get what's coming to you. I'm going to get rid of the house and live on my own.
He pulled away and walked on. Dilly followed quickly and tugged at his coat.
—Well, what is it? he said, stopping.
The bellman rang his bell behind them.
—Clang!
—Blast your noisy bell! Mr. Dedalus cried, turning on the bellman.
The bellman, noticing the angry look, shook his bell more weakly:
—Ding!
Mr. Dedalus glared at him.
—Watch him, he said to Dilly. Very educational. I wonder if he'll allow us to have a conversation.
—You got more than one shilling, Father, Dilly insisted.
—I'll show you exactly what I have, Mr. Dedalus said. I got two shillings from Jack Power and spent some on a shave and a haircut.
He pulled out a handful of copper coins nervously.
—Can't you look for money somewhere else? Dilly pleaded.
Mr. Dedalus thought about it and nodded.
—I will, he said seriously. I looked all along the gutter in O'Connell Street for loose coins. I'll try this street now.
—Very funny, Dilly said with a small grin.
—Here, Mr. Dedalus said, handing her two pennies. Get yourself a glass of milk and a bun or something. I'll be home soon.
He put the rest of his coins in his pocket and started walking away.
The Lord Lieutenant's procession of carriages passed by at that moment, greeted by saluting policemen.
—I'm sure you have another shilling, Dilly called after him.
The bellman banged his bell loudly.
Mr. Dedalus walked off through the noise, muttering sarcastically to himself:
—The little nuns! Such sweet little things! Oh, they would never teach a girl to be so bold! Little Sister Monica, indeed!
Mr. Kernan walked from the sundial toward James's Gate, pleased with the business order he had just secured. He'd handled the client well, smooth-talking him just right.
I smiled at him and talked about America, Kernan thought proudly. Said all the right things about imports. That's how you do it.
Business is business, he thought. Where there's money, there's always someone trying to get it.
He noticed a man looking at his fine coat. Appearance matters, Kernan thought. A good-looking frock coat makes all the difference.
—Hello, Simon, Father Cowley called out. How are things?
—Hello, Bob, old man, Mr. Dedalus answered, stopping to chat.
Mr. Kernan paused to admire himself in a shop mirror. A stylish coat, no question. It had been worth every penny he'd paid for it.
Must dress well for these customers, Kernan thought. Look the part of a gentleman. And would the customer like to place another order? The finest tea, of course.
Down the river, the crumpled religious flyer — "Elijah is Coming" — floated past ships and anchored boats, still drifting eastward.
Mr. Kernan took a last look at his reflection. Distinguished appearance, he thought. Grizzled mustache. Looked like a retired military officer. He squared his shoulders and walked on.
A good drop of gin was warming his insides and putting a spring in his step.
Down this very street, the Irish rebel Robert Emmet had been executed, back in the bad old days. Terrible times.
Bad times those were, Kernan thought. But over and done with. The men of that era were hard drinkers too.
He tried to remember where Emmet was buried. Some secret midnight burial. And now Dignam was buried too, just this morning. One day you're here, the next day gone.
Mr. Kernan turned and walked down the slope, past the Guinness visitors' waiting room and a distillery. A horse and carriage stood outside without a driver.
Denis Breen, the man with the rude postcard, walked across O'Connell Bridge with his wife. He'd been waiting an hour at the lawyer's office and was now heading to try another law firm.
Mr. Kernan continued along Island Street.
He thought about the old days of rebellion and the colorful characters of Irish history. Noble families, desperate times, courage and treachery side by side.
That was good gin, Kernan thought again.
He admired the old Irish rebels. Fine people, even if they'd been on the losing side. They rose up in dark times. Good blood in them.
A line from an old song ran through his head: "At the siege of Ross did my father fall."
A procession of carriages trotted past along the river — the Lord Lieutenant's cavalcade, with riders bouncing in their saddles, wearing fine coats and carrying cream-colored parasols.
Mr. Kernan hurried forward, puffing.
His Excellency the Lord Lieutenant! Too bad — he'd just missed the procession by a hair. What a pity!

Stephen Dedalus watched through a dusty shop window as an old jeweler's fingers tested a tarnished chain. Dust coated the window and the display trays. The old man's dark, grimy fingers worked with practiced skill.
Stephen thought about jewels born deep in the dark earth — cold sparks of fire, like fallen stars buried in the mud.
His thoughts turned dark and strange, imagining rough scenes from Dublin's back streets.
Old Russell the jeweler polished his gem with a shammy leather cloth, turned it in the light, and examined it close to his face through his long beard.
Stephen thought about ancient words and old wisdom, about grain standing eternally in the fields, about what endures and what fades.
Two old women fresh from a walk by the sea trudged through the neighborhood, one with a sandy, tired umbrella, the other carrying a midwife's bag with eleven cockles rattling inside.
The whirring of machinery and the hum of dynamos from the nearby power station urged Stephen onward. The world was always throbbing — outside you and inside you, like a heartbeat.
Yes, quite true, someone was saying nearby. A very large and wonderful clock. Keeps perfect time.
Stephen walked down Bedford Row, his walking stick clacking against his shoulder blade. In a shop window, he saw an old faded poster of a boxing match from 1860.
He turned and stopped by a slanting book cart.
—Twopence each, the seller said. Four for sixpence.
Stephen looked at the tattered books: The Irish Beekeeper, Life of the Curé of Ars, Pocket Guide to Killarney.
He wondered if he might find one of his old school prizes here, pawned and sold on.
Father Conmee, having finished his afternoon prayers, was at that moment walking through the village of Donnycarney.
Stephen picked up another book. "Eighth and Ninth Book of Moses. Secret of All Secrets." Its pages were well-thumbed. Full of charms and spells and folk remedies.
—Strange words and magic spells! Stephen read with amusement.
Who wrote this nonsense? Stephen wondered. Charms and blessings from some made-up holy man. Just as good as any other pretend magic.
—What are you doing here, Stephen?
It was Dilly — his sister. He noticed her thin shoulders and shabby dress.
He quickly closed the book he'd been looking at. Don't let her see.
—What are you doing? Stephen asked her.
She had their mother's face, he thought, with its pale oval shape. He remembered telling Dilly about Paris once. She'd listened with such hunger for the world beyond Dublin.
—What have you got there? Stephen asked.
—I bought it from the other book cart for a penny, Dilly said, laughing nervously. Is it any good?
My eyes, they say she has, Stephen thought. Do others see me in her face? Quick and far-seeing.
He took the coverless book from her hand. It was a French language primer.
—What did you buy that for? he asked. To learn French?
She nodded, blushing, and pressed her lips together tightly.
Don't show surprise, Stephen told himself. Act natural.
—Here, Stephen said kindly, handing it back. It's all right. Keep it. Just make sure Maggy doesn't pawn it. I suppose all my books at home are gone?
—Some of them, Dilly said quietly. We had to sell them.

She is drowning, Stephen thought with a terrible pang of guilt. My sister, my family — drowning in poverty. Save her! But she will drag me down with her if I let her. All of them, pulling me under with their need. I can feel the weight of it already.
We. All of us together.
Guilt. The sting of conscience.
Misery! Stephen thought. Misery!
—Hello, Simon, Father Cowley said. How are things?
—Hello, Bob, old man, Mr. Dedalus answered, stopping on the street.
They shook hands warmly outside a shop. Father Cowley nervously smoothed down his mustache.
—What's the latest? Mr. Dedalus asked.
—Well, not much good news, Father Cowley said. I'm under siege, Simon. I've got two men from a debt collector prowling around my house trying to get in.
—Lovely, Mr. Dedalus said sarcastically. Who sent them?
—Oh, Father Cowley said. A certain money-lender we both know.
—The one with the bad back? Mr. Dedalus asked.
—The very same, Father Cowley said. Reuben himself. I'm waiting for Ben Dollard. He's going to ask the sub-sheriff to call those two men off. All I need is a little time to sort things out.
He looked hopefully up and down the street, his Adam's apple bobbing nervously.
—I know, Mr. Dedalus said, nodding. Good old Ben! He's always helping someone out. Wait — hold on!
He put on his glasses and peered toward the metal bridge.
—There he is! Mr. Dedalus said. Big as life!
Ben Dollard — a large man in a loose blue jacket and square hat — crossed the bridge at a leisurely pace, scratching behind his coat tails.
As Ben came near, Mr. Dedalus greeted him:
—Hold on to that big fellow!
—Hold on! Ben Dollard agreed.
Mr. Dedalus looked Ben Dollard's large figure up and down with mock disapproval. Then he turned to Father Cowley and muttered:
—That's a fine outfit for a summer's day, isn't it?
—Why, curse it all, Ben Dollard growled, I've thrown out more clothes in my time than you've ever seen!
He stood beaming at them, and Mr. Dedalus flicked bits of lint off his roomy jacket, saying:
—They were made for someone in better health than you, Ben.
—Bad luck to the tailor who made them, Ben Dollard said. Thank goodness he hasn't been paid yet.
—And how is that wonderful bass voice of yours, Benjamin? Father Cowley asked.
At that moment, the eccentric Mr. Cashel Boyle O'Connor Fitzmaurice Tisdall Farrell strode past, muttering to himself through his thick glasses.
Ben Dollard frowned, shaped his mouth like a singer's, and let out a deep note.
—Ahhh! he sang.
—That's the stuff, Mr. Dedalus said, nodding along to the deep rumble.
—Not bad, eh? Ben Dollard said. What do you think?
He looked at both of them.
—That'll do nicely, Father Cowley agreed with a nod.
The clergyman from earlier — Reverend Hugh C. Love — was at that moment walking past an old church, accompanied in his imagination by the tall ghosts of the Fitzgerald clan.
Ben Dollard, leaning sideways from his great weight, led them forward, his cheerful fingers waggling in the air.
—Come along with me to the sub-sheriff's office, he said. I want to show you the new man they've hired. He's a sight to see! Come along.
—Tell the sub-sheriff I just need a few days, Father Cowley said anxiously.
Ben Dollard stopped and stared, his big mouth hanging open, a button dangling from his coat.
—A few days? he boomed. Hasn't your landlord already claimed the property for unpaid rent?
—He has, Father Cowley admitted.
—Then the money-lender's claim isn't worth the paper it's printed on, Ben Dollard declared. The landlord gets first claim. I explained all the details already.
—That's right, Father Cowley said. The Reverend Mr. Love is the landlord. He's a minister out in the countryside. But are you sure about this?
—Tell the money-lender, Ben Dollard said firmly, that his legal claim is worthless.
He took Father Cowley's arm and pulled him along.
—I believe the technicality involves filbert nuts, Mr. Dedalus muttered, following behind them with his glasses sliding down his nose.
—The youngster will be all right, Martin Cunningham said, as they walked out through the Castle gate. He was talking about young Patrick Dignam, whose father had just died.
A policeman touched his forehead in salute.
—God bless you, Martin Cunningham said cheerfully.
He signaled to the waiting carriage driver, who clicked the reins and set off toward Lord Edward Street.
At the Ormond Hotel, two barmaids — Miss Kennedy with bronze hair and Miss Douce with golden hair — appeared together above the window blind.
—Yes, Martin Cunningham said, stroking his beard. I wrote to Father Conmee and explained the whole situation about the Dignam family.
—You could try our friend for help too, Mr. Power suggested from the back seat.
—Boyd? Martin Cunningham said shortly. No, thank you.
John Wyse Nolan came hurrying after them down Cork Hill, reading a list.
On the steps of City Hall, Councillor Nannetti was coming down while other politicians were going up. They all greeted each other.
The castle carriage wheeled away, now empty.
—Look here, Martin, John Wyse Nolan said, catching up. I see Bloom put his name down for five shillings — a donation for the Dignam family.
—Quite right, Martin Cunningham said, taking the list. And he actually gave the money too.
—Without a moment's hesitation, Mr. Power added.
—Unusual but true, Martin Cunningham agreed.
John Wyse Nolan's eyes widened.
—I'll say there is much kindness in that man, he said thoughtfully.
They walked down Parliament Street.
—There's Jimmy Henry, Mr. Power said, heading into the restaurant.
—Right, Martin Cunningham said. Let's go.
Outside a restaurant, Blazes Boylan stopped someone he knew for a chat.
John Wyse Nolan fell back to walk with Mr. Power, while Martin Cunningham took the arm of a small, neatly dressed man — the assistant town clerk — who was hobbling along painfully.
—The poor fellow's corns are giving him terrible trouble, John Wyse Nolan whispered to Mr. Power.
They followed around the corner toward a wine bar. Martin Cunningham kept showing the charity list to Jimmy Henry, who kept waving it away — he had his own problems.
—And long John Fanning is here too, John Wyse Nolan said. Large as life.
The tall figure of long John Fanning filled the doorway.
—Good day, Mr. Sub-Sheriff, Martin Cunningham said, and everyone stopped to exchange greetings.
Long John Fanning didn't move aside. He removed his large hat and looked them all over with fierce, intelligent eyes.
—Are the city council members still arguing in there? he asked the assistant town clerk in his deep, rich voice.

Jimmy Henry said irritably that they were having a terrible row about the Irish language. Where was the marshal to keep order? And old Barlow the caretaker was useless — everyone was shouting and banging desks.
Long John Fanning blew a stream of smoke from his lips.
Martin Cunningham spoke to both the town clerk and the sub-sheriff, while John Wyse Nolan listened quietly.
—What Dignam was that? long John Fanning asked, hearing the name.
Jimmy Henry made a pained face and lifted his left foot.
—Oh, my poor corns! he complained. Come upstairs so I can sit down somewhere. Ouch!
He squeezed past long John Fanning and limped up the stairs.
—Come on up, Martin Cunningham said to the sub-sheriff. I don't think you knew Dignam — or perhaps you did?
Mr. Power followed them inside with John Wyse Nolan.
—He was a decent little fellow, Mr. Power said, speaking to Ben Dollard's broad back as they climbed the stairs.
—Smallish man, Martin Cunningham said. He worked at Menton's law office.
Long John Fanning couldn't remember him.
The clatter of horse hooves sounded from outside.
—What's that? Martin Cunningham asked.

Everyone turned to look. John Wyse Nolan went back down. From the cool shadow of the doorway, he saw horses pass along Parliament Street — harnesses gleaming, hooves shining in the sunlight. The Lord Lieutenant's carriages, passing grandly by.
—What was that? Martin Cunningham asked from the staircase.
—The Lord Lieutenant and Governor General of Ireland, John Wyse Nolan announced from below.
As they walked across the thick carpet of a café, Buck Mulligan whispered behind his Panama hat to Haines:
—Parnell's brother. Over there in the corner.
They chose a small table near the window, across from a long-faced man whose beard and intense gaze hung over a chessboard.
—Is that him? Haines asked, twisting in his seat to look.
—Yes, Mulligan said. That's John Howard Parnell, our city marshal. Brother of the famous leader.

John Howard Parnell quietly moved a white bishop on his chessboard and raised his gray hand to his forehead. For a brief instant, his eyes darted up — ghostly bright — at a mirror, then back to his game.
—I'll have a coffee with cream, Haines told the waitress.
—Two coffees, Buck Mulligan said. And bring us some scones with butter, and some cakes too.
When she had gone, he said with a laugh:
—We call this place D.B.C. because they have Dreadfully Bad Cakes. Oh, but you missed Stephen's talk about Hamlet at the library!
Haines opened his newly bought book.
—I'm sorry I missed it, he said. Shakespeare seems to attract all the unbalanced minds.
Outside on the street below, the one-legged sailor growled:
—England expects...
Buck Mulligan's yellow waistcoat shook with laughter.
—You should see Stephen, he said, when his mind goes off-balance. I call him Wandering Angus — after the restless poet of Irish myth.
—I'm sure he has some fixed idea, Haines said, pinching his chin thoughtfully. People like that always do. I wonder what his would be.
Buck Mulligan leaned across the table seriously.
—They've frightened him with visions of punishment, he said. He'll never achieve true poetic beauty because of it. That's his tragedy. He can never be free and easy like the great poets.

—Eternal punishment, Haines said, nodding. I see. I asked him about his beliefs this morning. There was clearly something on his mind. It's interesting because a professor in Vienna has written about the same thing — the idea of punishment in Irish mythology.
Mulligan's watchful eyes spotted the waitress returning. He helped her set down the tray.

—The professor can find no trace of a belief in punishment in ancient Irish myths, Haines said, stirring his cup. The sense of justice and consequences seems to be missing. It's strange that Stephen should have exactly that idea fixed in his mind.
Haines dropped two sugar lumps neatly into his cream coffee. Mulligan split a hot scone in two and spread butter over it generously.
—Ten years, he said, chewing and laughing. Stephen says he's going to write something in ten years.
—That seems a long way off, Haines said thoughtfully. Still, I wouldn't be surprised if he actually did it.
He tasted a spoonful of his creamy coffee.
—This is real Irish cream, I hope, he said. I don't want to be cheated.

The crumpled religious leaflet — "Elijah is Coming" — continued its journey eastward down the Liffey, floating past ships and fishing boats, past docks and wharves, riding the river's current out toward the sea.

Almidano Artifoni, the Italian music teacher, walked past Holles Street. Behind him, the eccentric Mr. Farrell was doing his peculiar walk — dodging around lampposts with his stick, umbrella, and dustcoat all dangling together.
Mr. Farrell walked as far as one end of Merrion Square, then turned and strode all the way back, his belongings still dangling.

At the corner of Oscar Wilde's old house, he stopped, frowned at a poster advertising the preacher Elijah, frowned at the distant park, and frowned through his monocle at the sun. With a fierce, defiant expression, he spoke a Latin phrase to himself.
—I was forced but I chose it! he muttered.
He strode on toward Clare Street, grinding out his angry words.
As he passed a dentist's office, his swinging dustcoat rudely knocked aside a thin tapping cane, bumping a frail body. It was the blind young man that Mr. Bloom had helped earlier.
—God curse you, whoever you are! the blind young man said bitterly. You're more blind than I am!

Outside a shop, young Patrick Dignam — the dead man's son — dawdled along warm Wicklow Street, carrying the pound and a half of pork chops his mother had sent him for. It was too hot for the thick black mourning suit he was wearing.
He stopped to look in a shop window at a display of boxing photos — two fighters stripped to the waist, ready to throw punches. In the side mirrors, he could see two reflections of the scene.

Master Dignam pulled his collar straight and dawdled on. He thought about boxers — Fitzsimons was the strongest, but there was another one, a comeback fighter, who was even better. He'd love to go see a boxing match someday.
On Grafton Street, young Dignam noticed a well-dressed man with a red flower in his mouth, wearing fancy shoes, listening to a man talking to him and grinning the whole time.
No Sandymount tram in sight.

Master Dignam walked along Nassau Street, shifting the pork chops to his other hand. His collar kept springing up and he tugged it down. The button on his shirt was too small for the hole. His father — his dead father — used to be much bigger than him. He wondered when he'd grow up to be as big.

The boy thought about his father's face in the coffin — how gray it had looked instead of its usual red color, and how a fly had walked across it. He remembered the terrible sound of the screws going into the coffin lid, and the bumps as the coffin was carried downstairs.

Pa was inside it, and Ma was crying in the parlor, and Uncle Barney was telling the men how to get the coffin around the bend in the staircase. It was a big coffin, heavy and tall. The night before, Pa had been downstairs, his face red from drinking too much. The boy remembered the sound of his father snoring when they'd put him to bed that last night.
William Humble, Earl of Dudley, Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, and Lady Dudley drove out after lunch from the Vice-Regal Lodge in Phoenix Park. Following carriages carried their distinguished guests.
The cavalcade passed through the park gates, saluted by police officers, and proceeded along the northern banks of the River Liffey. The procession was heading into the city.
The Lord Lieutenant was warmly greeted along the way by various citizens who bowed and tipped their hats.

Blazes Boylan, wearing a sky-blue tie, a wide straw hat at a jaunty angle, and an indigo suit, saluted the carriages with one hand in his pocket while the other held a just-lit cigar. He presented quite a picture.

He hummed a song as the carriages passed:
"But though she's a factory girl
     And wears no fancy clothes,
     Still I've a sort of
     fondness for
     My little Yorkshire rose."

On a nearby track, the half-mile bicycle race sprinted toward the finish line — riders with stretched necks, legs pumping. And many other people across Dublin went about their business as the Lord Lieutenant's grand procession rolled through the city streets.

chapters.title: Episode 11 — Sirens
paragraphs: Bronze hair beside gold hair heard the horses' hooves ringing on the street.
Impertinent boy with his sniffling!
Picking at his thumbnail. Chips.
Horrid! And the golden-haired one blushed.
A low note blew from a pipe.
Blew. Blue. Bloom is on the way.
Golden hair pinned up high.
A rose bounced on a dress of satin. The rose of Castile.
Singing, singing: sweet Dolores.
Peep! Who's hiding there? A glint of gold!
A bell rang out to the bronze-haired girl with pity.
And a call, pure and long and throbbing. A dying call.
A trick. A soft word. But look: the bright stars fade. Notes chirp in answer.
Oh, rose! Castile. The morning is breaking.
Jingle jingle went the bouncing carriage.
A coin rang. A clock ticked.
A promise. A bell rings. A goodbye. Sweetheart, goodbye!
Jingle. Bloom.
Crashing chords boomed. When love takes over. War! War! The drumbeat.
A sail! A veil waving on the waves.
Lost. A bird sang. All is lost now.
A horn. Hawthorn.
When first he saw her. How sad!
Full and throbbing.
Warbling. Ah, how tempting! Alluring.
Martha! Come!
Clap clap. Clap clap. Clapping.
Good heavens, he'd never heard anything like it.
Deaf bald Pat the waiter brought a pad and knife.
A moonlit night-call: far, far away.
I feel so sad. P.S. So lonely blooming.
Listen!
The cold spiraling seashell. Do you have one? Each sound, splashing and roaring silently.
Pearls: when she wore them. Piano music. Hissing.
You don't believe it?
Did not: no, no: believe. With a knock, with a tap.
Black. Deep sounding. Sing, Ben, sing.
Wait while you wait. Hee hee. Wait while you hee.
But wait!
Low in the dark earth. Hidden treasure.
A preacher, that's what he is.
All gone. All fallen.
Tiny, trembling fern-like strands of delicate hair.
Amen! He clenched his teeth in fury.
Back and forth. A baton sticking out coolly.
Bronze Lydia beside golden Mina.
By bronze, by gold, in ocean-green shadow. Bloom. Old Bloom.
One rapped, one tapped, with a tap, with a knock.
Pray for him! Pray, good people!
His stiff, gouty fingers plucking at the keys.
Big Ben. Big Ben Dollard.
Last rose of Castile of summer. Left bloom. I feel so sad alone.
Pee! A little wind piped softly.
True men. Good fellows. They'll lift their glasses together.
Pfft! Ooh!
Where is bronze? Where is gold? Where are the horses?
Rumble. Creak. Creaking.
Then, not till then. My epitaph. Let it be written.
Done.
Begin!
Bronze-haired Miss Douce and golden-haired Miss Kennedy, the two barmaids at the Ormond Hotel, peered over the window blind and heard the Lord Lieutenant's horse-drawn carriages go ringing past.
—Is that her? Miss Kennedy asked, meaning the Lord Lieutenant's wife.
Miss Douce said yes — the lady was sitting with her companion, dressed in pearl gray and pale green.
—What a beautiful contrast, Miss Kennedy said.
Then Miss Douce said eagerly:
—Look at the fellow in the tall silk hat!
—Who? Where? Miss Kennedy asked, even more eagerly.
—In the second carriage, Miss Douce said, laughing in the sunlight.
He's looking this way, she thought. Let me get a better view.
She darted to the back corner, pressing her face against the windowpane, her breath making a circle of mist on the glass.
Her lips giggled:
—He nearly broke his neck looking back at us!
She laughed:
—Oh, aren't men ridiculous!
With a touch of sadness.
Miss Kennedy walked sadly away from the bright window light, twisting a loose strand of golden hair behind her ear.
—It's men who have all the fun, she said sadly.
A man passed by outside.
Mr. Bloom walked past the hotel, carrying the book he had bought tucked close to his chest. He was on his way to find paper and envelopes to write a letter.
The boots — the young hotel servant — came into the bar with their tea. He banged the tray of rattling china on the counter.
—There's your teas, he said.
Miss Kennedy politely moved the tea tray down to an upturned crate, out of sight of the customers.
—What's going on? the boots asked rudely.
—Mind your own business, Miss Douce retorted.
—Is it your boyfriend out there?
Miss Douce replied haughtily:
—I'll complain to the manager about your rudeness if I hear any more.
The boots sniffed rudely and retreated, just as he had come.
Bloom was passing by outside.
Miss Douce, frowning at the flower on her blouse, said:
—That young brat is so annoying. If he doesn't behave himself, I'll give him a good scolding.
So ladylike, in contrast to her words.
—Take no notice of him, Miss Kennedy advised.

She poured tea into a cup, then poured some back into the teapot — too strong. The two barmaids crouched behind the counter on upturned crates, waiting for their tea to brew. They smoothed their blouses and touched their hair.
Yes, bronze from nearby, gold from far away, they heard the steel hooves ringing on the street as the Lord Lieutenant's procession passed.
—Am I terribly sunburned? Miss Douce asked, showing her neck.
Miss Douce unbuttoned the top of her blouse to check her skin.
—No, Miss Kennedy said. It turns brown after a while. Did you try that skin lotion?
Miss Douce half-stood to check her skin in the bar mirror, where glasses of wine glimmered on the shelves and a seashell sat in the middle.
—Look at my hands, she said.
—Try the glycerine, Miss Kennedy suggested.
Saying goodbye to her neck and hands for now, Miss Douce
—Those skin creams only give you a rash, she replied, sitting back down. I asked that old fellow in Boyd's chemist shop for something for my skin.
Miss Kennedy, pouring out a full cup of tea, made a face and groaned:
—Oh, don't remind me of that man!
—But wait till I tell you, Miss Douce begged.
Miss Kennedy plugged both ears with her little fingers, her tea poured with milk.
—No, don't! she cried.
—I won't listen! she cried.
But what about Bloom? He was still walking outside.
Miss Douce put on a deep, grumpy old man's voice:
—For your what? says he.
Miss Kennedy unplugged her ears to listen, then begged again:
—Don't make me think about him or I'll scream! The horrible old creature! That night at the concert hall.
She sipped her hot, sweet tea with distaste.
—There he was, Miss Douce said, tilting her bronze-haired head and sniffling like the old man. Sniff! Sniff!
A shriek of laughter burst from Miss Kennedy. Miss Douce snorted and sniffled, imitating the old man's twitching nose.
—Oh! Miss Kennedy screamed. Will you ever forget his goggling eyes?
Miss Douce joined in with deep, hearty laughter:
—And your other eye! she shouted.
Meanwhile, Mr. Bloom walked past various shops along the street, his dark eyes scanning.
His eyes moved on. The book he'd bought was tucked under his arm.
Sweet sin indeed.
The two young barmaids blended their giggling voices — golden and bronze — throwing their heads back, letting their laughter ring free through the bar.
At last, panting and sighing, their laughter died away.
Miss Kennedy sipped her tea again and giggled. Miss Douce rolled her eyes comically. They both collapsed in laughter once more.
—Oh, those greasy eyes! Imagine being married to a man like that! Miss Kennedy cried.
Miss Douce let out a tremendous yell of delight.
—Married to that greasy old fellow! she shrieked.
They urged each other into peal after peal of laughter — bronze and gold, gold and bronze — until they could laugh no more.
Married to Bloom, to greasy Bloom — that's what they were laughing about, though Bloom didn't know it.
—Oh, saints above! Miss Douce sighed. I wish I hadn't laughed so much.
—Oh, Miss Douce! Miss Kennedy protested. You're terrible!
And she blushed even more golden.
Mr. Bloom walked past more shops along the street, thinking about his work — he needed to see Nannetti about that advertisement.
The barmaids' blushes faded.
Into the bar strolled Mr. Dedalus — Stephen's father — picking at one of his thumbnails. He strolled in casually.
—Oh, welcome back! Miss Douce greeted him.
He took her hand. Had she enjoyed her holidays?
—Very much, thanks.
He hoped she'd had nice weather at the seaside.
—Gorgeous, she said. Look how sunburned I am. I was lying on the beach all day.
Bronze skin against white.
—That was very naughty of you, Mr. Dedalus teased, pressing her hand. Tempting innocent fellows like us.
Miss Douce pulled her arm away.
—Oh, go on! she said. You're not so innocent, I'm sure.
He was, though.
—Well, I used to be, he mused. I was so simple as a baby they called me Simple Simon.
—You must have been adorable, Miss Douce replied. And what will you have to drink today?
—Well now, he said, I think I'll have some fresh water and half a glass of whiskey.
Jingle — the sound of a carriage approaching.
—Right away, sir, Miss Douce agreed cheerfully.
With grace she turned to the mirror behind the bar, reached up to the shelf, and poured a measure of golden whiskey. Mr. Dedalus pulled coins from his pocket.
—By Jove, he mused, I've always wanted to see the Mourne Mountains. The air must be wonderful down there.
He dropped little pieces of fingernail into a bowl. Musing. Silent.
Nobody said anything for a moment.
Miss Douce polished a glass cheerfully, singing softly:
—Oh, Dolores, queen of the eastern seas!
—Was Mr. Lidwell in today? someone asked.
Just then, Lenehan came in through the door. Meanwhile, Mr. Bloom had reached Essex Bridge. He was thinking about buying paper to write a letter — to Martha, his secret pen-pal.
—He was here at lunchtime, Miss Douce said.
Lenehan came forward.
—Was Mr. Boylan looking for me?
He asked. She answered:
—Miss Kennedy, was Mr. Boylan in while I was upstairs?
Miss Kennedy answered without looking up from what she was reading, holding her teacup:
—No. He was not.
Miss Kennedy kept reading. Lenehan wandered around the counter.
—Peep! Who's hiding in the corner? he joked.
Jingle jingle went the carriage outside — that was Boylan's carriage, getting closer.
Jingle, jingle, bouncing along.
Miss Kennedy read her book and pretended not to notice Lenehan. He told her a silly story to try to make her laugh.
—A fox met a stork, Lenehan said in a silly voice. The fox said to the stork: Will you put your long beak down my throat and pull out a bone?
He tried in vain. Miss Douce turned away to her tea.
He sighed:
—Ah me! Oh my!
He greeted Mr. Dedalus and got a nod.
—Greetings from the famous son of a famous father! Lenehan said.
—Who would that be? Mr. Dedalus asked.
Lenehan spread his arms wide. Who indeed?
—Who? Can you not guess? Stephen, the brilliant young poet!
Dry reply from Dedalus.
Mr. Dedalus set aside his empty pipe.
—I see, he said. I didn't recognize the description for a moment. I hear he's keeping very interesting company. Have you seen him lately?
He had.
—I drank with him this very day, Lenehan said proudly. At Mooney's pub. He'd just been paid for bringing a letter to the newspaper.
Lenehan smiled at the barmaids:
—All the best writers and thinkers in Dublin were hanging on his every word. Professor MacHugh, and O'Madden Burke, and all the rest.
After a pause, Mr. Dedalus raised his drink:
—That must have been very entertaining, he said dryly.
He drank. His sad, faraway eyes looked into the distance. He set down his glass.
He looked toward the saloon door.
—I see you've moved the piano, he said.
—The tuner was in today, Miss Douce replied. He was tuning it for the concert tonight, and I've never heard such a wonderful player.
—Is that so? Mr. Dedalus said.
—Wasn't he wonderful, Miss Kennedy? He played real classical music. And he was blind, the poor fellow. Not even twenty years old, I'd say.
—Is that a fact? Mr. Dedalus said again.
He drank and wandered toward the saloon.
—So sad to see his face, Miss Douce said sympathetically.
A curse on his enemies, someone muttered.
A bell rang from the dining room. Bald Pat, the waiter at the Ormond, came hurrying to take the order.
Lenehan waited patiently for Boylan — jingly, jaunty Blazes Boylan.
Someone lifted the lid of the piano and looked at the wires inside. The same fingers ran gently along the keys.
Bloom, meanwhile, was at Daly's stationery shop buying cream paper and envelopes to write his letter to Martha.
A carriage jingled from the bridge toward the Ormond Hotel. Boylan was coming. At four o'clock — that was when Molly expected him.
—Twopence, sir, the shop girl said to Bloom.
—Ah... I was forgetting... Excuse me...
—And fourpence change.
The shop girl smiled at Bloom. He knew she smiled like that at everyone.
For all men, not just him.
In drowsy silence, golden Miss Kennedy bent over her page, reading.
From the saloon, a long, dying musical note rang out. It was a tuning fork that the blind piano tuner had left behind.
Bald Pat carried drinks to the dining room — for Richie Goulding and Mr. Bloom, who had come in for dinner.
Someone sang softly: —The bright stars fade...
A voiceless song seemed to sing from within:
—...the morning is breaking.
Bright notes chirped from the piano under skilled hands — all the keys twinkling and linking together in beautiful harmonies.
—The dewdrops sparkle...
Lenehan whistled softly from the counter, trying to get Miss Kennedy's attention.
—But look this way, he said. You're the rose of Castile.
Boylan's carriage jingled along the curb and stopped outside.
Miss Kennedy rose from her reading — like a rose of Castile — looking fretful and dreamy.
—Did she fall or was she pushed? Lenehan asked her, joking.
She answered coolly:
—Ask no questions and you'll hear no lies.
Very ladylike.
Blazes Boylan's smart tan shoes creaked on the bar floor as he strode in. Miss Kennedy and Miss Douce both noticed him. Lenehan called out:
—See the conquering hero comes!
Between the carriage and the window, carefully walking so as not to be seen, Bloom slipped into the hotel dining room.
From the piano: —And I from thee...
—I heard you were in the area, Blazes Boylan said to the barmaids.
He tipped his straw hat to Miss Kennedy with a charming smile. She smiled back. But Miss Douce outshone her, preening her richer bronze hair.
Smart Boylan ordered drinks.
—What'll you have? A glass of bitter? And a sloe gin for me. Any messages?
Not yet. At four o'clock. Bloom sat in the dining room, feeling the hour approaching.
Father Cowley appeared at the door of the sheriff's office nearby.
Bloom thought: Stay out of sight. But here's Richie Goulding. What's he doing here?
Bloom and Goulding sat down together in the dining room. Best value in Dublin, Goulding said.
Miss Douce reached high to a shelf to take down a bottle, stretching her arm up.
—Oh! Oh! Lenehan gasped, watching her stretch.
But she easily grabbed what she was after and brought it down.
—Why don't you grow taller? Blazes Boylan teased her.
Miss Douce poured the sweet drink for Boylan, smiling at the red flower in his buttonhole.
—Good things come in small packages, she said.
She poured neatly and carefully.
—Here's to good fortune, Blazes said.
He tossed a large coin onto the counter. It rang.
—Wait for me, said Lenehan.
—Good fortune, he wished, raising his glass.
—Sceptre will win the Gold Cup race easily, Lenehan predicted.
—I'm afraid not, Boylan said. I fancy a different horse.
Lenehan leaned across the counter, whispering about the race.
The clock was ticking toward four.
—Let me pay, Boylan said, draining his glass.
Lenehan saw Boylan pass a coin across.
—Wait, Lenehan protested.
—Sorry, must dash, Boylan said. See you later.
He was off. Boylan's carriage jingled away toward Eccles Street.
Miss Douce touched her lips where she'd drunk from his glass.
—Handsome fellow, isn't he? the boots remarked.
—Go away, you pest, Miss Douce said.
Miss Kennedy poured more tea. In the saloon, Mr. Dedalus was at the piano with Father Cowley and Ben Dollard.
—Come on, Simon, play us something, Father Cowley urged.
—What shall I play? Mr. Dedalus asked.
—Anything you like.
Mr. Dedalus ran his fingers along the keys.
—Here, try this one, Father Cowley suggested.
—Wait, Mr. Dedalus said. Is Mr. Lidwell here?
Yes, George Lidwell the solicitor had arrived. He stood at the bar, politely greeting Miss Douce.
Bloom, in the dining room, couldn't see them but could hear the music. He ordered his meal.
—Liver and bacon, please, Bloom told Pat the waiter.
Bald Pat, deaf in one ear, nodded and went.
From the saloon, beautiful piano music drifted through.
Richie Goulding talked about singers and concerts he'd been to.
Bloom could hear the piano through the wall. It sounded better after being tuned.
Father Cowley played some chords.
—That's lovely, Bob, Mr. Dedalus said.
The notes rose, clear and bright.
Bald Pat brought Bloom's dinner — liver and bacon on a hot plate.
Bloom ate quietly, listening.
—Do you hear that? Richie whispered. Beautiful.
Yes, Bloom heard. The piano played on.
Ben Dollard, the big man with the deep bass voice, leaned against the piano.
—Play us something, Simon, he urged.
—What shall I sing? Mr. Dedalus asked.
Someone suggested an old song.
Ben Dollard sat down and rumbled through some chords.
—No, wait, Father Cowley said. Let me play. You sing, Ben.
Father Cowley played warm chords while Ben Dollard prepared to sing.
Bloom ate his dinner and listened.
A song rose from the saloon.
—Those were the days, Ben Dollard said.
—Remember that night at the concert? Father Cowley asked.
—Do I remember! Ben Dollard said.
They reminisced about an old concert where everything went wrong — the pianist was terrible, and poor Ben had no proper concert clothes.
—Bloom helped me out that night, Mr. Dedalus recalled. Where's my pipe?
He went back to the bar to find his pipe. Bald Pat carried drinks. Father Cowley laughed, remembering.
—I saved the day, Ben, Father Cowley said.
—You did, Ben Dollard agreed. And those tight trousers were Bob Cowley's brilliant idea.
Father Cowley blushed to the tips of his ears.
—Love and War, Ben, Mr. Dedalus said. God be with old times.
Miss Douce's eyes turned from the window. She pulled down the blind and dreamily polished a glass.
—Poor old Goodwin was the pianist that night, Father Cowley reminded them. He had a slight argument with the grand piano.
There was indeed.
—He was impossible, Mr. Dedalus said. Already a bit unsteady on his feet.
—Lord, do you remember? Ben Dollard said, turning from the piano. And I had no proper concert clothes!
All three laughed together. He had nothing proper to wear!
—Bloom helped us out that night, Mr. Dedalus said.
Bald Pat brought more drinks. Father Cowley laughed.
—I managed to save things, Father Cowley said.
—You did, Ben agreed. Those tight trousers were Bob's idea.
Father Cowley's face turned purple with embarrassment.
—Bloom's wife had a wardrobe of beautiful clothes, Father Cowley remembered. Opera cloaks and fine things.
Ben Dollard remembered.
—She had some magnificent clothes.
Mr. Dedalus wandered back with his pipe.
—Grand dresses, he agreed. All kinds of costumes.
—Yes, Mr. Dedalus nodded. Mrs. Marion Bloom had quite a collection.
Boylan's carriage jingled down the street toward Eccles Street.
Liver and bacon for Bloom, steak and kidney pie for another. Pat took the orders.
Mrs. Marion Bloom. Bloom tried not to think about what was happening at four o'clock.
—What was her name again? A fine woman. Marion...
—Tweedy.
—Yes. Is she still around?
—Very much alive.
—She was a daughter of...
—A daughter of the regiment. Her father was a military man.
—Yes, indeed. I remember the old drum major.
Mr. Dedalus struck a match, lit his pipe, and puffed.
—Is she Irish? I don't know. Is she, Simon?
—Her father was from Dublin. An army man. But she was born in Gibraltar.
—Was she?
—Oh yes. Down south. The rock of Gibraltar. Her mother was Spanish. Or half so, at least.
—Beautiful woman.
—Handsome, yes, someone murmured.
In the dining room, Bloom could hear every word they said about Molly. His heart sank.
Pat brought more food. Steak and kidney pie.
The piano started up again. Father Cowley's fingers.
—Come on, Simon, everyone urged. Sing something.
—What shall I sing?
—Something from the opera.
Ben Dollard suggested a song from the opera Martha.
—Come on, Simon. You know the one. M'appari.
Mr. Dedalus smiled. In the dining room, Bloom sat very still, listening to their voices.
He should write that letter now. To Martha Clifford, his pen-pal. But the music held him in place.
—Play the introduction, Bob, Mr. Dedalus said to Father Cowley.
Cowley's fingers found the opening chords. Soft and expectant.
Bloom looked around the quiet dining room. Just him and Richie Goulding.
Tom Kernan came into the bar just then, pleased with his day's work.
More people gathered in the saloon to listen to the singing.
The blind piano tuner's forgotten tuning fork rang out. Its pure note hung in the air, calling.
Bloom reached across the table and pulled the elastic band off his writing paper. He'd write later.
Bloom's dinner arrived — hot and steaming. He began to eat, but kept one ear on the music.
Bald Pat stood near the dining room door, listening too — though he could barely hear.
—Your friends are inside, Mr. Lidwell, Miss Douce said.
George Lidwell held Miss Douce's hand in greeting.
Bloom ate his liver and bacon. At least it was clean here. No one noticed him in this quiet corner.
Piano again. Father Cowley playing. The way he sat at the piano, like they were one.
Boylan's carriage jingled along, getting farther away.
The piano played on. Lovely golden sound.
—Ah, I couldn't sing now, Mr. Dedalus said shyly.
Strongly they urged him.
—Go on! Ben Dollard growled. Get it out!
—M'appari, Simon, Father Cowley suggested — the famous aria from the opera Martha.
Mr. Dedalus walked a few paces from the piano, tall and dignified, arms outstretched. He cleared his throat.
Father Cowley sang the opening notes:
—M'appari — when first my eyes beheld her...
Miss Douce waved farewell through the window, like someone waving goodbye to a departing ship.
—Go on, Simon.
—Ah, my dancing days are done, Ben... Well, all right...
Mr. Dedalus set down his pipe beside the tuning fork and sat at the piano.
—No, Simon, Father Cowley said. Play it in the original key. One flat.
The keys rose and fell, searching for the melody.
Father Cowley stood up.
—Here, Simon, I'll play the accompaniment, he said. You get up and sing.
Outside, Boylan's carriage bounced past shops on its way to Eccles Street.
In the dining room, Bloom and Goulding ate — steak, kidney, liver, mashed potatoes — food fit for princes.
—The most beautiful song ever written, Richie said.
Bloom looked at Richie's strained face. Poor Richie, with his bad back.
Richie would never forget that night at the concert.
Richie paused.
Here comes another big story, Bloom thought. But you have to be kind.
—Which song is that? Bloom asked.
—All is Lost Now.
Richie pursed his lips and hummed a low note — sweet and sad, like a bird singing far away.
Bloom leaned closer. He knew this melody. The song was about someone walking in a dream.
—A beautiful song, Bloom said quietly. I know it well.
Never in all his life had Richie heard anything so fine.
Bloom knows it well too, Richie thought.
Bloom glanced at Richie's face — remembering better days.
The piano started again. It sounded wonderful now.
Dollard and Cowley urged Mr. Dedalus on.
—Come on, Simon.
—Sing it, Simon.
—Ladies and gentlemen, Mr. Dedalus said with mock formality, I am deeply grateful for your encouragement.
—Come on, Simon!
—I have no money, he said, but if you'll lend me your attention, I shall try to sing.
Miss Douce watched and waited at the bar, her grace giving and withholding.
The prelude chords closed. A long, expectant chord drew out a voice.
—When first I saw that form endearing...
Richie turned to listen.
—That's Simon Dedalus's voice, he told Bloom.
They listened, touched with feeling, as the beautiful melody flowed over them.
—Sorrow from me seemed to depart...
Through the hushed air, a voice sang to them — low and gentle, a human voice singing of love.
Love was singing: love's old sweet song. Bloom slowly unwound the elastic band from his writing paper.
—Full of hope and all delighted...
Singers attract people, Bloom mused. A beautiful voice can make anyone fall in love.
The voice rose, sighing, changing — becoming loud, full, shining, proud.
—But alas, 'twas idle dreaming...
What a glorious voice Simon Dedalus still has, Bloom thought. He could have made a fortune.
The music swelled — tender, slow, full, throbbing.
Words? Music? No — it's what's behind them that matters.
Bloom played with the elastic band, looping and unlooping it.
A flood of warm feeling flowed through Bloom with the music.
—...ray of hope is...
Miss Douce squeezed out a tiny sigh as she listened.
Martha — that's the name of the opera, Bloom realized. And he was about to write to his pen-pal named Martha.
The voice returned, weaker but still beautiful — it sang to Richie, to Bloom, to Miss Douce, to everyone.
Bloom wished he could see the singer's face.
—Each graceful look...
Bloom remembered the first night he saw Molly at the Dillons' party. She wore yellow with black lace. They played musical chairs.
—Charmed my eye...
She had been singing that night. Bloom remembered turning her music pages. Her perfume. Everything changed that night.
—Martha! Ah, Martha!
The singer cried out in grief, in passion — calling his lost love to return.
—Come, thou lost one!
Come, thou dear one!
Alone. One love. One hope. One comfort. Martha, come back!
—Come!
The voice soared like a bird — a swift, pure cry — silver and serene.
It rose and rose, sustained in the air.
Then, at its peak, it gently died away.
—To me!
Simon! Leopold! The music filled them both.
Consumed by the beauty of it.
Come. Well sung. Everyone clapped.
She ought to come. To me, to him, to her, to all of us.
—Bravo! Clap clap! Good man, Simon! Clapping! Encore! Bravo, Simon! More clapping!
Outside, Blazes Boylan's smart tan shoes carried him away. His carriage jingled past monuments — past Sir John Gray's statue, past Nelson's Pillar — heading toward Eccles Street.
The last echo of Father Cowley's accompaniment closed and died on the air, leaving it richer.
And Richie Goulding drank his whiskey, and Leopold Bloom drank his cider, and Lidwell drank his dark beer, and Pat served them all.
—Seven days in jail on bread and water, Ben Dollard joked. Then you'd really sing, Simon, like a songbird.
Simon Dedalus, the singer, laughed. Father Cowley played on softly. Miss Kennedy served drinks. Tom Kernan strutted about.
Admiring.
Richie praised Mr. Dedalus's glorious voice at length. He remembered another wonderful night.
Richie, his pale face flushed, told Bloom all about that night — at Ned Lambert's house — when Simon Dedalus sang even more beautifully.
He told and told. And Bloom listened while Richie told him everything.
They were brothers-in-law who rarely spoke anymore. A rift between them. But tonight the music brought them together.
That voice was a cry of sorrow, Bloom thought. Calmer now.
It's in the silence after the song that you really hear it. Vibrations. Now the air is silent.
Bloom plucked at a thin rubber band, stretching it like a guitar string. He drew and plucked. It buzzed faintly.
Thou lost one. All songs are on that theme, Bloom thought. People getting attached to each other, then losing each other. Cruel, it seems.
Let people get fond of each other. Then tear them apart.
Too much happiness is boring, Bloom mused. He stretched the band more. More. Snap — it broke.
Boylan's carriage jingled into Dorset Street. Getting closer.
Miss Douce pulled her satiny arm away from a customer, half reproachful, half pleased.
—Don't be so familiar, she said, until we know each other better.
George Lidwell told her something really and truly flattering. But she did not believe him.
Another man confirmed it. And a second. And a third.
Miss Douce did not believe. Miss Kennedy did not believe. George Lidwell — no. Nobody believed anybody.
But that was all part of the fun.
Better write that letter now, Bloom thought. Before the moment passed.
Bald Pat at a signal drew near. A pen and ink. He went to fetch them.
A pad. He went. A pad to blot. He brought them all, deaf, bald Pat.
—Yes, Bloom said, playing with the broken elastic band. It certainly is fine music. Just a few lines will do. I need to write a quick letter.
—That's the grandest number in the whole opera, Richie Goulding said.
—It is, Bloom agreed.
Everything is numbers when you think about it, Bloom thought. All music is mathematics. Two multiplied by two. Vibrations. Chords.
Listen to what Father Cowley is playing now, Bloom thought. Improvising. Could be anything until you hear the words. You have to listen sharp.
Bald, deaf Pat brought the flat pad and ink pen. Pat set them down flat.
Pat took the plate and dish and knife and fork. Pat went.
Someone said the real thing was Irish songs. Mr. Dedalus had heard them as a boy in the countryside — people singing on the shore by the sea.
Mr. Dedalus cupped his hands around his mouth and made a beautiful nighttime bird call — clear from nearby, far-sounding to those at a distance, a call from across a moonlit bay.
Bloom's eyes scanned his newspaper, looking for something. Also making sure nobody was watching him write.
He hoped nobody was looking. Clever as a cat, he hid behind his newspaper.
Bloom tapped his fingers gently on the flat pad that Pat had brought.
Boring, this. Bored, Bloom tapped gently on the pad.
He began to write carefully, shielding the paper with his newspaper. Accept my little present enclosed.
Ask no questions. You know what I mean.
Am I foolish to be writing this? Bloom wondered. Married men don't usually have secret pen-pals.
But Molly has her own secrets. What can he do?
A hackney cab — number three hundred and twenty-four — carrying Blazes Boylan bounced along toward 7 Eccles Street.
—Answering an advertisement? Richie Goulding noticed Bloom writing.
—Yes, Bloom said casually. A job posting. Town traveler. Nothing doing, I expect.
Bloom murmured something about references while he finished writing. He signed it with his pen-name: Henry.
Better add a postscript, he thought.
He blotted the ink quickly on Pat's pad. Envelope.
He addressed it, copying from a piece of paper.
Miss Martha Clifford, care of the Post Office, Dolphin's Barn Lane, Dublin.
He blotted over the writing so nobody could read what was on the pad. There. Right.
Something clever, he thought. A puzzle for anyone who might find the blotting paper.
Too sentimental, what he'd written about sadness. The music had made him that way. Shakespeare said music has charms. There's a quotation for every day of the year.
Bloom thought about Shakespeare walking in a garden, gray-haired. One life is all we get.
Done. He'd need a stamp. Post office further down the street. He also needed to meet people at Barney Kiernan's pub.
Bloom could hear the talk at the bar. Bald Pat was busy with napkins.
Bald Pat, who was hard of hearing, smoothed napkins neatly. He waited while you waited.
Miss Douce now. Miss Lydia Douce. Bronze and rose.
She'd had the most gorgeous time at the seaside. And look at the lovely shell she'd brought back!
She carried the spiraling seashell to the end of the bar for George Lidwell to hold to his ear.
—Listen! she told him.
While Tom Kernan talked about singers, Father Cowley played soft music on the piano.
Lidwell held the shell to his ear. He heard! Wonderful! She held it to her own ear and heard the sea.
Tap. The blind young man's cane tapped on the pavement outside.
Bloom saw the shell being held to their ears. He could hear faintly what they heard.
Bronze by weary gold, they listened to the shell.
Her ear is like a shell too, Bloom thought. She'd been to the seaside.
The sea — that's what they think they hear, Bloom thought. But really it's just the sound of blood in your own ear.
Wonderful, really. George Lidwell held the shell once more, then gently set it down.
—What are the wild waves saying? he asked her with a smile.
Miss Douce smiled charmingly back.
Tap. The blind man's cane.
Boylan's carriage turned onto Eccles Street at last.
Miss Kennedy went from the abandoned shell back to serving her customers. Not so lonely now, with Miss Douce nearby.
Father Cowley's fingers played softly in the high notes. He was telling someone about landlords and legal claims. Ben Dollard rumbled in agreement.
Sea, wind, leaves, thunder, water, cows lowing at the cattle market — there's music in everything, Bloom thought.
The world is full of sounds. If you listen carefully.
That's joyful music now, Bloom thought. He could feel it. Joy in the melody.
He thought about Molly's singing voice. Powerful and beautiful.
My wife and your wife, Bloom thought. Everyone has someone.
Boylan's carriage stopped. His fancy tan shoes hit the ground.
He had arrived. At Eccles Street.
Music echoes everywhere, Bloom thought. Even in everyday sounds. A cup on a saucer. A door closing.
Someone knocked on a door. One knock. Then another. A loud, proud knock. Knock knock knock.
Tap. The blind man's cane outside.
—Sing something in Italian, Ben, Father Cowley suggested from the piano.
—No, Ben, Tom Kernan interrupted. Sing The Croppy Boy. That's our own Irish song.
—Yes, do, Ben, Mr. Dedalus agreed. Good men and true.
—Do, do, they all begged as one.
I should go now, Bloom thought. Here, Pat. My bill. Come. How much?
—What key? Ben Dollard asked. Six sharps?
—F sharp major, Ben Dollard decided.
Father Cowley's outstretched fingers struck deep, dark, sounding chords on the black keys.
Must go, Bloom told Richie. No, Richie said, stay a moment. Yes, I must. Bloom paid his bill — one shilling and ninepence. A penny tip for Pat.
But wait. But listen. Dark chords. Solemn and deep. Like being underground in a cave. Buried treasure of music.
The voice of a dark, ancient, tired world approached — painful and grave. It came from far away, from old mountains. It called on good men and true.
The young man in the song sought a priest. He wanted to confess his sins before going off to fight for Ireland.
Tap. The blind man passed by outside.
Ben Dollard's voice. A deep, rumbling bass. He did his very best to tell the story.
