His voice was like a vast, moonless ocean.
The song told how the young man found a priest. But the priest's servant who welcomed him was a traitor in disguise.
The so-called holy father was really the enemy. The young man didn't know.
The powerful could ruin lives, Bloom thought. Build them up, then tear them down. Lullaby. Goodbye.
The solemn voice warned: the youth entered a lonely hall.
His footsteps echoed in the gloomy chamber. The fake priest sat waiting to hear his confession.
Poor fellow, Bloom thought. A decent soul caught in a trap.
Listen. Bloom listened. Richie Goulding listened.
And by the door, deaf bald Pat listened too.
The piano chords harped slower.
The voice of sorrow and repentance came slowly, beautifully, trembling. Ben's great voice confessed the young man's sins.
In God's name, the young man knelt. He beat his breast. My fault. My fault. My greatest fault.
Latin words again, Bloom thought. That's what holds them — the mystery of the ancient language.
Tap. The blind man's cane tapped outside.
They all listened. The barmaids. George Lidwell. Tom Kernan. Simon Dedalus.
The sorrowful voice sang on. The young man confessed: since Easter he had cursed three times. He had missed church. He had neglected to pray for his dead mother.
Miss Douce gazed far away, listening, by the beer pull. She didn't realize Bloom could see her.
The singer's voice rose bravely, emboldened.
The young man confessed his deepest, most dangerous secret.
He was going to fight for Ireland. For the green land across the sea.
His country — his life — all at stake.
Tap. Tap. The blind man's cane outside on the pavement.
Bloom stood near the door with his letter in his pocket. The voice sang on.
The chords swelled beneath the words.
A chord trembled. The last confession was made.
The ending approached. The terrible twist.
The young man was betrayed. The priest he'd confessed to was really an enemy captain.
The confession was a trap. All his secrets spilled.
The youth was seized. Captured. His brave fight over before it began.
Bloom heard the climax. The great chords crashed.
He gnashed his teeth in fury — the young man's fury, Bloom's fury, everyone's fury at the injustice.
A moment of terrible silence fell over the bar.
At this very moment, Bloom knew, Boylan was at his house. At 7 Eccles Street. With Molly.
He tried not to think about it.
The song ended. The very last chord died away into nothing.
—Bravo! everyone cried and clapped.
Ben Dollard stood breathing hard from the effort. Good singing.
—That was magnificent, Ben, Father Cowley said with feeling.
Everyone agreed. Tom Kernan nodded solemnly.
Miss Kennedy's eyes were moist with feeling. The song had touched everyone.
Bloom had to go. The music was over and now the thoughts came flooding back.
He rose from his chair.
He gathered his newspaper and his letter.
—Thank you, Pat, Bloom said to the deaf waiter.
Bald Pat smiled without hearing and cleared the table.
Bloom walked toward the door of the dining room.
He passed through the bar. The barmaids were chatting.
The empty seashell sat on the counter, silent now.
Must go, Bloom thought. Must post this letter first.
Through the bar and out the door he went.
The evening air was cooler on the quay.
Bloom walked along the river.
He thought about the music — Simon Dedalus singing, Ben Dollard's deep bass.
Beautiful. Sad. Like life itself.
Music fades, Bloom thought. Like everything. Like love.
He passed shops along the quay.
Must post this letter, he reminded himself. Martha is waiting for a reply.
He felt restless. He needed something.
Tap. Tap. Tap. Tap. Tap. The blind man's cane on the pavement.
—Very fine voice, Mr. Dedalus was saying back at the hotel, staring at a sardine on his plate.
Under the sandwich bell lay a single sardine on a piece of bread. The very last one. Lonely.
Bloom alone.
—Very fine, Mr. Dedalus repeated. Especially the lower register.
Tap. Tap. Tap. Tap. Tap. Tap. Tap. Tap.
Bloom walked on past Barry's and other buildings. He wished he could do something wonderful — like a magician.
He thought about how everyone discovers their calling. The fellow who plays the big drum in a band. How did he first realize? Probably sitting at home one day, banging on things.
Tap. Tap. The blind young man came tapping past Daly's window, unable to see the shop display.
His cane found the way where his eyes could not. A mermaid poster smiled unseen.
Any object can be an instrument, Bloom thought. A blade of grass. A shell held to your hands.
Even a comb with tissue paper. Molly used to play like that. Humming in her nightgown.
I really must go, Bloom thought. His stomach grumbled. Must be the cider.
The Shah of Persia, Bloom thought randomly — even kings have these problems. Embarrassing at a banquet, though.
A tired-looking woman in a black straw hat walked along the quay toward Mr. Bloom in the fading light.
When first he saw that form... No. Not her. Just a stranger passing.
In a shop window, Bloom saw old things for sale — battered candlesticks, a worn accordion oozing at the seams. Bargains. Six shillings each.
Must be the cider, he thought again. Or the burgundy from earlier.
Back at the Ormond, near bronze Miss Douce and near gold Miss Kennedy, the drinkers clinked their glasses together — bright-eyed and cheerful.
A last toast. The last rose of summer.
First Lidwell, then Dedalus, then Cowley, then Kernan, then Dollard.
Tap. The blind young man entered the lonely hallway of the Ormond.
Bloom paused at a shop window and gazed at a picture of Robert Emmet. The Irish rebel's last words were framed below. Seven last words.
—True men like you, they toasted inside the hotel.
—Ay, ay, Ben agreed.
—Will lift your glasses with us.
They lifted their glasses.
Clink. Clunk. The glasses rang.

Tip. The blind young man stood in the hotel doorway. He saw nothing — not bronze Miss Douce, not golden Miss Kennedy, not Ben nor Bob nor Tom nor Simon nor George nor the drinks nor Richie nor Pat. He could not see. But he could hear.
Bloom, standing alone on the darkening street, gazed at the words.
Seabloom. Greaseabloom, the barmaids had called him, though he didn't know that.
He read Robert Emmet's last words softly: "When my country takes her place among the nations of the earth..."
His stomach rumbled. Prrr.
Must be the burgundy wine.
Pfft. Ooh. Another rumble.
He looked around. Nobody behind him.

"Nations of the earth." Nobody was behind him. A woman had passed. "Then and not till then." A tram rattled past — good moment to cover any sound. "Let my epitaph be written." Those were Robert Emmet's last words before he was executed. Bloom walked on.
One last rumble as he turned the corner and headed into the evening.

chapters.title: Episode 12 — Cyclops
paragraphs: I was walking along near Arbour Hill when a chimney sweep almost poked me in the eye with his brush. I was about to give him a piece of my mind when I spotted Joe Hynes coming down the street.
"Hey, Joe!" I said. "Did you see that chimney sweep? He nearly took my eye out!"
"That's supposed to be good luck," said Joe. "Who was that old fellow you were talking to?"
"Old Troy," I said. "He used to be a policeman. I was half thinking of reporting that sweep for blocking the footpath with his brushes."
"What brings you round here?" said Joe.
"Not much," I said. "There's a fellow who owes money to a shopkeeper named Herzog — old Troy was telling me about him. Took loads of tea and sugar and won't pay up."
"Is he the one who lives by the church?" said Joe.
"That's the one," I said. "An old plumber named Geraghty. I've been chasing him for two weeks and can't get a penny out of him."
"Is that your job now?" said Joe.

"It is," I said. "Collecting bad debts. Not the most glamorous work, I'll tell you. And this Geraghty is the biggest cheat you'd ever meet. He told me he'd take me to court! And there he is, stuffing himself with the tea and sugar he never paid for."

The official record showed that Mr. Moses Herzog had sold five pounds of tea and three stone of sugar to Mr. Michael Geraghty, who was supposed to pay it back three shillings a week. The goods belonged to Mr. Herzog until the full amount was paid.
"Are you completely off the drink?" said Joe.
"Not exactly," I said with a wink.
"Shall we go pay our respects to our friend?" said Joe.
"Who?" I said. "He's gone off his head, poor man. They had to take him away."
"Was he drinking his own stuff?" said Joe.
"He was," I said. "Whiskey went straight to his brain."
"Come round to Barney Kiernan's pub," said Joe. "I want to see the citizen."
"Sounds good to me," I said. "Anything interesting happening?"
"Nothing special," said Joe. "I was up at a meeting earlier."
"What meeting was that?" I said.
"Cattle traders," said Joe. "About a disease going round the farms. I need to tell the citizen about it."

So we walked round by the barracks and the courthouse, chatting about this and that. Joe is a decent fellow, but he's never got any money. And I still couldn't stop thinking about that cheat Geraghty.

In the fair land of Ireland, there are great towers and sleeping heroes. The rivers are full of fish — trout and salmon and all kinds besides. Beautiful trees grow everywhere, and lovely maidens sit under them, singing songs and playing with golden treasures. Heroes come from all parts of Ireland to visit this magical place.
And there stands a shining palace that sailors can see from far out at sea. All kinds of food is brought there — mountains of vegetables and fruits and berries, more than you could ever imagine.
"I dare him!" shouted Geraghty. "Come out here, you robber!"

And along the roads came endless herds of animals — sheep and cows, horses and pigs, geese and calves, all kinds of creatures from every corner of Ireland, bringing milk and butter and cheese and eggs.
So we went into Barney Kiernan's pub and there, sure enough, was the citizen sitting in the corner, talking to himself and his mangy old dog, Garryowen, waiting for someone to buy him a drink.
"There he is," I said, "in his favourite spot, with his jug and his newspapers, working for the cause."
The old dog growled at us in a way that'd make your hair stand up. Someone really ought to do something about that dog. I heard he once tore the trousers off a policeman.
"Stand and deliver," said the citizen.
"It's all right, citizen," said Joe. "We're friends."
"Pass, friends," said the citizen.
Then he rubbed his eye and said:
"What's your opinion of how things are going?"
He was putting on a big act, like a rebel leader. But Joe knew how to handle him.
"I think business is picking up," said Joe casually.
The citizen slapped his knee and said:
"It's the foreign wars causing all the trouble."
And Joe said, with his thumb in his pocket:
"It's the Russians trying to take over."
"Oh, stop joking around, Joe," I said. "I'm dying of thirst."
"What'll you have, citizen?" said Joe.
"A pint of the local," said the citizen.
"And you?" said Joe.
"Same for me," I said.
"Three pints, Terry," said Joe. "And how are you keeping, citizen?"
"Never better," said the citizen. "Right, Garry? Are we going to win?"
And he grabbed the old dog by the scruff of the neck and nearly choked him.

The figure sitting on a large boulder at the foot of a round tower was enormous — broad-shouldered, deep-chested, with wild red hair and a shaggy beard. He was so big that his nostrils could have held a bird's nest, and his eyes were the size of cauliflowers. When he breathed, the ground shook, and when his heart beat, the walls of the cave trembled.

He wore a rough outfit made of animal skins, tied at the waist with a belt of straw. From his belt hung a row of stones carved with pictures of Irish heroes — everyone from the ancient warrior Cuchulin to Napoleon Bonaparte, from Julius Caesar to Captain Nemo, and even Adam and Eve. A huge stone spear rested beside him, and at his feet lay a savage dog, growling in its sleep.
So Terry brought the three pints that Joe was paying for, and I nearly fell over when I saw Joe pull out a whole gold coin to pay.
"And there's more where that came from," said Joe.
"Were you robbing the poor box, Joe?" I joked.
"Hard-earned money," said Joe. "A friend gave me a tip."
"I saw him earlier," I said, "sneaking around the fish market, counting every last fish."
Who comes through the land in dark armour? It is O'Bloom, the son of Rory! Fearless and wise is Rory's son.
"Look at this newspaper," said the citizen. "It's supposed to be for Irish workers, but look at what it's full of — English names and English news!"
And he started reading them out:
"Gordon of Exeter... Redmayne of Saint Anne's... weddings in Kensington... deaths in London... Is this what an Irish newspaper should look like?"
"I know that fellow," said Joe. "From bitter experience."
"Look at all these English names!" said the citizen. "And this is supposed to be an Irish national newspaper!"
"Ah well," said Joe, handing round the drinks. "At least they got a head start on us. Drink up, citizen."
"I will," said the citizen politely.
"Good health, Joe," I said. "And to everyone here."
I was so thirsty that first sip hit my stomach with a click. Wonderful.
And lo, a messenger came swiftly in, bright as sunshine, a cheerful young man, and behind him walked an elder of noble bearing, carrying scrolls of law, accompanied by his fine lady wife.

Little Alf Bergan popped in round the door, hiding behind the counter and laughing. And who was sitting in the corner, drunk and snoring? Bob Doran. Alf kept making signs at the door, and it turned out old Denis Breen was outside in his slippers, carrying two big books, with his poor wife trotting after him. I thought Alf would burst laughing.
"Look at him," said Alf. "Breen. He's going all over Dublin with a postcard someone sent him..."
And he doubled over laughing.
"What postcard?" I said.
"He wants to sue someone for it," said Alf. "For ten thousand pounds!"
"You're joking!" I said.
The old dog started growling, sensing something was up, but the citizen gave him a kick to quiet him.
"Hush, boy," said the citizen to the dog.
"Who's suing?" said Joe.
"Breen," said Alf. "He went to one lawyer, then another, and they all sent him on a wild goose chase. He's gone completely round the bend over this postcard."
"When are they going to hang that fellow in the prison?" said Joe.
"Bergan?" said Bob Doran, waking up. "Is that Alf Bergan?"
"Yes," said Alf. "Wait till I show you something. Terry, give us a drink. That silly old fool Breen! Ten thousand pounds!"
And he started laughing again.
"Who are you laughing at?" said Bob Doran. "Is that Bergan?"
"Hurry up with that drink, Terry," said Alf.
Terry heard him and brought a crystal cup filled with fine dark ale, brewed by master craftsmen who work day and night to create the perfect drink.
Then noble Terry presented the cup to the thirsty man, as one gentleman to another.
But the young chief of the O'Bergans would not be outdone in generosity. He paid with a fine bronze coin bearing the image of Queen Victoria herself, ruler of the great empire.
"What's that fellow doing walking up and down outside?" said the citizen.
"What fellow?" said Joe.
"Here, look at this," said Alf, pulling something from his pocket. "I'll show you something amazing. Letters from hangmen."
He took out a bundle of letters and envelopes.
"Are you serious?" I said.
"Completely," said Alf. "Read them."
So Joe picked up the letters.
"Who are you laughing at?" said Bob Doran again.
I could see trouble brewing. Bob gets a bit difficult when he's been drinking, so I changed the subject:
"How's Willy Murray these days, Alf?"
"I don't know," said Alf. "I just saw him in the street with Paddy Dignam. Only I was running after that..."
"You what?" said Joe, dropping the letters. "With who?"
"With Dignam," said Alf.
"Paddy Dignam?" said Joe.
"Yes," said Alf. "Why?"
"Don't you know he's dead?" said Joe.
"Paddy Dignam dead!" said Alf.
"Yes," said Joe.
"But I just saw him five minutes ago," said Alf, "clear as day."
"Who's dead?" said Bob Doran.
"You must have seen his ghost then," said Joe.
"What?" said Alf. "But he was right there... What? Dignam's dead?"
"What about Dignam?" said Bob Doran. "Who's talking about him?"
"Dead!" said Alf. "He can't be dead. I just saw him!"
"Maybe so," said Joe. "But they buried him this morning."
"Paddy?" said Alf.
"Yes," said Joe. "He's passed away, God rest him."
"I can't believe it!" said Alf.
He was completely shocked.

In the darkness, spirit hands were felt to flutter. A faint ruby light appeared — the ghost of the departed! When asked about the afterlife, he said he had been shown wonderful things. The spirits there had every modern comfort. He had one important message for the living: make sure his son Patsy finds the other boot, which is under the chest of drawers in the back room, and send the pair to the cobbler — the heels are still good. This had been greatly troubling his peace of mind in the next world.
Everyone promised to take care of the boot situation, which seemed to bring the ghost some peace.
He is gone from us! O'Dignam, light of our morning! Swift was his step! Cry for him, Ireland, and cry, O ocean!
"There he is again," said the citizen, staring out the window.
"Who?" I said.
"Bloom," said the citizen. "He's been walking up and down out there for the last ten minutes."
And sure enough, I saw Bloom peek in the door and then disappear again.
Little Alf was still in shock about Dignam.
"I could have sworn it was him I saw!" said Alf.
And Bob Doran, his hat on backwards and rather the worse for drink, said:
"Who said anything about that?"
"I beg your pardon," said Alf.
"Is it fair," said Bob Doran, "to take away poor little Willy Dignam?"
"Well," said Alf, trying to smooth things over, "at least he's at peace now."
But Bob Doran shouted out:
"It's terrible," he said, "to take away poor little Willy Dignam."
Terry came over and told him quietly to keep it down — they didn't want that kind of scene in the pub. And Bob started crying about Paddy Dignam.
"The finest man," Bob said, sniffling. "The finest, purest character."
He was nearly in tears. Of course, Bob always gets emotional when he's had a few drinks. You'd think he was the best friend Dignam ever had.
"The noblest, the truest," said Bob. "And he's gone. Poor little Paddy."
And with a heavy heart he mourned the loss of that good man.
Old Garryowen started growling again. Bloom was hovering around the door.
"Come in, come in," said the citizen. "He won't bite you."
So Bloom came in, keeping one eye on the dog, and asked Terry if Martin Cunningham had been there.
"Listen to this one," said Joe, reading one of the letters. "This is priceless."
And he started reading it out:
"7 Hunter Street, Liverpool."
"To the High Sheriff of Dublin."
"Dear Sir, I would like to offer my services. I have experience in this line of work, having done several jobs before..."
"Show us," I said.
"...I was assistant at several occasions and have the proper skills..."
"Unbelievable!" I said.
"...and I come highly recommended..."
The citizen grabbed at the letter.
"Wait," said Joe. "He says he has a special knack for the job and his fee is five guineas."
"Signed, H. Rumbold, Master Barber."
"What a brute," said the citizen.
"And look at the terrible handwriting," said Joe. "Here, Alf, take these away. Hello, Bloom — what'll you have?"
So they offered Bloom a drink, but he kept saying no thank you, he couldn't, excuse him — and finally said he'd just have a cigar. He was being very careful with his money.
"Give us one of your best cigars, Terry," said Joe.
And Alf was telling us that one applicant had even sent a mourning card with a black border.
"They're all the same," said Alf. "They'd do anything for a few coins."
He told us that after the job is done, people even buy bits of the rope as souvenirs.
In dark places the executioners hide, waiting with their deadly tools, as the Lord commands justice to be served.
So they started talking about whether punishment really stops crime, and of course Bloom had to join in with all his opinions and theories.
"There's one thing it doesn't stop," said Alf.
"What's that?" said Joe.
"Never mind," said Alf with a grin.
"Really?" said Joe.
"It's true," said Alf. "I heard it from someone who was there."
"The body does strange things," said Joe.
"That can be explained by science," said Bloom. "It's just a natural reaction, you see, because of the..."
And then he started using long scientific words that nobody could follow.

The distinguished scientist Professor Blumenduft explained in great detail, using the longest possible words, that it was simply a medical reaction — something that happens in the body at such moments, a phenomenon well known to science.

So then the citizen started going on about Irish heroes and rebels, and Joe joined in, talking about all the men who had fought and died for Ireland. Meanwhile, Bob Doran was making a fuss over the dog:
"Give us your paw! Good doggy! Give the paw!"
The dog wasn't having any of it, and Alf had to stop Bob from falling off his stool. Bob was feeding the dog bits of old biscuit, and the dog gobbled them up and wanted more.

The citizen and Bloom were arguing about Irish heroes and the fight for freedom. Bloom was puffing on his cigar and trying to make his points, while the narrator thought to himself that Bloom was just showing off. He'd heard that Bloom's wife was quite a character, and that Bloom had once tried to get on the good side of a rich old woman to get into her will.
"To the memory of the dead," said the citizen, raising his glass and glaring at Bloom.
"Hear, hear," said Joe.
"You don't understand my point," said Bloom. "What I mean is..."
"Ireland for the Irish!" said the citizen. "Our friends beside us and our enemies before us!"

The scene was described in the most dramatic way imaginable — bells tolling, drums beating, thunder crashing, and half a million people watching in the rain. The famous executioner Mr. Rumbold arrived in his best clothes, and the crowd went wild. There was a very emotional moment when a young bride threw herself at the prisoner. Everyone was crying, even the tough policemen. Then a handsome young man proposed to the bride right there, and everyone cheered. Even the stern military commander had to wipe away a tear.

Mr. Rumbold the executioner arrived looking very smart and received a great cheer from the crowd. Foreign visitors from all over the world were watching. There was an argument among the international guests about the correct date of Saint Patrick's Day, which led to a comical fight until a tall policeman settled it by suggesting the seventeenth of the month, which everyone agreed to.
"She's quite something," muttered the military man, wiping his eye. "She reminds me of my own sweetheart."

The citizen started talking about the Irish language and how Irish people should speak their own tongue. Bloom put in his thoughts about temperance — not drinking too much. But the narrator thought Bloom was a fine one to talk about temperance, since he'd happily drink anything put in front of him without ever buying a round himself.
The old dog, seeing the biscuit tin was empty, started nosing around us. If that dog were mine, I thought, I'd train him with a firm hand.
"Afraid he'll bite you?" teased the citizen.
"No," I said, "but he might mistake my leg for a lamppost."
So the citizen called the old dog over.
"What's the matter, Garry?" he said.
Then the citizen started talking to the dog in Irish, and the dog growled back, like they were having a conversation. A proper duet, the two of them.

For those interested in animal intelligence, the famous Irish setter Garryowen (recently renamed Owen Garry by his friends) gave an amazing performance. Experts say his growls bear a striking resemblance to ancient Celtic poetry. We include a sample of his verse, translated into English by a top scholar.

"The curse of my curses,
Seven days every day,
And seven dry Thursdays
On you, Barney Kiernan,
Who has no water
To cool my thirst,
And my belly rumbling
After eating the lights."
So the citizen told Terry to bring water for the dog, and you could hear the dog lapping it up from across the room. Joe asked the citizen if he'd have another drink.
"I will," said the citizen, "to show there's no hard feelings."
He's no fool, the citizen. Gets himself fed and watered by everyone else and never pays for a thing.
"Fancy another pint?" said Joe.
"Can a duck swim?" I said.
"Same again, Terry," said Joe. "Are you sure you won't have a proper drink?" he asked Bloom.

"No, thank you," said Bloom. "Actually, I just need to find Martin Cunningham. It's about poor Dignam's insurance. You see, there's a problem with the policy — Dignam didn't file the right papers, and now the insurance company might not pay out."
"Well, that's something," said Joe, laughing. "So the wife will get the money after all?"
"That's one way to look at it," said Bloom. "For the wife's benefit."
"For whose benefit?" said Joe.
"The wife's advisers, I mean," said Bloom.
Then Bloom started explaining all the legal details about mortgages and trusts until my head was spinning. He certainly knew his law, though some wondered how he knew so much about dodgy dealings.
Bob Doran came stumbling over, asking Bloom to tell Mrs. Dignam how sorry he was. He was shaking Bloom's hand and getting all emotional about poor Paddy Dignam.
"If I may be so bold," said the first gentleman, "though our friendship may be brief, I hope you will do me this favour."
"Of course," said the other. "Though the task is a sad one, your trust in me makes it easier to bear."
"Then let me shake your hand," said the first. "Your kind heart will know what to say better than I ever could."
And off went Bob Doran, trying to walk straight. He was always getting himself into trouble when he'd had too much to drink.
So Terry brought the three pints.
"Here you go," said Joe, handing them round. "Here, citizen."
"Cheers," said the citizen.
"Good health, Joe," I said. "And to everyone."
The citizen had half his pint gone before anyone else had started. It would take a fortune to keep him in drinks.
"Who's running for mayor, Alf?" said Joe.
"A friend of yours," said Alf.
"Nannan?" said Joe. "The councillor?"
"I won't say any names," said Alf.
"I thought so," said Joe. "I saw him at the cattle traders' meeting with the politician."
"That windbag," said the citizen. "The darling of every country and the idol of his own."

So Joe started telling the citizen about the cattle disease, and the citizen thought everyone involved was useless. Then Bloom chimed in with his ideas about remedies for sick animals. Bloom always had an opinion about everything — he'd once worked in a cattle yard until he got fired for being too clever.
Cluck cluck cluck. Our hen lays eggs. When she lays her egg she's so happy. Cluck cluck. Then comes nice Uncle Leo. He reaches under the hen and takes her fresh egg. Cluck cluck cluck.
"Anyway," said Joe, "the politicians are going to London tonight to ask about it in Parliament."
"Are you sure the councillor is going?" said Bloom. "I wanted to see him."
"He's going on the mail boat tonight," said Joe.
"That's a pity," said Bloom. "I particularly wanted to speak to him."
"He's been asked to bring up a question in Parliament about the police banning Irish games in the park," said Joe. "What do you think of that, citizen?"
Mr. Conacre asked: "Has the government ordered these animals destroyed without proper medical evidence?"
Mr. Allfours replied: "The evidence has already been presented. The answer is yes."
Mr. O'Reilly asked: "And what about the Irish people who dare to play Irish games in the park? Are they to be treated the same way?"
Mr. Allfours: "The answer is no."
Mr. Conacre: "Has the government's policy been inspired by violence?"
Mr. Allfours: "I'll need notice of that question."
Another member: "Don't hesitate to take action!"
(Sarcastic cheers from the opposition.)
The Speaker: "Order! Order!"
(The session ended with cheers.)
"There's the man," said Joe, pointing at the citizen. "He revived Gaelic sports. He was the champion of all Ireland at throwing the shot put. What was your best throw, citizen?"
"Ah, don't make a fuss," said the citizen modestly. "I was as good as anyone, once upon a time."
"You were more than good," said Joe. "You were the best."
"Is that really true?" said Alf.
"Yes," said Bloom. "It's well known."

So they all started talking about Irish sports versus English sports like tennis, and the citizen was all for building up the nation through athletics. And of course Bloom had to put in his view about how violent exercise can be bad for you. He'd talk about anything for an hour if you let him.

A fascinating discussion about reviving ancient Irish sports took place at Barney Kiernan's. After a magnificent speech by the chairman, everyone debated whether the old games should be brought back. Mr. Bloom spoke against too much exercise, which got a mixed reaction. The evening ended with a rousing rendition of "A Nation Once Again" by the citizen, who sang in fine form to great applause from all present.
Among those present were dozens of reverend fathers, priests, and brothers from every religious order in Ireland, too many to name individually.
"Speaking of exercise," said Alf, "were you at that boxing match?"
"No," said Joe.
"I heard someone made a lot of money on it," said Alf.
"Boylan?" said Joe.
And Bloom said:
"What I meant about tennis is that it's good for training the eye and improving agility."
"Yes, Boylan," said Alf. "He let it be known the fighter was drinking to raise the odds, while really the fighter was training hard."
"We know him," said the citizen. "A traitor's son. We know where his money comes from."
"True enough," said Joe.
And Bloom tried again to talk about tennis and exercise:
"Don't you think so, Bergan?"
"The Irish lad destroyed him," said Alf. "It was an incredible fight. The smaller man won through pure skill and one final punch."

It was a historic battle when the two fighters stepped into the ring for fifty gold coins. The smaller Irish fighter, Dublin's favourite, made up for his size with incredible skill. After rounds of fierce fighting, the Irish gladiator landed a tremendous punch that knocked the larger soldier flat. It was a clean knockout, and the crowd went wild, rushing into the ring to celebrate their champion.
"He knows which side his bread is buttered," said Alf. "I hear he's running concerts up north now."
"He is," said Joe. "Isn't he?"
"Oh, yes," said Bloom. "That's quite true. A kind of summer tour."
"Mrs. Bloom is the star of the show, isn't she?" said Joe.
"My wife? Yes, she's singing," said Bloom. "I think it will be a success. He's an excellent organiser."
I thought to myself, that explains a lot. Boylan organising concerts with Bloom's wife. Very interesting indeed.
The beautiful dark-haired daughter of Tweedy grew up where lemon trees and almonds scent the air. She is the fair wife of Leopold, Marion of the generous spirit.
And there entered a member of the O'Molloy clan, a handsome hero, learned in law, and with him the noble Lambert.
"Hello, Ned."
"Hello, Alf."
"Hello, Jack."
"Hello, Joe."
"Good day to you," said the citizen.
"Good day," said J. J. "What'll you have, Ned?"
"A small one," said Ned.
So J. J. ordered the drinks.
"Were you at the court?" said Joe.
"Yes," said J. J. "He'll sort that out, Ned."
"I hope so," said Ned.
I wondered what those two were up to. J. J. was trying to get Ned off jury duty, and they were both doing each other favours. Meanwhile Ned owed money everywhere and was always gambling.
"Did you see that crazy fellow Breen around there?" said Alf.
"Yes," said J. J. "He was looking for a private detective."
"He wanted to go straight to court," said Ned, "but Corny Kelleher talked him out of it, saying he should get the handwriting examined first."
"Ten thousand pounds!" said Alf, laughing. "I'd love to see him try that in court."
"Was it you who sent the postcard, Alf?" said Joe with a grin.
"Me?" said Alf. "Don't go accusing me!"
"Anything you say may be used against you," said Joe, joking.
"He could actually sue," said J. J. seriously. "The postcard implies he's not of sound mind."
"Not of sound mind is right!" said Alf, laughing. "Have you seen the size of his head? He needs a shoehorn to get his hat on!"
"But in law," said J. J., "even if it's true, that's no defence against a charge of publishing something harmful."
"Ha ha," said Joe to Alf.
"Still," said Bloom, "I feel sorry for his poor wife."
"Feel sorry for her?" said the citizen. "Or any woman who marries a fool."
"What do you mean by that?" said Bloom. "Do you mean he's..."
"I mean what I mean," said the citizen. "A man who's neither one thing nor the other."
"Nor anything useful," said Joe.
"Exactly," said the citizen. "A fool, if you know what I mean."

I could see trouble was coming. Bloom was trying to explain he was just worried about the poor wife having to run around after her foolish husband. But the narrator thought old Breen was a laughingstock, wandering around with his big beard, pretending to be important.
"Furthermore," said J. J., "a postcard counts as a public document in law. There's a legal case that proves it."
Who asked for his legal opinion? Can't a man drink his pint in peace?
"Good health, Jack," said Ned.
"Good health, Ned," said J. J.
"There he is again," said Joe.
"Where?" said Alf.
And there was old Breen passing the door with his books under his arm and his wife beside him, and Corny Kelleher walking with them, talking to Breen like a kindly father.
"How did that swindle case go?" said Joe.
"Postponed," said J. J.

It was about a fellow who put an advert in the paper saying he'd give you a ticket to Canada for almost nothing. Of course it was a scam. He cheated everyone — servants and workers and even his own people.
"Who was the judge?" said Joe.
"The Recorder," said Ned.
"Poor old Sir Frederick," said Alf. "You can fool him easily."
"He's got a heart of gold," said Ned. "Tell him a sad story about a sick wife and children, and he'll cry right there on the bench."
"True," said Alf. "Someone nearly got in trouble the other day for suing a poor watchman who guards stones by the bridge."
And Alf started imitating the old judge getting emotional:
"How terrible! This poor hardworking man! How many children does he have? Ten?"
"Yes, your honour. And my wife has a fever."
"His wife has a fever! Scandalous! Case dismissed! I won't make him pay a penny! How dare you bring this case before me!"

On that day, the learned judges gathered in their courts. Master Courtenay sat in his chamber, and Justice Andrews weighed the evidence in a complicated case about a will. And in the great Green Street court, Sir Frederick presided, with twelve good men of Ireland serving on the jury, sworn to deliver truth and justice.
"Nice characters coming over here," grumbled the citizen, "filling the country with trouble."
Bloom pretended not to hear and started talking to Joe about some business — asking him to put in a word with Mr. Crawford about an advertisement.
"The secret of advertising," said Bloom, "is repetition. You have to keep repeating the message."
"You can count on me," said Joe.
"Foreigners cheating our people," said the citizen. "We don't want strangers in our house."
"I'm sure it'll be fine," said Bloom. "It's just the Keyes advertisement, you see."
"Consider it done," said Joe.
"Very kind of you," said Bloom.
"Strangers," said the citizen. "Our own fault for letting them in. It was a betrayal that brought the English here in the first place."
"A legal ruling," said J. J.
Bloom pretended to be very interested in a spider's web in the corner, while the citizen glared at him and the old dog watched to see who it should growl at.
"A betrayed nation," said the citizen. "That's the root of all our problems."
"And here's something interesting," said Alf, pointing at a magazine Terry had on the counter.
"Let me see," I said.
It was just a silly American magazine with scandalous stories and pictures — nothing worth looking at.
"Would you look at that!" said Joe.
"Quite a sight," I agreed.
Then in came John Wyse Nolan and Lenehan, and Lenehan looked miserable.
"Well," said the citizen, "what's the latest? What did the city council decide about the Irish language?"

O'Nolan, clad in shining armour, brought news to the great chief of Ireland. The elders of the city had met and, after saying their prayers, had held a solemn discussion about how to bring the ancient Irish language back to life.
"Progress is being made," said the citizen. "Down with the English language!"
J. J. tried to be balanced, saying you have to look at both sides, and Bloom backed him up, talking about moderation and the benefits of civilisation.
"Their civilisation?" sneered the citizen. "Everything they have, they stole from us!"
"The European family..." said J. J.
"They're not European," said the citizen. "I've been to Europe. You won't find a trace of them anywhere."
And John Wyse said:
"Many a flower blooms unseen."
And Lenehan, who knew a bit of French, said:
"Down with the English!"
The great warrior raised his mighty cup of dark ale and, shouting his battle cry, drank to the defeat of his enemies — those mighty rulers of the waves who sit on thrones of stone.
"What's wrong with you?" I asked Lenehan. "You look like you've lost money."
"The Gold Cup race," he said.
"Who won?" asked Terry.
"Throwaway," said Lenehan. "A complete outsider, at twenty to one. Everyone else lost."
"And the favourite?" said Terry.
"Still running, probably," said Lenehan. "We all lost. Boylan put money on my tip, Sceptre, for himself and a lady friend."
"I bet on Zinfandel myself," said Terry.
"Twenty to one," said Lenehan sadly. "That's life. Throwaway wins and everyone else loses."
He went over to the biscuit tin to see if there was anything to eat, with the old dog following hopefully. But the tin was empty.
"Nothing there, I'm afraid," he said.
"Cheer up," said Joe. "Better luck next time."
J. J. and the citizen were arguing about law and history, with Bloom putting in a word here and there.
"Some people," said Bloom, "can see faults in others but not in themselves."

"Don't talk to me about blindness," said the citizen. "Where are the twenty million Irish who should be here? Where are our industries — our pottery, our textiles, our wool that was famous in Rome? Our lace, our glass, our silk? The Greeks used to trade here! Read the history books! And what did England do? Destroyed our trade, our homes, our forests, and wouldn't even drain the bogs to stop people dying of disease!"
"We'll be as bare as a desert soon," said John Wyse, "if we don't plant more trees."
"Save the great trees of Ireland!" said the citizen. "The giant ash of Galway, the mighty elm of Kildare! Save them for the future!"
"All of Europe is watching," said Lenehan.

A grand wedding took place between Mr. John Wyse de Neaulan, chief forester, and Miss Fir Conifer of Pine Valley. Among the guests were Mrs. Holly Hazeleyes, Miss Gladys Beech, Miss Olive Garth, Miss Grace Poplar, and Mrs. Arabella Blackwood. The bride wore a stunning green dress. The organist played 'Woodman, Spare That Tree.' After the ceremony, the happy couple were showered with hazelnuts, acorns, and holly berries.
"We used to trade with Spain and France long before England existed," said the citizen. "Spanish wine in Galway — that's our history."
"And we will again," said Joe.

"With God's help, we will," said the citizen, slapping his thigh. "Our empty harbours will be full again — Galway, Kinsale, Kerry. When the first Irish ship sails with our own flag, the oldest flag in the world, three crowns on a blue field!"
He finished his pint. All big talk, of course. He wouldn't dare make speeches like that in some parts of Ireland where people had real grievances against loudmouths like him.
"Hear, hear," said John Wyse. "What'll you have?"
"A special drink to celebrate," said Lenehan.
"A whiskey and a beer, Terry," said John Wyse. "Terry! Wake up!"
"Yes, sir," said Terry. "Small whiskey and a bottle. Coming right up."
Everyone was reading the newspaper, looking for interesting stories. There was a picture of a headbutting contest, and another horrible story from America. Terrible stuff.
"But what about the navy?" said Ned. "That keeps enemies away."
"The navy?" said the citizen. "Let me tell you about the navy. It's brutal. Read the papers about what happens on their training ships."
He told us about harsh punishment on navy ships — young boys being beaten for minor offences.
"They call it discipline," said the citizen. "I call it cruelty."
And John Wyse said:
"It's a rule more broken than followed."
Then the citizen described how officers on ships punished young sailors harshly for the smallest mistakes.
"That's your great empire," said the citizen. "Built on cruelty and slavery."
"The empire where the sun never rises," joked Joe.
"And the sad thing is," said the citizen, "they actually believe they're doing good."
They believe in the rod almighty, maker of misery, and in harsh punishment, and in endless work, and in being beaten and suffering, world without end.
"But isn't discipline the same everywhere?" said Bloom. "I mean, wouldn't it be the same here if you used force against force?"
There he goes again. Even on his last breath he'd try to argue that black was white.

"We'll meet force with force," said the citizen. "We have millions of Irish people around the world. They were driven from their homes during the Great Famine. Twenty thousand died on the ships. But those who made it to freedom remember where they came from, and they will return."
"That's perfectly true," said Bloom. "But my point was..."
"We've been waiting a long time for that day," said Ned.
"We fought for every cause but our own," said John Wyse. "We gave our best soldiers to France and Spain. And what did we ever get in return?"
"The French!" said the citizen. "They were never any help to Ireland. Now they're making friends with England!"
"Down with the French!" said Lenehan, drinking his beer.
"And the Germans were no better," said Joe. "All those foreign kings on our thrones."
Everyone laughed thinking about old Queen Victoria in her palace.
"Well, now we have Edward the Peacemaker," said J. J.
"Peacemaker!" scoffed the citizen. "He's no peacemaker."
"And can you believe," said Joe, "that the priests at Maynooth decorated his room in his racing colours?"
"They should have put up pictures of all his lady friends too," said little Alf.
And J. J. said:
"There wouldn't have been enough wall space for that."
"Will you have another, citizen?" said Joe.
"I will," said the citizen.
"You?" said Joe to me.
"Don't mind if I do, Joe," I said. "May your shadow never grow less."
"Same again all round," said Joe.
Bloom was deep in conversation with John Wyse, getting quite worked up about something.
"Persecution," said Bloom. "The whole history of the world is full of it. Nations hating each other for no good reason."
"But do you know what a nation really means?" said John Wyse.
"Yes," said Bloom.
"What is it?" said John Wyse.
"A nation?" said Bloom. "A nation is the same people living in the same place."
"Well then," laughed Ned, "I must be a nation myself, because I've been living in the same place for five years!"
Everyone laughed at Bloom, and he tried to fix his answer:
"Or also living in different places," he added.
"That covers my case too," said Joe.
"What is your nation, if I may ask?" said the citizen, staring at Bloom.
"Ireland," said Bloom. "I was born here. Ireland."
The citizen said nothing. He just spat into the corner.
"Pass the drink, Joe," said the citizen, wiping his mouth with his handkerchief.
"Here you go, citizen," said Joe. "Take this and repeat after me."

Then a beautiful ancient Irish cloth was brought out, embroidered with pictures of the four evangelists and decorated with scenes of Ireland's most famous places — from the lakes of Killarney to the brewery of Guinness, from the rock of Cashel to Fingal's Cave. All these wonderful scenes, made even more beautiful by the passage of time.
"Pass me my drink," I said. "Which one is mine?"
"That one's mine," said Joe.
"I belong to a people who have been hated and persecuted too," said Bloom quietly. "Right now, at this very moment."
He nearly burned his fingers on his cigar stub.
"Robbed," said Bloom, getting passionate. "Plundered. Insulted. Having what's rightfully ours taken away. Right now, people are being sold like cattle."
"Are you talking about a homeland?" said the citizen.
"I'm talking about injustice," said Bloom.
"Then stand up and fight for it," said John Wyse.
I had to smile at the thought of Bloom standing up to anyone. He's not exactly a fighter.
"But force is no use," said Bloom. "Force, hatred, history — that's not what life is really about. Everybody knows the opposite of hatred is what really matters."
"What opposite?" said Alf.
"Love," said Bloom. "I mean the opposite of hatred. I have to go now," he said to John Wyse. "Just popping round to the courthouse to find Martin. If he comes, tell him I'll be right back."
And off he went like a shot.
"A new preacher of love," said the citizen sarcastically.
"Well," said John Wyse, "isn't that what we're taught? Love your neighbour?"
"That fellow?" said the citizen. "His motto is look out for number one."
Love loves to love love. The nurse loves the new doctor. The policeman loves Mary Kelly. Everyone loves somebody. And God loves everybody.
"Well, Joe," I said, "your very good health."
"Cheers," said Joe.
"God bless you," said the citizen.
And he took a big gulp of his drink.

"We know those types," said the citizen. "Preaching love while picking your pocket. What about Cromwell? He had 'God is love' painted on his cannons while he was destroying Ireland! And did you see in today's paper about the African chief visiting England?"
"What about him?" said Joe.
The citizen picked up a newspaper and started reading:

A group of English businessmen visited an African chief to thank him for letting them trade in his country. The chief, through an interpreter, said how much he valued his friendship with England. His most treasured possession was a Bible given to him by Queen Victoria herself. Then he performed a traditional dance, which the audience enjoyed enormously.
"The old queen," said Ned. "I wonder if the chief actually read the Bible."
"Probably not in the usual way," said Lenehan with a grin.
"Who wrote that article?" said John Wyse.
"It's not signed properly," said the citizen. "Just the initial P."
"A fine initial," said Joe.
"That's how empire works," said the citizen. "Trade follows the flag."
"Well," said J. J., "if they're any worse than what the Belgians did in Africa, they must be truly terrible. Did you read that report by — what's his name?"
"Casement," said the citizen. "He's Irish."
"Yes, that's him," said J. J. "Terrible things happening there."
"I know where Bloom has gone," said Lenehan, snapping his fingers.
"Where?" I said.
"He had a bet on Throwaway," said Lenehan, "the horse that won. He's gone to collect his winnings."
"That sneaky fellow?" said the citizen. "He's never bet on a horse in his life!"
"That's where he's gone," said Lenehan. "I met someone who said Bloom gave them the tip. I bet he put a lot of money on it. He's the only one in Dublin who knew."
"He's a dark horse himself," said Joe.
"Watch out for him," I said.
"Here's your drink," said Terry.
I went out back for a moment, and all I could think about was whether Bloom really had bet on that horse and won all that money, while the rest of us were broke.

When I got back, they were deep in an argument. John Wyse was saying Bloom had given ideas to the Irish independence movement — all kinds of clever schemes. But the narrator thought, if Bloom is involved, it can't be any good. Bloom's own father had been a travelling salesman with a bad reputation.
"It's true," said John Wyse. "And here comes the man who can confirm it — Martin Cunningham."
Sure enough, a carriage pulled up with Martin Cunningham, Jack Power, and a quiet fellow named Crofton.
Our travellers reached the rustic inn and dismounted from their horses.
"Ho, servant!" cried their leader. "Come here!"
And he knocked on the door with his sword handle.
The innkeeper came out, putting on his apron.
"Good day, good masters," he said with a bow.
"Hurry up!" said the leader. "See to our horses. And bring us your best food and drink!"
"Alas, good masters," said the innkeeper. "My kitchen is nearly empty."
"What?" said the second traveller. "Is this how you treat the king's messengers?"
The innkeeper's expression changed immediately.
"Forgive me, gentlemen!" he said. "If you serve the king, you shall have everything!"
"Then get moving!" said the third, who looked very hungry. "What have you got?"
The innkeeper bowed and replied:
"How about pigeon pie, venison, veal, roast pork, custard, and a fine old wine?"
"Wonderful!" cried the hungry one. "Especially the pistachios!"
"A poor kitchen indeed!" laughed the second. "You're quite the joker."
So Martin came in and asked where Bloom was.
"He's probably off cheating someone," said Lenehan.
"Isn't it true what I was telling the citizen about Bloom and his ideas?" said John Wyse.
"So they say," said Martin.
"Who says?" said Alf.
"I do," said Joe. "I'm the one saying it."
"And why can't a Jewish person love his country like anyone else?" said John Wyse.
"Why not?" said J. J. "As long as he knows which country it is."
"But what exactly is he?" said Ned. "No offence meant."
"That's the question," said J. J.
"We don't need his sort," said Crofton quietly.
"He's originally from Hungary," said Martin. "It was his father who drew up plans based on the Hungarian system of independence. We know about it from government records."
"Isn't he related to Bloom the dentist?" said Jack Power.
"No, just the same name," said Martin. "The father's real name was Virag. He changed it legally."
"The new saviour of Ireland!" said the citizen sarcastically.
"Well, everyone's still waiting for a saviour," said Martin. "Including us."
J. J. made a joke that got a laugh from everyone.
"Always expecting something," said Lenehan.
"You should have seen Bloom before his son was born — the one who died," said Ned. "I met him six weeks before the birth, already buying baby food."
"Before the child was even born," said J. J.
"Do you call that a man?" said the citizen.
"I wonder about him sometimes," said Joe.
"Well, he does have two children," said Jack Power.
"And who does he suspect?" said the citizen with a sneer.
People said all sorts of nasty things about Bloom behind his back. And now here he was, leaving without buying anyone a drink. That's what bothered people most.
"We should be kind," said Martin. "But where is he? We can't wait."
"He's not what he seems," said the citizen. "A wolf in sheep's clothing."
"Have you time for a quick drink, Martin?" said Ned.
"Just one," said Martin. "We have to hurry."
"You, Jack? Crofton? Three small whiskies, Terry."
"Saint Patrick himself would have to come back to sort this country out," said the citizen, "after letting in people like that."
"Well," said Martin, raising his glass. "God bless all here."
"Amen," said the citizen.
"And I'm sure He will," said Joe.

Then came a grand procession of monks and friars and nuns from every religious order — Benedictines, Franciscans, Dominicans, Jesuits, and many more. Behind them came all the saints and martyrs of Ireland, carrying palms and harps and swords, wearing robes decorated with symbols of their lives. They walked through the streets singing hymns, performing miracles along the way. Finally, they arrived at Barney Kiernan's pub and blessed it from top to bottom.
"The Lord be with us."
"Who made heaven and earth."
"The Lord be with you."
"And with your spirit."
And he blessed everything and everyone prayed together:
A prayer in Latin asking God to bless all the food and drink in the pub.
"Hear, hear," said Jack.
"A good living," said Crofton.
"Right," said Ned, picking up his whiskey. "Cheers."
I was just looking around when who should walk back in but Bloom, pretending to be in a great hurry.
"I was just at the courthouse," he said, "looking for you. I hope I'm not late."
"No," said Martin. "We're ready to go."
I was thinking, here he is with his pockets full of winnings from the horse race, and he still won't buy anyone a drink. Not a penny.
"Don't tell anyone," said the citizen with a meaningful look.
"I beg your pardon?" said Bloom.
"Come on, everyone," said Martin, seeing trouble was brewing. "Let's go."
"Don't tell anyone!" shouted the citizen. "It's a secret!"
The old dog woke up and growled.
"Goodbye, all," said Martin.
He got them all out as fast as he could — Jack Power, Crofton, and Bloom — and up onto the horse-drawn carriage.
"Let's go," said Martin to the driver.
The white dolphin tossed its mane and the helmsman raised the sails. Beautiful sea nymphs clung to the sides of the noble ship, and they laughed as they sailed through the waves.
But I was just finishing my pint when I saw the citizen getting up and heading for the door, red in the face and cursing under his breath, with Joe and little Alf trying to calm him down.
"Let me go," said the citizen.
He made it to the door and shouted after the carriage:
"Three cheers for Israel!"
For heaven's sake, sit down and stop making a scene. There's always someone causing trouble over nothing.
A crowd gathered at the door. Martin was telling the driver to go, the citizen was shouting, and someone in the crowd started singing a rude song. A woman shouted at Bloom:
"Hey, mister! Your fly is open!"
And Bloom called back:
"Mendelssohn was Jewish, and Karl Marx, and Spinoza. And Jesus was Jewish too, and so was his father. Your God was Jewish."
"He had no earthly father," said Martin. "That's enough now. Driver, go!"
"Whose God?" shouted the citizen.
"Your God was Jewish," said Bloom. "Christ was Jewish, like me."
The citizen charged back into the pub.
"I'll teach him!" he roared. "How dare he use the holy name! Give me that biscuit tin!"
"Stop! Stop!" said Joe.

A huge crowd gathered to bid farewell to the great Mr. Leopold Bloom. He was presented with a beautiful scroll and a silver box. An orchestra played "Come Back" followed by a Hungarian march. Bonfires were lit on every hilltop in Ireland. The great ship slowly sailed away, saluted by flags from every building along the river. Goodbye, dear friend! Goodbye!
But the citizen grabbed the biscuit tin and ran outside, shouting, with little Alf hanging on to his arm:
"Where is he? Let me at him!"
Ned and J. J. were helpless with laughter.
"I'd better get going," I said.
Luckily the driver turned the horse around just in time.
"Wait, citizen!" said Joe. "Stop!"

The citizen drew back his arm and hurled the biscuit tin after the carriage. Thank goodness the sun was in his eyes, or he might have hit someone. The tin sailed through the air, the horse took fright, and the old dog went chasing after the carriage as the tin clattered along the street.

The impact was described as an earthquake registering on every scale. All the buildings in the neighbourhood were reported demolished. An article of clothing and an umbrella belonging to the judge were found at opposite ends of Ireland. An enormous glowing object was seen hurtling through the sky. Messages of sympathy poured in from around the world, and the Pope ordered special prayers.
You've never seen anything like it. If that biscuit tin had hit Bloom, he'd remember the Gold Cup race all right. But the driver saved the day with some furious driving.
"Did I hit him?" said the citizen. "Or what?"
And he shouted at the dog:
"After him, Garry! After him, boy!"
And the last we saw was the carriage turning the corner with Bloom waving his arms, and the old dog running after it as fast as his legs could carry him.

And then a great brightness appeared, and they saw a golden chariot rising into the sky. And in the chariot stood a figure clothed in glory, bright as the sun. A voice came from heaven calling: "Elijah! Elijah!" And he answered: "Father! Lord!" And they saw him — Ben Bloom Elijah — ascending into the brightness at an angle of forty-five degrees, like a rocket shot over the rooftops of Little Green Street.

chapters.title: Episode 13 — Nausicaa
paragraphs: The summer evening had begun to wrap the world in its gentle embrace. Far away in the west, the sun was setting and the last golden light of the day lingered lovingly on the sea and the sandy shore, on the proud headland of dear old Howth hill standing guard over the bay, on the weedy rocks along Sandymount shore, and on the quiet church from which the sound of evening prayers drifted out over the stillness.

Three girl friends were sitting on the rocks, enjoying the evening and the fresh sea air. They often came to this favourite spot for a chat beside the sparkling waves. There was Cissy Caffrey and Edy Boardman with a baby in a pushchair, and Tommy and Jacky Caffrey, two little curly-haired boys dressed in sailor suits with caps that said H.M.S. Belleisle. Tommy and Jacky were twins, barely four years old, noisy and spoiled sometimes but darling little fellows with bright, merry faces. They were playing in the sand with their spades and buckets, building castles and playing with their big coloured ball, happy as could be. Edy was rocking the chubby baby back and forth in the pushchair while the little fellow chuckled with delight. He was only eleven months old but was already beginning to babble his first words. Cissy bent over to tickle his plump little cheeks and the dimple in his chin.
"Now, baby," Cissy Caffrey said. "Say 'big, big.' I want a drink of water."
And baby babbled after her:
"A jink a jink a jawbo."

Cissy cuddled the little one because she was terribly fond of children, always so patient with them. Tommy Caffrey could never be made to take his medicine unless it was Cissy who held his nose and promised him the crusty end of the bread with golden syrup on it. What a gift that girl had! Baby Boardman was as good as gold in his new fancy bib. Cissy Caffrey was no fussy sort of girl. She was as true-hearted as they come, always with a laugh in her bright eyes and a cheerful word on her lips, a truly lovable girl. And Edy Boardman laughed too at the baby's funny babbling.

But just then there was a little fight between Tommy and Jacky. Boys will be boys, after all. The trouble was about a sandcastle that Jacky had built, which Tommy wanted to improve by adding a front door like the Martello tower had. But Jacky was just as stubborn as Tommy, and believing that every boy's castle is his own, he knocked his brother down and — sadly — the sandcastle tumbled too. Naturally, Tommy's cries drew the attention of the girls.
"Come here, Tommy," his sister called firmly. "Right now! And you, Jacky, shame on you for pushing poor Tommy into the dirty sand. Just wait till I catch you!"

With tears in his eyes, Tommy came when called, because their big sister's word was law. He was in a sorry state after his mishap — his little sailor suit was full of sand. But Cissy was an expert at smoothing over life's little troubles, and very quickly there wasn't a speck of sand left on him. But his blue eyes were still glistening with tears, so she kissed away the hurt and shook her finger at Jacky the troublemaker.
"Naughty Jacky!" she cried.
She put an arm around the little sailor and said softly:
"What's your name? Butter and cream?"
"Tell us who your sweetheart is," said Edy Boardman. "Is Cissy your sweetheart?"
"No," said tearful Tommy.
"Is Edy Boardman your sweetheart?" Cissy asked.
"No," Tommy said.
"I know," Edy Boardman said with a sly glance from her short-sighted eyes. "I know who Tommy's sweetheart is. Gerty is Tommy's sweetheart."
"No!" Tommy said, nearly in tears again.
Cissy guessed what was really the matter and she whispered to Edy to take him behind the pushchair to sort him out, and to be careful of his new tan shoes.
But who was Gerty?

Gerty MacDowell, who sat near her friends lost in thought and gazing far away into the distance, was a lovely example of Irish girlhood. Everyone who knew her said she was beautiful, though people often remarked she looked more like her mother's family, the Giltraps, than the MacDowells. She was slim and graceful, with a face that had an almost dreamlike quality to it. Her mouth was perfectly shaped, her hands were delicate with slender fingers, and she took great care of her appearance. There had been a silly rumour once, started by Bertha Supple during one of those little arguments that friends sometimes have, but it wasn't true at all. There was something naturally elegant about Gerty — you could see it in her graceful hands and the way she carried herself. If she'd been born into a wealthy family and had the finest education, Gerty MacDowell could easily have been a great lady. Perhaps it was this sense of what might have been that gave her beautiful blue eyes a dreamy, wistful look that few could resist. Gerty's eyes were the bluest Irish blue, framed by dark lashes and expressive brows. She had learned a few beauty tips from the magazines and never regretted trying them. But Gerty's greatest pride was her wonderful dark brown hair with its natural wave. She had trimmed it that very morning, and it fell beautifully around her pretty face. And just now, at Edy's teasing words, a delicate blush crept into her cheeks.

For a moment she was silent, looking down with rather sad eyes. She was about to answer back, but something stopped her. She wanted to speak but her pride told her to stay quiet. Her pretty lips pouted for a moment, but then she looked up and broke into a happy little laugh. She knew perfectly well what had made Edy say that — it was because of a boy she knew who rode his bicycle up and down her street. He was studying hard for his exams now, planning to go to university like his brother who raced bicycles. Maybe he didn't know how she felt, that ache in her heart sometimes. But he was young, and perhaps in time he might notice her. He was very handsome with a fine nose, every inch a gentleman, and she liked the way he could ride his bicycle with no hands. That was really why Edy was being so clever — because the boy hadn't been riding past Edy's garden.

Gerty was dressed simply but tastefully, because she had a feeling he might be out this evening. She wore a neat blue blouse and a navy skirt that showed off her slim figure nicely. She had spent all Tuesday looking for the perfect hat trimming at the summer sales, and when she finally found it at Clery's — just slightly marked down but you'd never notice — what joy it was when she tried it on and saw the lovely reflection in the mirror! Her shoes were the latest style with a smart buckle, and she knew she looked well. She had four sets of nice underclothes with pretty stitching in different colours — rose pink, pale blue, mauve, and pea green — and she washed and ironed them all herself because she wouldn't trust the laundry women not to scorch them. She was wearing the blue today for luck.

And yet there was a strained look on her face, a quiet sorrow always there. Deep down she wanted nothing more than to go to her own room and have a good cry. She had known from the start that her daydream of marrying young Reggy Wylie wasn't meant to be. He was too young to understand. At a party long ago, when they were both quite young, he had put his arm around her waist and she'd gone pale. He called her "little one" in a funny husky voice, but then he'd rushed off. Reggy wasn't very brave, and whoever won Gerty's heart would have to be a real man. She was tired of waiting. What she really dreamed of was someone older and wiser, a man with a kind, quiet face — perhaps with a touch of grey in his hair — who would understand her and care for her. For such a person she waited on this lovely summer evening.

While Edy Boardman was behind the pushchair with little Tommy, Gerty was just daydreaming about the future. She imagined a cosy home with pretty pictures on the walls, good food that she would cook herself — her griddle cakes and puddings were famous — and a tall husband with a fine moustache. They would go abroad for their honeymoon and then settle into a nice little house where every morning they'd have breakfast together before he went off to work.

Edy Boardman asked Tommy Caffrey if he was all right and he said yes, so she buttoned up his shorts and told him to run off and play with Jacky and be good. But Tommy said he wanted the ball, and Edy told him no, the baby was playing with it. Tommy stamped his foot on the ground. What a temper! Edy told him no and told Cissy not to give in to him either.
"You're not my sister," naughty Tommy said. "It's my ball."
But Cissy told baby Boardman to look up high at her finger, and she quickly snatched the ball and threw it along the sand, with Tommy chasing after it, having won the day.
"Anything for a quiet life," laughed Cissy.
She tickled the baby's cheeks to make him forget about the ball and played peekaboo with him. But Edy was cross about Tommy always getting his own way.
"I'd like to give him a smack," she said.
"On his bottom!" laughed Cissy.
Gerty blushed at Cissy saying such a thing out loud, and Edy said she was sure the gentleman sitting nearby had heard. But Cissy didn't care one bit.
"Let him!" she said with a toss of her head. "He deserves it too."

Madcap Cissy with her curly hair! You had to laugh at her sometimes. Like when she would say funny things about Chinese tea and raspberry jam, or draw funny faces on her fingernails with red ink, or the time she dressed up in her father's suit with a pretend moustache and walked down the road. No one was more fun than Cissy. But she was completely genuine and one of the kindest, truest people you could ever meet.

Then the sound of voices and organ music drifted out on the air from the church. It was the evening service led by Father Hughes, with prayers and singing. How sad those familiar prayers sounded to poor Gerty! If only her father hadn't had his troubles with drinking, things might have been so different for her family. She often sat alone at home, thinking about it by the dying fire, or gazing out the window at the rain falling. Her father's drinking had cast a shadow over her childhood. She had seen arguments at home caused by it, and she knew that anyone who treated their family unkindly because of drink was the lowest of the low.

Still the voices sang their prayers, and Gerty, lost in thought, barely noticed her friends or the twins playing or the gentleman walking along the beach that Cissy pointed out. You'd never see him behaving badly, but still Gerty wouldn't want him for a father because he was too old and had a rather bumpy red nose. Poor father of hers! With all his faults she loved him, especially when he sang his favourite songs. She remembered the evening they'd had stewed shellfish and salad for supper, and he sang with Mr Dignam who had died suddenly — God rest him — and it was her mother's birthday, with the whole Dignam family visiting, and they were going to have a photograph taken. Nobody could have guessed that Mr Dignam would die so soon.

Gerty was a wonderful daughter, like a second mother in the house, always helping and caring. When her mother had terrible headaches, it was Gerty who rubbed the menthol on her forehead, though they did sometimes argue about her mother's snuff habit. Everyone loved Gerty for her gentle ways. It was Gerty who turned off the gas every night and kept the house tidy. On the wall she had hung a pretty picture from the grocer's calendar showing a gentleman in old-fashioned clothes offering flowers to a lady through a window. The colours were beautiful. She often looked at it and dreamed about those romantic old times, because she had looked up the word 'halcyon' in her grandfather's dictionary and learned what it meant.

The twins were playing nicely now until Jacky, bold as ever, deliberately kicked the ball as hard as he could toward the seaweedy rocks. Poor Tommy cried out, but luckily the gentleman in black who was sitting by himself came to the rescue and caught the ball. The twins shouted for it, and Cissy called to the gentleman to throw it over please. He tossed it toward them, but it rolled down the slope and stopped right near Gerty. The twins shouted for it again, and Cissy told Gerty to kick it away. Gerty drew back her foot but missed, and Edy and Cissy laughed.
"If you miss, try again," said Edy Boardman.

Gerty smiled and bit her lip. A blush crept into her cheek, but she was determined to show them. She took careful aim and gave the ball a great kick, and it went flying, with the twins chasing after it. It was just jealousy of course — Edy drawing attention because of the gentleman sitting nearby. Gerty felt a warm flush in her cheeks. Until now she and the stranger had only exchanged the most casual glances, but now she peeked at him from under the brim of her new hat, and the face she saw there in the twilight seemed to her the saddest she had ever seen.

Through the open church window came the smell of incense, and with it the sound of the prayers — spiritual vessel, pray for us, mystical rose. There were tired and troubled people in that church, workers and wanderers, their eyes wet but still full of hope, because the priest had told them about the power of prayer.

The twins were playing happily again, as children do — their troubles passing like summer showers. Cissy played peekaboo with baby Boardman until he crowed with delight, clapping his little hands. She hid behind the hood of the pushchair and then popped up, and the baby loved it! Then she tried to teach him a new word.
"Say papa, baby. Say pa pa pa pa."

And baby did his very best to say it, because everyone agreed he was very clever for eleven months, and big for his age, and the picture of health — a perfect little bundle of joy who would surely grow up to be something special.
"Haja ja ja haja."

Cissy wiped his little mouth with his bib and tried to get him to sit properly, but when she undid his strap she discovered he needed changing and told Edy to fold the blanket the other way under him. Of course his little majesty fussed terribly at being changed:
"Habaa baaaahabaaa baaaa."

And two great big tears rolled down his cheeks. Nothing would comfort him — not talking about horses or trains — but Cissy, always quick-thinking, popped the bottle in his mouth and the little fellow was happy again.

Gerty wished they would take that noisy baby home and the bothersome twins too. She gazed out toward the distant sea. It was like a beautiful painting with all the colours of sunset, and such a shame that such beauty couldn't last, like those chalk drawings artists make on the pavement. The evening clouds were coming and the Bailey lighthouse was lit on Howth, and the music from the church was like a kind of perfume in the air. And as she gazed, her heart beat fast. Yes, it was her he was looking at, and there was something meaningful in his look. His eyes seemed to see right through her. They were wonderful eyes, dark and thoughtful, and she could tell at once from his pale, intelligent face that he was someone different — like a picture of a handsome actor she'd once seen. He was in dark mourning clothes, and there was clearly a story of sadness behind him. She would have given anything to know what it was. She noticed he was watching her intently, sitting very still. She was glad she'd put on her nice stockings and her best shoes with the bright buckles. Here, perhaps, was the person she had dreamed about. He seemed different from everyone else. Even if he had sorrows of his own, she didn't mind. She was sure that if she could only get to know him, she could help him forget whatever sadness he carried. She dreamed he might care for her just as she was.

The prayers continued inside the church — prayers to the comforter of the sad and the refuge of sinners. Gerty could picture the whole scene: the stained glass windows glowing, the candles, the flowers, and the blue banners. Father Conroy was helping Canon O'Hanlon at the altar, carrying things back and forth with his eyes downcast. He looked almost like a saint. He had been very kind to Gerty once when she'd gone to talk to him — he'd told her not to worry, that the things troubling her were perfectly natural and nothing to be ashamed of. He was so kind and gentle that she'd often thought about making him a nice gift, like an embroidered tea cosy or a picture album of Dublin views, but it was hard to know what would be right.

The annoying little twins started fighting again and Jacky threw the ball toward the sea and they both ran after it. Cissy and Edy shouted at them to come back because they were afraid the tide might catch them.
"Jacky! Tommy!"

But would they listen? Not a chance! What a pair! Cissy said it was the very last time she'd ever bring them out. She jumped up and ran down the slope after them, her hair flying behind her. Cissy was a bit of a tomboy and a show-off when she got the chance, and she ran in a rather ungainly way that wasn't very ladylike, with her skirt too tight and her heels too high.

The prayers in the church continued — Queen of Angels, Queen of all Saints — and Father Conroy swung the incense burner while Cissy caught the twins. She wanted to give them a good scolding but held back. Meanwhile Gerty could tell that the gentleman hadn't taken his eyes off her, and she swung her foot in time with the music. She was pleased she'd bought those nice stockings at Sparrow's for three shillings and eleven pence.

Cissy came back along the strand with the two twins and their ball, looking rather dishevelled after her run. Gerty took off her hat for a moment to fix her hair — and a prettier head of nut-brown hair was never seen on anyone's shoulders. She could almost feel the flash of admiration in the stranger's eyes. She put her hat back on so she could peek out from under the brim, and swung her buckled shoe as she noticed how intently he was watching her.

Edy Boardman was noticing it too, squinting at Gerty through her glasses, half smiling and pretending to nurse the baby. Nosy little thing she was, always poking into other people's business. She said to Gerty:
"A penny for your thoughts."
"What?" replied Gerty with a smile. "I was only wondering if it was getting late."

Because she wished they would all just go home so she could be alone with her thoughts, so she dropped a gentle hint about the time. When Cissy came over, Edy asked the time, and Cissy, cheeky as ever, said it was "half past kissing time, time to kiss again." But Edy wanted to know properly because they were supposed to be home early.
"Wait," said Cissy, "I'll run and ask that gentleman over there what time it is."

So over she went, and Gerty could see the gentleman get nervous, fiddling with his watch chain and looking toward the church. But despite whatever he was feeling, he had remarkable self-control — one moment he seemed fascinated, the next he was the picture of a calm, dignified gentleman.

Cissy politely asked would he mind telling her the time, and Gerty watched him take out his watch and listen to it. He said he was very sorry but his watch had stopped, though he thought it must be after eight because the sun had set. His voice had a pleasant, cultured sound, though there was a slight tremor in it. Cissy came back, stuck out her tongue, and said his watch was broken.

Then they sang the second verse of the hymn in church, and Canon O'Hanlon swung the incense again. One of the candles nearly set fire to the flowers and Father Conroy had to fix it. Gerty watched the gentleman wind his watch, and she swung her foot in time with the music. It was getting darker now. She felt a strange, exciting sensation — a kind of nervous flutter. His dark eyes watched her again, and she knew that he admired her. There was no question about it.

Edy began to get ready to leave, and Gerty was glad her hint had worked because it was a long walk home with the pushchair. Cissy took off the twins' caps and tidied their hair. Canon O'Hanlon was reading from the altar while Edy and Cissy kept asking about the time. Gerty gave polite but distant answers. Then Edy made a sharp remark about Gerty's boyfriend throwing her over. That stung! It cut deep because Edy had a mean way of saying hurtful things. Gerty's eyes stung with tears for a moment — she had truly cared for Reggy Wylie and he would never understand what he'd meant to her. But with a brave effort she smiled brightly and glanced at the stranger, her new admirer, so the others could see.
"Oh," Gerty said quick as lightning, laughing and lifting her head proudly. "I can choose whoever I like — it's leap year after all."

Her words rang out clear and musical, but with an edge of ice. There was something in her young voice that said she was not someone to be trifled with. As for Reggy Wylie and his showing off and his pocket money — she could forget him in a heartbeat and never give him another thought. Little Edy's face fell, and Gerty could see she was furious behind her fake smile, because that remark had hit home. They both knew Gerty was something special, different from them, and there was someone else who knew it too.

Edy straightened baby Boardman to get ready to go, and Cissy packed up the ball and the spades and buckets. It was high time because little Master Boardman was ready for his bed. Cissy told him the sandman was coming and baby looked just adorable, laughing up at her, and then she poked him gently in his tummy and the baby was sick all over his brand new bib.
"Oh my! What a mess!" cried Cissy. "He's ruined his bib!"
But in no time at all she had cleaned it up.

Gerty coughed quietly and Edy asked what was the matter. She was going to say something about the church but thought better of it, and simply said that the benediction bell was ringing from the steeple, because Canon O'Hanlon was giving the blessing with the golden vessel in his hands.

How beautiful the scene was in the gathering twilight — the last glimpse of the shore, the touching sound of the evening bells. A bat flew out from the church tower through the dusk with a tiny cry. Gerty could see the distant lighthouse lights, so beautiful she wished she could paint them, and soon the lamplighter would be making his rounds. Gerty had her private dreams that no one knew about. She loved to read poetry, and she had a lovely pink confession album where she wrote her thoughts. She kept it in her dresser drawer alongside her treasured things — her combs, her religious badge, her little bottles and ribbons. In the album she had copied out a beautiful poem she'd found in the newspaper: 'Art thou real, my ideal?' it was called, and the beauty of poetry, so sad in its loveliness, often brought tears to her eyes. She felt the years slipping by, and she had one small imperfection she always tried to hide — an old injury from falling on Dalkey hill. But she felt that this evening something might change. She would give everything to the right person. He would be her whole world. She dreamed of being a true friend and companion — they would understand each other perfectly, like a big brother and sister. She would follow her heart wherever it led. Nothing else mattered. She would be free.
