Canon O'Hanlon put the golden vessel back in its place and the choir sang a hymn of praise. When it was finished, he locked the tabernacle and Father Conroy handed him his hat. Cross little Edy asked Gerty if she wasn't coming, but just then Jacky Caffrey called out:
"Oh, look, Cissy!"
And they all looked — was it lightning? But Tommy saw it too, over the trees beside the church — blue and then green and purple.
"It's fireworks!" Cissy Caffrey said.
And they all ran down the strand to see over the houses and the church — Edy pushing the pushchair with baby Boardman, Cissy holding Tommy and Jacky by the hand so they wouldn't fall.
"Come on, Gerty!" Cissy called. "It's the bazaar fireworks!"

But Gerty stayed where she was. She had no intention of running after them. If they wanted to race around, fine, but she could see perfectly well from here. She felt the stranger's eyes on her and a kind of understanding passed between them. They were alone now, without the others to fuss and gossip, and she sensed he was a good, honourable man. She leaned back to watch the fireworks light up the sky, catching her knee with her hands to keep her balance. The evening was magical — just the two of them watching the fireworks paint the sky with colour while the sounds of prayer drifted from the church.

Jacky shouted to look — there was another one! And she leaned back to watch as a long Roman candle rose up over the trees, up, up, and everyone held their breath as it climbed higher and higher, almost out of sight. She was leaning back so far, watching it soar into the sky, and then — then it burst in a shower of light and everyone cried 'Oh!' in delight, and streams of golden sparks rained down like threads of gold, and they spread out like green dewy stars falling softly, so lovely, so gentle, so sweet.

Then it all faded away into the grey evening air, and everything was quiet. She glanced at the gentleman as she sat forward again, and he seemed lost in thought, leaning against the rock behind him. This was Leopold Bloom, and he stood with bowed head feeling ashamed of himself. He had been staring, and he knew it was rude. But there was kindness in her eyes, even forgiveness. This was their secret moment — just the two of them in the hiding twilight, with no one to know except the little bat that flew softly back and forth through the evening.
Cissy Caffrey whistled loudly, showing off:
"Gerty! Gerty! We're going. Come on. We can see from farther up."

Gerty had an idea. She took out her handkerchief and waved it in reply, then tucked it back. She wondered if he could see. She stood up. Was this goodbye? No — she felt they would see each other again somehow, here at this spot, and she would dream about this evening until then. She drew herself up to her full height. Their eyes met in one last long look, and she gave him a sad, sweet, forgiving smile — a smile that almost had tears in it — and then they parted.

Slowly, without looking back, she went down the uneven strand to Cissy, to Edy, to Jacky and Tommy, to little baby Boardman. It was darker now and there were stones and bits of wood on the strand, and slippery seaweed. She walked with quiet dignity but very carefully and slowly because — because Gerty MacDowell was...
Tight boots? No. She has a limp! Oh!

Mr Bloom watched her as she limped away. Poor girl! So that's why she'd stayed behind while the others ran. He'd thought something seemed different about the way she moved. He felt a pang of sympathy. A limp is harder for a girl. But it made her gentle and considerate. He was glad he hadn't known while she was nearby — it might have changed how he acted, and that wouldn't have been fair to her. She had beautiful eyes, that much was certain. And the quiet one with glasses — Edy — she seemed a bit under the weather. Strange how the moon affects people. His watch had stopped at half past four. Funny coincidence.
Ah!

The evening was making him thoughtful. He often noticed how girls walked by in the evenings, pouring out of offices at the end of the working day. People are so mysterious. Everyone has their own story. That girl — she probably had a whole life he'd never know about. Her pretty eyes, her careful way of dressing. Women notice everything about each other — friends whispering secrets, judging each other's clothes. His wife Molly and her old friend Josie Powell — they'd been close once, but now they hardly ever met. That's how friendships go. Everyone drifts apart.
Ah!

The evening air was cool now. He thought about his wife Molly and how different she was from everyone else. His mind wandered to all sorts of things — memories, observations, odd thoughts. He'd had a long day. He felt tired but oddly at peace sitting here on the rocks in the gathering darkness.

Mr Bloom straightened his shirt in the cool evening air. He was starting to feel chilly. Time to think about heading home. Still, it had been a nice rest here on the beach, watching the sunset and the fireworks. Sometimes you need to just sit and be quiet for a while. He remembered the actress names he'd seen on theatre posters — Nell Gwynn, Mrs Bracegirdle. Moonlight, music, the whole scene like a play. He wondered what he would have said if he'd actually spoken to the girl. Starting conversations with strangers is awkward — you never know how to end them. Better to just let the moment be what it was. He thought of his daughter Milly, and how she was growing up so fast.

Down there on the beach, Cissy and Tommy and Jacky were still watching the fireworks. His own private show. The twins were bouncing with excitement — children always want to see what happens next, always in a hurry to grow up. And Cissy looking after them all, understanding children the way some people just naturally do.

The girl hadn't looked back as she walked away. Proud. Girls like that — with beautiful clear eyes, the white of the eye makes them sparkle. Women notice everything, sharp as needles they are. When he'd once told Molly that a man on the corner was good-looking, she'd spotted instantly that he had a false arm. Where do women learn these things? His daughter Milly was the same — always clever little tricks, like drying her handkerchief on the mirror. Children learn from watching. He remembered Milly at three years old, playing in front of Molly's dressing table. How quickly they grow up.

Another firework burst — a monkey puzzle rocket, crackling and sputtering. Cissy and Tommy and Jacky ran out to watch, and Edy after them with the pushchair, and then Gerty beyond the curve of the rocks. He watched her go. He could see everything in the fading light.
Lord!

It had done him good to rest here, after the difficult day — Kiernan's pub, Dignam's funeral. He was grateful for the peace and quiet. His head had been swimming earlier but now he felt better. It was all the atmosphere of the evening — the music, the soft light, the sea air. He'd exchanged a kind of silent conversation with that girl, without any words at all.

Her maiden name was Jemima Brown
     And she lived with her mother in Irishtown.

This place made him think of silly rhymes. The ball had rolled right to her as if it understood where to go. Of course, he'd never been able to throw straight since school — crooked as anything. Sad though, how quickly youth passes. A few years of fun and then settling down to ordinary life. Babies, housework, all of it. Nature's way. He should probably visit the hospital to check on Mrs Purefoy — he'd heard she was having a baby. He wondered if Nurse Callan was still there. He remembered when his own daughter Milly was a baby, and Mrs Dignam and Mrs Breen were young too — how time changes everyone.
Ow!

Strange about his watch stopping. He lay back and thought about how everything in the world is connected — magnetism, the planets pulling at each other, the tides. The magnetic needle on a compass tells you what's happening far away in the sun and stars. A tiny piece of steel can feel forces from millions of miles away. Time itself is just movement, and if everything stopped moving, time would stop too. It's all connected, all arranged somehow.

He wondered what the girl was thinking now. Everyone puts on a brave face in front of others. His wife Molly was always honest about things, not pretending. He remembered Molly at a horse show years ago, and the time painters were working on their old house in Lombard street. So many memories tied to places.

Wait. That was her perfume he could still smell — that's why she had waved her handkerchief. She wanted him to remember her by the scent. What was it? Roses, he thought. Sweet and delicate. His wife Molly preferred a different kind of perfume, something richer. It's funny about smells — how they travel through the air, millions of tiny particles drifting on the breeze. Like the spice islands, where you can smell the cinnamon from miles away. Scent is like an invisible web that clings to everything. Even the cat at home liked to sniff Molly's clothes on the bed. Smells and memories — they're all tied together.

Maybe she could smell him too. What do men smell like to women? It must be something — cigars, soap, whatever they've eaten. Everyone has their own scent. Connected to something deep in nature, he supposed.
Mr Bloom sniffed the air. Then he sniffed his own waistcoat. Almonds? No. Lemons? No, that was just the soap from this morning.

Oh, speaking of soap — he'd forgotten to go back and pay for that lotion. And the soap wasn't paid for either. He didn't like carrying packages around. Hynes still owed him three shillings too. He could mention it casually, just to remind him. Two and nine. Still, if Hynes thought badly of him for asking — well, that's business. Shopkeepers lose customers by giving too much credit. People run up bills and then sneak off to shop somewhere else.

There went that well-dressed man again, walking past. Just strolling back and forth along the beach after his dinner. Probably had a nice government job and a comfortable bank balance. Mr Bloom imagined himself as a character in a story: 'The Mystery Man on the Beach, a prize story by Mr Leopold Bloom.' And that strange fellow in the brown coat at Dignam's funeral today — who was he? Nobody seemed to know. The evening air was damp — probably rain coming. The body feels the weather. Old Betty's joints always predicted rain. And the distant hills of Howth seemed to be coming nearer in the mist.

Howth. The Bailey lighthouse blinking. Two, four, six, eight, nine flashes. They have to change the pattern so ships don't mistake it for a house window. Grace Darling, the famous lighthouse keeper's daughter who rescued shipwrecked sailors. People are afraid of the dark. Glowworms and cyclists need lights too. The best time to water plants is in the shade after sunset. There was still some light left. Red rays travel farthest — he remembered learning the colours of the rainbow in school: Roy G. Biv — red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. Was that a star appearing? Venus? Can't tell yet. Two stars now. When you can see three, it's truly night.

Dew was falling. Not good to sit on cold stone for too long — it makes you stiff. He thought about the evening, how beautiful it had been. Green apples aren't ready yet — you have to wait. It's the evening that brings out feelings in people. Everything opens up, like flowers knowing their time has come — sunflowers, garden flowers in ballrooms, on lamplit avenues. He remembered kissing Molly's shoulder in Mat Dillon's garden long ago, on a June evening just like this one. The year comes around again. History repeats itself. Life, love — you go on a journey around your own little world and then come back to where you started. He felt sorry about the girl's limp, of course, but he mustn't let pity carry him away.
All quiet on Howth now. The distant hills, the rhododendrons where he and Molly had once been together. Names change, but the hill stays the same. Lovers come and go.

He felt tired now. Should he get up? Maybe just rest another moment. The evening had taken all his energy. Would the girl come back tomorrow? He'd like to think so, but no — you can never repeat a perfect moment. Like children returning to a place that thrilled them the first time — it's never quite the same. He thought about long ago, playing charades at Luke Doyle's house. Mat Dillon and all his daughters: Tiny, Atty, Floey, Maimy, Louy, Hetty. And Molly was there too. That was 1887. He and Molly had been so young. How strange that they were both only children. Life has a way of coming full circle. The longest way round is the shortest way home.

A bat flew past. What was that? A swallow? No, a bat probably. It must think he's a tree, being so still. Funny little creature. He wondered where it lived — up in the belfry, most likely, hanging upside down. The church bell must have scared it out. Mass seemed to be over — he could hear them finishing their prayers. Pray for us, pray for us, pray for us — the repetition was like advertising: buy from us, buy from us. There was a light in the priest's house now — they'd be having their simple supper. He remembered something about the houses from when he worked at Thom's directory. Bats are strange creatures — like birds crossed with mice. What scares them — light or noise? Better sit still. Clever things though, all instinct, like the bird in the fable that dropped pebbles into a jar to raise the water level. A bat is like a tiny man in a cloak with little hands. You can almost see their tiny bones shimmering in the dusk, kind of bluish-white. Colours depend on the light, of course — stare at the sun and then look at something and you see a yellow blob. Everything leaves its mark on everything else. Like that cat this morning, brown as peat. He thought about how Howth had looked purple a while ago, like amethyst. That reminded him of the story about the man with the magnifying glass who set things on fire. In dry weather, even broken bottles can focus sunlight and start fires. Archimedes! That was his name — he remembered now.

Another bat. Who knows why they fly about like that? Chasing insects probably. That bee last week that got into the room, playing with its shadow on the ceiling. Birds are amazing too — the nerve to fly across the whole ocean and back. Many must be killed in storms or hitting telegraph wires. Sailors have a hard life as well — great ships ploughing through dark seas, or little boats tossed about like nothing. Married sailors, sometimes away for years at the ends of the earth. Their wives waiting at home. When the anchor's weighed, off he goes with a lucky charm around his neck. All those superstitions — because when you set out, you never know what dangers you'll face. Clinging to wreckage in a storm, hoping to be rescued. Do fish ever get seasick, he wondered?
Then you imagine a beautiful calm — not a cloud, smooth sea, everything peaceful — and somewhere below, a shipwreck in Davy Jones' locker. The moon looking down, not caring.

A last lonely firework wandered up the sky from the bazaar and burst, dropping a cluster of violet and white stars. They floated and fell and faded. It was the shepherd's hour — the hour of going home. The postman was making his rounds, his little lamp gleaming through the hedges. Among the trees, a street lamp was lit. Through lighted windows, past neat gardens, came a boy's shrill voice crying: 'Evening Telegraph! Stop press! Result of the Gold Cup races!' From Dignam's house a boy ran out. The bat flew here, there. Far out over the sands, the grey surf crept in. Howth settled down to sleep, tired of long days, glad of the night breeze ruffling its ferns. The old hill lay down but kept one red eye open — the lighthouse, always watching. And far out on the Kish bank, the anchored lightship twinkled and winked at Mr Bloom.

Life must be strange for those lighthouse keepers, stuck in the same spot day after day. And coastguards too, always watching for ships in trouble with their lifeboats and rescue equipment. He remembered the day they'd gone on a pleasure cruise on the Erin's King — throwing old papers to the seals. A rough trip. Some passengers being sick over the side. But his daughter Milly had shown no fear at all — her blue scarf flying, laughing into the wind. Children don't think about danger at that age. He remembered playing hide and seek with her at Crumlin, and how frightened she'd got when she couldn't find them — 'Mamma! Mamma!' Like Babes in the Wood. Children's games could be a bit scary sometimes — hiding behind masks, tossing them in the air. He remembered getting her medicine once when she was ill, and how she slept in the bed with Molly afterwards. She had the very same teeth as her mother. 'Dearest Papli,' she used to call him — he remembered her little hand touching his, counting his waistcoat buttons. She was growing up so fast now. He remembered when Molly had first told young Milly about growing up and the changes that come — it had frightened the poor child at first. A strange moment for the mother too, remembering her own girlhood in Gibraltar, looking out from the tower at the seabirds and the sea.

Better not sit here all night like a barnacle on a rock. This weather makes you drowsy. Must be nearly nine by the fading light. Time to go home. Too late for the theatre — 'Lily of Killarney.' But he could still visit the hospital to check on Mrs Purefoy. Long day he'd had — Martha's letter, the bath, the funeral, the museum visit, Dedalus singing. Then that angry scene in Barney Kiernan's pub. He'd given as good as he got there, though — made the man wince with a clever remark. But maybe it's always a mistake to fight back. Better to go home and let it go. That bully with his ugly temper. But Dignam's funeral was the worst part of the day — funerals are so depressing because you never know when your own time will come. He had to visit those insurance people as he'd promised. 'Scottish Widows' — funny name for an insurance company, assuming the husband dies first. He thought of a widow he'd seen on Monday outside a shop. And that poor man O'Connor whose wife and five children were poisoned by bad mussels from the sewage. Terrible. He thought about dreams — he'd had a confused one last night. Something about red slippers. His mind jumped from thing to thing: must sort out that advertisement for Keyes, get Molly some new clothes. Then he noticed something in the sand.

Mr Bloom stooped and picked up a piece of paper from the strand. He held it close and squinted. A letter? No, he couldn't read it in this light. Better go. He was too tired to move. It was just a page from an old exercise book. All those pebbles on the beach — who could count them? You never know what you'll find — a message in a bottle, thrown from a shipwreck. Children always want to throw things in the sea. What's this? A bit of stick.
He felt exhausted. It had been a long day. Would the girl come here tomorrow? Should he come back and wait for her? He'd always return to this spot. Would he?
Mr Bloom used the stick to draw gently in the thick sand at his feet. He could write a message for her. It might still be here in the morning. What should he write?
I.

Some person would probably step on it in the morning anyway. Useless. The tide would wash it away. He could see a pool of water near where the girl had been sitting. If he leaned over he could see his own reflection in it, dark as a mirror. All these rocks with their lines and scars, worn by time and tide.
AM. A.
No room to write more. Let it go.
Mr Bloom rubbed out the letters with his boot. Hopeless thing, sand. Nothing grows in it. Everything fades. No big ships come up this far — only the brewery barges going round the coast.

He threw away his stick. It landed in the wet sand and stuck upright. If you tried to do that on purpose, you could never manage it. Pure chance. They'd never meet again, he and the girl. But it had been lovely. Goodbye. Thanks. She'd made him feel young again.

A short nap would be nice now. Must be close to nine. The Liverpool boat was long gone — not even the smoke visible. He'd just close his eyes for a moment. Not really sleeping — just half-dreaming. The bat flew past again. Harmless little thing. Just resting for a few moments...

His thoughts became muddled as sleep crept over him — fragments of the evening, the girl, the fireworks, the sunset, golden and sweet, everything blurring together in a dreamy haze, memories of the day floating past like clouds, round and round, coming back again and again...

A bat flew. Here. There. Here. Far away in the grey dusk, a church bell chimed. Mr Bloom, with his mouth open, leaning sideways, his boot half-buried in sand, breathed slowly. Just for a few moments...

Cuckoo
     Cuckoo
     Cuckoo.
The clock on the mantelpiece in the priest's house cuckooed while Canon O'Hanlon and Father Conroy and Father Hughes were having their tea and bread and butter and chops and talking about...

Cuckoo
     Cuckoo
     Cuckoo.

Because it was a little cuckoo bird that came out of its little clock-house to tell the time — the same one that Gerty MacDowell had noticed, because she was always quick to notice things like that. And she had noticed that the foreign gentleman sitting on the rocks was...

Cuckoo
     Cuckoo
     Cuckoo.

chapters.title: Episode 14 — Oxen of the Sun
paragraphs: To the hospital! To the hospital! Let us go to the hospital!
Send good wishes, bright hopes, for the mother and baby. Send good wishes, bright hopes, for the mother and baby. Send good wishes, bright hopes, for the mother and baby.
Hooray for the baby! Hooray for the baby! Hooray for the baby!

There is nothing more important in a nation's life than caring for mothers and their newborn children. Everyone knows this. The health and happiness of families is what makes a country truly great. And anyone who ignores this simple truth, or fails to care for mothers and babies, is making a terrible mistake.

This is why, in Ireland, doctors and nurses have always been held in great honour. The ancient Irish healers — the O'Shiels, the O'Hickeys, the O'Lees — wrote down all their knowledge about how to help the sick get well again. And they made sure that every mother, whether rich or poor, would have the best possible care when her baby was coming.

Everyone wanted the mothers to be safe and comfortable. The whole community cared about them, because they knew that the birth of a new child was something wonderful. When they saw a mother being brought to the hospital, everyone felt a rush of kindness and wanted to help.

Before the baby was born, everything was prepared. A comfortable bed with clean blankets, good food, and all the medicines and tools the doctors might need — everything was laid out and ready, so that when the time came, the mother could bring her child into the world safely.

A man who had been wandering far from home stood at the door of the hospital as night fell. He was Mr Leopold Bloom, and he had been walking through the city all day long. Something drew him to this house.

The hospital was run by Dr Horne. Seventy beds it had, for mothers who came there to have their babies, just as the angel told Mary long ago. Two nurses walked the wards day and night in their white uniforms, always watching, always caring. They were the best and most faithful helpers Dr Horne could have.

In the hallway, a kind nurse saw Mr Bloom coming and opened the door wide for him. Outside, lightning flashed across the western sky over Ireland. The nurse was a little frightened that a storm was coming, and she made the sign of the cross and invited him to come inside out of the rain. Mr Bloom gratefully stepped into the hospital.

Mr Bloom stood shyly in the hallway, holding his hat. He had once lived near here with his dear wife and lovely daughter, nine years ago now it seemed. Once he had passed the nurse in town and forgotten to tip his hat to her. He wanted to apologise for that now, and she kindly forgave him, because she remembered how young his face had looked back then. Her eyes brightened and she blushed at his kind words.

She noticed his dark clothes and was worried someone had died. She was relieved when it wasn't what she feared. He asked if there was any news of Dr O'Hare, and the nurse sadly told him that Dr O'Hare had passed away. That made Mr Bloom very sorrowful indeed. She told him all about it — how the young doctor had died peacefully, with a priest beside him, and she prayed for his soul in heaven. They stood there together for a while, both sad and sorry.
So remember, everyone, that life is short and precious, and we should make the most of every day.

Mr Bloom then asked the nurse about the woman who was having her baby. The nurse told him that the poor woman had been in labour for three full days now, and it was going to be a very difficult birth. She had seen many births, she said, but never one as hard as this. She told him all about it, because she knew he had once lived nearby. Mr Bloom listened with great sympathy, feeling deeply for the suffering of mothers, and he noticed that the nurse herself, though she had a kind face, had spent many long years caring for others without having children of her own.

While they were talking, the door of the dining hall opened and they heard a great noise of people eating and talking inside. A young medical student named Dixon came out to greet them. Dixon knew Mr Bloom — they had met at the hospital once before when Mr Bloom had come in for treatment of a chest injury. Dixon said he should come in and join the group for supper. Mr Bloom wasn't sure — he was a cautious man — and the nurse also thought he might be better off staying out here, but Dixon wouldn't take no for an answer and said what a wonderful place it was. So Mr Bloom went in to rest for a while, because he was tired from walking all over Dublin that day.

Inside the dining hall, a table was set with all sorts of food. There were sharp knives and forks laid out on a birchwood table, and glasses and plates, and bottles of ale, and a tin of sardines in oil from Portugal, and bread that had risen wonderfully, and long sticks of asparagus with butter.

Young Dixon poured Mr Bloom a drink, and everyone else drank too. Mr Bloom politely lifted his glass but only pretended to sip — he didn't much care for beer — and when no one was looking, he quietly poured most of his into his neighbour's glass. Then he sat down with them to rest. Thank goodness.

Meanwhile, the good nurse stood by the door and begged them all, for heaven's sake, to keep the noise down because upstairs a woman was about to have her baby. Mr Bloom heard a cry from the upper floor and wondered whether it was the mother or the baby. It seemed to be taking a very long time. An older man named Lenehan, who was sitting nearby, joked that the baby would arrive 'any moment now.' Lenehan was a cheerful fellow who enjoyed his ale, and he raised a toast to good health. Mr Bloom, who was the gentlest and kindest man there, raised his glass politely in return, still thinking of the poor woman upstairs.

Now let us describe who else was at the table. There were several medical students: Dixon, Lynch, and Madden. There was Lenehan the older fellow, a Scotsman named Crotthers, and young Stephen Dedalus sitting at the head of the table, with a thoughtful, serious look about him. There was also Costello, whom everyone called Punch because of his wild behaviour — he was the most rowdy of them all. And sitting quietly among them was gentle Mr Bloom. They were all waiting for their friend Mulligan, who was late as usual. Mr Bloom was there because he was an old friend of Stephen's father, and he felt a fatherly concern for young Stephen.

The students were very clever and they loved to debate big questions. Young Madden started a discussion about what should happen if a mother's life was in danger during a birth — should the doctors save the mother or the baby? Everyone had strong opinions. Some said the mother must be saved first, others disagreed. Lenehan kept pouring more ale to keep everyone happy. Then Madden told them a sad true story about a woman who had died in this very hospital. Stephen, who was drinking too much, said some confusing things about life and death that were hard to understand. Dixon made a joke, and Costello said something rude that made everyone laugh — well, almost everyone. Mr Bloom and Stephen didn't laugh, because they were both feeling sad for the woman upstairs.

Mr Bloom was deeply troubled by the cries he could hear from the birthing room. He remembered how his own wife Molly had once given him a baby boy, but the child had died after only eleven days, and no doctor could save him. That was the saddest thing that had ever happened to them. They had wrapped the tiny baby in the softest lamb's wool blanket. Now Mr Bloom had no son, and as he looked at young Stephen — his friend's boy — he felt both pride in the lad and worry, because Stephen was spending his time with wild young men who were not a good influence.

Stephen, meanwhile, was in a talkative mood and poured more drinks for everyone. He pulled out some coins and notes — about two pounds and nineteen shillings — that he said he'd earned from a piece of writing. Everyone was impressed, because money was scarce. Stephen made a little speech about time and creation and words and meaning, but much of it was hard to follow because he had been drinking.

Then Punch Costello started to sing a rude song, but the head nurse, a serious older woman, appeared at the door and told them all firmly to be quiet because of the patient upstairs. Everyone was embarrassed and shushed Costello. Mr Bloom, who was always considerate and gentle, agreed with the nurse completely. In this hospital, there should be peace and quiet.

Shortly after, Dixon asked Stephen why he hadn't become a priest, and Stephen joked that he'd taken a vow of poverty — the involuntary kind! Lenehan teased him, and the others joined in with jokes and stories. Stephen, being very well-read, quoted from old plays and books, making clever remarks that were sometimes funny and sometimes hard to understand. The conversation bounced from one topic to another, with everyone trying to be wittier than the last.

Then Costello started boasting loudly again about things he would do, and a great clap of thunder shook the building. The storm outside was getting worse! Lynch told Costello to watch his tongue — perhaps the thunder was a warning from above. Costello, who had been acting so brave, suddenly went pale and shrank back in his chair. Some of the others laughed at him for being scared. Mr Bloom, sitting beside the frightened young man, spoke to him in calming tones, explaining that thunder was simply a natural thing — just water drops releasing from clouds. Nothing to be afraid of at all.

But was Costello truly brave at heart? Not really. He had worries and guilt that no amount of joking could make disappear. He heard the thunder and wondered if it meant something. Was it just nature, as Mr Bloom said, or was it something more? He couldn't decide. He was a young man who couldn't quite settle between being good and being wild, and the storm outside seemed to mirror the storm inside him.

This is what all the young men at the table struggled with, deep down. They joked and laughed and pretended nothing mattered, but each of them had doubts and fears. They called each other funny names — Mr Cautious Calmer for Bloom, Young Boasthard for Costello — as though life were just a game. But the thunder reminded them that there are things bigger than any of them.

So on this Thursday, the sixteenth of June, Mr Dignam had been buried, and after a long dry spell, it finally rained. A bargeman on the river said the crops had been withering for weeks, but now the rain came pouring down after sunset, with sheet lightning first and then a great thunderclap. Everyone in the streets scrambled for cover. Meanwhile, young Mulligan's friend Alec Bannon had come to town from the countryside, and they met in the rain and headed together to the hospital. Inside, Mr Bloom was sitting with the group of students — Dixon, Lynch, Madden, Lenehan, Stephen, and the others. Mrs Purefoy was still upstairs, three days past her due date, and the midwives were doing everything they could to help. This would be her ninth child.

Lenehan arrived at the table with news about a letter in the evening newspaper, and settled himself comfortably. He was a sociable type who spent his time in coffeehouses picking up gossip, always ready with a joke or a funny story. Costello asked what the news was about, and Lenehan said it was about sick cattle being sent away. The conversation turned to farming and cattle, with Mr Bloom — who had once worked for a cattle dealer — asking sensible questions, and Stephen making clever jokes. Dixon joined in with a story about a famous bull, and soon everyone was making up ridiculous tales about bulls and cows and farming, each trying to outdo the other. The stories got sillier and sillier, with imaginary bulls wearing gold coats and eating only green grass, until Stephen finished with a grand tale about men sailing off to America on a homemade raft.
And someone sang out a little verse:
"A man's a man for all that."
Look at the house that Jack built, they laughed — all the food and drink, the friends and the stories, stacked up like a tower of jokes and memories in that grand old hospital dining room.

Then Mr Mulligan arrived at last, soaking wet from the rain, with his friend Alec Bannon beside him. Mulligan was in fine form and had printed up funny cards calling himself 'Mr Malachi Mulligan, Fertiliser and Incubator, Lambay Island.' He launched into a long, amusing speech about his plans to help increase Ireland's population by setting up a farm on an island, eating a special diet of root vegetables and rabbit meat. Everyone was greatly entertained by this ridiculous scheme. His friend Bannon was bursting to tell his own story about a girl he'd met.

Mulligan, who was quite pleased with himself, dried off his wet clothes while everyone praised his silly plan. His friend Bannon could barely contain his excitement about the girl he'd met. Mulligan noticed the food on the table and asked who it was all for. When he saw Mr Bloom, he bowed politely and asked if he could help. Mr Bloom explained that he was there to check on a woman having a baby, and he sighed deeply. Then the students started teasing each other with jokes about medicine and babies, while Mulligan's friend Bannon pulled out a small locket with a picture of his sweetheart — a pretty girl from the countryside.

The Scottish student, Crotthers, congratulated Bannon and asked to hear more about this girl. Bannon launched into a romantic description of his beloved, becoming quite poetic about her charms. He told how they'd met on a beautiful May evening under chestnut trees in bloom. Lenehan offered him a drink, and Bannon gratefully accepted. Then there was more joking about rain and umbrellas, and Lynch's girlfriend's funny opinions about clothes, until — just at the most interesting moment — a bell rang from the delivery ward.

The bell rang and the room fell quiet. Nurse Callan appeared, whispered something to young Dixon, and left with a deep curtsy. The moment she was gone, the students started being silly again. Costello made a rude remark, but Dixon, the young surgeon, stood up seriously. He had been told that the baby had finally been born! A healthy bouncing boy! Dixon made a short but passionate speech about the noble profession of medicine, defending Nurse Callan's honour against the rude comments, and left to attend to the new mother. Everyone felt a little ashamed after that, and even Costello admitted he hadn't really meant any harm.

Mr Bloom, who had been sitting quietly through all the rude jokes, had borne them patiently. He understood that young people sometimes say silly things, even cruel things, without really meaning to. He was older and wiser, and he'd learned to let such things wash over him. What had truly bothered him was Costello's rudeness about the nurse — Mr Bloom could not stand to hear anyone be cruel about a woman, especially one who was doing such important work. But now that the baby had been born safely, he felt deeply grateful.

Mr Bloom told his neighbour that anyone with a heart ought to be overjoyed at this wonderful news. Mr Crotthers banged the table and announced that the proud father, Mr Purefoy — 'Old Glory Hallelujah' as they called him — had been there earlier, asking after his wife. What a man! Nine children! Everyone was impressed and amused, though some of the students made jokes about it.

Then came a sharp passage where someone criticised Mr Bloom behind his back — calling him an outsider, questioning his loyalty, making fun of his private life and his marriage. This was cruel and unfair gossip, the kind that small-minded people spread about anyone who is different. Mr Bloom, thankfully, did not hear most of it.

The nurse came a second time to announce officially that a healthy baby boy had been born. When the young doctor left to attend the birth, the students burst into excited conversation about every topic they could think of — babies, twins, medicine, superstitions about pregnancy, old wives' tales, and scientific theories. Mr Bloom tried to keep the peace among all these excited young voices, but there was no stopping them. Every possible subject was debated with great energy and loud opinions.

Then Mulligan told a spooky ghost story that made everyone's skin crawl. He described a secret panel sliding open and a mysterious figure appearing with a bottle of poison, confessing to a terrible crime. 'I am the murderer!' the figure cried. But it was all just a story, of course — a made-up tale for entertainment. Then the figure vanished behind the panel. Everyone was both frightened and amused.

How old is the soul? It changes with our mood, just as our face changes. Mr Bloom sat there thinking, and suddenly he wasn't the tired middle-aged man anymore — in his mind, he was young Leopold again, walking to school on a crisp morning with a sandwich his mother had made, or selling trinkets door-to-door for his father's business, charming the housewives with his dark eyes and polite manner. He remembered his father reading foreign newspapers by the fire after supper. But then the memory faded, and he was back in the present. Now he was the older one, and these young men around him could be his sons. He thought about his own lost boy, and about Milly growing up, and about how time rushes past and never comes back.

The voices faded into silence — a vast silence like space itself. In his mind's eye, Mr Bloom saw ghostly images: grey twilight falling over green fields, animals moving like shadows, ancient herds trooping through the darkness. Wild and strange visions passed through his imagination — bulls and elephants and mammoths moving toward a dark sea, horned shapes against the clouds.

Then the vision changed to something brighter: a star rising on the horizon, a beautiful figure appearing in the sky, draped in flowing colours — emerald, sapphire, mauve — like a queen among the stars, a mysterious sign of hope.

Stephen's friend Lenehan reminded him of their school days, asking about old classmates. Where were they now? Neither could say. Stephen grew thoughtful and spoke about the past and memory — how we are the keepers of our friends' stories. Lenehan mentioned Stephen's mother, and Stephen's face darkened. Everyone could see that the memory of his recently dead mother still hurt him terribly. But the conversation moved on. Lenehan told them about the horse race that afternoon — how the favourite, Sceptre, had been in the lead the whole way until, at the very last moment, a horse called Throwaway had overtaken her and won. Poor Sceptre! Bannon spoke tenderly about his sweetheart, describing a beautiful day they'd spent together under blossoming chestnut trees. As for Mr Bloom, his thoughts had drifted far away, lost in memories of his own. Mulligan noticed and whispered to the others to let him be — it was painful to be woken from a dream.

Actually, Mr Bloom wasn't daydreaming at all. He had been staring at a bottle of Bass ale across the table with its red label, lost in thought about his own private memories. When he finally noticed that Mulligan was watching him, he reached across, picked up the bottle, and poured some for the young man — which was what Mulligan had been hoping for all along.

The debate in the grand old dining hall of the hospital was quite a spectacle. All the young men were gathered there: Crotthers in his Scottish clothes, Lynch with his sharp face, Costello the wild one, steady Madden, Bannon the explorer, elegant Mulligan, serious Stephen at the head of the table, cheerful Lenehan, and patient Mr Bloom, whose heart was full of thoughts about his wife.

The students argued about every scientific and medical question imaginable: what determines whether a baby is a boy or a girl? Why do some babies die young while others survive? Mulligan blamed dirty air and ugly streets for poor health, and said that beautiful art and music would help mothers have healthier babies. Crotthers talked about the dangers working women faced. Lynch suggested that all of nature follows hidden mathematical patterns. The most important question — why does a healthy baby from healthy parents sometimes die? — nobody could answer. Stephen said something strange and morbid that nobody quite understood. Mr Bloom, when asked his opinion, gave a careful and diplomatic answer that satisfied everyone, as was his way.

Meanwhile, the doctor had helped Mrs Purefoy safely deliver her baby. What a long and difficult time it had been — three whole days! But the brave woman had come through it, and now she was wonderfully happy. Everyone could imagine the touching scene upstairs: the new mother gazing lovingly at her baby, whispering a prayer of thanks, wishing her dear husband Doady could be there to hold their newest child. The Purefoys already had eight children — Charley, Mary Alice, Mamy, Budgy, Tom, Violet, little Bobsy, and another who sadly hadn't survived. This new baby boy would be called Mortimer Edward. Mr Purefoy was an ordinary, decent man — a bank accountant who liked to fish on weekends with his boys. A good man, a good father. Rest now, Mina Purefoy, rest.

There are secret sorrows that people carry in their hearts, memories they try to forget but never quite can. A chance word, a familiar scene, even a dream, can bring these memories rushing back — not to punish, but simply because the past never truly goes away.

Mr Bloom looked at Stephen and saw something familiar in the young man's face — a sadness behind the cleverness, a pain behind the bravado. A memory came to him: a soft May evening in a garden, playing bowls on the lawn. Lilac trees, purple and white. And girls standing nearby — Floey, Atty, Tiny, and one darker girl wearing cherry earrings, so pretty against her warm skin. A little boy of four or five stood on the garden wall, held safe by gentle hands, trying to look brave. Somewhere nearby, a mother watched with a faint shadow of worry on her face.

Then the vision shifted again, and Mr Bloom remembered a young man — Stephen as he once was — walking through the world full of questions, searching for answers. Some things in life cannot be taught; they can only be lived.

The moment came suddenly. A new energy swept through the room. The students had been sitting around the table all evening, but now something changed — like storm clouds building before lightning strikes. One moment they were calm, the next...

"Burke's pub!" shouted Stephen, jumping up, and the whole crowd leapt to their feet and scrambled for their hats and walking sticks and coats. What a scramble! What a racket! Nurse Callan tried to stop them in the hallway but couldn't. Even the doctor coming downstairs with the good news — a healthy nine-pound baby! — couldn't hold them. Off they went, racing each other through the streets. Mr Bloom hung back a moment to send kind wishes up to the new mother and baby, then he whispered to the nurse, asking when she herself might have a little one.
Outside, the night air was fresh and gleaming with raindrops under the stars. What a wonderful thing — a new baby born into the world!

Well done, Theodore Purefoy! Well done indeed! Nine children! What energy, what determination! While others complained and worried, you just got on with living. Your wife is a brave woman, and together you've built something amazing — a big, noisy, wonderful family. Don't envy those with fewer cares; they have fewer joys too. Life is full and messy and difficult, but it's life! So raise your glass, Theodore Purefoy!

And off they all went, tumbling down the street, shouting and laughing in the rain. Slattery's pub? No, Burke's! Where's everyone? Come on! Someone started singing. Tramp, tramp, tramp went their feet on the wet pavement. What a crew they were, these medical students and their friends, racing through the Dublin night!

"Who's paying for this round?" asked someone. Nobody seemed to have much money. Mr Bloom was there, quiet as always. They ordered drinks. Five pints. Ginger cordial for someone. Absinthe for the brave ones. A clock ticked. Time was getting on. But who cared? The night was young!

In they went, crowding into the pub. Tight fit! Someone had been to the barber. Someone else was singing about the Rose of Castile. A man nearly fainted and needed water. Someone mentioned a horse racing tip. There was talk of lucky bets and unlucky ones. Stephen was there, and Madden, and all the rest, getting louder and sillier as the evening went on.

"Another round?" said someone. "Absolutely!" said another. "Landlord, more drinks!" It was closing time, but nobody wanted to leave. Someone asked about Mr Bloom — where had he got to? Off in the corner somewhere, being quiet and sensible as always. Someone needed help getting home. "Kind stranger, can you help a young man find a place to lay his head tonight?" The night was getting very late indeed.

Who was that strange man in the long coat? Dusty Rhodes, some called him. A poor fellow, down on his luck, wandering through the rainy streets. They'd seen him at the funeral that morning. Someone felt sorry for him. Life can be hard. Then someone else changed the subject to cars and racing and horses. Eleven o'clock already! Time to go. "Forward, wobbly friends!" someone cried. "Good night! Good night! May heaven watch over you all tonight!"
"Attention everyone! We're not that drunk! We can still stand up straight! Well, mostly."
"Watch out for that fellow being sick over there. Good night! Good night, my love! Good night!"
Listen! What's that noise? A fire engine! There it goes, bells clanging, racing down the street toward Mount Street! Off we go!

"Lynch! Come with me!" called Stephen. "This way, down Denzille Lane!" And off went Stephen and Lynch together into the dark Dublin night. "Who's that man in the black clothes?" someone whispered. But never mind. Somewhere in the distance, a street preacher was shouting about salvation and the end of the world: "Elijah is coming! Come on, you sinners! The Almighty is no small-time operation — He's the greatest thing going and don't you forget it!" And the fire engine's bell rang again in the distance.

chapters.title: Episode 15 — Circe
paragraphs: _(The entrance to a strange part of the city at night. Dim streetlamps cast rainbow-coloured shadows. An ice cream cart gleams white and blue. Children gather around it, eating wafers with coloured ice cream. Whistles call and answer in the darkness, like a mysterious code.)_
THE CALLS: Wait for me, and I'll catch up!
THE ANSWERS: Over here, behind the corner!
_(A confused-looking boy stumbles past, bumping into things. A chain of children holding hands blocks his way, giggling.)_
THE CHILDREN: Hello there! Say hello!
THE IDIOT: _(Waves his left arm and gurgles happily.)_ Grhahello!
THE CHILDREN: Where's the big light?
THE IDIOT: _(Mumbling.)_ Ghaghahest.

_(The children let him go and he stumbles on. A small woman swings on a rope between two railings, counting. Someone sleeps against a wall, snoring loudly. An old rag-and-bone man with a pointed cap shoulders his sack and hobbles away. An old woman with a lamp shuffles back to her doorway, and a small child scrambles after her, clutching her skirt. A tired worker holds onto railings, swaying. Two night watchmen stand tall at a corner. Somewhere a plate crashes, a woman cries out, a child wails. From a lane, Cissy Caffrey's young voice sings.)_
CISSY CAFFREY:

I gave it to Molly
     Because she was jolly,
     The leg of the duck,
     The leg of the duck.
_(Private Carr and Private Compton, soldiers with swagger sticks, march unsteadily and burst out laughing. More laughter comes from the lane.)_
THE WOMAN: Ha! Good on the Cavan girl!

CISSY CAFFREY: More luck to me. Cavan, Cootehill and Belturbet. _(She
sings.)_

I gave it to Nelly
     To put in her belly,
     The leg of the duck,
     The leg of the duck.
_(Private Carr and Private Compton turn around, their red uniforms bright under a streetlamp. Stephen Dedalus and Lynch pass through the crowd near them.)_
PRIVATE COMPTON: _(Jerks his finger.)_ Way for the parson.
PRIVATE CARR: _(Turns and calls.)_ What ho, parson!
CISSY CAFFREY: _(Her voice soaring higher.)_

She has it, she got it,
     Wherever she put it,
     The leg of the duck.

_(Stephen, flourishing the ashplant in his left hand, chants with joy
the_ introit _for paschal time. Lynch, his jockeycap low on his brow,
attends him, a sneer of discontent wrinkling his face.)_
STEPHEN: _Vidi aquam egredientem de templo a latere dextro. Alleluia_.
_(An old woman peers out from a doorway.)_
THE OLD WOMAN: _(Whispering.)_ Sst! Come here! I've got something to show you!
STEPHEN: _(Chanting louder.)_ And everyone touched by this water...
THE OLD WOMAN: _(Muttering after them.)_ University students. All brains and no money.

_(Edy Boardman, sniffling, crouched with Bertha Supple, draws her shawl
across her nostrils.)_

EDY BOARDMAN: _(Bickering.)_ And says the one: I seen you up Faithful
place with your squarepusher, the greaser off the railway, in his
cometobed hat. Did you, says I. That’s not for you to say, says I. You
never seen me in the mantrap with a married highlander, says I. The
likes of her! Stag that one is! Stubborn as a mule! And her walking
with two fellows the one time, Kilbride, the enginedriver, and
lancecorporal Oliphant.
STEPHEN: _(Triumphaliter.) Salvi facti sunt._

_(He flourishes his ashplant, shivering the lamp image, shattering
light over the world. A liver and white spaniel on the prowl slinks
after him, growling. Lynch scares it with a kick.)_
LYNCH: So that?

STEPHEN: (_Looks behind_.) So that gesture, not music not odour, would
be a universal language, the gift of tongues rendering visible not the
lay sense but the first entelechy, the structural rhythm.
LYNCH: Pornosophical philotheology. Metaphysics in Mecklenburgh street!

STEPHEN: We have shrewridden Shakespeare and henpecked Socrates. Even
the allwisest Stagyrite was bitted, bridled and mounted by a light of
love.
LYNCH: Ba!

STEPHEN: Anyway, who wants two gestures to illustrate a loaf and a jug?
This movement illustrates the loaf and jug of bread or wine in Omar.
Hold my stick.
LYNCH: darn your yellow stick. Where are we going?

STEPHEN: foolish lynx, to _la belle dame sans merci,_ Georgina
Johnson, _ad deam qui laetificat iuventutem meam._

_(Stephen thrusts the ashplant on him and slowly holds out his hands,
his head going back till both hands are a span from his breast, down
turned, in planes intersecting, the fingers about to part, the left
being higher.)_

LYNCH: Which is the jug of bread? It skills not. That or the
customhouse. Illustrate thou. Here take your crutch and walk.

_(They pass. Tommy Caffrey scrambles to a gaslamp and, clasping, climbs
in spasms. From the top spur he slides down. Jacky Caffrey clasps to
climb. The navvy lurches against the lamp. The twins scuttle off in the
dark. The navvy, swaying, presses a forefinger against a wing of his
nose and ejects from the farther nostril a long liquid jet of snot.
Shouldering the lamp he staggers away through the crowd with his
flaring cresset._

_Snakes of river fog creep slowly. From drains, clefts, cesspools,
middens arise on all sides stagnant fumes. A glow leaps in the south
beyond the seaward reaches of the river. The navvy, staggering forward,
cleaves the crowd and lurches towards the tramsiding. On the farther
side under the railway bridge Bloom appears, flushed, panting, cramming
bread and chocolate into a sidepocket. From Gillen’s hairdresser’s
window a composite portrait shows him gallant Nelson’s image.

_At Antonio Rabaiotti’s door Bloom halts, sweated under the bright
arclamp. He disappears. In a moment he reappears and hurries on.)_
BLOOM: Fish and taters. N. g. Ah!

_(He disappears into Olhausen’s, the porkbutcher’s, under the
downcoming rollshutter. A few moments later he emerges from under the
shutter, puffing Poldy, blowing Bloohoom. In each hand he holds a
parcel, one containing a lukewarm pig’s crubeen, the other a cold
sheep’s trotter, sprinkled with wholepepper. He gasps, standing
upright. Then bending to one side he presses a parcel against his ribs
and groans.)_
BLOOM: Stitch in my side. Why did I run?

_(He takes breath with care and goes forward slowly towards the lampset
siding. The glow leaps again.)_
BLOOM: What is that? A flasher? Searchlight.
_(He stands at Cormack’s corner, watching.)_

BLOOM: _Aurora borealis_ or a steel foundry? Ah, the brigade, of
course. South side anyhow. Big blaze. Might be his house. Beggar’s
bush. We’re safe. _(He hums cheerfully.)_ London’s burning, London’s
burning! On fire, on fire! (_He catches sight of the navvy lurching
through the crowd at the farther side of Talbot street._) I’ll miss
him. Run. Quick. Better cross here.
_(He darts to cross the road. Urchins shout.)_
THE URCHINS: Mind out, mister!

(_Two cyclists, with lighted paper lanterns aswing, swim by him,
grazing him, their bells rattling._)
THE BELLS: Haltyaltyaltyall.
BLOOM: _(Halts erect, stung by a spasm.)_ Ow!

_(He looks round, darts forward suddenly. Through rising fog a dragon
sandstrewer, travelling at caution, slews heavily down upon him, its
huge red headlight winking, its trolley hissing on the wire. The
motorman bangs his footgong.)_
THE GONG: Bang Bang Bla Bak Blud Bugg Bloo.

_(The brake cracks violently. Bloom, raising a policeman’s whitegloved
hand, blunders stifflegged out of the track. The motorman, thrown
forward, pugnosed, on the guidewheel, yells as he slides past over
chains and keys.)_
THE MOTORMAN: Hey, shitbreeches, are you doing the hat trick?

_(Bloom trickleaps to the curbstone and halts again. He brushes a
mudflake from his cheek with a parcelled hand.)_

BLOOM: No thoroughfare. Close shave that but cured the stitch. Must
take up Sandow’s exercises again. On the hands down. Insure against
street accident too. The Providential. _(He feels his trouser pocket.)_
Poor mamma’s panacea. Heel easily catch in track or bootlace in a cog. Day the wheel of the black Maria peeled off my shoe at Leonard’s
corner. Third time is the charm. Shoe trick. Insolent driver. I ought
to report him. Tension makes them nervous.

_(A sinister figure leans on plaited legs against O’Beirne’s wall, a
visage unknown, injected with dark mercury. From under a wideleaved
sombrero the figure regards him with evil eye.)_
BLOOM: _Buenas noches, señorita Blanca, que calle es esta?_

THE FIGURE: (_Impassive, raises a signal arm._) Password. _Sraid
Mabbot._

BLOOM: Haha. _Merci._ Esperanto. _Slan leath. (He mutters.)_ Gaelic
league spy, sent by that fireeater.

_(He steps forward. A sackshouldered ragman bars his path. He steps
left, ragsackman left.)_
BLOOM: I beg.
(_He leaps right, sackragman right._)
BLOOM: I beg.
(_He swerves, sidles, stepaside, slips past and on._)

BLOOM: Keep to the right, right, right. If there is a signpost planted
by the Touring Club at Stepaside who procured that public boon? I who
lost my way and contributed to the columns of the _Irish Cyclist_ the
letter headed _In darkest Stepaside_. Keep, keep, keep to the right.
Rags and bones at midnight. A fence more likely. First place villain
makes for. Wash off his sins of the world.

_(Jacky Caffrey, hunted by Tommy Caffrey, runs full tilt against
Bloom.)_
BLOOM: O.

_(Shocked, on weak hams, he halts. Tommy and Jacky vanish there, there.
Bloom pats with parcelled hands watch, fobpocket, bookpocket,
pursepoke, sweets of sin, potato soap.)_

BLOOM: Beware of pickpockets. Old thieves’ dodge. Collide. Then snatch
your purse.

_(The retriever approaches sniffing, nose to the ground. A sprawled
form sneezes. A stooped bearded figure appears garbed in the long
caftan of an elder in Zion and a smokingcap with magenta tassels.
Horned spectacles hang down at the wings of the nose. Yellow poison
streaks are on the drawn face.)_

RUDOLPH: Second halfcrown waste money today. I told you not go with
dizzy goy ever. So you catch no money.

BLOOM: _(Hides the crubeen and trotter behind his back and,
crestfallen, feels warm and cold feetmeat.) Ja, ich weiss, papachi._

RUDOLPH: What you making down this place? Have you no soul? _(With
feeble vulture talons he feels the silent face of Bloom.)_ Are you not
my son Leopold, the grandson of Leopold? Are you not my dear son
Leopold who left the house of his father and left the god of his
fathers Abraham and Jacob?

BLOOM: _(With precaution.)_ I suppose so, father. Mosenthal. All that’s
left of him.

RUDOLPH: _(Severely.)_ One night they bring you home dizzy as dog after
spend your good money. What you call them running chaps?

BLOOM: _(In youth’s smart blue Oxford suit with white vestslips,
narrowshouldered, in brown Alpine hat, wearing gent’s sterling silver
waterbury keyless watch and double curb Albert with seal attached, one
side of him coated with stiffening mud.)_ Harriers, father. Only that
once.

RUDOLPH: Once! Mud head to foot. Cut your hand open. Lockjaw. They make
you kaputt, Leopoldleben. You watch them chaps.

BLOOM: _(Weakly.)_ They challenged me to a sprint. It was muddy. I
slipped.

RUDOLPH: _(With contempt.) Goim nachez!_ Nice spectacles for your poor
mother!
BLOOM: Mamma!

ELLEN BLOOM: _(In pantomime dame’s stringed mobcap, widow Twankey’s
crinoline and bustle, blouse with muttonleg sleeves buttoned behind,
grey mittens and cameo brooch, her plaited hair in a crispine net,
appears over the staircase banisters, a slanted candlestick in her
hand, and cries out in shrill alarm.)_ O blessed Redeemer, what have
they done to him! My smelling salts! _(She hauls up a reef of skirt and
ransacks the pouch of her striped blay petticoat. A phial, an Agnus
Dei, a shrivelled potato and a celluloid doll fall out.)_ Sacred Heart
of Mary, where were you at all at all?

_(Bloom, mumbling, his eyes downcast, begins to bestow his parcels in
his filled pockets but desists, muttering.)_
A VOICE: _(Sharply.)_ Poldy!

BLOOM: Who? _(He ducks and wards off a blow clumsily.)_ At your
service.

_(He looks up. Beside her mirage of datepalms a handsome woman in
Turkish costume stands before him. Opulent curves fill out her scarlet
trousers and jacket, slashed with gold. A wide yellow cummerbund
girdles her. A white yashmak, violet in the night, covers her face,
leaving free only her large dark eyes and raven hair.)_
BLOOM: Molly!

MARION: Welly? Mrs Marion from this out, my dear man, when you speak to
me. _(Satirically.)_ Has poor little hubby cold feet waiting so long?
BLOOM: _(Shifts from foot to foot.)_ No, no. Not the least little bit.

_(He breathes in deep agitation, swallowing gulps of air, questions,
hopes, crubeens for her supper, things to tell her, excuse, desire,
spellbound. A coin gleams on her forehead. On her feet are jewelled
toerings. Her ankles are linked by a slender fetterchain. Beside her a
camel, hooded with a turreting turban, waits. A silk ladder of
innumerable rungs climbs to his bobbing howdah. He ambles near with
disgruntled hindquarters. Fiercely she slaps his haunch, her goldcurb
wristbangles angriling, scolding him in Moorish.)_
MARION: Nebrakada! Femininum!

_(The camel, lifting a foreleg, plucks from a tree a large mango fruit,
offers it to his mistress, blinking, in his cloven hoof, then droops
his head and, grunting, with uplifted neck, fumbles to kneel. Bloom
stoops his back for leapfrog.)_

BLOOM: I can give you... I mean as your business menagerer... Mrs
Marion... if you...

MARION: So you notice some change? _(Her hands passing slowly over her
trinketed stomacher, a slow friendly mockery in her eyes.)_ O Poldy,
Poldy, you are a poor old stick in the mud! Go and see life. See the
wide world.

BLOOM: I was just going back for that lotion whitewax, orangeflower
water. Shop closes early on Thursday. But the first thing in the
morning. _(He pats divers pockets.)_ This moving kidney. Ah!

_(He points to the south, then to the east. A cake of new clean lemon
soap arises, diffusing light and perfume.)_
THE SOAP:

We’re a capital couple are Bloom and I.
     He brightens the earth. I polish the sky.

_(The freckled face of Sweny, the druggist, appears in the disc of the
soapsun.)_
SWENY: Three and a penny, please.
BLOOM: Yes. For my wife. Mrs Marion. Special recipe.
MARION: _(Softly.)_ Poldy!
BLOOM: Yes, ma’am?
MARION: _Ti trema un poco il cuore?_

_(In disdain she saunters away, plump as a pampered pouter pigeon,
humming the duet from_ Don Giovanni.)
BLOOM: Are you sure about that _Voglio_? I mean the pronunciati...

_(He follows, followed by the sniffing terrier. The elderly old woman seizes
his sleeve, the bristles of her chinmole glittering.)_

THE OLD WOMAN: Ten shillings a maidenhead. Fresh thing was never touched.
Fifteen. There’s no-one in it only her old father that’s dead dizzy.

_(She points. In the gap of her dark den furtive, rainbedraggled,
Bridie Kelly stands.)_
BRIDIE: Hatch street. Any good in your mind?

_(With a squeak she flaps her bat shawl and runs. A burly rough pursues
with booted strides. He stumbles on the steps, recovers, plunges into
gloom. Weak squeaks of laughter are heard, weaker.)_

THE OLD WOMAN: _(Her wolfeyes shining.)_ He’s getting his pleasure. You
won’t get a maiden in the flash houses. Ten shillings. Don’t be all
night before the polis in plain clothes sees us. Sixtyseven is a bitch.

_(Leering, Gerty Macdowell limps forward. She draws from behind,
ogling, and shows coyly her bloodied clout.)_

GERTY: With all my worldly goods I thee and thou. _(She murmurs.)_ You
did that. I hate you.
BLOOM: I? When? You’re dreaming. I never saw you.

THE OLD WOMAN: Leave the gentleman alone, you cheat. Writing the gentleman
false letters. Streetwalking and soliciting. Better for your mother
take the strap to you at the bedpost, hussy like you.

GERTY: _(To Bloom.)_ When you saw all the secrets of my bottom drawer.
_(She paws his sleeve, slobbering.)_ Dirty married man! I love you for
doing that to me.

_(She glides away crookedly. Mrs Breen in man’s frieze overcoat with
loose bellows pockets, stands in the causeway, her roguish eyes
wideopen, smiling in all her herbivorous buckteeth.)_
MRS BREEN: Mr...

BLOOM: _(Coughs gravely.)_ Madam, when we last had this pleasure by
letter dated the sixteenth instant...

MRS BREEN: Mr Bloom! You down here in the haunts of sin! I caught you
nicely! Scamp!

BLOOM: _(Hurriedly.)_ Not so loud my name. Whatever do you think of me?
Don’t give me away. Walls have ears. How do you do? It’s ages since I.
You’re looking splendid. Absolutely it. Seasonable weather we are
having this time of year. Black refracts heat. Short cut home here.
Interesting quarter. Rescue of fallen women. Magdalen asylum. I am the
secretary...

MRS BREEN: _(Holds up a finger.)_ Now, don’t tell a big fib! I know
somebody won’t like that. O just wait till I see Molly! _(Slily.)_
Account for yourself this very sminute or woe betide you!

BLOOM: _(Looks behind.)_ She often said she’d like to visit. Slumming.
The exotic, you see. Negro servants in livery too if she had money.
Othello black brute. Eugene Stratton. Even the bones and cornerman at
the Livermore christies. Bohee brothers. Sweep for that matter.

_(Tom and Sam Bohee, coloured coons in white duck suits, scarlet socks,
upstarched Sambo chokers and large scarlet asters in their buttonholes,
leap out. Each has his banjo slung. Their paler smaller negroid hands
jingle the twingtwang wires. Flashing white Kaffir eyes and tusks they
rattle through a breakdown in clumsy clogs, twinging, singing, back to
back, toe heel, heel toe, with smackfatclacking nigger lips.)_
TOM AND SAM:

There’s someone in the house with Dina
     There’s someone in the house, I know,
     There’s someone in the house with Dina
     Playing on the old banjo.

_(They whisk black masks from raw babby faces: then, chuckling,
chortling, trumming, twanging, they diddle diddle cakewalk dance
away.)_

BLOOM: _(With a sour tenderish smile.)_ A little frivol, shall we, if
you are so inclined? Would you like me perhaps to embrace you just for
a fraction of a second?
MRS BREEN: _(Screams gaily.)_ O, you ruck! You ought to see yourself!

BLOOM: For old sake’ sake. I only meant a square party, a mixed
marriage mingling of our different little conjugials. You know I had a
soft corner for you. _(Gloomily.)_ ’Twas I sent you that valentine of
the dear gazelle.

MRS BREEN: Glory Alice, you do look a holy show! Killing simply. _(She
puts out her hand inquisitively.)_ What are you hiding behind your
back? Tell us, there’s a dear.

BLOOM: _(Seizes her wrist with his free hand.)_ Josie Powell that was,
prettiest deb in Dublin. How time flies by! Do you remember, harking
back in a retrospective arrangement, Old Christmas night, Georgina
Simpson’s housewarming while they were playing the Irving Bishop game,
finding the pin blindfold and thoughtreading? Subject, what is in this
snuffbox?

MRS BREEN: You were the lion of the night with your seriocomic
recitation and you looked the part. You were always a favourite with
the ladies.

BLOOM: _(Squire of dames, in dinner jacket with wateredsilk facings,
blue masonic badge in his buttonhole, black bow and mother-of-pearl
studs, a prismatic champagne glass tilted in his hand.)_ Ladies and
gentlemen, I give you Ireland, home and beauty.
MRS BREEN: The dear dead days beyond recall. Love’s old sweet song.

BLOOM: _(Meaningfully dropping his voice.)_ I confess I’m teapot with
curiosity to find out whether some person’s something is a little
teapot at present.

MRS BREEN: _(Gushingly.)_ Tremendously teapot! London’s teapot and I’m
simply teapot all over me! _(She rubs sides with him.)_ After the
parlour mystery games and the crackers from the tree we sat on the
staircase ottoman. Under the mistletoe. Two is company.

BLOOM: _(Wearing a purple Napoleon hat with an amber halfmoon, his
fingers and thumb passing slowly down to her soft moist meaty palm
which she surrenders gently.)_ The witching hour of night. I took the
splinter out of this hand, carefully, slowly. _(Tenderly, as he slips
on her finger a ruby ring.) Là ci darem la mano._

MRS BREEN: _(In a onepiece evening frock executed in moonlight blue, a
tinsel sylph’s diadem on her brow with her dancecard fallen beside her
moonblue satin slipper, curves her palm softly, breathing quickly.)
Voglio e non._ You’re hot! You’re scalding! The left hand nearest the
heart.

BLOOM: When you made your present choice they said it was beauty and
the beast. I can never forgive you for that. _(His clenched fist at his
brow.)_ Think what it means. All you meant to me then. _(Hoarsely.)_
Woman, it’s breaking me!

_(Denis Breen, whitetallhatted, with Wisdom Hely’s sandwichboards,
shuffles past them in carpet slippers, his dull beard thrust out,
muttering to right and left. Little Alf Bergan, cloaked in the pall of
the ace of spades, dogs him to left and right, doubled in laughter.)_
ALF BERGAN: _(Points jeering at the sandwichboards.)_ U. p: up.

MRS BREEN: _(To Bloom.)_ High jinks below stairs. _(She gives him the
glad eye.)_ Why didn’t you kiss the spot to make it well? You wanted
to.
BLOOM: _(Shocked.)_ Molly’s best friend! Could you?

MRS BREEN: _(Her pulpy tongue between her lips, offers a pigeon kiss.)_
Hnhn. The answer is a lemon. Have you a little present for me there?

BLOOM: _(Offhandedly.)_ Kosher. A snack for supper. The home without
potted meat is incomplete. I was at _Leah_, Mrs Bandmann Palmer.
Trenchant exponent of Shakespeare. Unfortunately threw away the
programme. Rattling good place round there for pigs’ feet. Feel.

_(Richie Goulding, three ladies’ hats pinned on his head, appears
weighted to one side by the black legal bag of Collis and Ward on which
a skull and crossbones are painted in white limewash. He opens it and
shows it full of polonies, kippered herrings, Findon haddies and
tightpacked pills.)_
RICHIE: Best value in Dub.

_(Bald Pat, bothered beetle, stands on the curbstone, folding his
napkin, waiting to wait.)_

PAT: _(Advances with a tilted dish of spillspilling gravy.)_ Steak and
kidney. Bottle of lager. Hee hee hee. Wait till I wait.
RICHIE: Goodgod. Inev erate inall...

_(With hanging head he marches doggedly forward. The navvy, lurching
by, gores him with his flaming pronghorn.)_

RICHIE: _(With a cry of pain, his hand to his back.)_ Ah! Bright’s!
Lights!

BLOOM: _(Points to the navvy.)_ A spy. Don’t attract attention. I hate
stupid crowds. I am not on pleasure bent. I am in a grave predicament.

MRS BREEN: Humbugging and deluthering as per usual with your cock and
bull story.

BLOOM: I want to tell you a little secret about how I came to be here.
But you must never tell. Not even Molly. I have a most particular
reason.
MRS BREEN: _(All agog.)_ O, not for worlds.
BLOOM: Let’s walk on. Shall us?
MRS BREEN: Let’s.

_(THE OLD WOMAN makes an unheeded sign. Bloom walks on with Mrs Breen. The
terrier follows, whining piteously, wagging his tail.)_
THE OLD WOMAN: Jewman’s melt!

BLOOM: _(In an oatmeal sporting suit, a sprig of woodbine in the lapel,
tony buff shirt, shepherd’s plaid Saint Andrew’s cross scarftie, white
spats, fawn dustcoat on his arm, tawny red brogues, fieldglasses in
bandolier and a grey billycock hat.)_ Do you remember a long long time,
years and years ago, just after Milly, Marionette we called her, was
weaned when we all went together to Fairyhouse races, was it?

MRS BREEN: _(In smart Saxe tailormade, white velours hat and spider
veil.)_ Leopardstown.

BLOOM: I mean, Leopardstown. And Molly won seven shillings on a three
year old named Nevertell and coming home along by Foxrock in that old
fiveseater shanderadan of a waggonette you were in your heyday then and
you had on that new hat of white velours with a surround of molefur
that Mrs Hayes advised you to buy because it was marked down to
nineteen and eleven, a bit of wire and an old rag of velveteen, and
I’ll lay you what you like she did it on purpose...
MRS BREEN: She did, of course, the cat! Don’t tell me! Nice adviser!

BLOOM: Because it didn’t suit you one quarter as well as the other
ducky little tammy toque with the bird of paradise wing in it that I
admired on you and you honestly looked just too fetching in it though
it was a pity to defeat it, you cruel naughty creature, little mite of a
thing with a heart the size of a fullstop.
MRS BREEN: _(Squeezes his arm, simpers.)_ Naughty cruel I was!

BLOOM: _(Low, secretly, ever more rapidly.)_ And Molly was eating a
sandwich of spiced beef out of Mrs Joe Gallaher’s lunch basket.
Frankly, though she had her advisers or admirers, I never cared much
for her style. She was...
MRS BREEN: Too...

BLOOM: Yes. And Molly was laughing because Rogers and Maggot O’Reilly
were mimicking a cock as we passed a farmhouse and Marcus Tertius
Moses, the tea merchant, drove past us in a gig with his daughter,
Dancer Moses was her name, and the poodle in her lap bridled up and you
asked me if I ever heard or read or knew or came across...
MRS BREEN: _(Eagerly.)_ Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes, yes, yes.

_(She fades from his side. Followed by the whining dog he walks on
towards hellsgates. In an archway a standing woman, bent forward, her
feet apart, pisses cowily. Outside a shuttered pub a bunch of loiterers
listen to a tale which their brokensnouted gaffer rasps out with
raucous humour. An armless pair of them flop wrestling, growling, in
maimed sodden playfight.)_

THE GAFFER: _(Crouches, his voice twisted in his snout.)_ And when
Cairns came down from the scaffolding in Beaver street what was he
after doing it into only into the bucket of porter that was there
waiting on the shavings for Derwan’s plasterers.
THE LOITERERS: _(Guffaw with cleft palates.)_ O jays!

_(Their paintspeckled hats wag. Spattered with size and lime of their
lodges they frisk limblessly about him.)_

BLOOM: Coincidence too. They think it funny. Anything but that. Broad
daylight. Trying to walk. Lucky no woman.

THE LOITERERS: Jays, that’s a good one. Glauber salts. O jays, into the
men’s porter.

_(Bloom passes. Cheap strangers, singly, coupled, shawled, dishevelled,
call from lanes, doors, corners.)_
THE strangers:
Are you going far, queer fellow?
How’s your middle leg?
Got a match on you?
Eh, come here till I stiffen it for you.

_(He plodges through their sump towards the lighted street beyond. From
a bulge of window curtains a gramophone rears a battered brazen trunk.
In the shadow a shebeenkeeper haggles with the navvy and the two
redcoats.)_
THE NAVVY: _(burp.)_ Where’s the blooming house?

THE SHEBEENKEEPER: Purdon street. Shilling a bottle of stout.
Respectable woman.

THE NAVVY: _(Gripping the two redcoats, staggers forward with them.)_
Come on, you British army!
PRIVATE CARR: _(Behind his back.)_ He aint half balmy.
PRIVATE COMPTON: _(Laughs.)_ What ho!

PRIVATE CARR: _(To the navvy.)_ Portobello barracks canteen. You ask
for Carr. Just Carr.
THE NAVVY: _(Shouts.)_
We are the boys. Of Wexford.
PRIVATE COMPTON: Say! What price the sergeantmajor?
PRIVATE CARR: Bennett? He’s my pal. I love old Bennett.
THE NAVVY: _(Shouts.)_

The galling chain.
     And free our native land.

_(He staggers forward, dragging them with him. Bloom stops, at fault.
The dog approaches, his tongue outlolling, panting.)_

BLOOM: Wildgoose chase this. Disorderly houses. Lord knows where they
are gone. Drunks cover distance double quick. Nice mixup. Scene at
Westland row. Then jump in first class with third ticket. Then too far. Train with engine behind. Might have taken me to Malahide or a siding
for the night or collision. Second drink does it. Once is a dose. What
am I following him for? Still, he’s the best of that lot. If I hadn’t
heard about Mrs Beaufoy Purefoy I wouldn’t have gone and wouldn’t have
met.

_(He gazes ahead, reading on the wall a scrawled chalk legend_ Wet
Dream _and a phallic design._) Odd! Molly drawing on the frosted
carriagepane at Kingstown. What’s that like? _(Gaudy dollwomen loll in
the lighted doorways, in window embrasures, smoking birdseye
cigarettes. The odour of the sicksweet weed floats towards him in slow
round ovalling wreaths.)_
THE WREATHS: Sweet are the sweets. Sweets of sin.

BLOOM: My spine’s a bit limp. Go or turn? And this food? Eat it and get
all pigsticky. Absurd I am. Waste of money. One and eightpence too
much. _(The retriever drives a cold snivelling muzzle against his hand,
wagging his tail.)_ Strange how they take to me. Even that brute today. Better speak to him first. Like women they like _rencontres._ Stinks
like a polecat. _Chacun son goût_. He might be mad. Dogdays. Uncertain
in his movements. Good fellow! Fido! Good fellow! Garryowen!

_(With regret he lets the unrolled crubeen and trotter slide. The
mastiff mauls the bundle clumsily and gluts himself with growling
greed, crunching the bones. Two raincaped watch approach, silent,
vigilant. They murmur together.)_
THE WATCH: Bloom. Of Bloom. For Bloom. Bloom.
_(Each lays hand on Bloom’s shoulder.)_
FIRST WATCH: Caught in the act. Commit no nuisance.
BLOOM: _(Stammers.)_ I am doing good to others.

_(A covey of gulls, storm petrels, rises hungrily from Liffey slime
with Banbury cakes in their beaks.)_
THE GULLS: Kaw kave kankury kake.
BLOOM: The friend of man. Trained by kindness.

_(He points. Bob Doran, toppling from a high barstool, sways over the
munching spaniel.)_
BOB DORAN: Towser. Give us the paw. Give the paw.

_(The bulldog growls, his scruff standing, a gobbet of pig’s knuckle
between his molars through which rabid scumspittle dribbles. Bob Doran
falls silently into an area.)_
SECOND WATCH: Prevention of cruelty to animals.

BLOOM: _(Enthusiastically.)_ A noble work! I scolded that tramdriver on
Harold’s cross bridge for illusing the poor horse with his harness
scab. Bad French I got for my pains. Of course it was frosty and the
last tram. All tales of circus life are highly demoralising.

_(Signor Maffei, passionpale, in liontamer’s costume with diamond studs
in his shirtfront, steps forward, holding a circus paperhoop, a curling
carriagewhip and a revolver with which he covers the gorging
boarhound.)_

SIGNOR MAFFEI: _(With a sinister smile.)_ Ladies and gentlemen, my
educated greyhound. It was I broke in the bucking broncho Ajax with my
patent spiked saddle for carnivores. Lash under the belly with a
knotted thong. Block tackle and a strangling pulley will bring your
lion to heel, no matter how fractious, even _Leo ferox_ there, the
Libyan maneater. A redhot crowbar and some liniment rubbing on the
burning part produced Fritz of Amsterdam, the thinking hyena.
FIRST WATCH: Come. Name and address.

BLOOM: I have forgotten for the moment. Ah, yes! _(He takes off his
high grade hat, saluting.)_ Dr Bloom, Leopold, dental surgeon. You have
heard of von Blum Pasha. Umpteen millions. _Donnerwetter!_ Owns half
Austria. Egypt. Cousin.
FIRST WATCH: Proof.
_(A card falls from inside the leather headband of Bloom’s hat.)_

BLOOM: _(In red fez, cadi’s dress coat with broad green sash, wearing a
false badge of the Legion of Honour, picks up the card hastily and
offers it.)_ Allow me. My club is the Junior Army and Navy. Solicitors:
Messrs John Henry Menton, 27 Bachelor’s Walk.

FIRST WATCH: _(Reads.)_ Henry Flower. No fixed abode. Unlawfully
watching and besetting.
SECOND WATCH: An alibi. You are cautioned.

BLOOM: _(Produces from his heartpocket a crumpled yellow flower.)_ This
is the flower in question. It was given me by a man I don’t know his
name. _(Plausibly.)_ You know that old joke, rose of Castile. Bloom. The change of name. Virag. _(He murmurs privately and confidentially.)_
We are engaged you see, sergeant. Lady in the case. Love entanglement. _(He shoulders the second watch gently.)_ Dash it all. It’s a way we
gallants have in the navy. Uniform that does it.
_(A dark mercurialised face appears, leading a veiled figure.)_

THE DARK MERCURY: The Castle is looking for him. He was drummed out of
the army.

MARTHA: _(Thickveiled, a crimson halter round her neck, a copy of the_
Irish Times _in her hand, in tone of reproach, pointing.)_ Henry!
Leopold! Lionel, thou lost one! Clear my name.
FIRST WATCH: _(Sternly.)_ Come to the station.

BLOOM: _(Scared, hats himself, steps back, then, plucking at his heart
and lifting his right forearm on the square, he gives the sign and
